{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Apple Inc. 10-K for the period ending 2025-09-27, filed 2025-10-31 (accession 0000320193-25-000079): Item 1A (Risk Factors), paragraphs mentioning outsourcing partners, China mainland, Greater China, single or limited sources. Page 1 of 1 (8,295 characters).

The Company has a large, global business with sales outside the U.S. representing a majority of the Company’s total net sales, and the Company believes that it generally benefits from growth in international trade. A significant majority of the Company’s manufacturing is performed in whole or in part by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, in addition to sourcing from partners and facilities located in the U.S. Restrictions on international trade, such as tariffs and other controls on imports or exports of goods, technology or data, can materially adversely affect the Company’s business and supply chain. The impact can be particularly significant if these restrictive measures apply to countries and regions where the Company derives a significant portion of its revenues and/or has significant supply chain operations. Restrictive measures can increase the cost or limit the availability of the Company’s products and the components and rare earths and other raw materials that go into them. Restrictive measures can also require the Company to change suppliers, restructure business relationships and operations, refrain from offering and distributing or cease to offer and distribute affected products, services and third-party applications to its customers, and increase the prices of its products and services. Changing the Company’s business and supply chain in accordance with new or changed restrictions on international trade can be expensive, time-consuming and disruptive to the Company’s business and results of operations. Trade and other international disputes can also have an adverse impact on the overall macroeconomic environment and result in shifts and reductions in consumer spending and negative consumer sentiment for the Company’s products and services, all of which can further adversely affect the Company’s business and results of operations. Such restrictions can be announced with little or no advance notice, which can create uncertainty, and the Company may not be able to effectively mitigate any or all adverse impacts from such measures. Global supply chains can be highly concentrated, and an escalation of geopolitical tensions or conflict could result in significant disruptions. Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on imports to the U.S. (“U.S. Tariffs”), including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the European Union (“EU”), among others. In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, reciprocal tariffs on imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures. Various modifications to the U.S. Tariffs have been announced and further changes could be made in the future, which may include additional sector-based tariffs or other measures. For example, the U.S. Department of Commerce has initiated an investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, into, among other things, imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including downstream products that contain semiconductors. The ultimate impact remains uncertain and will depend on several factors, including whether additional or incremental U.S. Tariffs or other measures are announced or imposed, to what extent other countries implement tariffs or other retaliatory measures in response, and the overall magnitude and duration of these measures. If disputes and conflicts further escalate, actions by governments in response could be significantly more severe and restrictive.
Following any interruption to its business, the Company can require substantial recovery time, incur significant expenditures to resume operations, and lose significant sales. Because the Company relies on single or limited sources for the supply and manufacture of many critical components, a business interruption affecting such sources would exacerbate any negative consequences to the Company. While the Company maintains insurance coverage for certain types of losses, such insurance coverage may be insufficient to cover all losses that may arise. Any of the foregoing can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
The Company depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S.
A significant majority of the Company’s manufacturing is performed in whole or in part by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, in addition to sourcing from partners and facilities located in the U.S. The Company relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe to supply and manufacture many components, and on partners primarily located in Asia, for final assembly of substantially all of the Company’s hardware products. The Company has also outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management. While these arrangements can lower operating costs, they also reduce the Company’s direct control over production and distribution. Such diminished control has from time to time had, and may in the future have, an adverse effect on the cost, quality or quantity of products manufactured or services provided, or adversely affect the Company’s flexibility to respond to changing conditions. Although arrangements with these partners may contain provisions for product defect expense reimbursement, the Company generally remains responsible to the consumer for warranty and out-of-warranty service in the event of product defects and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities from time to time. While the Company relies on its partners to adhere to its supplier code of conduct, violations of the supplier code of conduct occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
Because the Company currently obtains certain components from single or limited sources, the Company is subject to significant supply and pricing risks. Many components, including those that are available from multiple sources, are at times subject to industry-wide shortages and significant commodity pricing fluctuations that can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price. For example, the global semiconductor industry has in the past experienced high demand and shortages of supply, which adversely affected the Company’s ability to obtain sufficient quantities of components and products on commercially reasonable terms, or at all. Such disruptions could occur in the future.
The Company distributes its products and certain of its services through third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers. The Company also sells its products and services directly to small and mid-sized businesses and education, enterprise and government customers. A substantial majority of the Company’s outstanding trade receivables are not covered by collateral, third-party bank support or financing arrangements, or credit insurance, and a significant portion of the Company’s trade receivables can be concentrated within cellular network carriers or other resellers. The Company’s exposure to credit and collectibility risk on its trade receivables is higher in certain international markets. The Company also has unsecured vendor non-trade receivables resulting from purchases of components by outsourcing partners and other vendors that manufacture subassemblies or assemble final products for the Company. In addition, the Company has made prepayments associated with long-term supply agreements to secure supply of inventory components. As of September 27, 2025, the Company’s vendor non-trade receivables were concentrated among a few individual vendors located primarily in Asia. If the Company is unable to monitor and limit exposure to credit risk on its trade and vendor non-trade receivables, as well as long-term prepayments, the Company’s results of operations, financial condition and stock price could be materially adversely affected.

CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA — Apple ® today announced financial results for its fiscal 2026 third quarter ended June 27, 2026. rows.finding: In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of net sales ($196,515M, +22.4% y/y) and Services 25.2% ($91,728M, +14.1%); the FY2025 mix was iPhone 50.4%, Services 26.2%, Mac 8.1%, iPad 6.7%, Wearables 8.6% ($416,161M total).
rows.mechanism: Hardware sell-in into an iPhone 17 upgrade cycle, plus a favourable FX swing in Europe and Greater China, outgrew the subscription-like services layer; mix therefore rotated back toward the more cyclical, lower-margin leg.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 mix of iPhone 52.3% and Services 22.2%; FY2023-FY2025 total revenue CAGR of 4.2% versus 9M FY2026 growth of 16.1%.
rows.weakens: The narrative that Apple is steadily becoming a services company: services' revenue share fell 1.0 point year on year and services' share of gross profit fell from 41.3% to 39.1%.
rows.implication: The durability of earnings depends on the hardware cycle more than the mix story implies, so the watchlist case must price a hardware downturn, not only a regulatory one.
rows.confidence: high - two primary filings (10-K FY2025, 8-K/10-Q FY2026) give the category table directly.
rows.follow_up: What were iPhone units and ASP in FY2026? Apple discloses net sales only, so unit volume must come from third-party shipment data.

rows.finding: Services earned a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026 (75.4% in FY2025, 70.8% in FY2023) against 39.9% for Products, and Services supplied 42.2% of FY2025 gross profit on 26.2% of revenue.
rows.mechanism: The App Store commission, advertising, iCloud and licensing are recognised net of near-zero marginal cost on an installed base already paid for by hardware buyers, so incremental service revenue carries almost pure margin.
rows.benchmark: Blended gross margin of 67.9% at Microsoft FY2026 and 59.7% at Alphabet FY2025; Apple's blended 46.9% is the lowest of the three because hardware dominates revenue.
rows.weakens: The 76% services margin is a gross margin before the content, payment and cloud costs that sit in cost of sales; and the Services gross-profit share fell to 39.1% in FY2026 because hardware margins rose faster.
rows.implication: Services is the right asset to own for durability, but at 25% of revenue it cannot by itself offset a hardware margin shock of 100-200bp.
rows.confidence: high - segment gross margin is disclosed in the 10-K and 10-Q MD&A.
rows.follow_up: How much of Services gross profit is App Store commission versus advertising and iCloud? Apple does not disaggregate services gross margin by line.

rows.finding: Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 is 26% on App Store In-App Purchase (15% for small-business, mini-app and video programmes and for auto-renewing subscriptions after year one), 20% on in-app alternative payment, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on external-link purchases after a 2025 contempt finding, and the DOJ Section 2 case filed 2024-03-21 is unresolved but in reported settlement talks.
rows.mechanism: Regulators and courts, not Apple, now set the ceiling on the commission; each reduction moves a share of third-party developer revenue from Apple's 76%-margin services line to developers or payment processors.
rows.benchmark: The 30% standard In-App Purchase commission Apple charged before the DMA and Epic litigation (15% for small developers); Google Play has faced the same structural pressure, so this is an industry re-rating, not an Apple-specific one.
rows.weakens: The EU package is a settlement-style simplification agreed with the Commission, which reduces the tail risk of escalating fines; a 26% base rate is a 4-point cut, not the elimination of the toll.
rows.implication: Services growth from FY2027 must come from installed-base growth, advertising and cloud rather than take-rate increases, which caps the multiple the services stream can support.
rows.confidence: medium-high - the rate card is Apple's own disclosure; the US 5-15% proposal still needs court approval and the DOJ outcome is open.
rows.follow_up: What share of Services revenue is EU App Store commission? Apple does not disclose it, which is the largest single unknown in the services margin.

rows.finding: Per active device, annualising the nine months to 2026-06-27 across the disclosed base of more than 2.5bn active devices gives about $194 of revenue, $95 of gross profit (49.1%), $30 of R&D and SG&A, $65 of operating profit (33.6%), $3.6 of capex and $59 of free cash flow.
rows.mechanism: R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base that grows about 6% a year, so each added device and each added dollar of services revenue drops through at a high incremental margin; the operating structure breaks even at roughly $153bn of annual revenue, 31.5% of the current run-rate.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 per-device figures of $166 revenue, $78 gross profit, $53 operating profit and $40 free cash flow; the FY2026 step-up is 22% in gross profit per device on 16% revenue growth.
rows.weakens: The per-device figure is an average that hides a wide spread: an iPhone buyer generates several times the services revenue of an iPad or Mac buyer, and Apple does not disclose the split.
rows.implication: The fixed-cost operating leverage is real and large: a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company profitable, which supports a lower risk premium than a hardware cyclical normally earns.
rows.confidence: medium - built from disclosed statements and the disclosed installed base; the annualisation and the divisor are estimates.
rows.follow_up: How does services revenue per device differ between iPhone, iPad and Mac cohorts, and is the base still growing in the premium segments?

rows.finding: Samsung Electronics reported Q3 2026 revenue of KRW 195.3tn and operating profit of KRW 107.4tn, a 55.0% operating margin, on record memory earnings from HBM4, while IDC expects 2026 smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% and the industry ASP to rise 27.6% to $581.
rows.mechanism: A memory shortage transfers profit from device assemblers to component suppliers; Apple's response is price (iPhone revenue +22% on shipment growth in the low teens) and mix (Pro models), which works only while demand is inelastic.
rows.benchmark: Apple's Products gross margin of 39.9% in 9M FY2026 versus 36.9% a year earlier, a rise the company attributes to mix and tariff refunds but not to component costs, which it says will intensify.
rows.weakens: Apple's hardware margin rose rather than fell in FY2026, so the memory transfer has not yet hit reported numbers; tariff refunds and mix more than offset it.
rows.implication: The single largest threat to the model is a cost shock Apple cannot pass on; the Samsung margin is the clearest evidence of who is capturing the value in the 2026 handset stack.
rows.confidence: high on the reported margins; medium on the causal link to Apple's FY2027 margins.
rows.follow_up: What memory cost inflation is embedded in Apple's FY2027 purchase commitments and to what extent have iPhone 18 prices been raised to offset it?

rows.finding: Apple returned $73,872M to shareholders in 9M FY2026 ($62,094M buybacks, $11,778M dividends) against $110,197M of free cash flow, while R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M to $38,220M with no acquisition line in investing cash flow.
rows.mechanism: Apple funds capability through the income statement and licensed intangibles rather than owned data-centre capex, which keeps reported free cash flow intact while competitors absorb the AI build in capex.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's TTM capex of $135,921M (39% of revenue) left TTM free cash flow of $59,957M, and Alphabet's $159,804M left $19,747M; Apple's $10,041M of capex left $136,683M.
rows.weakens: The capital-light model means Apple's access to AI capability depends on partners and licences it does not control, and the $13.3bn intangible build is unexplained in the 10-Q.
rows.implication: Buyback capacity is structurally protected, but the buyback slowed 12% year on year while R&D and intangibles rose, so the per-share compounding engine is being partly diverted.
rows.confidence: high on the cash figures; medium on what the intangibles represent.
rows.follow_up: What are the $13.3bn of gross intangibles added in FY2026, over what life are they amortised, and does the amortisation begin to pressure FY2027 operating margin?

plan.decision_question: How does Apple make money, and how durable are the economics of hardware plus services?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 40% product gross margin and then for the life of each device at a 76% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the profit acceleration came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not from the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth.
plan.why_different: The market and product sections judge demand, share and capability; this section judges the revenue model and the arithmetic of a single device and a single service dollar, and it is the only section that prices the take rate as a regulated input rather than a competitive one.
plan.mechanism: Installed-base monetisation: hardware buys the device at roughly 40% gross margin and installs the base; services then earn 76% gross margin on that base with near-zero marginal cost. The moat is the switching cost of the base, the leak is that the take rate on third-party transactions is now set by courts and regulators, and the 2026 cost shock is that memory suppliers are taking the hardware margin back.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own history (FY2023-FY2025 mix and margins), Microsoft and Alphabet as high-margin software comparables, Samsung as the memory supplier now capturing the handset stack's profit, and the pre-DMA 30% App Store rate as the regulatory base rate.
plan.counter_evidence: iPhone concentration at 53.9% of 9M FY2026 revenue and rising; services take rates cut in the EU to a 26% base and proposed at 5-15% for US link-outs; memory costs flagged by Apple as intensifying while Samsung earns a 55% operating margin; and hardware, not services, produced 71% of the FY2026 incremental gross profit, so the durable leg is not the one that is growing.
plan.visual: Unit-economics table per active device (FY2025 versus annualised 9M FY2026) plus a pricing table of the App Store rate card by region and effective date.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, moat (unqualified), ecosystem flywheel, about/many/several with a number

{"url":"https://fortune.com/2026/08/31/apple-new-ceo-john-ternus-tim-cook-ai-competition-corporate-succession/","title":"Apple’s John Ternus era: Can a low-key engineer win the AI race? | Fortune","text":"In late July, current and former Apple product developers gathered for a reunion at the company’s Cupertino, Calif., headquarters. As evening fell and guests sipped drinks and ate hors d’oeuvres, John Ternus slipped into the Observatory building, an event space embedded in a landscaped hillside with a large oval window that looks out toward Apple’s main building.

Some guests were surprised to see Ternus at the gathering, held to celebrate a design team executive’s 30th anniversary at the company. Ternus, who was anointed Apple’s next CEO in April, had just finished a long day of reporting the company’s quarterly earnings. But he hung around and worked the crowd, flashing his signature warm smile and reminiscing.

Ternus gave no formal speech, but he projected calm confidence, and in individual conversations, he spoke with genuine excitement about Apple’s product road map over the next several years. “It was super reassuring,” one event attendee told Fortune, asking to remain anonymous to discuss a private Apple gathering. “He holds a tremendous amount of optimism and belief that hard things can be worked out.”

Ternus will certainly have plenty of hard things to work out at the $4.6 trillion company that he’ll lead as of Tuesday, when Tim Cook ends his tenure as CEO and becomes executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors. While the consumer giant’s reach has never been wider, it’s also confronting some of the biggest trials of its 50-year history. 

Cook has made Apple a cash-flow king and one of the world’s supply-chain titans, but as Ternus inherits the iPhone-maker from the legendary CEO, Apple is grappling with questions about its strategy on artificial intelligence, where it is facing competition from rivals such as OpenAI. Meanwhile, a memory chip shortage threatens to squeeze its margins, its revenue growth is slowing, and even longtime Apple fans admit the maker of aspirational tech has lost some of its product design mojo. 

Though Apple accounts for roughly one in five smartphones shipped worldwide, it’s been a while since the company truly surprised consumers. Recent launch events have mostly settled into a predictable cadence of incremental camera upgrades and routine spec bumps. There have been notable misfires, too, including the Vision Pro headset and updates to its Siri voice-activated assistant. Major software overhauls, like the polarizing Liquid Glass iOS redesign, faced sharp criticism over legibility and performance. Meanwhile, Apple’s long-rumored foldable phone will arrive years after competitors like Samsung defined the category.

The stakes are even higher now in many ways, because every tech company that matters in Silicon Valley is racing to build out new form factors specifically designed for the AI era. That poses a massive risk for Apple, which has been behind the curve in popular products like AI-enabled glasses. 

There’s little question that Ternus is an able, trusted, product-literate leader, by all accounts well-liked and respected within the company whose hardware he has helped shape for more than two decades. But it remains to be seen whether an insider, however accomplished, is the right choice to lead the company through an era when it may well need a more disruptive leader—someone who can move faster in AI, make bigger bets, and perhaps reawaken the bold product instincts that made Apple one of Silicon Valley’s most consequential companies.

John Ternus (left) poses for a selfie at a press reception in June.Andrej Sokolow—picture alliance/Getty Images

The Ternus era begins

Jean-Louis Gassée, a former Apple executive, told Fortune that based on his interactions with Ternus and those in the Apple orbit, he doesn’t expect to see the new CEO make major changes to start. “I don’t think he’s intent on rushing to make a name for himself,” he said. “He doesn’t want to roil the waters. It’s going to be small touches here and there until they have something really new.”

That focus on continuity is perhaps unsurprising given that Ternus, at 51, has spent 25 years climbing Apple’s corporate ladder. Originally hired by Apple’s product design team, Ternus became vice president of hardware engineering in 2013, overseeing Macs and iPads. In 2021, he became a member of Apple’s senior executive team and has also taken on the development of iPhones, AirPods, and other devices. As his role expanded, Ternus became a more visible presenter at Apple product events, particularly around Mac hardware, Apple silicon, and iPad announcements.

To those who have worked with him or have known him throughout his life, a few things are clear: Ternus is widely admired as a confident, steadfast person with a reputation for being a man of the people, a product-engineer savant with an encyclopedic memory of Apple product minutiae, and an all-around nice guy who has played a significant part in building many of Apple’s most successful hardware products. (Like almost any product leader, he has also worked on products that haven’t been as successful, like the Vision Pro.) 

Ternus is not the irascible, never-satisfied tech savant that Apple cofounder Steve Jobs was. Nor is he a design virtuoso, like former chief design officer Jony Ive, who’s now working with OpenAI. “If you’re looking for an iconic product visionary person to come in, that’s not Ternus,” Apple investor Gene Munster told Fortune.

But it’s worth noting: The job description for the chief executive at Apple—and the standards by which success is measured—have often been defined by the person in the role. Over its half-century history, as Apple has reshaped numerous industries, from computing and music to manufacturing and communications, the business has repeatedly evolved to capitalize on the opportunities and address the challenges of each phase.

The question now: Will the Ternus era bring Apple into its next age of smashing success, whatever that may look like?

rows.mechanism: Revenue growth is price and mix-led (iPhone +22.4% on third-party shipment growth in the low teens plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing), while cost of sales was reduced by a one-off Supreme Court-driven tariff refund; both flatter the margin without changing the underlying volume run-rate.
rows.weakens: The margin expansion is real in reported terms and broader than one quarter, and services gross margin also rose to 76.3%; a simple 'all one-off' dismissal would overstate the downside.

rows.benchmark: Microsoft TTM free cash flow of $59,957M on net income of $142,631M (0.42x) and Alphabet $19,747M on $235,694M (0.08x), both burdened by AI capex.
rows.confidence: high - cash flow statements are explicit and the State Aid note reconciles the FY2025 dip.
rows.finding: Trailing free cash flow is $136,683M, 1.06x net income, on capex of $10,041M (2.2% of sales); FY2025's 0.88x conversion is explained by the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement paid that year, and nine-month FY2026 working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash.
rows.follow_up: What is the maintenance capex floor, and how much of the FY2026 cash benefit from receivables and vendor receivables is a one-time collection cycle?
rows.implication: Cash conversion is not a concern and Apple's free cash flow is roughly 1.7 times Microsoft's and Alphabet's combined, which is the strongest single argument for owning it in a capex-heavy technology market.
rows.mechanism: Apple leases or outsources manufacturing capacity and pays suppliers on 98-day terms while collecting receivables in 24 days, so growth releases rather than absorbs capital; competitors that build data centres convert a third or less of profit into free cash.
rows.weakens: The 1.06x is flattered by a $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables, and by $10,016M of other liabilities; a normalised year would convert closer to 0.95-1.00x.

rows.benchmark: FY2025 DSO of 34.9, DIO of 9.4 and DPO of 115.4; Microsoft TTM DSO of 65.4 and DPO of 138.8.
rows.confidence: medium - balances are disclosed, but the reason for the inventory build (memory pre-buy versus weak sell-through) is not disclosed.
rows.finding: Inventories rose to $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,718M at 2025-09-27 (+94%; +87% year on year), lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 while the cash conversion cycle stayed negative at -56.8 days and deferred revenue rose to $14.9bn, 64% of it current.
rows.follow_up: Is the inventory build finished goods ahead of price increases or unsold channel stock, and what is the write-down risk if demand softens?
rows.implication: The negative cash cycle is intact, but the inventory build is the first balance-sheet signal that the memory shortage is now costing Apple cash, and it should be watched as the leading indicator of a gross-margin miss.
rows.mechanism: Apple is pre-buying components into a shortage and paying for them before they ship, which raises inventory days and absorbs cash precisely when component prices are rising; a negative cash cycle elsewhere covers the cost.
rows.weakens: Inventory is still only $11.1bn against $109.4bn of quarterly revenue, so the absolute risk is small; a 6-day rise in inventory days is not yet a working-capital problem.

rows.benchmark: Pristine peer sets: Microsoft's 18.2% goodwill and intangibles to assets and Alphabet's 5.6%.
rows.confidence: high on the balance-sheet figures; low on what the intangibles represent, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate.
rows.finding: Net cash is $62,173M at 2026-06-27 (cash and marketable securities $146,517M less debt $84,344M), with term-debt maturities of $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, purchase obligations of $4,752M due in 2026 and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate.
rows.follow_up: What are the $13.3bn of gross intangibles added in nine months, over what life are they amortised, and could the unrecognised tax benefits crystallise?
rows.implication: Balance-sheet risk is not a constraint on the position; the intangible build is, because it is the one line that could turn into future amortisation that the current margin does not carry.
rows.mechanism: Debt is cheap, long-dated and matched against a $146.5bn liquidity pool, so the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months) rather than paying it; the intangible addition is a use of that liquidity that bypassed both capex and the acquisition line.
rows.weakens: Gross intangibles rose $13,270M with no corresponding acquisition in investing cash flow, and the current portion is already $5,075M, so amortisation is beginning; the item is unexplained rather than adverse on its face.

rows.benchmark: Microsoft TTM ROIC 35.2% and ROA 20.1%; Alphabet TTM ROIC 30.1% and ROA 30.6%; a cost of capital estimated at 9-10% from a 4.99% ten-year Treasury plus a 4.5-5.0% equity risk premium.
rows.confidence: high on the inputs and direction; the cost-of-capital estimate is the analyst's, not a disclosed figure.
rows.finding: ROA is 36.1% and ROE 148.8% on the trailing twelve months, while the mechanically computed ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of near-zero invested capital after $263.2bn of buybacks in FY2023-FY2025; on net operating assets of roughly $100bn the after-tax return is about 128%, and on total assets about 33%.
rows.follow_up: What is the incremental return on the new R&D and intangible spend, and does management report any AI-attributable revenue?
rows.implication: Returns are far above any plausible cost of capital, so the case does not rest on capital efficiency; it rests on whether the margin level persists, which is a pricing question rather than a returns question.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the equity and invested-capital denominators, so ROE and ROIC rise mechanically as the company returns capital; the economic return is the cash profit earned on operating assets, which is high but not 300%.
rows.weakens: The 128% and 33% are the analyst's restatements; the reported ratios are the ones most screens and index models use, and they overstate the true return by an order of magnitude.

rows.benchmark: A 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield and a 2.7% trailing free-cash-flow yield; Microsoft's 0.8% buyback yield against Apple's 1.6%.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the judgement that buybacks at this multiple are value-neutral rather than value-destructive.
rows.finding: Apple bought back $82,226M of stock over the trailing twelve months and paid $15,640M of dividends, about 72% of free cash flow, retiring 1.6% of the diluted share count a year and lifting EPS growth (22.4%) above net income growth (20.0%) in nine months; the buyback has slowed from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5%.
rows.follow_up: Will the buyback be cut further to fund AI investment, and is any part of the $13.3bn intangible spend capitalised R&D that would otherwise have hit the operating margin?
rows.implication: At roughly 40x trailing earnings the buyback retires shares at a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.99% risk-free rate, so it supports the share price more than it compounds value — a point the position sizing should reflect.
rows.mechanism: A company trading above the inverse of its cost of capital converts buybacks into per-share engineering rather than value creation; the cash still leaves the balance sheet, but the return per dollar is below the risk-free alternative.
rows.weakens: Buybacks remain 72% covered by free cash flow and the company is net cash, so there is no solvency or leverage argument against them; the critique is about return per dollar, not affordability.

PV of 10 years: 128.7 × Σ(1.15/1.095)^t = ratio 1.050228. Σ t=1..10:

So: at a 9.5% WACC, today's price implies FCF growing 15% a year for ten years, then 3% forever. Alternatively at 8% WACC the implied growth is ~11-12% for a decade (computed earlier ~12%). I'll show two discount rates in the reverse DCF: 
- At 9.5%: 15%/yr for 10 years.
- At 8.0%: let me compute precisely. Need EV 5,030 with FCF0 128.7, terminal 3%, g1 for 10 years. Try 11%:
FCF10 = 128.7 × 1.11^10 = 128.7 × 2.83942 = 365.5B.
PV10: ratio 1.11/1.08 = 1.027778. Σ t=1..10: 1.027778, 1.056327, 1.085758, 1.115918, 1.147060, 1.178957, 1.211706, 1.245376, 1.280080, 1.315849 → sum: 1.027778+1.056327=2.084105; +1.085758=3.169863; +1.115918=4.285781; +1.14706=5.432841; +1.178957=6.611798; +1.211706=7.823504; +1.245376=9.068880; +1.280080=10.348960; +1.315849=11.664809.
PV = 128.7 × 11.6648 = 1,501.3B.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Apple Inc. 10-K for the period ending 2025-09-27, filed 2025-10-31 (accession 0000320193-25-000079): Item 3 (Legal Proceedings). Page 1 of 1 (5,398 characters).

Item 3. Legal Proceedings
Digital Markets Act Investigations
On March 25, 2024, the Commission announced that it had opened a formal noncompliance investigation against the Company under Article 5(4) of the EU DMA (“Article 5(4) Investigation”). The Article 5(4) Investigation relates to how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users for apps distributed through the App Store, as well as how developers may conclude contracts with those end users. On June 24, 2024, the Commission announced that it had opened an additional formal investigation against the Company regarding whether the Company’s new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA (“Article 6(4) Investigation”). On April 23, 2025, the Commission fined the Company €500 million in the Article 5(4) Investigation and issued a cease and desist order requiring the Company to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. The Company has appealed the Commission’s Article 5(4) decision. Also on April 23, 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) Investigation. If the Commission makes a final determination in the Article 6(4) Investigation that there has been a violation, it can issue a cease and desist order and may impose fines up to 10% of the Company’s annual worldwide net sales. The Commission may also seek to impose additional fines if it deems that the Company has violated a cease and desist order. The Company believes that it complies with the DMA and has continued to make changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission.
Department of Justice Lawsuit
On March 21, 2024, the DOJ and a number of state and district attorneys general filed a civil antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against the Company alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for “performance smartphones” and “smartphones” in violation of U.S. antitrust laws. The DOJ is seeking equitable relief to redress the alleged anticompetitive behavior. In addition, various civil litigation matters have been filed in state and federal courts in the U.S. alleging similar violations of U.S. antitrust laws and seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief. The Company believes it has substantial defenses and intends to vigorously defend itself.
Epic Games
Epic Games, Inc. filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (“California District Court”) against the Company alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California’s unfair competition law based upon the Company’s operation of its App Store. The California District Court found that certain provisions of the Company’s App Review Guidelines violate California’s unfair competition law and issued an injunction (the “2021 Injunction”) enjoining the Company from prohibiting developers from including in their apps buttons, external links, or other calls to action that direct customers to purchasing mechanisms other than the Company’s in-app purchase system. The 2021 Injunction applies to apps on the U.S. storefronts of the iOS and iPadOS App Stores. On January 16, 2024, the Company implemented a plan to comply with the 2021 Injunction and filed a statement of compliance with the California District Court. On September 30, 2024, the Company filed a motion with the California District Court to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction. On April 30, 2025, the California District Court found the Company to be in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined the Company from imposing any commission or any fee on purchases that consumers make outside an app; restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app; or otherwise interfering with a consumer’s choice to proceed in or out of an app. The California District Court also denied the Company’s motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred the Company to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California for a determination whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. The Company will continue to vigorously defend its actions and employees, and has appealed the California District Court’s most recent decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (“Ninth Circuit Court”). Although the Company’s request to stay the decision pending appeal was denied, the Ninth Circuit Court has agreed to consider the Company’s appeal on an expedited basis, with oral arguments heard in October 2025.
Other Legal Proceedings
The Company is subject to other legal proceedings and claims that have not been fully resolved and that have arisen in the ordinary course of business. The Company settled certain matters during the fourth quarter of 2025 that did not individually or in the aggregate have a material impact on the Company’s financial condition or operating results. The outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain. If one or more legal matters were resolved against the Company in a reporting period for amounts above management’s expectations, the Company’s financial condition and operating results for that reporting period could be materially adversely affected.

arguments.markdown:
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for the life of that device at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the profit acceleration came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not from the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth.

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the incremental profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%; by 9M FY2026 iPhone was back to 53.9% and Services down to 25.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%, Europe 16.1%, the Americas 11.4% and Japan 10.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The mechanism is a device upgrade cycle (iPhone 17 Pro mix) layered on a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the installed base, which the company reported at more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year — about 6.4%, roughly a third of the 16.1% revenue growth. For an investor, the mix tells you which risk to underwrite: a hardware cycle that is currently doing the work, priced at hardware margins, rather than a subscription base compounding on its own.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue that is recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it works out at roughly $49 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew about 6.4%; so two-thirds of services growth is monetisation per device (advertising, cloud, App Store) rather than more devices. The margin is not, however, a free parameter. Apple's own EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, and a 5% Core Technology Commission now applies to apps distributed outside the App Store; in the US, Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases completed through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case filed on 2024-03-21 remains unresolved while the two sides reportedly talk settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue — not Apple's own — from a 76%-margin line to the developer, so the effect on Apple is concentrated in the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for the reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |

:::

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

Annualising the nine months to 2026-06-27 across the 2.5-billion-device base gives the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow. Revenue per device is $194, of which $145 is hardware and $49 services; gross profit is $95; the fixed cost base of R&D and SG&A is $30; operating profit is $65; capex is $3.6; free cash flow is $59. Two numbers matter. First, the operating structure breaks even at roughly $153bn of annual revenue — 31.5% of the current run-rate — because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base that grows 6% a year; a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable. Second, using a four-year device life as an assumption, cumulative gross profit per device is about $381 against $11.90 of annual SG&A, a 32:1 ratio that is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates several times the services revenue of an iPad buyer, and Apple does not disclose the split, so the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and the two risks are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin [S6].
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission, with 5% for distribution outside the App Store, versus the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA [S56, S65].
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify [S59].
- Apple's capital-light model keeps free cash flow intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months [S11, S13].
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

Apple funds the model from a negative cash cycle rather than from capital: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days produce a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days. That is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring about 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the more interesting signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Read together, Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow and the buyback, but also means the per-share compounding engine is being partly diverted, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that the two legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%; Apple is winning share in a market that is shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%+ operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are the iPhone unit volume that Apple no longer discloses, the EU share of Services revenue that Apple does not break out, and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years (about $4.4bn a year of additional expense) or ten.

arguments.markdown:
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for the life of that device at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the profit acceleration came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not from the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth.

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%; by 9M FY2026 iPhone was back to 53.9% and Services down to 25.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%, Europe 16.1%, the Americas 11.4% and Japan 10.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle (Pro-model mix) plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, about 6.4%, roughly a third of the 16.1% revenue growth. The mix therefore says which risk to underwrite — a hardware cycle doing the work at hardware margins, not a subscription base compounding on its own.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is roughly $49 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew about 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case filed on 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect is concentrated in the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| Offer | Pricing metric | Rate | Effective | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| App Store In-App Purchase, EU | % of developer transaction | 26% (15% for small-business, mini-app and video programmes and auto-renewing subscriptions after year one) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, alternative in-app payment | % of developer transaction | 20% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| Alternative marketplaces and web distribution, EU | % of digital transactions | 5% Core Technology Commission; per-install Core Technology Fee removed | 2026-10-01 | S56, S57 |
| App Store, US, In-App Purchase | % of developer transaction | 15-30% by developer size and category | current | S65 |
| App Store, US, external-link purchases | % (proposed, needs court approval) | 5-15% tiers; 0% was ordered in April 2025 | 2026-08-14 | S64 |
| iPhone | $ of revenue per unit | not disclosed; the 10-K reports iPhone net sales with no unit count | n/a | S5 |

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

Annualising the nine months to 2026-06-27 (multiplying by four-thirds) across the 2.5-billion-device base gives the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow; the per-device divisor and the annualisation are estimates, the dollars are disclosed.

| Line, per active device per year | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 (estimate) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $166 | $194 | S5, S6, S58 |
| — Products / Services | $123 / $44 | $145 / $49 | S5, S6 |
| Gross profit (margin) | $78 (46.9%) | $95 (49.1%) | S5, S6 |
| R&D | $13.8 | $18.2 | S5, S6 |
| SG&A, the acquisition-cost proxy | $11.0 | $11.9 | S5, S6 |
| Operating profit (margin) | $53 (32.0%) | $65 (33.6%) | S5, S6 |
| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | $40 | $59 | S5, S47 |
| LTV at a four-year device life (assumption) | $312 | $381 | S5, S6 |
| LTV : acquisition cost | 28:1 | 32:1 | S5, S6 |

Two numbers matter beyond the waterfall. The operating structure breaks even at roughly $153bn of annual revenue — 31.5% of the current run-rate — because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6% a year, so a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable. And the 32:1 lifetime-to-acquisition ratio is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates several times the services revenue of an iPad buyer, Apple does not disclose the split, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin [S6].
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA [S56, S65].
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify [S59].
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months [S11, S13].
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring about 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow, but partly diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years, about $4.4bn a year of extra expense, or over ten.

{"url":"https://9to5mac.com/2026/02/03/apple-search-deal-with-google-could-face-renewed-scrutiny-as-doj-appeals-antitrust-ruling/","title":"Apple’s search deal with Google could face renewed scrutiny as DOJ appeals antitrust ruling","text":"Last year, a federal judge ruled that Google had illegally maintained a search monopoly, but allowed the company to keep paying to be the default search engine on Apple devices (with very few caveats). Now, the Department of Justice and a group of states are appealing the overall decision. ￼Here are the details.

A bit of background

In August 2024, Judge Amit Mehta ruled that Google had resorted to illegal means to maintain its monopoly in the U.S. online search market.

Part of that decision involved Google’s exclusionary agreements with companies such as Apple, as they created steeper anticompetitive effects.

With that decision in the books, the case moved to a year-long remedies phase, during which multiple witnesses from all sides, including from associated companies such as Apple, tried to make their case as to what, exactly, should happen to Google.

From forcing the company to spin off Chrome to barring it from exclusive agreements like the one with Apple, everything seemed on the table.

It was during one such hearing that Apple SVP of Services Eddy Cue famously downplayed Apple’s deal with Google, suggesting that AI would make search (and even the iPhone) obsolete to the point of rendering their current exclusive deal irrelevant.

Finally, last September, Judge Mehta issued his opinion, which was overwhelmingly beneficial to Google.

As we reported back then:

Here’s what Google can and cannot do when it comes to partnerships with Apple going forward:

What is allowed

Apple’s search partnership with Google may continue. Judge Mehta rejected a blanket “payment ban,” finding it would harm partners and consumers. For this reason, Google gets to keep paying Apple to be the default (albeit not exclusive) search engine on Safari;

Google will still be allowed to pay browser developers (including Apple) for default status, provided the browser is allowed to promote other search engines, set different defaults by OS version or private mode, and change the default on an annual basis;

And speaking of defaults, the court found that choice screens weren’t shown to improve search competition, so this means that Apple won’t have to add new choice UIs in Safari or iOS because of this ruling;

When it comes to generative AI, the ruling bars contracts that would stop a Google partner from simultaneously distributing generative AI products (as well as other general search engines and browsers). In practice, this means that Apple will be free to promote or integrate non-Google assistants or chatbots even while Google Search remains the default on Safari.

What is not allowed

No exclusivity, including for generative AI products or features. This means that Google can’t require Apple to make Google the only option, block Apple from featuring rivals, or tie the deal for one Google app (like Search) to another (like Gemini);

No exclusivity-adjacent incentives. Google can’t offer higher revenue-share tiers or bonuses in exchange for exclusivity or for bundling multiple Google apps together;

12-month default limit. Google can’t condition revenue share on keeping any Google service as the default for more than one year. This means that Google’s competitors will get a yearly shot at offering Apple a better deal.

Last December, the court handed down its final judgment, which Google appealed to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals last month.

Google also asked the federal court to put parts of the ruling on hold while the appeals court reviews the case, which brings us to today.

DOJ and multiple states file an appeal

As revealed in court documents today, the Department of Justice and a group of states are also formally appealing the decision to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals.

arguments.markdown:
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for the life of that device at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the profit acceleration came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not from the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth.

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%; by 9M FY2026 iPhone was back to 53.9% and Services down to 25.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%, Europe 16.1%, the Americas 11.4% and Japan 10.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle (Pro-model mix) plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, about 6.4%, roughly a third of the 16.1% revenue growth. The mix therefore says which risk to underwrite — a hardware cycle doing the work at hardware margins, not a subscription base compounding on its own.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is roughly $49 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew about 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case filed on 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect is concentrated in the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| Offer | Pricing metric | Rate | Effective | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| App Store In-App Purchase, EU | % of developer transaction | 26% (15% for small-business, mini-app and video programmes and auto-renewing subscriptions after year one) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, alternative in-app payment | % of developer transaction | 20% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| Alternative marketplaces and web distribution, EU | % of digital transactions | 5% Core Technology Commission; per-install Core Technology Fee removed | 2026-10-01 | S56, S57 |
| App Store, US, In-App Purchase | % of developer transaction | 15-30% by developer size and category | current | S65 |
| App Store, US, external-link purchases | % (proposed, needs court approval) | 5-15% tiers; 0% was ordered in April 2025 | 2026-08-14 | S64 |
| iPhone | $ of revenue per unit | not disclosed; the 10-K reports iPhone net sales with no unit count | n/a | S5 |

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

Annualising the nine months to 2026-06-27 (multiplying by four-thirds) across the 2.5-billion-device base gives the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow; the per-device divisor and the annualisation are estimates, the dollars are disclosed.

| Line, per active device per year | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 (estimate) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $166 | $194 | S5, S6, S58 |
| — Products / Services | $123 / $44 | $145 / $49 | S5, S6 |
| Gross profit (margin) | $78 (46.9%) | $95 (49.1%) | S5, S6 |
| R&D | $13.8 | $18.2 | S5, S6 |
| SG&A, the acquisition-cost proxy | $11.0 | $11.9 | S5, S6 |
| Operating profit (margin) | $53 (32.0%) | $65 (33.6%) | S5, S6 |
| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | $40 | $59 | S5, S47 |
| LTV at a four-year device life (assumption) | $312 | $381 | S5, S6 |
| LTV : acquisition cost | 28:1 | 32:1 | S5, S6 |

Two numbers matter beyond the waterfall. The operating structure breaks even at roughly $153bn of annual revenue — 31.5% of the current run-rate — because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6% a year, so a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable. And the 32:1 lifetime-to-acquisition ratio is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates several times the services revenue of an iPad buyer, Apple does not disclose the split, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin [S6].
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA [S56, S65].
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify [S59].
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months [S11, S13].
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring about 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow, but partly diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years, about $4.4bn a year of extra expense, or over ten.

No mention of Apple AI agreement in Alphabet's 10-Q extract — so the Gemini/Siri deal is not publicly disclosed in filings. That is itself a finding: "not publicly disclosed in either company's SEC filings as of 2026-10-29; reported at about $1bn a year by trade press — unverified." I can cite S13 for the absence (careful: absence in a keyword-filtered search isn't proof, but it's a reasonable statement: "neither company's latest filing discloses the arrangement").

I'll register one media source for the reported Gemini deal, low confidence. Actually, do I need it? The competition section on AI assistants would benefit. I'll include it as "reported, unverified" citing a media source registered with low confidence. Let me register androidheadlines or tech-insider. I'll pick the WWDC 2026 recap/AppleInsider? Use "androidheadlines" (2026-06). Fine — one call.

Now let me write the evidence blocks. First market.

Deep Evidence Table rows (4+), each cell argued:

M1. Global handset market shrinks in units but grows in value — IDC: 2026 shipments -16.7% to just over 1bn, ASP +27.6% to $581, market value +6.3% to $613bn; memory up ~300% YoY. Mechanism: memory shortage raises BOM, forces price increases and kills sub-$100 segment (173M units in 2025), value migrates to premium where Apple and Samsung have supply and mix. Benchmark: 2025 1.25-1.26bn units. Weaken: IDC's own forecast was cut from -13.9% one quarter earlier, so forecast error is large (±); Counterpoint says -11% in Q2 vs IDC -7.4%. Implication: Apple's revenue can grow while its unit market shrinks; do not underwrite Apple on unit growth. Confidence high on direction, medium on magnitude. Follow-up: when does memory pricing peak (2028 per IDC)?

M2. Premium pool concentration — Counterpoint H1 2026: premium 29% of units (25% H1 2025), Apple 65% of premium units (+9%), Apple+Samsung 84%. Mechanism: premium is where profit is; Apple's share of value ~40% of the $613bn. Weaken: premium share measured in units not profit; Huawei's China premium mix not quantified. Implication: at 65% of premium, Apple's incremental growth must come from price and services rather than share. Confidence medium.

M3. Apple's regional growth re-accelerating, led by Greater China — 10-Q: 9M FY2026 Greater China $64.8bn (+30%), Europe $95.6bn (+16%), Americas $149.4bn (+11%), Japan $24.4bn (+10%), RoAP $30.2bn (+19%); FY2025 Greater China was -4% to $64.4bn. Mechanism: price discipline vs Android's memory-driven increases + iPhone 17 demand + RMB strength. Benchmark: China market -4.2% in 1H 2026. Weaken: FX contributed; pull-forward ahead of price rises; IDC expects China decline ~20% in H2 2026. Implication: China is cyclical, not structurally lost — but the swing is a one-time share gain, not a trend. High confidence on figures.

M4. Services is the growth engine but smaller in absolute dollars — Services TTM $120.5bn (+12.3% CAGR from FY2023 $85.2bn), 76.3% gross margin 9M FY2026; app ecosystem $1.4tn billings (company-funded), consumer IAP $167bn (+10.6%). Mechanism: installed base 2.5bn monetised at ~$48/device/year; services margin 2x products. Weaken: Google TAC at risk from DOJ remedies; EU take-rate cuts (5%/20% from Oct 2026); App Store commission slice not disclosed. Implication: services durability, not growth, is the valuation question. Confidence medium-high.

M5. India is the only large volume market with a structural premium runway — 33.2M units in Q2 2026 (-11.1%), ASP ₹30,000 (+14.4%), Apple led by value; 1H26 64.2M lowest in 5 years; Apple 28% value share in Q1 2026. Mechanism: premiumisation at low penetration (smartphone penetration ~?) — I don't have penetration. Weaken: Apple's revenue share from India is small (not disclosed separately; inside RoAP $30.2bn 9M). Implication: optionality, not a near-term driver. Confidence medium.

That's 5 rows. Good.

Plan for market section:
- decision_question: How large is the profit pool in Apple's markets, how fast is it growing by product and region, and where does the next growth come from?
- thesis_sentence: "Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value — global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 while market value rises 6.3% to $613bn — and Apple already takes about 40% of that value ($245.5bn of iPhone revenue in the twelve months to 2026-06-27), so the next leg of growth must come from price, services attach and share gains in China and India rather than from a rising unit tide."
- why_different: This section sizes the pool and its growth by product/region; competition names rivals and share; business model explains monetisation; financials quantify margins. Market answers "how big and how fast", not "who wins" (competition) or "how profitable" (financials).
- mechanism: memory shortage → BOM inflation → sub-$100 segment collapse → premium mix shift → Apple's value share rises even as units fall; services levered to installed base.
- comparison_set: Samsung/Xiaomi unit growth in Q2 2026 under the same shock; historical: 2025 market +1.5% units vs 2026 -16.7%.
- counter_evidence: IDC's forecast was cut from -13.9% to -16.7% in one quarter; replacement cycles elongate to 2028-29 recovery; China could fall ~20% in H2 2026; services take-rate regulation.
- visual: market size table (top-down and bottom-up) + regional table.
- prohibited: "huge market", "strong demand", "favorable tailwinds", "well positioned".

Gate items 1-9 all met.

Now competition block:
Rows:
C1. Global unit share Q2 2026 — IDC: Apple 20.2% (+3.9pp, +14.9% units) vs Samsung 22.7% (+8.1%), Xiaomi 11.3% (-26.4%), OPPO 10.5%, vivo 7.7%; Apple on track for record 22% in 2026. Mechanism: scale + early memory supply lock + premium mix determine survival. Benchmark: 2Q25 Apple 16.3%. Weaken: pull-forward demand; Counterpoint has Samsung at 24% (different share base). Implication: Apple is gaining share in a shrinking market — evidence against commoditisation. High.
C2. Premium segment — Apple 65% of $600+ units H1 2026 (+9%), Apple+Samsung 84%. Benchmark: 62% H1 2025. Weaken: Huawei is #3 premium globally and #1 in China; premium share measured in units. Implication: pricing power intact; the competitive risk is at the edges (China, AI). Medium.
C3. China — Huawei 22.6% (#1, +19.4%) vs Apple 18.1% (#2, +24.4%); Xiaomi -21.7%. Mechanism: Huawei's domestic brand + price discipline + distribution; Apple's counter is price hold + trade-in. Weaken: Apple grew faster than Huawei in Q2 2026, so Huawei is not gaining on Apple now. Implication: Huawei caps Apple's China premium ceiling; watch H2 2026 when China market may fall 20%. High (IDC).
C4. PC — Apple 9.9% units (Q2 2026), +10% vs market -4.9%; Lenovo 24.4%, HP 19.1%, Dell 13.6%. Mechanism: Mac gains from AI PC refresh + M-series; but unit share stays ~10%. Implication: Mac is a share-taker at the margin, not a growth engine. Medium (media-reported IDC).
C5. Wearables — Huawei 20.2%, Apple 17%, Xiaomi 17%, Samsung 5.8%, Garmin 5.1% (Q1 2026). Mechanism: Apple's watch ASP and attach vs Huawei/Xiaomi breadth. Weaken: category mix (bands vs smartwatches); Counterpoint smartwatch data has Apple at 23% with +21%. Implication: Apple has lost the unit lead in wrist-worn but keeps smartwatch profit. Low-medium.
C6. Services substitutes/regulatory — EU: 5% CTC from Oct 2026, 20% external payments; DOJ v Google remedies (Sept 2025) threaten Google TAC; DOJ v Apple monopolisation suits. Mechanism: take-rate compression lowers services gross margin (76.3%) and removes the highest-multiple revenue. Weaken: >90% of ecosystem billings commission-free already; EU is ~1/4 of revenue but a smaller share of services profit (not disclosed). Implication: price a regulatory haircut; watch services margin. High for the policy facts.
C7. AI assistants — Siri rebuilt on Google Gemini per trade press (~$1bn/yr), unverified; neither Apple's nor Alphabet's latest filings disclose it; Gemini powers Samsung Galaxy AI too. Mechanism: commoditised assistant layer shifts differentiation to hardware/integration, but also creates dependency and possible margin leakage. Implication: Apple's "AI premium" is not yet evidenced in share data. Low confidence.

That's 7 rows; I'll use 6.

Competition plan:
- thesis: "Apple's competitive position is stronger in value than in units and stronger at the high end than at the edges: it holds 65% of $600+ premium unit sales and 20.2% of global smartphone units in Q2 2026 while sitting at about 10% of PCs and second in wrist-worn devices, and the competitor that matters most is Samsung, which is the only rival gaining share at scale in a shrinking market and profits from the memory shortage through its own memory division, with Huawei the binding constraint inside China's premium tier."
- why_different: per-product competitor mapping and share; market sizes the pool; financials quantify the economics.
- mechanism: vertical integration in memory (Samsung) + brand and domestic policy protection (Huawei) vs Apple's silicon/OS/installed-base integration.
- comparison: historical premium shares (62% H1 2025 → 65% H1 2026), 2Q25 unit shares.
- counter_evidence: Apple gained 3.9pp share and 65% of premium, contradicting "Android closing the gap"; Huawei's growth is bounded outside China by absence of Google services.
- visual: competitor table + quad (SWOT) + positioning table.

Components: evidence, quad. Tables: competitor table, positioning table.

Character limits: 2,500-9,000; target 7,000-8,500.
