rows.finding: Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1bn units — the steepest annual contraction recorded — while ASP rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to $613bn; memory costs are up nearly 300% YoY and exceed 65% of low-end bill of materials.
rows.mechanism: The AI-datacenter memory shortage raises bill-of-materials cost, wiping out the sub-$100 tier (173M units shipped in 2025) and forcing price increases; volume migrates to vendors with secured supply and premium mix, so the market's value grows while its unit base shrinks.
rows.benchmark: 2025: about 1.25-1.26bn units and roughly 1.5-2.3% unit growth, with a broadly flat ASP; 2026 is the first year value and volume move in opposite directions at this scale.
rows.weakens: IDC cut its own 2026 forecast from -13.9% to -16.7% in one quarter, so the magnitude is unreliable; Counterpoint put Q2 2026 shipments at -11% YoY against IDC's -7.4%, a 3.6pp tracker disagreement on the same quarter.
rows.implication: Size Apple's opportunity in value, not units: a revenue model built on unit growth would understate Apple and overstate volume Android vendors; price lower any assumption of a volume recovery before 2028.
rows.confidence: High on direction (value up, units down); medium on the magnitude of the 2026 decline.
rows.follow_up: When does memory pricing peak — IDC expects increases until at least 2028 — and does Apple's early supply lock extend beyond the iPhone 18 cycle?

rows.finding: Premium handsets ($600+ wholesale) reached a record 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% in H1 2025; Apple held 65% of premium units, with premium sales up 9% YoY, and Apple plus Samsung held 84% of the segment.
rows.mechanism: Premiumisation is the market's adjustment mechanism to higher component costs: trade-in, financing and buyback programmes let buyers absorb higher prices, concentrating profit in the two vendors with the deepest premium franchises.
rows.benchmark: Apple held 62% of premium units in H1 2025, so its share rose about 3pp in a year even as its absolute premium volume grew 9% against a low-single-digit premium market.
rows.weakens: Premium share is measured in units, not profit; Huawei is the third-largest premium brand globally and leads China, and the Counterpoint release was read as a search extract rather than opened in full.
rows.implication: At 65% of the premium pool, Apple's incremental growth has to come from price and services attach rather than from further share gains — the ceiling on share is a ceiling on mix-driven growth.
rows.confidence: Medium — single research house, extract only, unit not value basis.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's share of premium segment gross profit, and how much of the premium pool is China, where Huawei is the leader?

rows.finding: Apple's Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64.8bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 (from $49.9bn), with Q3 FY2026 up 22%, after falling 4% in FY2025 and 8% in FY2024; Apple's China unit share rose to 18.1% in Q2 2026 from 13.9% a year earlier while China's total market fell 4.3%.
rows.mechanism: Apple and Huawei held prices while Android rivals raised theirs on memory costs, and Apple signalled second-half price increases, pulling iPhone 17 demand forward; renminbi strength added a translation tailwind. Share gain in a shrinking market, not market growth, drove the number.
rows.benchmark: China's market fell 4.2% to 134M units in H1 2026 and IDC expects the decline to widen to about 20% YoY in H2 2026, with recovery around 2028-29.
rows.weakens: Part of the gain is pull-forward and FX; if Android pricing normalises after the memory cycle, Apple's price-discipline advantage disappears. IDC's own outlook for H2 2026 China is markedly worse than H1.
rows.implication: Treat China as cyclical and price-driven rather than structurally lost — but do not extrapolate 30% growth; the sustainable read is share defended at 18%, not a new growth engine.
rows.confidence: High — company filings for revenue, IDC for share.
rows.follow_up: How much of the 30% is FX, how much is price, how much is units — and what happens to Apple's China share when Android prices stabilise?

rows.finding: Services reached $120.5bn on a trailing-twelve-month basis to 2026-06-27 (from $85.2bn in FY2023, about 12.3% a year) at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months, against 36.8% product gross margin in FY2025; Apple's installed base passed 2.5bn active devices in the December 2025 quarter.
rows.mechanism: Services monetise an installed base that no longer grows quickly: about $48 of services revenue per active device a year, at roughly twice the gross margin of hardware, so a 12% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 5% iPhone growth rate.
rows.benchmark: Global consumer in-app purchase spend was $167bn in 2025, up 10.6%; the App Store ecosystem facilitated over $1.4tn of developer billings and sales, more than 90% of it commission-free.
rows.weakens: The commission-bearing slice of that $1.4tn is not disclosed; Google search-licensing revenue is exposed to US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02, and EU take rates fall from October 2026 (5% outside the App Store, 20% on external payment links).
rows.implication: The valuation question is services durability, not services growth: a take-rate haircut on a 76%-margin stream is worth more per point than hardware share.
rows.confidence: High on the reported figures; medium on the durability of the take rate.
rows.follow_up: What share of services revenue is App Store commission, Google licensing and EU-exposed, and how much of the DOJ Google remedy is already reflected in guidance?

rows.finding: Apple's regional mix shifted toward Greater China in FY2026: nine-month revenue of $149.4bn Americas (+11%), $95.6bn Europe (+16%), $64.8bn Greater China (+30%), $24.4bn Japan (+10%) and $30.2bn rest of Asia-Pacific (+19%), versus FY2025 shares of 42.9% Americas, 26.7% Europe, 15.5% Greater China, 6.9% Japan and 8.1% rest of Asia-Pacific.
rows.mechanism: The two largest regions grow at low-to-mid teens while Greater China grows at 30%, so group growth of 16.2% in the nine months is unusually dependent on a market that is itself contracting in units.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 total revenue grew 6.4% with Greater China down 4%; Europe's FY2026 growth benefits from euro strength against the dollar.
rows.weakens: Europe's 16% includes a disclosed favourable FX effect and Greater China's includes renminbi strength, so constant-currency growth is lower than reported in both.
rows.implication: The Americas — 41% of nine-month revenue — is the swing factor for FY2027: a US replacement-cycle pause would matter more than another quarter of China share gains.
rows.confidence: High — filed regional net sales.
rows.follow_up: What is US carrier upgrade activity and iPhone replacement-cycle length in 2026, and how much of Americas growth is services versus iPhone?

rows.finding: India shipped 33.2M smartphones in Q2 2026, down 11.1% YoY, with the first half at 64.2M units — the lowest in five years — while ASP rose 14.4% to about INR 30,000 and Apple led the market by value.
rows.mechanism: The same memory shock that shrinks Indian volumes raises prices, and Apple's premium position converts the shift into value share even as the unit market contracts; India sits inside a rest-of-Asia-Pacific region that grew 19% in the nine months.
rows.benchmark: India's Q2 2026 decline of 11.1% is steeper than the global 7.4%, and its ASP is roughly a tenth of Apple's implied iPhone ASP.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose India revenue; the country is a small part of the $30.2bn rest-of-Asia-Pacific line, and the value-share claim comes from trade-press reporting of IDC data.
rows.implication: India is optionality for the next decade, not a driver of FY2027 earnings — worth a diligence question, not a valuation adjustment today.
rows.confidence: Medium — IDC data via trade press, no company disclosure.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's India revenue and unit share, and how much of iPhone assembly for the US market has moved to India?

plan.decision_question: How large is the profit pool in Apple's markets, how fast is it growing by product and region, and where does Apple's next growth come from?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value — global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 while market value rises 6.3% to $613bn — and Apple already captures about 40% of that value through $245.5bn of iPhone revenue in the twelve months to 2026-06-27, so the next leg of growth must come from price, services attach and share gains in China and India rather than from a rising unit tide.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the pool and its growth by product and region and locates Apple's position in it; the competition section names rivals and their shares, the business-model section explains how Apple monetises the pool, and the financials section turns the pool into margins and cash. Market answers 'how big and how fast', not 'who wins' or 'how profitable'.
plan.mechanism: The AI-datacenter memory shortage raises handset bill-of-materials cost, collapses the sub-$100 tier, forces Android vendors to raise prices, and shifts volume and value toward premium vendors with secured supply; Apple's revenue therefore grows on a falling unit base, while services compound off a 2.5bn-device installed base whose growth has slowed to a crawl.
plan.comparison_set: Samsung and Xiaomi under the same memory shock in Q2 2026 (+8.1% and -26.4% units); Apple's own history — 2025 unit growth of 1.5-2.3% with flat ASP versus 2026 value growth of 6.3% with a 27.6% ASP jump; premium share of 25% in H1 2025 versus 29% in H1 2026.
plan.counter_evidence: IDC cut its 2026 forecast from -13.9% to -16.7% in one quarter and expects no replacement-cycle recovery before 2028-29; China may fall about 20% in H2 2026; Apple's FY2026 China and Europe growth includes disclosed FX tailwinds and pull-forward demand; services take rates face EU and US legal compression.
plan.visual: A two-method market size table (top-down from IDC market value and premium share, bottom-up from installed base times services revenue per device) followed by a five-region table of Apple's position, barriers and competitors.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong demand; favorable tailwinds; well positioned; large addressable market; secular growth story; clear runway

arguments.markdown:
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for its life at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the growth came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth. The investor implication is that earnings durability has to be underwritten as a hardware cycle with a services annuity attached, not the other way round [S5, S6].

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Europe 16.1% and the Americas 11.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle with Pro-model mix plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, or 6.4%, against 16.1% revenue growth. iPhone concentration also rose to 53.9% of sales from 50.4%, which is the number to watch if the upgrade cycle rolls over.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is $48.9 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case from 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect lands on the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| Offer | Pricing metric | Rate | Effective | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| App Store In-App Purchase, EU | % of developer transaction | 26% (15% for small-business, mini-app and video programmes and auto-renewing subscriptions after year one) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, alternative in-app payment | % of developer transaction | 20% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| Alternative marketplaces and web distribution, EU | % of digital transactions | 5% Core Technology Commission; per-install Core Technology Fee removed | 2026-10-01 | S56, S57 |
| App Store, US, In-App Purchase | % of developer transaction | 15-30% by developer size and category | current | S65 |
| App Store, US, external-link purchases | % (proposed, needs court approval) | 5-15% tiers; 0% was ordered in April 2025 | 2026-08-14 | S64 |
| iPhone | $ of revenue per unit | not disclosed; the 10-K reports iPhone net sales with no unit count | n/a | S5 |

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

Annualising the nine months to 2026-06-27 (multiplying by four-thirds) across the 2.5-billion-device base gives the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow; the divisor and the annualisation are estimates, the dollars are disclosed.

| Line, per active device per year | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 (estimate) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $166 | $194 | S5, S6, S58 |
| — Products / Services | $123 / $44 | $145 / $49 | S5, S6 |
| Gross profit (margin) | $78 (46.9%) | $95 (49.1%) | S5, S6 |
| R&D | $13.8 | $18.2 | S5, S6 |
| SG&A, the acquisition-cost proxy | $11.0 | $11.9 | S5, S6 |
| Operating profit (margin) | $53 (32.0%) | $65 (33.6%) | S5, S6 |
| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | $40 | $59 | S5, S47 |
| LTV at a four-year device life (assumption) | $312 | $381 | S5, S6 |
| LTV : acquisition cost | 28:1 | 32:1 | S5, S6 |

Beyond the waterfall, two numbers set the risk envelope. The operating structure breaks even at an estimated $153bn of annual revenue, 31.5% of the current run-rate, because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6.4% a year, so a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable; and the 32:1 lifetime-to-acquisition ratio is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates more services revenue than an iPad or Mac buyer, Apple does not disclose the split, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin (Source: S6).
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA (Source: S56, S65).
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify (Source: S59).
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months (Source: S11, S13).
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow, but partly diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years — $4.4bn a year of extra expense — or over ten.

plan.decision_question: In each market Apple sells into, is it gaining or losing share and share of the profit pool?
plan.mechanism: Three different competitive mechanisms operate at once: vertical integration in memory (Samsung) converts an input-cost shock into share and profit; domestic brand plus policy protection (Huawei) caps Apple inside China's premium tier; and platform regulation plus AI commoditisation erode the services take rate and the assistant layer where Apple's differentiation was software.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; well positioned; strong moat; best-in-class; dominant ecosystem; robust pipeline
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is winning the value pool and merely holding the unit pool: it holds 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales and 20.2% of global smartphone units in Q2 2026, about 10% of PCs and second place in wrist-worn devices, and the most dangerous competitor is Samsung — the only rival gaining share at scale in a shrinking market while its memory division profits from the shortage that is squeezing everyone else — with Huawei the binding constraint on Apple inside China's premium tier.
plan.visual: A per-product competitor table (iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, services) with share, price position and source, a positioning table by product, and a SWOT component carrying the share-gain counter-evidence.
plan.why_different: This section maps rivals product by product and measures share and profit-pool movement; the market section sizes the pool and its growth; the strategy section asks what Apple should do about it; the risk section prices the failure modes. Competition answers 'who is taking the pool and how'.

rows.benchmark: Q2 2025: Apple 16.3%, Samsung 19.4%, Xiaomi 14.2%; Apple is on track for a record 22% full-year share in 2026 against about 20% in 2025.
rows.confidence: High — final IDC historical data; the share direction is confirmed by Counterpoint's independent Q2 2026 series, though Counterpoint puts Samsung at 24%.
rows.finding: Q2 2026 global smartphone units: Samsung 22.7% (+8.1% YoY), Apple 20.2% (+14.9% YoY, +3.9pp share), Xiaomi 11.3% (-26.4%), OPPO 10.5% (-17.1%), vivo 7.7% (-19.6%) in a market down 7.4% to 276.3M units.
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's FY2027 share hold once the pull-forward from expected price rises fades and Android vendors reprice?
rows.implication: Apple is taking share in a contracting market, which is the opposite of commoditisation — the competitive risk is at the margin (price-led Android flagships, Huawei in China), not in the core.
rows.mechanism: Vendors that secured memory supply early and sell where memory is a smaller share of bill of materials gain; vendors whose volume sits below $200 absorb the cost shock and lose both volume and pricing room.
rows.weakens: Some of Apple's unit growth is demand pulled forward by fear of its own second-half price increases, so the share gain may not repeat; Xiaomi's decline is partly deliberate low-end pruning to protect margin.

rows.benchmark: H1 2025: Apple 62% of premium units; premium was 25% of the market. Apple's premium volumes grew 9% YoY.
rows.confidence: Medium — one research house, and the release was available only as a search extract rather than a full page.
rows.finding: Premium handsets ($600+ wholesale) reached a record 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026; Apple held 65% of premium units with sales up 9% YoY, and Apple plus Samsung held 84%, up from 82% a year earlier.
rows.follow_up: What is Huawei's share of China's $600+ segment specifically, and how much premium profit does Apple earn per unit outside the US?
rows.implication: The profit pool is concentrating in two vendors; Apple's pricing power is intact, but at 65% share the incremental gain has to come from price and mix rather than from taking more of the segment.
rows.mechanism: Trade-in, financing and buyback programmes let consumers absorb higher prices, and the premium tier is where the memory cost increase is a smaller share of the price, so it grows as a share of a shrinking market.
rows.weakens: Unit share is not profit share; Huawei is the third-largest premium brand globally and the leader in China, where Apple's premium position is contested.

rows.benchmark: Q2 2025 China: Huawei 18.1%, Apple 13.9%, Xiaomi 15.1%. China's total market fell 4.2% in H1 2026 to 134M units, and IDC expects the decline to widen to about 20% YoY in H2 2026.
rows.confidence: High on the shares (IDC table); low on the durability of the relative position, since both leaders gained by holding prices rather than by winning on product.
rows.finding: China Q2 2026: Huawei 22.6% (+19.4% YoY), Apple 18.1% (+24.4%), OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% (-21.7%), Honor 11.3%; the top six hold about 96% of the market.
rows.follow_up: What happens to Huawei's and Apple's China shares when Android vendors stop raising prices, and how much of Apple's China revenue is services and accessories rather than iPhone?
rows.implication: Huawei caps Apple's China premium ceiling at a level Apple has not exceeded since 2023; plan on 18% share, not on a return to former highs.
rows.mechanism: Huawei's domestic brand loyalty, policy-backed prestige and widening price ladder let it hold price while Android rivals raised theirs; Apple matched with price holds and trade-in, so both took share from the price-raising middle.
rows.weakens: Apple grew faster than Huawei in Q2 2026, so Huawei is not gaining on Apple right now; and Huawei's reach outside China is limited by the absence of Google Mobile Services.

rows.benchmark: Global PC market Q2 2026 fell 4.9% to 68.2M units after nine quarters of growth; Lenovo 24.4%, HP 19.1%, Dell 13.6%, Apple 9.9%.
rows.confidence: Medium — IDC figures via trade press rather than IDC's release; unit share understates Apple's revenue share.
rows.finding: Mac shipments grew about 10% in Q2 2026 while the PC market fell 4.9%, leaving Apple at 9.9% unit share against Lenovo's 24.4%, HP's 19.1% and Dell's 13.6%.
rows.follow_up: What is Mac revenue share of the PC market, and how much of the Q2 2026 growth is AI-PC refresh versus education and enterprise wins?
rows.implication: Mac is a share-taker at the margin, not a growth engine: a 10% unit share cannot move group revenue the way iPhone or services can.
rows.mechanism: Memory shortages hit low-priced consumer PCs hardest while Apple's M-series pricing and vertical integration protect gross margin; AI-PC replacement demand favours premium configurations.
rows.weakens: Apple reports Mac revenue of $33.7bn in FY2025, only 8% of total revenue, so even strong Mac growth moves the group by less than a point.

rows.benchmark: Wrist-worn category grew 2.2% in Q1 2026; Counterpoint's smartwatch-only series put Apple at 23% share with 21% growth, so category definition changes the ranking.
rows.confidence: Low — trade-press summary of IDC, category mix distorts the comparison.
rows.finding: Q1 2026 wrist-worn shipments of 47.05M units: Huawei 20.2%, Apple 17%, Xiaomi 17%, Samsung 5.8% (-20.7%), Garmin 5.1%.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's share of smartwatch revenue and of attach rates to iPhone, and is Huawei's lead inside China only?
rows.implication: Apple has lost the unit lead in wrist-worn devices to cheaper Chinese hardware but likely retains profit leadership; the wearables line fell 4% in FY2025 to $35.7bn, so this is a shrinking contributor.
rows.mechanism: Huawei and Xiaomi win on price and breadth in China and emerging markets; Apple competes on health sensing and iPhone attach, which supports ASP rather than unit share.
rows.weakens: The category bundles smartwatches with basic bands, and Apple does not sell a band, so the headline share understates its position in the profitable segment.

rows.benchmark: App Store ecosystem billings of over $1.4tn in 2025 (company-commissioned study), more than 90% commission-free; services gross margin 76.3% in the nine months to 2026-06-27.
rows.confidence: High on the policy facts and the remedies timeline; medium on the revenue at risk, which Apple does not disclose.
rows.finding: Apple's App Store terms face three simultaneous pressures: EU terms restructured in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links from October 2026; US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02 in the Google search case could bar Google from paying Apple for distribution; and US civil antitrust suits allege monopolisation in smartphones.
rows.follow_up: How much services revenue comes from App Store commission, Google licensing and EU-exposed commerce, and what has Apple guided for services margin in FY2027?
rows.implication: Price a haircut to the highest-multiple revenue stream rather than a binary break-up: each point of services gross margin is worth more than a point of hardware share.
rows.mechanism: Regulation compresses the take rate on the only part of the ecosystem where Apple charges a commission, while the assistant layer commoditises: Siri was rebuilt on Google's Gemini models at WWDC in June 2026, reported at about $1bn a year and not disclosed in either company's latest SEC filing.
rows.weakens: Most of the $1.4tn ecosystem was already commission-free, the EU is a minority of services profit (not disclosed), and Apple still charges on external distribution, so the revenue loss may be smaller than the headlines imply.

events.text: Gate passed. Now the team evidence block.

plan.comparison_set: Apple's own 2011 handover from Cook's operations background; Microsoft FY2026 ($182.9bn operating cash flow against $139.5bn investing outflows, capex up $51.4bn); Apple's own stated benchmark of the 80th-90th percentile of peer CEO pay; base rate: internally promoted operations CEOs at hardware incumbents rarely deliver a new product category in their first two years.
plan.counter_evidence: Independent reporting of an unresolved AI gap, Siri misses and product misfires; zero insider purchases in twelve months against $208m of sales; a board with only one new independent since 2021; CEO, COO, CFO and GC all changed between January 2025 and March 2026; R&D intensity rising partly because of catch-up spending.
plan.decision_question: Does management's execution and capital-allocation record justify a premium valuation at a market value near $5.0trn, or is the premium a balance-sheet and buyback artefact?
plan.mechanism: Capital allocation substitutes for growth: the buyback adds roughly 1pp to EPS a year, so the premium depends on gross margin holding above 49% while R&D intensity rises from 8.3% to above 9% and while a first-time CEO with a hardware-engineering background runs the AI transition.
plan.prohibited: well positioned, strong team, experienced management, clear strategy, risks are manageable, about/many/several, recently
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's capital-allocation record is exceptional and its 2025-2026 product execution is not: the company returned $73.9bn, 63% of operating cash flow, in nine months while growing revenue 16%, but that growth needed a 33% rise in R&D and a $13.3bn build in gross intangibles, and the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed inside twenty months.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix across Ternus, Cook, Khan and Parekh, with an evidence component on the succession and the capital-allocation record.
plan.why_different: It judges the people and their decisions - pay, succession, insider behaviour, where the cash goes - rather than the products, the market or the price.

AAPL 8-K Item 5.02 filed 2025-07-25, 2025-12-05 and 2026-04-20: COO, general counsel and CEO transitions
AAPL 2026 DEF 14A: director biographies, tenure and ages, CEO pay structure, named executive officers, ownership
AAPL 10-Q 2026-06-27: R&D expense trend and drivers, repurchases, dividends, share count, intangible build and purchase obligations
AAPL FY2025 10-K Item 7: R&D by year, buyback authorisation, dividend increase
MSFT FY2026 10-K Item 7: operating cash flow and investing outflows (peer capital deployment)
Fortune profile of John Ternus, 2026-08-31 (independent evidence on the AI gap and succession expectations)

rows.benchmark: Cook himself was an operations executive promoted internally in 2011, a base rate of Apple preferring continuity; Fortune reports Gassée and Munster expect continuity rather than a reset.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: John Ternus, 50 at appointment, became CEO and a director on 2026-09-01; he joined Apple in 2001, was vice president of hardware engineering from 2013 and a member of the senior executive team from 2021; Tim Cook moved to executive chair and Art Levinson from chair to lead independent director.
rows.follow_up: Does Ternus change capital allocation (capex, M&A, licensing) or only product cadence in FY2027?
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a strategy reset: the premium should rest on the installed base and margin, not on a new-category bet from the new CEO.
rows.mechanism: A planned insider succession preserves operational continuity and product cadence but leaves the AI strategy owned by the same executive team that produced the 2024-2026 Siri delays.

rows.benchmark: Apple's tenured cohort: Khan joined in 1995 (31 years), Ternus in 2001 (25 years), Cook in 1998 (28 years); the GC replacement is the only external senior hire in the group.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Four of the top jobs turned over in twenty months: CFO (Kevan Parekh, January 2025), COO (Sabih Khan, 2025-07-25, aged 58, at Apple since August 1995), general counsel (Jennifer Newstead from 2026-03-01, with Kate Adams, GC since 2017, retiring late 2026) and CEO (2026-09-01).
rows.follow_up: Who is the designated AI/product leader below the CEO, and is that role on the executive team?
rows.implication: Institutional knowledge is intact but external refresh is thin; key-person dependency concentrates in Ternus and Khan at the moment of an AI transition.
rows.mechanism: A retirement wave in a long-tenured leadership cohort replaced operating experience with operating experience, not with new capability.

rows.benchmark: Microsoft in FY2026 retained capital: $182.9bn operating cash flow against $139.5bn investing outflows with capex up $51.4bn.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Capital allocation is disciplined and shareholder-first: $73.9bn returned in nine months of FY2026 ($62.1bn repurchases, $11.8bn dividends) equal to 63% of $117.0bn operating cash flow while capex was only $6.8bn; FY2025 returned $104.7bn ($89.3bn plus $15.4bn) and the share count fell 1.1% in nine months.
rows.follow_up: Is Apple buying capability it used to build - and at what price and exclusivity?
rows.implication: The record justifies a premium for capital discipline but not for reinvestment; a buyer paying ~$5trn is paying for returns of capital, not for a new growth engine.
rows.mechanism: Returning most operating cash flow and holding capex near 2% of revenue maximises per-share metrics and ROIC while leaving AI compute to partners and licensing.

rows.benchmark: R&D was 8% of revenue in FY2023-FY2025, so 9.3% is a step change, not a drift.
rows.confidence: high on figures; medium on what the spend buys
rows.finding: R&D rose from $29,915m (FY2023) to $31,370m (FY2024) to $34,550m (FY2025) and reached $34,035m in nine months of FY2026, up 33% year on year, or 9.3% of revenue, with the quarter at 10.7%; at the same time gross intangible assets rose to $38,220m from $24,950m and other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn.
rows.follow_up: What is the counterparty, term and exclusivity of the licensing commitments behind the intangible build?
rows.implication: Apple is buying capability as well as building it; that is a rational catch-up route but it transfers margin to a licensor whose identity is not disclosed.
rows.mechanism: AI catch-up is being funded through the P&L (infrastructure and headcount) and through licensed IP on the balance sheet, which is why operating margin (33.6%) held only because gross margin rose 2.3pp.

rows.benchmark: Apple positions Cook's total target pay at the 80th-90th percentile of its peer group by its own statement.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Pay is tied to relative total shareholder return, not to AI or product milestones: Cook's 2025 target equity was $50m, 75% performance-based, his base salary is unchanged since 2016, and 2021-granted performance RSUs vested at 187% of target on 2024-10-01 (477,301 shares); he has already met the age-65, ten-year retirement-vesting condition.
rows.follow_up: What is Ternus's pay package and does it include AI or product-cycle metrics?
rows.implication: Alignment with shareholder returns is strong and alignment with strategic transformation is weak - the incentive structure rewards the status quo the market is worried about.
rows.mechanism: Relative-TSR scorecards pay for outperforming the S&P 500, a target reachable through buybacks and margin management without a new product cycle.

rows.benchmark: A 14,608,963-thousand-share company where no officer or director bought a share at $300-345.
rows.confidence: high on the facts; low as a standalone signal
rows.finding: Insiders sold and did not buy: 46 sale transactions of 687,127 shares for $208.0m in the twelve months to 2026-10-29, 43 of them under Rule 10b5-1 plans, with zero purchases; the largest were director Art Levinson at $86.7m, executive chair Tim Cook at $80.4m and Deirdre O'Brien at $23.1m, and new CEO John Ternus sold $8.5m on 2026-10-02.
rows.follow_up: Does any officer buy after the 2026-11-02 results, and does Ternus keep selling on the same schedule?
rows.implication: Treat as neutral-to-negative corroboration, not a thesis driver: scheduled diversification explains the sales, but no informed buyer is signalling that the shares are cheap.
rows.mechanism: Scheduled plans mute the information content of sales, so the informative signal is the absence of any discretionary purchase at a ~$5trn valuation.

rows.benchmark: Committee chairs are substantive: Ron Sugar (77, since 2010) chairs audit after serving as Northrop Grumman's CFO; Sue Wagner (64, since 2014) co-founded BlackRock.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: The board is experienced but stale: after the transition it has nine directors aged 51-77, including Levinson (75, a director since 2000), Sugar (77, since 2010), Jung (67, since 2008) and Wagner (64, since 2014), with Wanda Austin (2024) the only new independent since 2021.
rows.follow_up: Will the board add an operating AI or developer-platform director within twelve months?
rows.implication: Oversight of the AI transition rests with a board that has deep finance and consumer-brand experience and little current AI-operator experience.
rows.mechanism: Low refresh and long tenure preserve institutional memory but reduce the external challenge a first-time CEO needs during a technology discontinuity.

rows.benchmark: Fortune quotes an investor that Ternus is not 'an iconic product visionary' and reports Vision Pro as a misfire, Siri updates as a miss, the Liquid Glass redesign as criticised and the foldable phone as years behind Samsung.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Independent reporting on the handover describes an unresolved AI gap versus OpenAI, a memory-chip shortage squeezing margins, slowing revenue growth and product misfires (Vision Pro, Siri updates, the Liquid Glass redesign), while describing Ternus as a well-liked hardware engineer expected to make only 'small touches' at first.
rows.follow_up: Which AI features ship in the FY2027 cycle and are they Apple-built or licensed?
rows.implication: The counter-case is about product, not people: the team is competent and the pipeline is the open question, which is what the FY2027 cycle will settle.
rows.mechanism: A continuity CEO inherits both the operating discipline and the innovation gap, so the valuation premium cannot be justified by succession alone.

arguments.markdown:
Apple turns nearly all of its profit into cash — $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income on capex of 2.2% of sales — but the fiscal 2026 margin of 49.1% gross and 33.6% operating includes at least 2 points of non-recurring tariff refunds and a $13,270M intangible build that the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise [S5, S6, S47].

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than with operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still sitting in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is close to 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at roughly 1.7 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, comfortably covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months) rather than paying it, so coverage is not a metric that binds. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin [S6, S5].

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On roughly $100bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is about 128%, and on total assets about 33% — still a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest way to say it is that Apple earns about $128bn of after-tax operating profit on about $100bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital that Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity [S7, S10, S11, S13].

### Capital allocation: 72% of free cash flow returned, at a 2.5% earnings yield

Trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow, retired 1.6% of diluted shares and lifted nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The arithmetic that matters for a long-only holder is the price paid: at $348.91 on 2026-10-29 the shares trade at roughly 40 times trailing EPS of $8.72, so each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%. That does not make the buyback wrong — it is funded by cash the company does not need and it is 1.4 times covered by free cash flow — but it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, not value creation, and it explains why the pace fell 12% year on year while R&D and intangibles rose. The investor implication is that EPS growth of 20%-plus is roughly half operating and half capital-structure driven, and that the operating half is the half at risk from memory costs [S7, S10, S47].

### Base, upside and downside: gross margin is the variable that moves the outcome

On a base case of $504bn of FY2027 revenue (+6%), a 48.0% gross margin and 15.6% operating expense, operating income is about $163bn (32.4%) and EPS about $9.3; an upside case of 10% revenue growth with a 49.5% margin gives about $10.3, and a downside of 2% revenue decline with a 45.0% margin gives about $7.5. Every 100bp on gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, about 3% of base-case net income; 100bp on the tax rate is $1.6bn, about 1%. Gross margin dominates, and it is the line management has already flagged — memory and storage costs that "may not" be offset by price. That is the one variable to underwrite: not revenue growth, which has a visible iPhone cycle behind it, but whether Apple can hold a 48% margin when Samsung is earning 55% on the components inside its phones [S59, S60].

::: info warning
The fiscal 2026 margin is not a clean run-rate: 2 points of the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds the company says are a one-off, inventories rose 94% to $11,092M from the FY2025 year-end close, and $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition in investing cash flow and no note disaggregating them (Source: S6, S47). Amortisation of that build is the most likely source of an FY2027 operating-margin surprise that no current line item shows.
:::

rows.mechanism: The premium is the price of mix (Services $91.7B of the $364.4B nine-month revenue) and of a revenue acceleration to 14.8% in FY2026 from 6.4% in FY2025; the market is capitalising a higher-quality, faster-growing stream at a lower discount rate than the peer set receives.

rows.weakens: Apple's FY2026 revenue growth of 14.8% is far above the peer set, and its EV/Sales premium is only 51% against a 88% P/E premium, so part of the gap is earned by mix rather than pure re-rating; Alphabet's 14.8x trailing P/E appears depressed by a trailing item and drags the median down.
rows.implication: An entry at 40x means the multiple, not the business, determines the return: hold the multiple and the buyer earns EPS growth of about 8%; lose a third of the multiple and two years of compounding is erased. Price lower or wait.
rows.confidence: high — multiples computed from SEC XBRL filings and 2026-10-29 closing prices, with two independent consensus reads agreeing.
rows.follow_up: What Services growth and gross margin does a 40x multiple capitalise, and does the FY2027 consensus of +10.3% revenue support it?

rows.finding: A two-stage DCF on $128.7B of owner free cash flow (consensus FY2026 FCF $142.36B less $13.7B stock-based compensation) at a 9.5% WACC, 8% growth for five years, 4% for five more and 3% terminal, values the equity at $2,667B or $183 a share — 48% below the $348.91 close. Across an 8.5%-10.5% WACC and 2.5%-3.5% terminal grid the range is $153-$230; each 100bp on the discount rate moves the value 15-18%.
rows.mechanism: Duration: at 40x earnings the cash flows that matter sit a decade out, so the discount rate and terminal growth set the price. Terminal value is 56% of the $2,605B enterprise value, which is why the grid, not the point estimate, is the honest output.
rows.benchmark: Revenue CAGR of 5.5% from FY2021 ($365.8B) to FY2026E ($477.6B); consensus FY2027 revenue growth of 10.3%; 10-year Treasury at 4.99%.
rows.weakens: The terminal assumption dominates: a single-stage perpetual-growth reverse DCF needs only 5.3% perpetual FCF growth at an 8.0% WACC (6.9% at 9.5%) to justify $5,030B, and Apple has compounded FCF at about 9% a year for five years — so the DCF is not proof of overvaluation, it is proof that the price depends on assumptions I cannot verify.
rows.implication: There is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return; a buyer is underwriting a second growth engine (AI devices, Services) that is not in the model. Position size for a 15-25% drawdown if the required return rises.
rows.confidence: medium — the arithmetic is exact and reproducible, but the growth path is judgement, and the peer-consistent discount rate is an assumption (beta 1.1 is mine, not sourced).
rows.follow_up: Which disclosed cash flows would have to arrive by FY2031 for the 15%-growth case to be visible in filings rather than in narrative?

rows.finding: Consensus already sits below the market: average 12-month target $332.39 across 43 analysts (median $337.50, low $245, high $405) is 4.7% below the $348.91 close, corroborated by a 44-analyst median of $338; Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from 1 in May 2026 to 6 in October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6% in twelve months.
rows.mechanism: The sell side's own discounted values do not support the price, so the marginal buyer is not rating-driven; when targets lag the price, upgrades cannot supply the next leg and downgrades become the asymmetric risk.
rows.benchmark: 43 analysts polled by S&P Global; the high target of $405 implies +16.1% and the low of $245 implies -29.8%.
rows.weakens: Targets lag prices mechanically in a momentum run, and five named houses (Evercore ISI $380, HSBC $366, JPMorgan $360, BofA $370, Monness $355) sit above the average; the average is dragged by a long tail of low targets.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a re-rating to consensus — there is none. The watchlist case must rest on earnings beats, not on multiple expansion.
rows.confidence: medium-high — two independent consensus aggregators agree within 1.6% on the median.
rows.follow_up: How much of the FY2027 EPS estimate depends on the Google default payment and on tariff-refund gross margin?

rows.finding: At a $5,092.1B market cap Apple's trailing earnings yield is 2.50% against a 4.99% 10-year Treasury yield — a negative spread of 249bp — with the 10-year up 93bp year on year, the 2-year at 4.67%, fed funds at 4.00%, VIX at 17.20 (52nd percentile) and investment-grade spreads at 86bp.
rows.mechanism: A negative earnings-yield spread means the buyer is paid less for owning the equity than for owning the bond and must recover the difference through growth; it also makes the multiple mechanically sensitive to any further rise in the discount rate, which is the exact channel through which 2022 compressed Apple's P/E from 37.5x to 24.6x.
rows.benchmark: 10-year Treasury 4.99%, 2-year 4.67%, fed funds upper limit 4.00%, IG OAS 86bp versus 76bp a year earlier, VIX 17.20 versus a 13.47-31.05 one-year range.
rows.weakens: Credit spreads at 86bp and a VIX in the middle of its range describe a calm market, not a stressed one; a fall in the 10-year yield would re-expand the multiple and my scenario weights would be wrong.
rows.implication: Size the position for rate duration, not just for earnings risk: a 100bp rise in the required return removes 15-18% of my DCF value without any change in Apple's business.
rows.confidence: high on the data, medium on the causal link between yields and this multiple.
rows.follow_up: What is the historical beta of Apple's P/E to the 10-year yield in 2022-2026, and has it fallen as Services grew?

rows.finding: FQ3 FY2026 (quarter ended 2026-06-27) revenue rose 16.4% to $109.4B with gross margin of 50.1% that included about 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, iPhone +21.7%, Greater China +22.4%, Services +12.1% and R&D +32.2%; the release contains no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance.
rows.mechanism: The margin peak is partly a refund, and R&D growing twice as fast as revenue is the cost of the AI build; extrapolating a 50.1% gross margin into FY2027 overstates earnings power by roughly two points, which on $527B of consensus FY2027 revenue is about $10B of gross profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 gross margin 46.9% and revenue growth 6.4%; FQ3 FY2025 gross margin 46.5% ($43.7B on $94.0B).
rows.weakens: The growth is broad-based — every geographic segment and iPhone, Mac and Services all grew double digits — and Greater China's 22.4% rebound contradicts the share-loss narrative, so the acceleration is not a one-product or one-refund artefact.
rows.implication: Underwrite FY2027 margins at 48-49%, not 50%, and discount the first clean quarter from the new CEO on 2026-11-02 rather than extrapolating the refund-flattered one.
rows.confidence: high — read from the 8-K exhibit filed with the SEC.
rows.follow_up: What is the gross margin excluding tariff refunds, and how much of the refund is recurring?

rows.finding: Trailing free cash flow of $136.7B is flattered by a working-capital release: days sales outstanding fell to 24.5 from 34.9 a year earlier with receivables $8.4B lower, so FCF/net income is 1.06x against 0.88x in FY2025 and a 0.98-1.16x five-year range; normalised FCF is about $129B, a 2.5% yield rather than 2.7%.
rows.mechanism: Cash conversion mean-reverts: a one-off collection of receivables raises reported FCF without changing earnings power, so anyone valuing Apple on trailing FCF yield overstates the cash return by roughly 20bp.
rows.benchmark: FY2021-FY2025 FCF/net income 0.98x, 1.12x, 1.03x, 1.16x, 0.88x; consensus FY2026 FCF $142.36B.
rows.weakens: Apple's conversion has averaged about 1.03x over five years, so 1.06x is not an outlier and the adjustment is small relative to the multiple question.
rows.implication: Use $129-142B of FCF as the base and resist the 2.7% yield headline; on either figure the cash yield is below the 4.99% Treasury, which is the whole valuation argument in one line.
rows.confidence: medium-high — the working-capital swing is in the filed balance sheet; the normalisation is my judgement.
rows.follow_up: Is the receivables decline a vendor-non-trade-receivable reclassification or genuine collection, and does it reverse in FQ4?

plan.decision_question: What is Apple worth, and what does the $348.91 share price imply about future cash flow and risk?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple at $348.91 is priced at 40.0x trailing earnings — an 88% premium to its peer median and above every fiscal-year-end multiple since 2021 — so the share price rather than the business is the risk: it requires roughly 15% annual free-cash-flow growth for a decade at a 9.5% discount rate, or a 5-7% perpetual growth rate accepted at a sub-9% required return, and leaves a long-only buyer no margin of safety at today's quote.
plan.why_different: The other sections judge the business, its products, its market and its risks; this one prices them, converting the filed numbers into per-share value and stating which growth the market has already paid for so the Lead can size a position rather than describe a company.
plan.mechanism: Multiple duration: a 40x P/E is a claim on cash flows a decade out, so the discount rate (10-year Treasury 4.99%) and the terminal growth rate set the value more than the next quarter does; with a 2.50% earnings yield sitting 249bp under the risk-free rate, each 100bp of required return removes 15-18% of my DCF value.
plan.comparison_set: Four named peers (MSFT 27.7x, GOOGL 14.8x, META 21.3x, Samsung 12.9x; median 18.1x), Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 fiscal-year-end P/E of 24.6x/27.9x/37.5x/34.2x and EV/Sales of 6.1x-9.1x, consensus FY2027 EPS of $9.56, and a 5.5% revenue CAGR from FY2021 to FY2026E.
plan.counter_evidence: Revenue grew 16.4% in FQ3 FY2026 with Greater China up 22.4% and gross margin at 50.1%, consensus FY2026 EPS was revised up 18.5%, the shares made a new high on 2026-10-29 and VIX sits at its 52nd percentile — a genuine AI-driven acceleration could hold a 40x multiple, and with terminal value at 56% of my DCF the $183 figure is an assumption rather than an observation.
plan.visual: Trading snapshot table, then the peer multiples table with Samsung added to the four-peer median, then the valuation methods table carrying peer P/E, own-history P/E, the two-stage DCF range and the reverse DCF.
plan.prohibited: 'expensive', 'overvalued' or 'bubble' as standalone labels without the arithmetic; 'huge market', 'strong team', 'high barriers to entry', 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned'; vague counts ('about 5', 'many'); any sentence about how the section or report is written.

arguments.markdown:
Apple turns nearly all of its profit into cash — $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income on capex of 2.2% of sales — but the fiscal 2026 margin of 49.1% gross and 33.6% operating includes at least 2 points of non-recurring tariff refunds and a $13,270M intangible build that the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise [S5, S6, S47].

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.6% | 17.3% | S3-S6 |
| Diluted EPS, $ | 6.13 | 6.08 | 7.46 | 6.88 | 8.72 | S3-S6 |

| Net cash | 51,011 | 50,021 | 33,763 | 62,173 | 62,173 | S3-S6 |

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is close to 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at roughly 1.7 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin [S6, S5].

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On roughly $100bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is about 128%, and on total assets about 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns about $128bn of after-tax operating profit on about $100bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity [S7, S10, S11, S13].

| Return on assets | 27.5% | 26.1% | 30.9% | 36.1% | 20.1% | 30.6% | S5, S11, S13 |
| ROIC as computed | 1,527% | 1,036% | 479% | 320.6% | 35.2% | 30.1% | S5, S11, S13 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 33.2% | 47.1% | 33.3% | S5, S11, S13 |
| Days sales outstanding | 28.1 | 31.2 | 34.9 | 24.5 | 65.4 | 56.4 | S5, S11, S13 |
| Days inventory outstanding | 10.8 | 12.6 | 9.4 | 16.9 | 6.0 | 26.3 | S5, S11, S13 |
| Days payables outstanding | 106.7 | 119.7 | 115.4 | 98.3 | 138.8 | 43.5 | S5, S11, S13 |
| Cash conversion cycle, days | -67.8 | -75.8 | -71.1 | -56.8 | -67.5 | 39.2 | S5, S11, S13 |
| Capex / revenue | 2.9% | 2.4% | 3.1% | 2.2% | 39.2% | 33.9% | S5, S11, S13 |

### Capital allocation: 72% of free cash flow returned, at a 2.5% earnings yield

Trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow, retired 1.6% of diluted shares and lifted nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The arithmetic that matters for a long-only holder is the price paid: at $348.91 on 2026-10-29 the shares trade at roughly 40 times trailing EPS of $8.72, so each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%. That does not make the buyback wrong — it is funded by cash the company does not need and covered 1.4 times by free cash flow — but it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, and it explains why the pace fell 12% year on year while R&D and intangibles rose. EPS growth of 20%-plus is therefore partly operating and partly capital-structure driven, and the operating part is the part at risk from memory costs [S7, S10, S47].

### Base, upside and downside: gross margin is the variable that moves the outcome

On a base case of $504bn of FY2027 revenue (+6%), a 48.0% gross margin and 15.6% operating expense, operating income is about $163bn (32.4%) and EPS about $9.3; an upside case of 10% revenue growth with a 49.5% margin gives about $10.3, and a downside of a 2% revenue decline with a 45.0% margin gives about $7.5. Every 100bp on gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, about 3% of base-case net income; 100bp on the tax rate is $1.6bn, about 1%. Gross margin dominates, and it is the line management has already flagged: memory and storage costs that price increases "may not" offset. That is the variable to underwrite — whether Apple can hold a 48% margin when Samsung is earning 55% on the components inside its phones [S59, S60].

::: info warning
The fiscal 2026 margin is not a clean run-rate: 2 points of the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds the company calls a one-off, inventories rose 94% to $11,092M from the FY2025 year-end close, and $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition in investing cash flow and no note disaggregating them (Source: S6, S47). Amortisation of that build is the most likely source of an FY2027 operating-margin surprise that no current line item shows.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple at 2026-10-30 is an iPhone business with a services margin bolted on — 53.9% of nine-month FY2026 revenue comes from iPhone while 76.3%-gross-margin Services supply a quarter of sales — and that shape, not the $62.2bn of net cash, is what the next twelve months test.

Apple Inc. is a California corporation whose shares trade on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars, with one class of common stock and no dual-class control block: 50,400,000 thousand shares authorised at $0.00001 par, 14,608,963 thousand outstanding at 2026-06-27 against 14,773,260 thousand at 2025-09-27. Ownership is index-dominated. Vanguard held 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% of the 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, all directors and executive officers together held 9,079,765 shares, or 0.062%, and CEO-turned-executive-chair Tim Cook held 3,280,295 shares. There is no controlling shareholder, no VIE and no second voting class, so structural governance risk is low and policy risk arrives through regulators rather than through a controller [S6, S52].

The legal-entity map is a jurisdiction map, not an intellectual-property map: Exhibit 21 names 19 subsidiaries, omits the rest as insignificant and states no entity's function. Four of the named entities are Irish — the largest foreign cluster — and the tax note records that the FY2025 provision fell $10.7bn year on year because of the State Aid Decision, leaving an effective rate of 15.6% in FY2025 and 17.6% in the first nine months of FY2026. No filing in the register discloses which entity owns the trademarks or the cost-sharing arrangement, which is the single largest unquantified structural item for anyone modelling a tax-rate normalisation [S5].

| iTunes K.K. | Japan | Limited company | Not stated | Subsidiary, % not disclosed | S5 |

The business model is an installed-base annuity on top of a hardware franchise. Apple sells through 40% direct and 60% indirect channels to consumers, small and mid-sized businesses, education, enterprise and government, and monetises the base through the App Store, iCloud, AppleCare, advertising, payments and Apple TV at a 76.3% Services gross margin against 39.9% on products. It employed approximately 166,000 full-time-equivalent staff at 2025-09-27. Growth in FY2026 came from the opposite end of that mix: Services rose 14% to $91.7bn in nine months while iPhone rose 22% to $196.5bn, so the highest-margin line grew slower than the group [S5, S6].

Geographically the company is majority non-US — 57.1% of FY2025 revenue and 59.0% of nine-month FY2026 revenue — and the segment disclosure hides more than it shows. India, the Middle East and Africa sit inside the Europe segment, so the fastest-growing large market is not visible as a line. Greater China is visible, and it reversed: from $72,559m in FY2023 it fell 8% to $66,952m, fell another 4% to $64,377m in FY2025, then produced $64,839m in nine months of FY2026, up 30% and above the whole of the prior year, with management attributing the increase to iPhone and a stronger renminbi. Manufacturing remains concentrated where the tariffs are: a significant majority of production runs through outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, with single-source partners for many components [S6, S5].

The balance sheet is capacity, not protection. Cash and marketable securities of $146.5bn against $84.3bn of debt — $2.0bn commercial paper, $11.0bn current and $71.3bn non-current term debt — left $62.2bn of net cash at 2026-06-27 against roughly $33.7bn nine months earlier, helped by inventories doubling to $11,092m ahead of component shortages. Apple returned $73.9bn in nine months ($62.1bn of repurchases, $11.8bn of dividends), equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, while spending $6.8bn on property, plant and equipment. Buybacks have already slowed by $8.5bn against the prior-year period and the share count fell only 1.1%, so per-share compounding is a support rather than the engine. Net cash equals 1.2% of a $5.02trn market value at $343.36, the price of an insider sale executed on 2026-10-27; the press valued the company at $4.6trn on 2026-08-31 [S6, S5].

The structure's weak points are supply, policy and price rather than demand. Management states that component supply constraints and rising costs for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM "may materially negatively impact" revenue, cost and gross margin, and expects the trend to intensify; Q3 FY2026 gross margin of 50.1% and EPS of $2.02 included roughly 2 percentage points and $0.11 from tariff refunds after the US Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, while the 2026-01-14 Section 232 semiconductor results imposed nothing additional on Apple products and Section 301 measures have since been imposed. In Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering rule in 2025 and Apple changed its EU App Store fees in August 2026. Against Microsoft, which funded $139.5bn of FY2026 investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow to build AI capacity, Apple converts operating cash into buybacks and almost none into owned compute — coherent for an installed-base franchise and fragile if AI features become the upgrade reason. Confidence is high on the reported figures (filings through 2026-06-27) and medium on the mix judgement; FY2026 results are not due until 2026-11-02. The open questions are whether Services outgrows iPhone in FY2027, how much of Q3's margin was the tariff refund, what the counterparty and term are behind the $14.5bn increase in other purchase obligations to $29.3bn, which entity owns the IP and at what rate, and whether Greater China holds if the renminbi weakens [S47, S84, S50].

rows.benchmark: Apple's own 10-K total-return graph to September 2025: Apple $234, S&P 500 $217, Dow Jones U.S. Technology $287 on a $100 base — 18.5% a year against 16.8% for the S&P and 23.5% for the technology index.
rows.confidence: high — every component is from a filing or a dated price series and the three components multiply back to the actual price change.
rows.finding: Over the five years to 2026-10-29 Apple's price rose 134.2% (18.5% a year) on diluted EPS growth of 55.4% ($5.61 in FY2021 to $8.72 trailing) and a P/E re-rating from 26.6x to 40.0x (+50.7%), with dividends adding about 2.3% cumulatively; multiple expansion accounts for roughly 48% of the logarithmic return.
rows.follow_up: What multiple would a holding-period return of 8% a year require at exit, and what would force it down?
rows.implication: A repeat of the last five years requires the multiple to reach 60x on 8% EPS growth; without that, the holding-period return is the EPS growth rate plus the dividend, about 8.4% a year, which is below the 9.5% required return used in the valuation.
rows.mechanism: Re-rating, not earnings, supplied half the return: with the multiple now at a five-year high the same mechanism cannot repeat from a higher base, so the return distribution is asymmetric — earnings still compound, the multiple can only give back.
rows.weakens: EPS still compounded at 9.2% a year through a pandemic, a China slowdown and a tariff cycle, so the underlying engine did two-thirds of the work even though the multiple did half of the return.

rows.benchmark: Buyback yield 1.6% against a 2.5% normalised FCF yield; $82.2B trailing repurchases against $90.7B in FY2025 and $94.9B in FY2024.
rows.confidence: high — authorisation, spend and prices are filed figures; only the residual balance is my arithmetic.
rows.finding: Apple has $99.779B of buyback authorisation left at 2025-09-27 under the May 2025 $100B programme, of which $62.1B was used in the nine months to 2026-06-27, leaving roughly $37.7B absent a new programme; trailing repurchases of $82.2B equal 1.6% of market cap, and in FQ4 FY2025 Apple bought 89.5M shares for about $20.0B at roughly $223.5 each, 36% below today's close.
rows.follow_up: What did Apple authorise in May 2026, and is the buyback being slowed as the multiple rises?
rows.implication: Do not treat the buyback as a bid under the stock: at 40x it shrinks the share count 1.6% a year while transferring value to sellers, and its capacity is about 2% of market cap a year, far too small to absorb index selling.
rows.mechanism: A buyback adds value only when the price is below intrinsic value; above it, each repurchased share is a transfer from continuing holders to selling ones, so the 1.6% buyback yield is a share-count effect rather than a return source at a 40x multiple.
rows.weakens: The programme is large, recurring and renewed annually, and 1.6% of annual share shrinkage is a real contributor to EPS growth that my 8% EPS estimate already embeds.

rows.benchmark: Microsoft/Activision Blizzard $68.7B (2023), Dell/EMC $67B (2016), Broadcom/VMware $61B (2023) — the three largest technology transactions ever.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the deal values, which come from one near-primary release and one ranking.
rows.finding: No strategic exit exists: the largest technology acquisition ever, Microsoft's $68.7B purchase of Activision Blizzard, equals 1.35% of Apple's $5,029.9B enterprise value, every comparable deal since 2016 was struck for a company one to two orders of magnitude smaller, and a leveraged buyout would need more than $5T of equity that no sponsor or consortium can raise.
rows.follow_up: Is there any regulatory or political path to a foreign or domestic acquisition of a US$5T company, and would antitrust review not end it first?
rows.implication: The exit is the secondary market, full stop; a holder should not pay anything for takeover optionality, and the trim decision must be made on valuation and catalyst dates rather than on a bid.
rows.mechanism: Deal size is bounded by the acquirer's balance sheet and by antitrust review; at $5.03T Apple is roughly 73 times the largest technology deal ever, so the distribution of exit outcomes has no takeover premium in it at all.
rows.weakens: A stock-for-stock merger with another mega-cap, an activist-driven break-up, or a sovereign-backed consortium are theoretical routes my arithmetic rules out by assumption rather than by evidence.

rows.benchmark: Average daily value traded $13.22B (20 days) and $13.55B (3 months); Apple is one of three stocks that together make up 21% of the S&P 500.
rows.confidence: high on liquidity; medium on the index concentration, which comes from a single media report without Apple's individual weight.
rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: 38.67M shares a day worth $13.22B trade in Apple, so a $250M position is 1.9% of one day's volume and can be exited in under a day at a fifth of normal participation; the shares sit 0.8% below their 52-week high of $351.73 and above the 50-day ($332.37) and 200-day ($296.13) averages.
rows.follow_up: What share of Apple's float is held by index and passive vehicles, and how does that change the drawdown behaviour versus 2022?
rows.implication: Exit cost is not the risk and does not argue for a smaller position; the risk is the price at which the exit happens, which is set by the multiple rather than by the order book.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity cuts both ways: it lets a holder leave without a discount, and it lets index-driven selling arrive without a discount too, so concentration in the index amplifies drawdowns rather than protecting the price.
rows.weakens: An all-time-high price with a 44.5% fifty-two-week range ($243.42 to $351.73) shows the stock can lose 30% in a year even with this liquidity, so liquidity protects the exit, not the return.

rows.mechanism: With EPS growth fixed at 8% by consensus, the exit multiple does most of the work: each 6x of P/E is about 15% of terminal value, so a return to the FY2025 year-end multiple alone erases two years of compounding.
rows.weakens: If revenue growth holds at 14-16% and the AI device cycle extends, 40x is defensible and the bull case is the base case; my 30% bear weight is the single most consequential judgement in the table.

Circuit appeal in which the DOJ and states are cross-appealing remedies that let Google keep paying Apple for default placement on non-exclusive, annually renegotiable terms.

Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism, not a cyclical accident, since the memory-intensive cost structure that is squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist to at least 2028. What is not durable is the FY2026 growth rate: 30% in Greater China rests on price discipline that only works while rivals are raising prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases.

Confidence in the direction is high, because the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and in two independent trackers. Confidence in the magnitude is lower: IDC cut its 2026 unit forecast from -13.9% to -16.7% within one quarter, and the trackers disagree by 3.6 points on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the $1.4 trillion App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (so the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions can be separated), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of group growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much of the FY2026 iPhone strength was pulled forward from FY2027? Second, does China hold an 18% unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to a 5% EU commission and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?
