arguments.markdown:
Apple's statements show a business that converts almost all of its profit into cash on capex that is trivial for a company of its size, but the fiscal 2026 margin rests on a tariff refund the company itself calls one-off and on an intangible build the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise.

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, the company's own approximation, and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at 1.71 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin. The question to put to management is what those intangibles are and over what life they amortise [S6, S5].

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On $100.4bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is 128%, and on total assets 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns $128.1bn of after-tax operating profit on $100.4bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity. The capital-allocation version of the same point: trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow and retired 1.6% of diluted shares, lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth; but at $348.91 on 2026-10-29, or 40.0 times trailing EPS, each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%, so it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, covered 1.4 times by free cash flow and already slowing — $62,094M in nine months against $70,579M [S7, S10, S11, S13, S47].

### Base, upside and downside: gross margin is the variable that moves the outcome

On a base case of $504bn of FY2027 revenue (+6% on an estimated FY2026 of $475bn), a 48.0% gross margin and 15.6% operating expense, operating income is $163.3bn (32.4%) and EPS $9.30; an upside case of 10% revenue growth with a 49.5% margin gives $10.24, and a downside of a 2% revenue decline with a 45.0% margin gives $7.58. Every 100bp on gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, 3.1% of base-case net income; 100bp on the tax rate is $1.6bn, 1.2%. Gross margin dominates, and it is the line management has already flagged: memory and storage costs that price increases "may not" offset. That is the variable to underwrite — whether Apple can hold a 48% margin when Samsung is earning 55% on the components inside its phones [S59, S60].

::: info warning
The fiscal 2026 margin is not a clean run-rate: 2 percentage points of the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds the company calls a one-off, inventories rose 94% to $11,092M from the FY2025 year-end close, and $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition in investing cash flow and no note disaggregating them (Source: S6, S47). Amortisation of that build is the most likely source of an FY2027 operating-margin surprise that no current line item shows.
:::

arguments.markdown:
**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just above 1.0 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth about $135 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter; against that base, trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million is about $48 per device per year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 5% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 30% in Greater China to $64,839 million, 16% in Europe, 11% in the Americas, 10% in Japan and 19% in the rest of Asia-Pacific, lifting Greater China from 15.5% of FY2025 revenue to 17.8%. China's own market fell 4.2% in the first half of 2026, so Apple's gain was share rather than tide: its unit share rose to 18.1% from 13.9% because it held prices while Android rivals raised theirs, and IDC expects the Chinese market to fall about 20% in the second half. India repeats the pattern at a different scale — 33.2 million units in the second quarter of 2026, down 11.1%, average prices up 14.4% and Apple leading by value — while in the United States, where iOS carries 58.35% of mobile web traffic, growth runs through carrier trade-in programmes rather than new users. [S6, S80, S96, S89]

Policy both creates and caps this demand, and the dates are live. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation published initial results on 2026-01-14 without imposing tariffs on Apple's products, and the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, for which Apple has claimed refunds; Section 301 duties and further sector measures remain open. In Europe, Apple restructured its App Store terms in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, effective October 2026. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. Demand that was subsidy-created is now subsidy-dependent; demand that is trade-in-driven has held. [S6, S81, S80]

::: evidence
**Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on roughly 1.0 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at about $48 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]
:::

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism, not a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist to at least 2028. What is not durable is the FY2026 growth rate: 30% in Greater China rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its 2026 unit forecast from -13.9% to -16.7% within one quarter, and the trackers disagree by 3.6 points on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed: the commission-bearing slice of the $1.4 trillion App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much FY2026 iPhone strength was pulled forward from FY2027? Second, does China hold an 18% unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to a 5% EU commission and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?

arguments.markdown:
Apple's statements show a business that converts almost all of its profit into cash on capex that is trivial for a company of its size, but the fiscal 2026 margin rests on a tariff refund the company itself calls one-off and on an intangible build the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise.

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, the company's own approximation, and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at 1.71 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin. The diligence question that follows: what are those intangibles, over what life are they amortised, and does the expense arrive in FY2027 [S6, S5]?

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On $100.4bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is 128%, and on total assets 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns $128.1bn of after-tax operating profit on $100.4bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity. The capital-allocation version of the same point: trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow and retired 1.6% of diluted shares, lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth; but at $348.91 on 2026-10-29, or 40.0 times trailing EPS, each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%, so it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, covered 1.4 times by free cash flow and already slowing — $62,094M in nine months against $70,579M [S7, S10, S11, S13, S47].

### Base, upside and downside: gross margin is the variable that moves the outcome

On a base case of $504bn of FY2027 revenue (+6% on an estimated FY2026 of $475bn), a 48.0% gross margin and 15.6% operating expense, operating income is $163.3bn (32.4%) and EPS $9.30; an upside case of 10% revenue growth with a 49.5% margin gives $10.24, and a downside of a 2% revenue decline with a 45.0% margin gives $7.58. Every 100bp on gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, 3.1% of base-case net income; 100bp on the tax rate is $1.6bn, 1.2%. Gross margin dominates, and it is the line management has already flagged: memory and storage costs that price increases "may not" offset. That is the variable to underwrite — whether Apple can hold a 48% margin when Samsung is earning 55% on the components inside its phones [S59, S60].

Amortisation of that build is the most likely source of an FY2027 operating-margin surprise that no current line item shows.

arguments.markdown:
Apple at 2026-10-30 is an iPhone business with a services margin bolted on — 53.9% of nine-month FY2026 revenue comes from iPhone while 76.3%-gross-margin Services supply a quarter of sales — and that shape, not the $62.2bn of net cash, is what the next twelve months test.

Apple Inc. is a California corporation whose shares trade on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars, with one class of common stock: 50,400,000 thousand shares authorised at $0.00001 par and 14,608,963 thousand outstanding at 2026-06-27, down from 14,773,260 thousand at 2025-09-27. Ownership is index-dominated. Vanguard held 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% of the 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, while all directors and executive officers together held 9,079,765 shares, or 0.062%, and Tim Cook held 3,280,295. There is no controlling shareholder, no VIE and no second voting class, so structural governance risk is low and policy risk arrives through regulators rather than a controller [S6, S52].

The entity map is a jurisdiction map, not an intellectual-property map: Exhibit 21 names 19 subsidiaries, omits the rest as insignificant and states no entity's function. Four are Irish, the largest foreign cluster, and the tax note records that the FY2025 provision fell $10.7bn year on year because of the State Aid Decision, leaving an effective rate of 15.6% in FY2025 and 17.6% in nine months of FY2026. No filing in the register discloses which entity owns the trademarks or the cost-sharing arrangement, the largest unquantified item for anyone modelling tax normalisation [S5].

| Apple Operations International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Not stated | Subsidiary | S5 |
| Apple Operations Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Not stated | Subsidiary | S5 |
| Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. | China | Limited company | Not stated | Subsidiary | S5 |
| Apple India Private Ltd | India | Limited company | Not stated | Subsidiary | S5 |
| Braeburn Capital, Inc. | Nevada, US | Corporation | Not stated | Subsidiary | S5 |

The business model is an installed-base annuity on a hardware franchise. Apple sells through 40% direct and 60% indirect channels to consumers, small and mid-sized businesses, education, enterprise and government, and monetises the base through the App Store, iCloud, AppleCare, advertising, payments and Apple TV at a 76.3% Services gross margin against 39.9% on products, with 166,000 full-time-equivalent staff at 2025-09-27. Growth in FY2026 came from the other end of that mix: Services rose 14% to $91.7bn in nine months while iPhone rose 22% to $196.5bn, so the highest-margin line grew slower than the group [S5, S6].

Geographically the company is majority non-US — 57.1% of FY2025 revenue and 59.0% of nine-month FY2026 revenue — and the segment disclosure hides more than it shows: India, the Middle East and Africa sit inside Europe, so the fastest-growing large market is not a line. Greater China is visible, and it reversed: from $72,559m in FY2023 it fell 8% to $66,952m, fell another 4% to $64,377m in FY2025, then produced $64,839m in nine months of FY2026, up 30% and above the whole prior year, with management citing iPhone and a stronger renminbi. Manufacturing remains where the tariffs are: a significant majority of production runs through outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, with single-source partners for many components [S6, S5].

The balance sheet is capacity, not protection. Cash and marketable securities of $146.5bn against $84.3bn of debt — $2.0bn commercial paper, $11.0bn current and $71.3bn non-current term debt — left $62.2bn of net cash at 2026-06-27 against roughly $33.7bn nine months earlier, with inventories doubled to $11,092m. Apple returned $73.9bn in nine months ($62.1bn of repurchases, $11.8bn of dividends), equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, and spent $6.8bn on capital expenditure. Buybacks were $8.5bn below the prior-year period and the share count fell only 1.1%, so per-share compounding is a support rather than the engine. Net cash equals 1.2% of the $5.02trn market value implied by $343.36, the price of an insider sale executed on 2026-10-27; the press valued the company at $4.6trn on 2026-08-31 [S6, S5].

The weak points are supply, policy and price, not demand. Management states that component constraints and rising costs for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM "may materially negatively impact" revenue, cost and gross margin, and expects the trend to intensify. Q3 FY2026 gross margin of 50.1% and EPS of $2.02 included roughly 2 percentage points and $0.11 from tariff refunds after the US Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20; the 2026-01-14 Section 232 semiconductor results added nothing on Apple products, but Section 301 measures have since been imposed. In Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering rule in 2025 and Apple changed its EU App Store fees in August 2026. Against Microsoft, which funded $139.5bn of FY2026 investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow to build AI capacity, Apple converts operating cash into buybacks and almost none into owned compute: coherent for an installed-base franchise, fragile if AI becomes the upgrade reason. Confidence is high on the figures (filings through 2026-06-27) and medium on the mix judgement; FY2026 results are not due until 2026-11-02. Open questions: whether Services outgrows iPhone in FY2027, how much of Q3 margin was the refund, what sits behind the $14.5bn rise in other purchase obligations to $29.3bn, and whether Greater China holds if the renminbi weakens [S47, S84, S50].

The question is whether it deserves 40.0x, and that is a question only a discount-rate-and-growth model can answer.

The model I trust least is the one that looks most precise, so it is worth stating its inputs plainly. Taking consensus FY2026 free cash flow of $142.36B and deducting $13.7B of stock-based compensation as a real cost gives $128.7B of owner cash flow; discounting eight years of growth at 8% tapering to 4% for five years and 3% in perpetuity, at a 9.5% WACC built from a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity-risk premium and a 1.1 beta (my assumption, not a sourced figure), produces an equity value of $2,667B, or $183 a share. Terminal value is 56% of the $2,605B enterprise value, which is why the sensitivity grid matters more than the point estimate: $153 a share at a 10.5% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth, $230 at 8.5% and 3.5%.

| Peer median P/E | 18.1x × TTM EPS $8.72 | $158 | −55% | S6, S93, S94 |
| Own four-year average year-end P/E | 31.1x × TTM EPS $8.72 | $271 | −22% | S6, S7 |
| Two-stage DCF, base | $128.7B FCF; 8%/4%/3%; 9.5% WACC | $183 | −48% | S6, S93, S10 |
| DCF sensitivity | 8.5–10.5% WACC; 2.5–3.5% terminal | $153 – $230 | −34% to −56% | Author's model |
| Reverse DCF | $5,029.9B EV at 9.5% WACC | needs ~15% FCF growth a year for ten years | — | Author's model |
| Perpetual-growth reverse | $128.7B FCF at 8.0% WACC | needs 5.3% growth in perpetuity | — | Author's model |
| Cash yield at the price | $136.7B FCF / $5,092.1B | 2.68% vs 4.99% ten-year Treasury | −231bp spread | S6, S10 |

The reverse calculation is the cleanest statement of what the price assumes, and it cuts both ways. At a 9.5% required return, today's enterprise value needs free cash flow to compound at about 15% a year for ten years before settling to 3%; that is nearly triple the 5.5% revenue compound from FY2021 ($365.8B) to FY2026E ($477.6B). At an 8.0% required return the bar falls to 5.3% perpetual growth, which Apple's roughly 9% five-year free-cash-flow compound has already cleared. The honest conclusion is therefore not that the shares are obviously mispriced but that the buyer is underwriting a second growth engine — AI devices, Services, new categories — that no filing yet evidences, and is paying a price that assumes it arrives. The 2.68% cash yield against a 4.99% risk-free rate is the same fact in one line: the equity offers less current cash than the bond and must make up the difference with growth.

The sell side has stopped keeping up with the price. The consensus of 43 analysts polled by S&P Global carries an average 12-month target of $332.39 and a median of $337.50, which is 3.3-4.7% below the $348.91 close, with a high of $405 and a low of $245; a separate 44-analyst median of $338 agrees. Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one in May 2026 to six in October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6%. Forward numbers are respectable — consensus FY2026 revenue $477.64B (+14.8%) and EPS $8.84 (+18.5%), FY2027 $526.79B (+10.3%) and $9.56 (+8.1%) — but they imply a sharp deceleration already: subtracting nine-month actuals from the full-year estimate gives a September quarter of about $113.3B and $1.96 of EPS, or +10.6% and +6.5%, against +16.4% and +29% in the June quarter. Apple publishes no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance — the July 2026 results release contains none — so the consensus is the only forward anchor and it is falling, not rising, in growth terms [S93].

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the acceleration is real and broad. June-quarter revenue rose 16.4% with double-digit growth in iPhone, Mac and Services and in every geographic segment, Greater China rebounded 22.4% to $18.8B, and R&D rose 32.2% to $11.7B — the profile of a company investing into a cycle rather than harvesting one. Against that, the 50.1% gross margin included about two points of tariff refunds, so underlying margin was 48.1%, and a 50% margin extrapolated into FY2027 overstates gross profit by roughly $10B on consensus revenue. Peak margin plus peak multiple plus a 4.99% ten-year yield is the combination that hurt Apple in 2022, when the multiple fell from 37.5x to 27.9x in a year without any deterioration in the business [S47, S5].

For a long-only watchlist the implication is a price, not a story. At $348.91 there is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return, the expected return in my scenario set is negative, and the buyback does not defend the price at a 2.7% cash yield. The conditions that would justify adding are concrete: revenue growth of 10% or more in FY2027 with gross margin of 48% or higher excluding tariff refunds, and an entry multiple of 30-34x forward earnings — about $287-$325 on FY2027 EPS of $9.56, which is still above the peer median and in line with Apple's own 2024-2025 multiples. Until one of those appears, the shares belong on a watchlist with a trim discipline, not in a position sized for compounding.

Diligence questions the evidence leaves open: how much of Services gross profit is the Google default payment, and how much of FY2027 EPS depends on it; whether the 24.5-day receivables figure marks a genuine collection or a classification shift that reverses in the September quarter; what buyback authorisation replaced the May 2025 programme, and whether Apple slows repurchases as the multiple rises; and what Services growth a 40x multiple requires if hardware growth reverts to the 6% of FY2025. Each is answerable from the 2026-11-02 results, the FY2026 10-K and the next buyback announcement, and each moves the value more than a further 5% move in the share price does.

arguments.markdown:
**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth $134.9 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter. Trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million has compounded at 12.3% a year from $85,200 million in FY2023 and divides into $48.19 per active device a year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12.3% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 7.0% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. **Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on just over 1 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40.0% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at $48.19 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism rather than a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist through the forecast horizon. What is not durable is the current growth rate: the Greater China acceleration rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its own unit forecast within a single quarter, and the trackers disagree materially on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much iPhone strength was pulled forward? Second, does China hold its current unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to the EU's restructured commissions and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?

Against its own history the same message is sharper. At the last four fiscal year ends Apple traded at 24.6x (2022), 27.9x (2023), 37.5x (2024) and 34.2x (2025) earnings, with EV/Sales of 6.1x, 6.9x, 8.8x and 9.1x; today's 40.0x and 10.8x sit above all four years on both measures. The re-rating is not random: revenue growth accelerated to 14.8% in FY2026 from 6.4% in FY2025 on consensus, gross margin rose to 48.6% from 46.9%, and the mix shifted toward Services at $91.7B of the $364.4B nine-month revenue. A higher-quality, faster-growing stream deserves a higher multiple than the 24.6x of fiscal 2022. The question is whether it deserves 40.0x, and that is a question only a discount-rate-and-growth model can answer.

The model I trust least is the one that looks most precise, so its inputs are worth stating plainly. Taking consensus FY2026 free cash flow of $142.36B and deducting $13.7B of stock-based compensation as a real cost gives $128.7B of owner cash flow; discounting eight years of growth at 8% tapering to 4% for five years and 3% in perpetuity, at a 9.5% WACC built from a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity-risk premium and a 1.1 beta (my assumption, not a sourced figure), produces an equity value of $2,667B, or $183 a share. Terminal value is 56% of the $2,605B enterprise value, which is why the sensitivity grid matters more than the point estimate: $153 a share at a 10.5% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth, $230 at 8.5% and 3.5%.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peer median P/E | 18.1x × TTM EPS $8.72 | $158 | −55% | S6, S93, S94 |
| Own four-year average year-end P/E | 31.1x × TTM EPS $8.72 | $271 | −22% | S6, S7 |
| Two-stage DCF, base | $128.7B FCF; 8%/4%/3%; 9.5% WACC | $183 | −48% | S6, S93, S10 |
| DCF sensitivity | 8.5–10.5% WACC; 2.5–3.5% terminal | $153 – $230 | −34% to −56% | Author's model |
| Reverse DCF | $5,029.9B EV at 9.5% WACC | needs ~15% FCF growth a year for ten years | — | Author's model |
| Perpetual-growth reverse | $128.7B FCF at 8.0% WACC | needs 5.3% growth in perpetuity | — | Author's model |
| Cash yield at the price | $136.7B FCF / $5,092.1B | 2.68% vs 4.99% ten-year Treasury | −231bp spread | S6, S10 |

The reverse calculation is the cleanest statement of what the price assumes, and it cuts both ways. At a 9.5% required return, today's enterprise value needs free cash flow to compound at about 15% a year for ten years before settling to 3%; that is nearly triple the 5.5% revenue compound from FY2021 ($365.8B) to FY2026E ($477.6B). At an 8.0% required return the bar falls to 5.3% perpetual growth, which Apple's roughly 9% five-year free-cash-flow compound has already cleared. The honest conclusion is not that the shares are obviously mispriced but that the buyer is underwriting a second growth engine — AI devices, Services, new categories — that no filing yet evidences, and is paying a price that assumes it arrives. The 2.68% cash yield against a 4.99% risk-free rate is the same fact in one line: the equity offers less current cash than the bond and must make up the difference with growth.

The sell side has stopped keeping up with the price. The consensus of 43 analysts polled by S&P Global carries an average 12-month target of $332.39 and a median of $337.50, which is 3.3-4.7% below the $348.91 close, with a high of $405 and a low of $245; a separate 44-analyst median of $338 agrees. Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one in May 2026 to six in October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6%. Forward numbers are respectable — consensus FY2026 revenue $477.64B (+14.8%) and EPS $8.84 (+18.5%), FY2027 $526.79B (+10.3%) and $9.56 (+8.1%) — but they imply a sharp deceleration already: subtracting nine-month actuals from the full-year estimate gives a September quarter of about $113.3B and $1.96 of EPS, or +10.6% and +6.5%, against +16.4% and +29% in the June quarter. Apple publishes no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance — the July 2026 results release contains none — so the consensus is the only forward anchor and it is falling, not rising, in growth terms [S93].

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the acceleration is real and broad. June-quarter revenue rose 16.4% with double-digit growth in iPhone, Mac and Services and in every geographic segment, Greater China rebounded 22.4% to $18.8B, and R&D rose 32.2% to $11.7B — the profile of a company investing into a cycle rather than harvesting one. Against that, the 50.1% gross margin included about two points of tariff refunds, so underlying margin was 48.1%, and a 50% margin extrapolated into FY2027 overstates gross profit by roughly $10B on consensus revenue. Peak margin plus peak multiple plus a 4.99% ten-year yield is the combination that hurt Apple in 2022, when the multiple fell from 37.5x to 27.9x in a year without any deterioration in the business [S47, S5].

For a long-only watchlist the implication is a price, not a story. At $348.91 there is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return, the expected return in my scenario set is negative, and the buyback does not defend the price at a 2.7% cash yield. The conditions that would justify adding are concrete: revenue growth of 10% or more in FY2027 with gross margin of 48% or higher excluding tariff refunds, and an entry multiple of 30-34x forward earnings — about $287-$325 on FY2027 EPS of $9.56. Until one appears the shares belong on a watchlist with a trim discipline. Two questions remain open and move the value more than another 5% in the share price: how much of Services gross profit is the Google default payment, and what buyback authorisation replaced the May 2025 programme.

**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth $134.9 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter. Trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million implies a 12.3% CAGR from $85,200 million in FY2023 and divides into $48.19 per active device a year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12.3% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 7.0% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 30% in Greater China to $64,839 million, 16% in Europe, 11% in the Americas, 10% in Japan and 19% in the rest of Asia-Pacific, lifting Greater China from 15.5% of FY2025 revenue to 17.8%. China's own market fell 4.2% in the first half of 2026, so Apple's gain was share rather than tide: its unit share rose to 18.1% from 13.9% because it held prices while Android rivals raised theirs, and IDC expects the second-half decline in China to widen to 20% year on year. India repeats the pattern at a different scale — 33.2 million units in the second quarter of 2026, down 11.1%, average prices up 14.4% and Apple leading by value — while in the United States, where iOS carries 58.35% of mobile web traffic, growth runs through carrier trade-in programmes rather than new users. [S6, S80, S96, S89]

Policy both creates and caps this demand, and the dates are live. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation published initial results on 2026-01-14 without imposing tariffs on Apple's products, and the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, for which Apple has claimed refunds; Section 301 duties and further sector measures remain open. In Europe, Apple restructured its App Store terms in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, effective October 2026. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. Demand that was subsidy-created is now subsidy-dependent; demand that is trade-in-driven has held. [S6, S81, S80]

::: evidence
**Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on just over 1 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40.0% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at $48.19 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]
:::

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism rather than a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist through the forecast horizon. What is not durable is the current growth rate: the Greater China acceleration rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its own unit forecast within a single quarter, and the trackers disagree materially on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much iPhone strength was pulled forward? Second, does China hold its current unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to the EU's restructured commissions and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?

The reverse calculation is the cleanest statement of what the price assumes. At a 9.5% required return, today's enterprise value needs free cash flow to compound at about 15% a year for ten years before settling to 3%; that is nearly triple the 5.5% revenue compound from FY2021 ($365.8B) to FY2026E ($477.6B). At an 8.0% required return the bar falls to 5.3% perpetual growth, which Apple's roughly 9% five-year free-cash-flow compound has already cleared. The honest conclusion is not that the shares are obviously mispriced but that the buyer is underwriting a second growth engine — AI devices, Services, new categories — that no filing yet evidences, and is paying a price that assumes it arrives. The 2.68% cash yield against a 4.99% risk-free rate is the same fact in one line: the equity offers less current cash than the bond and must make up the difference with growth.

The sell side has stopped keeping up with the price. The consensus of 43 analysts polled by S&P Global carries an average 12-month target of $332.39 and a median of $337.50, which is 3.3-4.7% below the $348.91 close, with a high of $405 and a low of $245; a separate 44-analyst median of $338 agrees. Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one in May 2026 to six in October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6%. Forward numbers are respectable — consensus FY2026 revenue $477.64B (+14.8%) and EPS $8.84 (+18.5%), FY2027 $526.79B (+10.3%) and $9.56 (+8.1%) — but they imply a sharp deceleration already: subtracting nine-month actuals from the full-year estimate gives a September quarter of about $113.3B and $1.96 of EPS, or +10.6% and +6.5%, against +16.4% and +29% in the June quarter. Apple publishes no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance — the July 2026 results release contains none — so the consensus is the only forward anchor [S93].

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the acceleration is real and broad. June-quarter revenue rose 16.4% with double-digit growth in iPhone, Mac and Services and in every geographic segment, Greater China rebounded 22.4% to $18.8B, and R&D rose 32.2% to $11.7B — the profile of a company investing into a cycle rather than harvesting one. Against that, the 50.1% gross margin included about two points of tariff refunds, so underlying margin was 48.1%, and a 50% margin extrapolated into FY2027 overstates gross profit by roughly $10B on consensus revenue. Peak margin plus peak multiple plus a 4.99% ten-year yield is the combination that hurt Apple in 2022, when the multiple fell from 37.5x to 27.9x in a year while the business did not deteriorate [S47, S5].

For a long-only watchlist the implication is a price, not a story. At $348.91 there is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return, the expected return in my scenario set is negative, and the buyback does not defend the price at a 2.7% cash yield. The conditions that would justify adding are concrete: revenue growth of 10% or more in FY2027 with gross margin of 48% or higher excluding tariff refunds, and an entry multiple of 30-34x forward earnings — about $287-$325 on FY2027 EPS of $9.56. Until one appears the shares belong on a watchlist with a trim discipline. Two open questions move the value more than another 5% of price: how much of Services gross profit is the Google default payment, and what buyback authorisation replaced the May 2025 programme.

The Company recognizes revenue at the amount to which it expects to be entitled when control of products or services is transferred to its customers. Control is generally transferred when the Company has a present right to payment and title and the significant risks and rewards of ownership of products or services are transferred to its customers. For most of the Company’s Products net sales, control transfers when products are shipped. For the Company’s Services net sales, control transfers over time as services are delivered. Payment for Products and Services net sales is collected within a short period following transfer of control or commencement of delivery of services, as applicable.
The Company records reductions to Products net sales related to future product returns, price protection and other customer incentive programs based on the Company’s expectations and historical experience.
For the sale of third-party products where the Company obtains control of the product before transferring it to the customer, the Company recognizes revenue based on the gross amount billed to customers. The Company considers multiple factors when determining whether it obtains control of third-party products, including evaluating if it can establish the price of the product, retains inventory risk for tangible products or has the responsibility for ensuring acceptability of the product. For third-party applications sold through the App Store, the Company does not obtain control of the product before transferring it to the customer. Therefore, the Company accounts for all third-party application–related sales on a net basis by recognizing in Services net sales only the commission it retains.
(1) Services net sales include amortization of the deferred value of services bundled in the sales price of certain products.
The Company has non-trade receivables from certain of its manufacturing vendors resulting from the sale of components to these vendors who manufacture subassemblies or assemble final products for the Company. The Company purchases these components directly from suppliers. The Company does not reflect the sale of these components in products net sales. Rather, the Company recognizes any gain on these sales as a reduction of products cost of sales when the related final products are sold by the Company. As of September 27, 2025, the Company had two vendors that individually represented 10% or more of total vendor non-trade receivables, which accounted for 46 % and 23 %. As of September 28, 2024, the Company had two vendors that individually represented 10% or more of total vendor non-trade receivables, which accounted for 44 % and 23 %.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's capital-allocation record is exceptional and its 2025-2026 product execution is not: the company returned $73.9bn, 63% of operating cash flow, in nine months while growing revenue 16%, but that growth needed a 33% rise in R&D and a $13.3bn build in gross intangibles, and the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed inside twenty months. The bench is deep in operators and thin in outsiders. John Ternus, 50 when appointed, became chief executive and a director on 2026-09-01; Tim Cook, 65, moved to executive chair after fifteen years as CEO and keeps a board seat; Sabih Khan, 58, has been chief operating officer since 2025-07-25 and joined Apple in August 1995; Kevan Parekh has been chief financial officer since January 2025; Deirdre O'Brien is a senior vice president and named executive officer; Jennifer Newstead became general counsel on 2026-03-01. The six named executive officers in the 2026 proxy — Cook, Kate Adams, Khan, Luca Maestri, O'Brien and Parekh — include no AI or machine-learning title, so the function's leadership is not disclosed through Section 16 or proxy channels [S54, S52].

The succession is continuity by design, and that is the point to price. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 through the product design team, ran hardware engineering as vice president from 2013 with Macs and iPads in scope, joined the senior executive team in 2021 and added iPhone and AirPods; Art Levinson moved from chair to lead independent director as Cook became executive chair. Apple has done this before: Cook was an operations executive promoted from within in 2011, and the base rate for the company is internal succession, not a strategic reset. Independent reporting on the handover says the same thing from the outside — a well-liked product engineer expected to make "small touches" rather than a disruptive break, and explicitly not the product visionary type, against a record that includes Vision Pro, delayed Siri work and a criticised Liquid Glass redesign. For an investment case resting on the installed base and a 76.3% Services gross margin, continuity protects the cash engine; it supplies no evidence of a new product cycle, so a premium cannot be underwritten on the handover itself [S87, S55].

Capital allocation is where this team earns its premium, and where the contrast with peers is starkest. In nine months of FY2026 Apple returned $73.9bn — $62.1bn of repurchases and $11.8bn of dividends — equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, while spending $6.8bn, or 1.9% of revenue, on capital expenditure; FY2025 was $89.3bn of repurchases plus $15.4bn of dividends under a $100bn authorisation, with the quarterly dividend raised to $0.26 and then $0.27. Microsoft chose the opposite trade in FY2026, funding $139.5bn of investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow and lifting capital spending by $51.4bn for AI capacity. Apple's returns on capital are high because it owns almost no compute; if AI features require owned infrastructure or licensed models, that return structure, not just the margin line, is what changes [S6, S5, S50].

The spending pattern says the company knows it is behind. Research and development went from $29,915m in FY2023 to $31,370m in FY2024 and $34,550m in FY2025, then reached $34,035m in nine months of FY2026 — up 33% year on year, 9.3% of revenue and 10.7% in the June quarter — with management attributing the increase to infrastructure, including artificial intelligence, and headcount. In the same nine months gross intangible assets rose to $38,220m from $24,950m and other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn. Apple is buying capability as well as building it; the filing discloses neither the counterparty nor the exclusivity, and operating margin held at 33.6% only because gross margin rose 2.3 percentage points. A licensing commitment of that size is a permanent transfer of margin to an unnamed party, which is why it belongs in the valuation work as an assumption, not a footnote [S6, S5].

Pay and board composition reinforce the status quo. Cook's 2025 target equity was $50m with 75% performance-based, his base salary has not changed since 2016, his total target compensation sits in the 80th to 90th percentile of the primary peer group by the committee's own statement, and 2021-granted performance RSUs vested at 187% of target on 2024-10-01, or 477,301 shares, on relative total shareholder return measured against the S&P 500; he has already met the age-65, ten-year condition for retirement vesting. After the transition the board has nine directors aged 51 to 77, including Levinson (75, a director since 2000), Ron Sugar (77, since 2010), Andrea Jung (67, since 2008) and Sue Wagner (64, since 2014), with Wanda Austin (2024) the only new independent since 2021. Relative-TSR scorecards pay for beating the index, a target reachable through buybacks and margin management without a new product cycle, and oversight of the AI transition sits with a board whose current members have finance, consumer-brand and aerospace backgrounds rather than AI operating experience [S52, S54].

Insider behaviour gives no support to the price. Over the twelve months to 2026-10-29 there were 46 sale transactions of 687,127 shares for $208.0m, 43 of them under Rule 10b5-1 plans, and no purchases at all; Art Levinson sold $86.7m, Cook $80.4m, O'Brien $23.1m and Ternus $8.5m on 2026-10-02, his first sale as CEO. Scheduled plans mute the information in the sales, so the signal is the absence of a single discretionary purchase between $300 and $345. The counter-case is about product rather than people: independent reporting describes an unresolved AI gap versus OpenAI, a memory shortage squeezing margins and product misfires, while the same filings show 16% revenue growth and 22% iPhone growth, so the team is executing the current cycle well and the next one is unproven. Confidence is high on the record and low on the forward judgement; no education data for any of these executives appears in the SEC filings, and the company leadership pages or university records would settle it. Four checks matter: Ternus's pay package and whether it carries AI or product-cycle metrics, the identity of the executive who owns AI, the counterparty behind the licensing commitments, and whether the board adds an operating AI director [S41, S87].

Item 3. Legal Proceedings
Digital Markets Act Investigations
On March 25, 2024, the Commission announced that it had opened a formal noncompliance investigation against the Company under Article 5(4) of the EU DMA (“Article 5(4) Investigation”). The Article 5(4) Investigation relates to how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users for apps distributed through the App Store, as well as how developers may conclude contracts with those end users. On June 24, 2024, the Commission announced that it had opened an additional formal investigation against the Company regarding whether the Company’s new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA (“Article 6(4) Investigation”). On April 23, 2025, the Commission fined the Company €500 million in the Article 5(4) Investigation and issued a cease and desist order requiring the Company to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. The Company has appealed the Commission’s Article 5(4) decision. Also on April 23, 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) Investigation. If the Commission makes a final determination in the Article 6(4) Investigation that there has been a violation, it can issue a cease and desist order and may impose fines up to 10% of the Company’s annual worldwide net sales. The Commission may also seek to impose additional fines if it deems that the Company has violated a cease and desist order. The Company believes that it complies with the DMA and has continued to make changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission.
Department of Justice Lawsuit
On March 21, 2024, the DOJ and a number of state and district attorneys general filed a civil antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against the Company alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for “performance smartphones” and “smartphones” in violation of U.S. antitrust laws. The DOJ is seeking equitable relief to redress the alleged anticompetitive behavior. In addition, various civil litigation matters have been filed in state and federal courts in the U.S. alleging similar violations of U.S. antitrust laws and seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief. The Company believes it has substantial defenses and intends to vigorously defend itself.
Epic Games
Epic Games, Inc. filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (“California District Court”) against the Company alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California’s unfair competition law based upon the Company’s operation of its App Store. The California District Court found that certain provisions of the Company’s App Review Guidelines violate California’s unfair competition law and issued an injunction (the “2021 Injunction”) enjoining the Company from prohibiting developers from including in their apps buttons, external links, or other calls to action that direct customers to purchasing mechanisms other than the Company’s in-app purchase system. The 2021 Injunction applies to apps on the U.S. storefronts of the iOS and iPadOS App Stores. On January 16, 2024, the Company implemented a plan to comply with the 2021 Injunction and filed a statement of compliance with the California District Court. On September 30, 2024, the Company filed a motion with the California District Court to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction. On April 30, 2025, the California District Court found the Company to be in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined the Company from imposing any commission or any fee on purchases that consumers make outside an app; restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app; or otherwise interfering with a consumer’s choice to proceed in or out of an app. The California District Court also denied the Company’s motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred the Company to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California for a determination whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. The Company will continue to vigorously defend its actions and employees, and has appealed the California District Court’s most recent decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (“Ninth Circuit Court”). Although the Company’s request to stay the decision pending appeal was denied, the Ninth Circuit Court has agreed to consider the Company’s appeal on an expedited basis, with oral arguments heard in October 2025.
Other Legal Proceedings
The Company is subject to other legal proceedings and claims that have not been fully resolved and that have arisen in the ordinary course of business. The Company settled certain matters during the fourth quarter of 2025 that did not individually or in the aggregate have a material impact on the Company’s financial condition or operating results. The outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain. If one or more legal matters were resolved against the Company in a reporting period for amounts above management’s expectations, the Company’s financial condition and operating results for that reporting period could be materially adversely affected.

arguments.markdown:
**Apple wins the value pool and only holds the unit pool, and the competitor that matters most is Samsung.** In the second quarter of 2026 Apple shipped 20.2% of the world's smartphones, up 3.9 percentage points and 14.9% in units in a market that fell 7.4%, while holding 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales in the first half and taking 84% of that tier together with Samsung. In PCs it sits at 9.9% of units against Lenovo's 24.4%, and in wrist-worn devices it is second at 17% behind Huawei's 20.2%; Apple's own annual report concedes "a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables markets". The reading is not that Apple is losing — it gained share in every category where it competes at the top — but that its position is concentrated in one tier, and the rival most able to attack that tier is the one that makes the memory Apple now has to buy. [S79, S77, S90, S88, S5]

iPhone competition is now a contest of supply and balance sheets rather than of features. Samsung grew units 8.1% in a contracting quarter and leads at 22.7%; Xiaomi fell 26.4%, OPPO 17.1% and vivo 19.6% as memory costs consumed more than 65% of the bill of materials at the low end. Apple's counter is scale and early supply commitments, which is why IDC has it on track for a record 22% annual share in 2026. Counterpoint's series has Samsung higher, at 24%, and the market 11% smaller, but both trackers agree on the direction: the premium vendors are separating from the volume vendors. The asymmetry is that Samsung's memory division is on the winning side of the same cost shock that is squeezing Xiaomi and OPPO, so Samsung can fund handset price competition longer than any Android rival — that, not product superiority, is what makes it the most dangerous competitor. [S79, S78]

Inside China the constraint has a name. Huawei leads with 22.6% of a market that fell 4.3% in the second quarter of 2026, growing 19.4%, while Apple rose to 18.1% from 13.9% and grew 24.4%; between them they took share from OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi and Honor, which all fell by 9.5% to 21.7%. Huawei is the only competitor that has beaten Apple at the premium end of a large market at scale, and it does so with a group revenue of CNY880.9 billion, net profit of CNY68 billion and R&D of CNY192.3 billion, 21.8% of revenue, in 2025. Its weakness is geographic: without Google Mobile Services it cannot convert that position outside China, so the threat is a ceiling on Apple's China premium share rather than a global assault. Apple's China revenue grew 30% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 precisely because it did not follow Android vendors into price increases; that advantage disappears when they stop raising prices. [S80, S82, S6]

PCs and wearables show what happens when Apple competes without a premium monopoly. Mac shipments grew about 10% in a quarter when the PC market fell 4.9% to 68.2 million units, yet Apple remains fourth at 9.9% behind Lenovo, HP and Dell, and Mac is 8.1% of FY2025 revenue at $33,708 million. In wrist-worn devices Huawei leads at 20.2%, Apple and Xiaomi are tied at 17%, and Samsung fell 20.7% to 5.8% — a category where cheap Chinese hardware has taken the unit lead and Apple keeps the profit through attach and price. Neither line can move the group: Mac and wearables together were $69.4 billion of FY2025 revenue against iPhone's $209.6 billion, and wearables fell 4% in FY2025. The competition that matters for the watchlist is not here. [S90, S88, S5]

The services franchise faces substitutes and rule-makers at the same time. Google Play is the substitute on Android, Microsoft and Meta compete for the advertising and subscription dollars Apple is growing into, and Apple's own disclosures put the regulatory risk in concrete terms: EU terms restructured in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links from October 2026, US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02 that could bar Google from paying Apple for search distribution, and civil antitrust suits alleging monopolisation in "performance smartphones". The assistant layer has been licensed rather than won: Siri was rebuilt on Google's Gemini models at WWDC in June 2026, reported at about $1 billion a year and disclosed in neither company's latest SEC filing. A 76.3%-gross-margin services stream is the most valuable revenue Apple has, and it is the revenue most exposed to someone else's decisions. [S81, S5, S13, S6]

::: evidence
**Apple's share gains are real but concentrated: it is taking the premium tier of a shrinking market, not building a broader franchise.**

Apple raised unit share by 3.9 points to 20.2% and held 65% of $600-plus premium units in H1 2026, while Samsung grew 8.1% and Xiaomi fell 26.4% under the same memory shock. Huawei leads China at 22.6% and grew 19.4% there. Outside the premium tier Apple's positions are fourth in PCs at 9.9% and second in wrist-worn devices at 17%. [S79, S77, S80, S90, S88]
:::

::: quad

| Weaknesses | 9.9% PC share, second in wrist-worn devices and no volume position below $200; iPhone at 52.6% of trailing-twelve-month revenue concentrates the franchise in one product; the assistant layer is licensed from Google rather than owned; wearables revenue fell 4% in FY2025 | S90, S88, S6, S5 |

| Threats | Samsung converting memory profits into handset price competition; Huawei holding China's premium ceiling; EU fees of 5% and 20% from October 2026 plus US remedies against Google's search payments; memory costs rising until at least 2028; Android flagships differentiating on AI while Siri depends on Gemini | S79, S80, S81, S5, S13 |
:::

The competitive evidence supports a durable franchise without a widening advantage. Apple's share of the premium tier and its installed-base annuity are the strongest positions in consumer hardware, and the memory shock has strengthened both by removing weaker vendors from the low end. But every gain in this record is either cyclical, borrowed from Android vendors' price increases, or dependent on a supply window that closes when memory pricing normalises; the durable advantages are silicon, operating system and the installed base, and none of them is expanding at the rate the FY2026 numbers imply.

Confidence is high on the shares, which come from two independent trackers and filed revenue, and lower on the durability of the premium lead, because the only public evidence on AI capability is press reporting rather than company disclosure. Two questions would settle it: what proportion of iPhone 17 and 18 buyers upgraded earlier than planned because they expected Apple's own price increases, and what does Apple's FY2027 guidance imply for services gross margin once the EU's restructured commissions take effect? A third, for the next review: whether the Gemini arrangement carries a revenue share that would show up in services cost of sales.

The re-rating is not random: revenue growth accelerated to 14.8% in FY2026 from 6.4% in FY2025 on consensus, gross margin rose to 48.6% from 46.9%, and the mix shifted toward Services at $91.7B of the $364.4B nine-month revenue. Funding is entirely internal — no equity has been issued to support this: FY2021-FY2025 buybacks of $438.6B and dividends of $75.0B were paid out of operating cash flow while total debt fell to $84.3B from $124.7B. A higher-quality, faster-growing, self-funding stream deserves a higher multiple than the 24.6x of fiscal 2022; whether it deserves 40.0x is a question only a discount-rate-and-growth model can answer [S5, S6, S7].

Apple publishes no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance — the July 2026 results release contains none — so the consensus is the only forward anchor [S93].

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the acceleration is real and broad. June-quarter revenue rose 16.4% with double-digit growth in iPhone, Mac and Services and in every geographic segment, Greater China rebounded 22.4% to $18.8B, and R&D rose 32.2% to $11.7B — the profile of a company investing into a cycle rather than harvesting one. Against that, the 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds, so underlying margin was 48.1%, and a 50% margin carried into FY2027 overstates gross profit by $10.5B on consensus revenue; peak margin plus peak multiple plus a 4.99% ten-year yield is the combination that hurt Apple in 2022, when the multiple fell from 37.5x to 27.9x in a year while the business did not deteriorate. For a long-only watchlist the implication is a price, not a story: at $348.91 there is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return, the expected return in my scenario set is negative, and the buyback does not defend the price at a 2.7% cash yield. The conditions that would justify adding are concrete — revenue growth of 10% or more in FY2027 with gross margin of 48% or higher excluding tariff refunds, and an entry multiple of 30-34x forward earnings, or $287-$325 on FY2027 EPS of $9.56. Two open questions move the value more than another 5% of price: how much of Services gross profit is the Google default payment, and what buyback authorisation replaced the May 2025 programme [S47, S5, S93].

arguments.markdown:
Apple's capital-allocation record is exceptional and its 2025-2026 product execution is not: the company returned $73.9bn, 63% of operating cash flow, in nine months while growing revenue 16%, but that growth needed a 33% rise in R&D and a $13.3bn build in gross intangibles, and the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed inside twenty months. The bench is deep in operators and thin in outsiders. John Ternus, 50 when appointed, became chief executive and a director on 2026-09-01; Tim Cook, 65, moved to executive chair after fifteen years as CEO and keeps his board seat; Sabih Khan, 58, has been chief operating officer since 2025-07-25 and joined Apple in August 1995; Kevan Parekh has been chief financial officer since January 2025; Deirdre O'Brien is a senior vice president; Jennifer Newstead became general counsel on 2026-03-01. The six named executive officers in the 2026 proxy — Cook, Kate Adams, Khan, Luca Maestri, O'Brien and Parekh — include no AI or machine-learning title, so the function's leadership is not disclosed through Section 16 or proxy channels [S54, S52].

The succession is continuity by design, and that is the point to price. Ternus joined Apple in 2001 through the product design team, ran hardware engineering as vice president from 2013 with Macs and iPads in scope, joined the senior executive team in 2021 and added iPhone and AirPods; Art Levinson moved from chair to lead independent director as Cook became executive chair. Apple has done this before: Cook was an operations executive promoted from within in 2011, and the base rate for the company is internal succession, not a strategic reset. Independent reporting says the same from outside — a well-liked product engineer expected to make "small touches" rather than a disruptive break, and explicitly not the product visionary type, against a record including Vision Pro, delayed Siri work and a criticised Liquid Glass redesign. For a case resting on the installed base and a 76.3% Services gross margin, continuity protects the cash engine; it supplies no evidence of a new product cycle, so a premium cannot be underwritten on the handover itself [S87, S55].

Capital allocation is where this team earns its premium, and the peer contrast is stark. In nine months of FY2026 Apple returned $73.9bn — $62.1bn of repurchases and $11.8bn of dividends — equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, while spending $6.8bn, 1.9% of revenue, on capital expenditure; FY2025 was $89.3bn of repurchases plus $15.4bn of dividends under a $100bn authorisation, with the quarterly dividend raised to $0.26 and then $0.27. Microsoft chose the opposite trade in FY2026, funding $139.5bn of investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow and lifting capital spending by $51.4bn for AI capacity. Apple's returns on capital are high because it owns almost no compute; if AI features require owned infrastructure or licensed models, that return structure, not just the margin line, is what changes [S6, S5, S50].

The spending pattern says the company knows it is behind. Research and development went from $29,915m in FY2023 to $31,370m in FY2024 and $34,550m in FY2025, then reached $34,035m in nine months of FY2026 — up 33% year on year, 9.3% of revenue and 10.7% in the June quarter — management attributing it to AI infrastructure and headcount. In the same nine months gross intangible assets rose to $38,220m from $24,950m and other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn. Apple is buying capability as well as building it; the filing discloses neither the counterparty nor the exclusivity, and operating margin held at 33.6% only because gross margin rose 2.3 percentage points. A licensing commitment of that size is a permanent transfer of margin to an unnamed party, which is why it belongs in the valuation work as an assumption, not a footnote [S6, S5].

Pay and board composition reinforce the status quo. Cook's 2025 target equity was $50m with 75% performance-based, his base salary has not changed since 2016, his total target compensation sits in the 80th to 90th percentile of the primary peer group by the committee's own statement, and 2021-granted performance RSUs vested at 187% of target on 2024-10-01, or 477,301 shares, on relative total shareholder return measured against the S&P 500; he has already met the age-65, ten-year condition for retirement vesting. After the transition the board has nine directors aged 51 to 77, including Levinson (75, since 2000), Sugar (77, since 2010), Jung (67, since 2008) and Wagner (64, since 2014), with Wanda Austin (2024) the only new independent since 2021. Relative-TSR scorecards pay for beating the index, a target reachable through buybacks and margin management without a new product cycle, and oversight of the AI transition sits with a board whose members have finance, consumer-brand and aerospace backgrounds rather than AI operating experience [S52, S54].

Insider behaviour gives no support to the price. Over the twelve months to 2026-10-29 there were 46 sale transactions of 687,127 shares for $208.0m, 43 of them under Rule 10b5-1 plans, and no purchases at all; Art Levinson sold $86.7m, Cook $80.4m, O'Brien $23.1m and Ternus $8.5m on 2026-10-02, his first sale as CEO. Plans mute the sales; the signal is no discretionary purchase between $300 and $345. The counter-case is about product rather than people: independent reporting describes an unresolved AI gap versus OpenAI, a memory shortage squeezing margins and product misfires, while the same filings show 16% revenue growth and 22% iPhone growth, so the team is executing the current cycle well and the next one is unproven. Confidence is high on the record and low on the forward judgement; no education data for these executives appears in the SEC filings, and company leadership pages would settle it. Four checks matter: Ternus's pay metrics, the executive who owns AI, the licensing counterparty, and whether the board adds an operating AI director [S41, S87].
