| Memory suppliers | DRAM and NAND; talks reported with CXMT and YMTC for China sales | 2026-07, reported | Negotiating, unconfirmed by Apple | S113 |
| Indian assembly partners | Final assembly of iPhones for export and domestic sale | Not disclosed | 23% of global output in 2025 | S119 |

### What must be true within twelve months

Four tests decide whether this is a durable annuity or a melting ice cube. First, gross margin must hold near the mid-40s once the 2-point tariff refund washes out of the comparison, while memory costs rise; the December 2026 quarter is the first clean read [S6]. Second, services growth must stay in double digits with advertising and cloud replacing any commission lost to the Epic order and the DMA — a mix the company has not yet had to prove for a full year. Third, the iPhone Duo must sell into its 10 million-unit plan, because a miss would confirm that Apple's premium pricing has reached the limit of what its installed base will pay. Fourth, no adverse final remedy should land in Brussels or at the Ninth Circuit that removes commission revenue retroactively.

Against those tests, the signposts to watch are concrete: the December-quarter gross margin print, the split between advertising and App Store revenue in the FY2026 10-K, any disclosure of the Gemini contract's size in either company's filings, IDC's China share for Q4 2026, and the Commission's Article 6(4) decision. What the record cannot settle is the economics of the AI arrangement — the fee, the term and whether Apple retains query data — and the value of the health and finance adjacencies, neither of which is broken out; Apple discloses no services sub-segment revenue, so the durability of the margin engine has to be inferred from aggregate growth. Confidence in the direction of the strategy is high; confidence in its durability is medium, because the plan is well funded and well executed but its two binding constraints are a regulator and a competitor.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is a defence that is working, but it is a defence. Services at a 75.4% gross margin, a premium multi-launch product cadence and Indian assembly are turning a maturing hardware franchise into a higher-margin, less tariff-exposed annuity — while the two forces that set the ceiling, competition law in Brussels and Washington and the cost of renting intelligence from Google, are outside management's control [S115]. The plan protects cash generation; it does not restore growth.

### Services carry the margin, and the law is repricing them

Services reached $109,158m in FY2025, up 13.5% from $96,169m, at a 75.4% gross margin against 73.9% a year earlier, and grew 14% to $91,728m in the nine months to 2026-06-27 with a 75.6% margin in the June quarter. Because Apple books only its commission on third-party App Store sales, on a net basis, a dollar of services revenue carries 75 cents of gross profit against a consolidated gross margin of 46.9% in FY2025 and 50.1% in Q3 FY2026, so every point of mix shift raises group profitability without a single extra iPhone sold. That engine is now being repriced by courts and regulators rather than by competitors. On 2025-04-30 the California District Court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction and barred it from imposing any commission on purchases made outside an app, referring the matter to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt, with the Ninth Circuit hearing Apple's expedited appeal in October 2025; in Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 and its Article 6(4) investigation into Apple's contract terms remains open, carrying potential fines of up to 10% of worldwide net sales; and the Department of Justice's antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21, seeks equitable relief over the same conduct [S5]. Because Apple has already introduced alternative fee structures and external purchase links in the EU, some revenue migrates rather than vanishing, but the direction is one-way: from commission, which scales with third-party commerce and costs nothing, to advertising, subscriptions and device price, which Apple must earn back every year.

### Manufacturing diversification is real but partial

India assembled 23% of global iPhone output in 2025, up from 14% in 2024, and is projected to reach 28% in 2026, while China's share fell from 83% to 74% [S119, S6]. That is the fastest supply-chain shift in Apple's history and it is being paid for twice: duplicated tooling and lower ramp yields on one side, dependence on Chinese components on the other, since Indian final assembly still imports much of what it screws together. Scale is the offset. Apple secured components for 80 million new-model phones for the second half of 2026 and plans more than 220 million units of production in 2026, which lets it pre-buy memory while Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo cut targets below 100 million units each, and inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m in nine months. Tariff policy remains live: the U.S. Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple has applied for refunds, while Section 301 duties and the Section 232 semiconductor investigation continue.

### China: revenue up, units down, share up

Greater China revenue rose 22% to $18,816m in Q3 FY2026 and 30% to $64,839m in nine months, after falling 4% in FY2025 and 8% in FY2024. The unit picture is different: China's smartphone market fell 15.4% year on year in Q3 2026, Apple's shipments fell 4.3%, its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%, and Huawei grew 17.3% to 21.1% [S5, S122]. Apple is therefore monetising a shrinking market through mix and price rather than winning volume — defensible while the installed base upgrades to Pro and foldable models, fragile if Huawei's domestic supply chain keeps improving or price elasticity bites. The "China share loss" bear case was right about the trend through FY2025 and wrong about 2026 so far.

### Capital allocation is the strategy's quiet centre

Apple spent $6,799m on property, plant and equipment in nine months, 1.9% of revenue, while raising R&D 33% to $34,035m: the AI build is an operating cost, not a capital programme. That leaves cash for shareholders — $10.0bn of accelerated share repurchases entered in May 2026 and a $0.27 quarterly dividend — against $146.5bn of cash and marketable securities and $82.3bn of term debt at 2026-06-27. Net income rose 27% and diluted EPS 29% in the June quarter, so buybacks added 1.6 points of per-share growth [S6, S47]. The risk is not leverage but under-investment: buying capability from Google protects the margin while leaving Apple without owned compute or models, and gross intangibles rising from $24,950m to $38,220m in nine months suggests more value is being purchased than built.

### Resources fit the plan, with one exception

The organisation changed at the top on 2026-09-01, when John Ternus moved from Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering to CEO and Tim Cook became Executive Chair. A hardware engineer running a hardware-led strategy is continuity, and the first launch under him came in on schedule [S54]. The exception is political capital: the decisions that matter most over the next three years — the DMA Article 6(4) remedy, the Ninth Circuit appeal and the DOJ case — are legal negotiations in which a product engineer has less experience than the chair he replaced.

The iPhone Duo must sell into its planned volume, because a miss would confirm that premium pricing has reached the limit of what the installed base will pay. And no adverse final remedy should land in Brussels or at the Ninth Circuit that removes commission revenue retroactively. The signposts are concrete: the December-quarter margin, the advertising-versus-App-Store split in the FY2026 10-K, any disclosed size for the Gemini contract, IDC's China share for Q4 2026 and the Article 6(4) decision.

For a long-only watchlist the conclusion is that Apple's strategy earns ownership of the cash flow rather than payment for growth: the services annuity justifies a premium multiple while growth holds in double digits, the buyback compounds per-share value, and the plan creates no new growth engine before 2028. What the record cannot settle is the economics of the AI arrangement — the fee, the term and whether Apple retains query data — and the value of the health and finance adjacencies, neither of which is broken out; Apple discloses no services sub-segment revenue, so the durability of the margin engine has to be inferred from aggregate growth. Confidence in the direction of the strategy is high and in its durability medium, because the plan is well funded and well executed but its two binding constraints are a regulator and a competitor.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a new A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable wherever Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thinning at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: a narrow lead, defended by integration

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design — not transistor count — is what lets a phone chip deliver desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The measured lead has narrowed to a rounding error at the top: the A19 Pro scored 4,019 on Geekbench 6 single-core against 3,846 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 4.5% gap in Apple versus Qualcomm single-core performance, and the same comparison reportedly favours Qualcomm in multi-threaded and graphics tests [S117]. Apple's answer is to compete on what the benchmark does not measure: an in-house modem, battery life, imaging and a protected hinge.

| R&D expense, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |
| Foldable units planned for 2026 | 10m, from 7-8m | Supply-chain reporting | S113 |

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple frames this as hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it unveiled "all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 in June 2026, shipping it on the iPhone 18 Pro that reached stores on 2026-09-18. R&D rose 33% to fund AI infrastructure and headcount while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, or 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so Apple buys capability as an operating cost instead of building a hyperscale compute base. The strategic cost is that model quality, query data and the pace of improvement now sit with a competitor that also sells phones.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**
The next generation of Apple Foundation Models is built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the ceiling of the assistant is set by a competitor while the differentiation left to Apple is integration, privacy and distribution.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | No assistant | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S116 |
| Cellular modem | In-house | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S116 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Apple is unique among the five in owning the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image, and Qualcomm sells silicon to the rest. Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant.

### Form factors: the stagnation critique is out of date

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Suppliers were told to prepare 10 million foldables for 2026, up from 7-8 million, inside at least five new iPhone models spread across the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027 [S113, S121]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units, the Duo changes the price ladder and the narrative rather than the revenue base. The patent record shows the mechanics were engineered before launch: the granted patent US 12,164,344 covers a multi-link hinge with interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch, and US2025/0120026 adds a folding expandable display.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | 2023 (app. US2023/0049811) | Date not disclosed | Granted | iPhone Duo hinge mechanics | S121 |
| US2025/0120026A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | 2025 | — | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |
| Not disclosed | Aggregate portfolio | Global | — | — | "Pursuing thousands of applications" | No patent count given | S5 |

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared its Hypertension Notification Feature on 2025-09-11, its Sleep Apnea Notification Feature on 2024-09-13, granted the Hearing Aid Feature a De Novo on 2024-09-12, and cleared a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, which raises the wearable's value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration: Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 4% in FY2025 to $35,686m and grew 6% in Q3 FY2026 to $7,883m.

| Vision Pro | Shipping | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | None disclosed | S5 |

### What would break the story

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability. The Q3 FY2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM; inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m [S6]. Strip out 2 percentage points of tariff refund and the 50.1% gross margin is nearer 48%, so the technology premium is being defended by price increases while memory costs rise. The unverifiable pieces matter too: no Vision Pro units, no product-level margins, no patent counts, and one benchmark cannot show whether the A20 Pro sustains performance under thermal load.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power management designed as one product | 3-4 years | S116 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | All-time-high active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Foundry, custom components | 7 | Single-source parts; scale secures leading capacity | 2-3 years | S5 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team with Apple's published patents could match the hinge and the foldable within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and the regulatory record, medium on durability, because memory costs are eating into the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the A20 Pro's process node, the Gemini fee and term, and iPhone Duo sell-through.

Text:

Apple's ESG exposure is not a carbon or governance problem but a platform-regulation problem: enforcement in five jurisdictions is aimed at the 75.4%-gross-margin Services pool, which in FY2025 produced $109.2bn of sales and $82.3bn of gross profit — 26.2% of net sales but 42.2% of total gross profit — while the fines to date (€500m in the EU, €150m in France, $15.5m in Korea) are 0.1% of $416.2bn of net sales and the remedies can permanently lower the highest-margin revenue Apple has. [S5, S134, S137, S136]

### The EU has established the principle; the size is still open

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering obligation and ordered the restrictions removed within 60 days; the separate Article 6(4) investigation into Apple's contractual terms, opened 2024-06-24, remains unresolved, with a statutory ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales — $41.6bn on FY2025 sales. The fine is a rounding error, but the principle is durable: the General Court rejected Apple's challenge to its DMA gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08, narrowing its appeal route. The cash question is not the fine but the effective commission Apple can charge on EU link-outs and alternative distribution after the cease-and-desist. [S6, S134, S135]

### The US is the largest and slowest remedy risk

The DOJ and 15 states plus the District of Columbia sued Apple for monopolization on 2024-03-21 in New Jersey, seeking equitable relief rather than damages; the motion to dismiss failed, and by July 2026 the parties were in early settlement talks, with fact discovery scheduled to late May 2027 and no trial date. The faster US case is Epic v. Apple: the district court found contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred fees on out-of-app purchases, the Ninth Circuit on 2025-12-11 preserved parity requirements but allowed some link-out commission, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari on the contempt standard on 2026-06-30. Separately, the Google search remedies entered in December 2025 threaten the distribution payments that flow through Services; Apple does not disclose their size, so that exposure cannot be quantified from filings. [S6, S62, S138]

### Enforcement is fragmenting; privacy is now an antitrust issue

The UK CMA designated Apple with strategic market status on 2025-10-22 and by 2026-10-20 was consulting on steering and NFC access conduct requirements. Korea's communications regulator fined Apple KRW 20.81bn ($15.5m) on 2026-10-28 and ordered external payment links and revised commissions within three months, ruling that a 26% fee on third-party billing evaded the 30% norm. Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act took effect on 2025-12-18, with Apple designated in March 2025, and 48 Chinese developers complained to SAMR on 2026-06-23. In France, the competition authority fined Apple €150m on 2025-03-31 over how it implemented App Tracking Transparency, treating a privacy feature as an abuse of dominance. The pattern is not one catastrophic penalty but convergence of the global take rate toward the mid-teens, with compliance built once and exported. [S132, S136, S140, S139, S141, S137]

### Environmental and labour risks are real but not cash-flow drivers

Apple's 2025 emissions were more than 60% below 2015 and flat versus 2024, against a 2030 target of a 75% cut before carbon removals balance the remainder; the residual gap sits in supplier energy and product use, and the volume and cost of removals are not disclosed, so the carbon-neutral claim is only partially verified. On labour, manufacturing remains concentrated in China, India and Vietnam, and the 10-K flags supplier industrial-accident risk; India's PLI has shifted capacity — cumulative iPhone exports passed $50bn by December 2025 and reached ₹2 lakh crore in FY2026, the scheme's final year — but that is subsidy-supported diversification, not proof of a structural cost advantage. Neither issue carries a plausible fine large enough to move a $133.1bn operating-income base. [S144, S145, S146, S143, S5]

### Governance is clean where it is measurable

Apple has one share class, an independent chair in Art Levinson and eight directors; the 2026 proxy discloses no material related-party transactions beyond a former operating chief's family member earning above $120,000, and Tim Cook's 2025 target pay was $59m with 92% support on the 2025 say-on-pay vote. The live governance issues are succession (Cook is 65) and political exposure: shareholders rejected a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal on 2026-02-24, which signals that China is now a governance theme as well as a revenue exposure. There is no dual-class control discount to apply, and the SEC record shows no disclosure-quality problem. [S52, S100]

### Policy is two different risks: sunk tax and reversible trade

The policy matrix below separates them. The State Aid case is finished cash — the ECJ confirmed the Commission's 2016 decision on 2024-09-10 and the bill has been paid — so it is a precedent risk rather than an open liability. Tariffs are the opposite: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple is claiming refunds, the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs affecting Apple's products on 2026-01-14, but Section 301 actions remain live. Trade policy should be priced as gross-margin volatility around a hardware business, not as a permanent impairment.

### What the investor should price

Separate the fine from the remedy. Fines to date are immaterial against one year of net sales, and even a maximum DMA fine would be a one-year charge, not a solvency event. The durable exposure is the commission pool: the sensitivity table shows the operating-income effect of a 5-20% cut in Services gross profit. That is the number to underwrite, and it argues for a haircut to Services earnings, not for avoiding the stock. My confidence is medium because Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or take rates, and the DOJ and EU timetables have slipped repeatedly.

### Diligence questions

Five questions would change the assessment: what share of Services revenue and gross profit is App Store commission revenue by region; what effective commission Apple now collects on US and EU link-outs; whether the Commission's Article 6(4) decision imposes periodic penalties or structural separation; the annual value of Google search-distribution payments and what remedy would remove them; and the contracted volume and cost of carbon removals behind Apple 2030. The first two sit in court and company records outside the public filing set, and a data request for the PACER exhibits has been filed. If App Store commission revenue is below a tenth of Services gross profit, regulation is a sentiment issue; if it is a quarter or more, it is an earnings issue.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's ESG exposure is not a carbon or governance problem but a platform-regulation problem: enforcement in five jurisdictions targets the 75.4%-gross-margin Services pool — $109.2bn of FY2025 sales and $82.3bn of gross profit, 42.2% of total gross profit — while fines to date (€500m EU, €150m France, $15.5m Korea) are 0.1% of $416.2bn of net sales and the remedies can permanently lower the highest-margin revenue Apple has. [S5, S134, S137, S136]

### The EU has established the principle; the size is still open

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering obligation and ordered the restrictions removed within 60 days; a separate Article 6(4) investigation into its developer contract terms, opened 2024-06-24, remains unresolved with a statutory ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales ($41.6bn). The fine is a rounding error, but the principle is durable: the General Court rejected Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08. The cash question is the effective commission Apple can charge on EU link-outs and alternative distribution. [S6, S134, S135]

### The US is the largest and slowest remedy risk

The DOJ and 15 states plus DC sued Apple for monopolization on 2024-03-21 in New Jersey seeking equitable relief; the motion to dismiss failed and by July 2026 the parties were in early settlement talks, with discovery running to late May 2027 and no trial date. In Epic v. Apple the district court found contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred fees on out-of-app purchases; the Ninth Circuit on 2025-12-11 allowed some link-out commission, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari on the contempt standard on 2026-06-30. The Google search remedies ordered in September 2025 and finalised in December 2025 also threaten distribution payments that flow through Services, but Apple does not disclose their size. [S6, S62, S138]

### Enforcement is fragmenting; privacy is now an antitrust issue

The UK CMA designated Apple with strategic market status on 2025-10-22 and by 2026-10-20 was consulting on steering and NFC access conduct requirements. Korea's communications regulator fined Apple KRW 20.81bn ($15.5m) on 2026-10-28 and ordered external payment links and revised commissions within three months, ruling that a 26% fee on third-party billing evaded the 30% norm. Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act took effect on 2025-12-18, and 48 Chinese developers complained to SAMR on 2026-06-23. France's competition authority fined Apple €150m on 2025-03-31 over its App Tracking Transparency implementation, treating a privacy feature as an abuse of dominance. The pattern is convergence of the global take rate toward the mid-teens, not one catastrophic penalty. [S132, S136, S140, S139, S141, S137]

### Environmental and labour risks are real but not cash-flow drivers

Apple's 2025 emissions were more than 60% below 2015 and flat versus 2024, against a 2030 target of a 75% cut before carbon removals balance the remainder; the volume and cost of removals are not disclosed, so the carbon-neutral claim is only partially verified. Manufacturing remains concentrated in China, India and Vietnam, and the 10-K flags supplier industrial-accident risk; India's production-linked incentive has shifted capacity — cumulative iPhone exports passed $50bn by December 2025 and reached ₹2 lakh crore in FY2026, the scheme's final year — but this is subsidy-supported diversification, not a structural cost advantage. Neither issue can plausibly move a $133.1bn operating-income base. [S144, S145, S146, S143, S5]

### Governance is clean where it is measurable

Apple has one share class, an independent chair in Art Levinson and eight directors; the 2026 proxy discloses no material related-party transactions beyond a former operating chief's family member earning above $120,000, and Tim Cook's 2025 target pay was $59m with 92% support on the 2025 say-on-pay vote. The live issues are succession (Cook is 65) and political exposure: shareholders rejected a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal on 2026-02-24. There is no dual-class discount to apply and no disclosure-quality problem in the SEC record. [S52, S100]

### Policy is two different risks: sunk tax and reversible trade

The policy matrix below separates them. The State Aid case is finished cash — the ECJ confirmed the Commission's 2016 decision on 2024-09-10 and the bill has been paid — so it is a precedent risk, not an open liability. Tariffs are the opposite: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple is claiming refunds, the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs affecting Apple's products on 2026-01-14, but Section 301 actions remain live. Price trade policy as gross-margin volatility, not permanent impairment.

### What the investor should price

Separate the fine from the remedy. Fines to date are immaterial against one year of net sales, and even a maximum DMA fine would be a one-year charge, not a solvency event. The durable exposure is the commission pool: the sensitivity table shows the operating-income effect of a 5-20% cut in Services gross profit. That argues for a haircut to Services earnings, not for avoiding the stock. Confidence is medium because Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or take rates, and the DOJ and EU timetables have slipped repeatedly.

### Diligence questions

Five questions would change the assessment: what share of Services revenue and gross profit is App Store commission revenue by region; what effective commission Apple now collects on US and EU link-outs; whether Article 6(4) brings periodic penalties or structural separation; the annual value of Google search-distribution payments and what remedy would remove them; and the contracted volume and cost of carbon removals behind Apple 2030. The first two sit outside the public filing set, and a data request for the PACER exhibits has been filed. If App Store commission revenue is below a tenth of Services gross profit, regulation is a sentiment issue; if it is a quarter or more, it is an earnings issue.

Apple's ESG exposure is a platform-regulation problem, not a carbon or governance one: enforcement in five jurisdictions targets the 75.4%-gross-margin Services pool — $109.2bn of FY2025 sales and $82.3bn of gross profit, 42.2% of the total — while fines to date (€500m EU, €150m France, $15.5m Korea) are 0.1% of $416.2bn of net sales and the remedies can permanently lower the highest-margin revenue Apple has. [S5, S134, S137, S136]

### The EU has established the principle; the size is still open

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering obligation and ordered the restrictions removed within 60 days; a separate Article 6(4) case on developer contract terms, opened 2024-06-24, remains unresolved with a statutory ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales ($41.6bn). The fine is a rounding error, but the principle is durable: the General Court rejected Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08. The cash question is the commission Apple can charge on EU link-outs and alternative distribution. [S6, S134, S135]

### The US is the largest and slowest remedy risk

The DOJ and 15 states plus DC sued Apple for monopolization on 2024-03-21 in New Jersey seeking equitable relief; the motion to dismiss failed and by July 2026 the parties were in early settlement talks, with discovery to late May 2027 and no trial date. In Epic v. Apple the district court found contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred fees on out-of-app purchases; the Ninth Circuit on 2025-12-11 allowed some link-out commission and the Supreme Court granted certiorari on the contempt standard on 2026-06-30. The Google search remedies finalised in December 2025 also threaten distribution payments inside Services, but Apple does not disclose their size. [S6, S62, S138]

### Enforcement is fragmenting; privacy is now an antitrust issue

The UK CMA designated Apple with strategic market status on 2025-10-22 and by 2026-10-20 was consulting on steering and NFC access conduct requirements. Korea's communications regulator fined Apple KRW 20.81bn ($15.5m) on 2026-10-28 and ordered external payment links and revised commissions within three months, ruling that a 26% fee on third-party billing evaded the 30% norm. Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act took effect on 2025-12-18, and 48 Chinese developers complained to SAMR on 2026-06-23. France's competition authority fined Apple €150m on 2025-03-31 over its App Tracking Transparency implementation, treating a privacy feature as abuse of dominance. The pattern is convergence of the global take rate toward the mid-teens, not one catastrophic penalty. [S132, S136, S140, S139, S141, S137]

### Environmental and labour risks are real but not cash-flow drivers

Apple's 2025 emissions were more than 60% below 2015 and flat versus 2024, against a 2030 target of a 75% cut before carbon removals balance the remainder; removal volumes and costs are not disclosed, so the carbon-neutral claim is only partially verified. Manufacturing remains concentrated in China, India and Vietnam, and the 10-K flags supplier industrial-accident risk; India's production-linked incentive has shifted capacity — cumulative iPhone exports passed $50bn by December 2025 and reached ₹2 lakh crore in FY2026, the scheme's final year — but this is subsidy-supported diversification, not a structural cost advantage. Neither issue can move a $133.1bn operating-income base. [S144, S145, S146, S143, S5]

### Governance is clean where it is measurable

Apple has one share class, an independent chair in Art Levinson and eight directors; the 2026 proxy discloses no material related-party transactions beyond a former operating chief's family member earning above $120,000, and Tim Cook's 2025 target pay was $59m with 92% support on the 2025 say-on-pay vote. The live issues are succession (Cook is 65) and political exposure: shareholders rejected a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal on 2026-02-24. There is no dual-class discount and no disclosure-quality problem in the SEC record. [S52, S100]

### Policy is two different risks: sunk tax and reversible trade

The policy matrix separates sunk tax from reversible trade. State Aid is finished cash — the ECJ confirmed the Commission's 2016 decision on 2024-09-10 and the bill has been paid — so it is a precedent risk, not an open liability. Tariffs are the opposite: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple is claiming refunds, the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs affecting Apple's products on 2026-01-14, but Section 301 actions remain live. Price trade policy as gross-margin volatility, not permanent impairment.

### What the investor should price

Separate the fine from the remedy. Fines to date are immaterial against one year of net sales, and even a maximum DMA fine would be a one-year charge. The durable exposure is the commission pool: the sensitivity table below converts a 5-20% cut in Services gross profit into operating-income terms. That argues for a haircut to Services earnings, not for avoiding the stock. Confidence is medium because Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or take rates, and the DOJ and EU timetables have slipped repeatedly.

### Diligence questions

Five questions would change the assessment: what share of Services revenue and gross profit is App Store commission revenue by region; what commission Apple now collects on US and EU link-outs; whether Article 6(4) brings periodic penalties or structural separation; the annual value of Google search-distribution payments and what would remove them; and the contracted volume and cost of carbon removals behind Apple 2030. arguments.markdown:
Apple's ESG exposure is a platform-regulation problem, not a carbon or governance one: five jurisdictions target the 75.4%-gross-margin Services pool — $109.2bn of FY2025 sales and $82.3bn of gross profit, 42.2% of the total — while fines to date (€500m EU, €150m France, $15.5m Korea) are 0.1% of $416.2bn of net sales and the remedies can permanently lower the highest-margin revenue Apple has. [S5, S134, S137, S136]

### The EU has established the principle; the size is still open

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering obligation and ordered the restrictions removed within 60 days; a separate Article 6(4) case on developer contract terms, opened 2024-06-24, remains unresolved with a statutory ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales ($41.6bn). The fine is a rounding error, but the principle is durable: the General Court rejected Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08. The cash question is the commission on EU link-outs. [S6, S134, S135]

### The US is the largest and slowest remedy risk

The DOJ and 15 states plus DC sued Apple for monopolization on 2024-03-21 in New Jersey seeking equitable relief; the motion to dismiss failed and by July 2026 the parties were in early settlement talks, with discovery to late May 2027 and no trial date. In Epic v. Apple the district court found contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred fees on out-of-app purchases; the Ninth Circuit on 2025-12-11 allowed some link-out commission and the Supreme Court took the contempt standard on 2026-06-30. Google search remedies finalised in December 2025 also threaten distribution payments inside Services, of undisclosed size. [S6, S62, S138]

### Enforcement is fragmenting; privacy is now an antitrust issue

The UK CMA designated Apple with strategic market status on 2025-10-22 and by 2026-10-20 was consulting on steering and NFC conduct requirements. Korea's communications regulator fined Apple KRW 20.81bn ($15.5m) on 2026-10-28 and ordered payment links and revised commissions, ruling a 26% fee on third-party billing evaded the 30% norm. Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act took effect on 2025-12-18, and 48 Chinese developers complained to SAMR on 2026-06-23. France's competition authority fined Apple €150m on 2025-03-31 over App Tracking Transparency, treating a privacy feature as abuse of dominance. The pattern is convergence of the global take rate toward the mid-teens, not one catastrophic penalty. [S132, S136, S140, S139, S141, S137]

### Environmental and labour risks are real but not cash-flow drivers

Apple's 2025 emissions were more than 60% below 2015 and flat versus 2024, against a 2030 target of a 75% cut before carbon removals balance the remainder; removal volumes and costs are undisclosed, so the claim is only partially verified. Manufacturing remains concentrated in China, India and Vietnam, and the 10-K flags supplier industrial-accident risk; India's production-linked incentive has shifted capacity — cumulative iPhone exports passed $50bn by December 2025 and reached ₹2 lakh crore in FY2026 — but this is subsidy-supported diversification, not a structural cost advantage. Neither issue can move a $133.1bn operating-income base. [S144, S145, S146, S143, S5]

### Governance is clean where it is measurable

Apple has one share class, an independent chair in Art Levinson and eight directors; the 2026 proxy discloses no material related-party transactions beyond a former operating chief's family member earning above $120,000, and Tim Cook's 2025 target pay was $59m with 92% support on the 2025 say-on-pay vote. The live issues are succession (Cook is 65) and political exposure: shareholders rejected a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal on 2026-02-24. There is no dual-class discount or disclosure-quality problem. [S52, S100]

### Policy is two different risks: sunk tax and reversible trade

The policy matrix separates sunk tax from reversible trade. State Aid is finished cash — the ECJ confirmed the Commission's 2016 decision on 2024-09-10 — a precedent risk, not an open liability. Tariffs are the opposite: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple is claiming refunds, the Section 232 semiconductor review imposed no tariffs on Apple's products on 2026-01-14, but Section 301 actions remain live. Price trade policy as gross-margin volatility, not permanent impairment.

### What the investor should price

Separate the fine from the remedy. Fines to date are immaterial, and even a maximum DMA fine would be a one-year charge. The durable exposure is the commission pool: the policy matrix shows what a 10% cut in Services gross profit would do to operating income. That argues for a haircut to Services earnings, not for avoiding the stock. Confidence is medium because Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or take rates, and the DOJ and EU timetables have slipped repeatedly.

### Diligence questions

Five questions would change the assessment: what share of Services revenue and gross profit is App Store commission revenue by region; what commission Apple collects on US and EU link-outs; whether Article 6(4) brings periodic penalties or structural separation; the annual value of Google search-distribution payments; and the contracted volume and cost of carbon removals behind Apple 2030. The first two sit outside the public filing set; a data request for PACER exhibits has been filed. If App Store commission revenue is below a tenth of Services gross profit, regulation is a sentiment issue; if a quarter or more, an earnings issue.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,814 characters)
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for its life at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the growth came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth. The investor implication is that earnings durability has to be underwritten as a hardware cycle with a services annuity attached, not the other way round [S5, S6].

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Europe 16.1% and the Americas 11.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle with Pro-model mix plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, or 6.4%, against 16.1% revenue growth. iPhone concentration also rose to 53.9% of sales from 50.4%, which is the number to watch if the upgrade cycle rolls over.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is $48.9 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case from 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect lands on the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |

| App Store, US, In-App Purchase | % of developer transaction | 15-30% by developer size and category | current | S65 |
| App Store, US, external-link purchases | % (proposed, needs court approval) | 5-15% tiers; 0% was ordered in April 2025 | 2026-08-14 | S64 |
| iPhone | $ of revenue per unit | not disclosed; the 10-K reports iPhone net sales with no unit count | n/a | S5 |

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

The table below is the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow: an estimate in its construction, disclosed in its dollars.

| Revenue | $166 | $194 | S5, S6, S58 |
| — Products / Services | $123 / $44 | $145 / $49 | S5, S6 |
| Gross profit (margin) | $78 (46.9%) | $95 (49.1%) | S5, S6 |
| R&D | $13.8 | $18.2 | S5, S6 |
| SG&A, the acquisition-cost proxy | $11.0 | $11.9 | S5, S6 |
| Operating profit (margin) | $53 (32.0%) | $65 (33.6%) | S5, S6 |
| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |

Beyond the waterfall, two numbers set the risk envelope, both computed on the disclosed 2.5-billion-device base with nine months annualised at four-thirds. The operating structure breaks even at an estimated $153bn of annual revenue, 31.5% of the current run-rate, because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6.4% a year, so a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable; and the 32:1 lifetime-to-acquisition ratio is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates more services revenue than an iPad or Mac buyer, Apple does not disclose the split, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin (Source: S6).
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA (Source: S56, S65).
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify (Source: S59).
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months (Source: S11, S13).
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow, but partly diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years — $4.4bn a year of extra expense — or over ten."}],"isError":false}

Apple's statements show a business that converts almost all of its profit into cash on capex that is trivial for a company of its size, but the fiscal 2026 margin rests on a tariff refund the company itself calls one-off and on an intangible build the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise.

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, the company's own approximation, and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at 1.71 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin. The diligence question that follows: what are those intangibles, over what life are they amortised, and does the expense arrive in FY2027 [S6, S5]?

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On $100.4bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is 128%, and on total assets 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns $128.1bn of after-tax operating profit on $100.4bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity. The capital-allocation version of the same point: trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow and retired 1.6% of diluted shares, lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth; but at $348.91 on 2026-10-29, or 40.0 times trailing EPS, each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%, so it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, covered 1.4 times by free cash flow and already slowing — $62,094M in nine months against $70,579M [S7, S10, S11, S13, S47].

Half of Apple's 134% five-year price gain came from its multiple rising from 26.6x to 40.0x, and with the consensus target already 4.7% below the $348.91 close the next five years can be earned only from earnings and dividends — 8.4% a year if the multiple holds, and a negative return if it reverts to 34x — so the discipline for a long-only holder is a trim rule tied to the multiple, not an exit on news. The decomposition is exact and closes: from the $148.96 close on 2021-11-01 to $348.91 on 2026-10-29 the shares returned 134.2%, while diluted EPS moved from $5.61 to $8.72 (+55.4%, 9.2% a year) and the P/E paid for those earnings moved from 26.6x to 40.0x (+50.7%); dividends added 3.3% cumulatively, and multiple expansion accounts for 48% of the logarithmic return [S5, S6, S7].

That history is the base rate a buyer is fighting. Apple's own filing puts the five years to September 2025 at $234 on a $100 invested in September 2020, against $217 for the S&P 500 and $287 for the Dow Jones U.S. Technology index — 18.5% a year against 16.8% for the market and 23.5% for the technology sector, so the quality compounder delivered only 8% cumulative outperformance against the index and lagged its own sector by 24%. The mechanism behind the next five years is different from the last five: with the multiple at a five-year high, re-rating can no longer carry half the return, and Apple's remaining levers are 8.1% consensus EPS growth for FY2027, a 0.31% dividend and a buyback worth 1.6% of shares a year. At a held 40x with 8.1% EPS growth the arithmetic gives 8.4% a year before any multiple change — below the 9.5% required return the valuation section uses, and dependent on the buyback continuing [S5, S93].

The exit routes are short because the company is too large to be bought. Every incremental dollar of return has to come from the market, and the market will pay whatever multiple prevails when the holder sells; there is no bid to negotiate, no premium to extract and no lock-up to wait out. Liquidity is not the constraint — 38.67M shares and $13.22B change hands daily, so exit cost is a rounding error — but index concentration cuts the other way: three stocks at 21% of the S&P 500 means passive flows amplify both directions, and the stock's own 52-week range of $243.42 to $351.73 is a 44.5% spread in a year in which the business did nothing but improve [S7, S97].

What the precedents do establish is the ceiling — an acquirer large enough to write a $5T cheque would face antitrust review in every major jurisdiction before it faced financing, and the DOJ's own monopolisation case against Apple, filed on 2024-03-21, shows how the company's scale is treated by regulators [S91, S98, S5].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 技术与产品 Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,947 characters)
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a new A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable wherever Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thinning at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: a narrow lead, defended by integration

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design — not transistor count — is what lets a phone chip deliver desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The measured lead has narrowed to a rounding error at the top: the A19 Pro scored 4,019 on Geekbench 6 single-core against 3,846 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 4.5% gap in Apple versus Qualcomm single-core performance, and the same comparison reportedly favours Qualcomm in multi-threaded and graphics tests [S117]. Apple's answer is to compete on what the benchmark does not measure: an in-house modem, battery life, imaging and a protected hinge.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship SoC, iPhone 18 Pro | A20 Pro | Announced 2026-09-09 | S116 |
| A19 Pro, Geekbench 6 single-core | 4,019 | Published benchmark run | S117 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same test | 3,846 | Published benchmark run | S117 |
| Apple's single-core lead | 4.5% | Computed from the two scores | S117 |
| iPhone revenue, Q3 FY2026 | $54,252m, +22% YoY | Reported, quarter ended 2026-06-27 | S47 |
| R&D expense, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |
| Foldable units planned for 2026 | 10m, from 7-8m | Supply-chain reporting | S113 |

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple frames this as hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it unveiled "all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 in June 2026, shipping it on the iPhone 18 Pro that reached stores on 2026-09-18. R&D rose 33% to fund AI infrastructure and headcount while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, or 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so Apple buys capability as an operating cost instead of building a hyperscale compute base. The strategic cost is that model quality, query data and the pace of improvement now sit with a competitor that also sells phones.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**
The next generation of Apple Foundation Models is built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the ceiling of the assistant is set by a competitor while the differentiation left to Apple is integration, privacy and distribution.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | No assistant | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S116 |
| Cellular modem | In-house | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S116 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Apple is unique among the five in owning the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image, and Qualcomm sells silicon to the rest. Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant.

### Form factors: the stagnation critique is out of date

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Suppliers were told to prepare 10 million foldables for 2026, up from 7-8 million, inside at least five new iPhone models spread across the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027 [S113, S121]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units, the Duo changes the price ladder and the narrative rather than the revenue base. The patent record shows the mechanics were engineered before launch: the granted patent US 12,164,344 covers a multi-link hinge with interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch, and US2025/0120026 adds a folding expandable display.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Published | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | 2023 (app. US2023/0049811) | Date not disclosed | Granted | iPhone Duo hinge mechanics | S121 |
| US2025/0120026A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | 2025 | — | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |
| Not disclosed | Aggregate portfolio | Global | — | — | "Pursuing thousands of applications" | No patent count given | S5 |

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared its Hypertension Notification Feature on 2025-09-11, its Sleep Apnea Notification Feature on 2024-09-13, granted the Hearing Aid Feature a De Novo on 2024-09-12, and cleared a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, which raises the wearable's value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration: Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 4% in FY2025 to $35,686m and grew 6% in Q3 FY2026 to $7,883m.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,906 characters)
**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth $134.9 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter. Trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million implies a 12.3% CAGR from $85,200 million in FY2023 and divides into $48.19 per active device a year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12.3% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 7.0% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 30% in Greater China to $64,839 million, 16% in Europe, 11% in the Americas, 10% in Japan and 19% in the rest of Asia-Pacific, lifting Greater China from 15.5% of FY2025 revenue to 17.8%. China's own market fell 4.2% in the first half of 2026, so Apple's gain was share rather than tide: its unit share rose to 18.1% from 13.9% because it held prices while Android rivals raised theirs, and IDC expects the second-half decline in China to widen to 20% year on year. India repeats the pattern at a different scale — 33.2 million units in the second quarter of 2026, down 11.1%, average prices up 14.4% and Apple leading by value — while in the United States, where iOS carries 58.35% of mobile web traffic, growth runs through carrier trade-in programmes rather than new users. [S6, S80, S96, S89]

Policy both creates and caps this demand, and the dates are live. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation published initial results on 2026-01-14 without imposing tariffs on Apple's products, and the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, for which Apple has claimed refunds; Section 301 duties and further sector measures remain open. In Europe, Apple restructured its App Store terms in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, effective October 2026. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. Demand that was subsidy-created is now subsidy-dependent; demand that is trade-in-driven has held. [S6, S81, S80]

India) | India 33.2 million units in Q2 2026, -11.1% | $33,696m in FY2025; +19% in 9M FY2026; 8.3% of nine-month revenue | Entered; Apple led India by value in Q2 2026 | Indian import duties and local-manufacturing rules | Xiaomi, vivo, Samsung, OPPO, Transsion | S5, S6, S96 |

::: evidence
**Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on just over 1 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40.0% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at $48.19 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]
:::

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism rather than a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist through the forecast horizon. What is not durable is the current growth rate: the Greater China acceleration rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its own unit forecast within a single quarter, and the trackers disagree materially on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much iPhone strength was pulled forward? Second, does China hold its current unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to the EU's restructured commissions and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,937 characters)
**Apple wins the value pool and only holds the unit pool, and the competitor that matters most is Samsung.** In Q2 2026 Apple's global smartphone market share rose 3.9 points to 20.2% and its units 14.9% in a market that fell 7.4%, while it held 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales in the first half and took 84% of that tier together with Samsung. In PCs it is fourth at 9.9% and in wrist-worn devices second at 17%; Apple's annual report concedes "a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables markets". It is not losing, but the position is concentrated in one tier whose most dangerous attacker makes the memory Apple must buy. [S79, S77, S90, S88, S5]

iPhone competition is now a contest of supply and balance sheets rather than features. Samsung grew units 8.1% and leads at 22.7%; Xiaomi fell 26.4%, OPPO 17.1% and vivo 19.6% as memory costs exceeded 65% of the bill of materials at the low end. Apple's counter is scale and early supply commitments, and IDC has it on track for a record 22% annual share in 2026. Counterpoint has Samsung at 24% and the market 11% smaller; both agree on direction. The asymmetry is that Samsung's memory division sits on the winning side of the same cost shock squeezing Xiaomi and OPPO, so Samsung can fund handset price competition longer than any Android rival — that, not product superiority, makes it the most dangerous competitor. [S79, S78]

Inside China the constraint has a name. Huawei leads with 22.6% of a market that fell 4.3% in the second quarter of 2026, growing 19.4%, while Apple rose to 18.1% from 13.9% and grew 24.4%, taking share from OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi and Honor, which fell 9.5% to 21.7%. Huawei is the only rival that has beaten Apple in a large premium market, on 2025 revenue of CNY880.9 billion, net profit of CNY68 billion and R&D of CNY192.3 billion (21.8% of revenue). Its weakness is geographic: without Google Mobile Services it cannot convert that position outside China, so the threat is a ceiling on Apple's China premium share rather than a global assault. Apple's China revenue grew 30% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 because it did not follow Android vendors into price increases; that advantage ends when they stop raising prices. [S80, S82, S6]

PCs and wearables show what happens without a premium monopoly. Mac shipments grew about 10% in a quarter when the PC market fell 4.9% to 68.2 million units, yet Apple is fourth at 9.9% behind Lenovo, HP and Dell, with Mac at 8.1% of FY2025 revenue ($33,708 million). In wrist-worn devices Huawei leads at 20.2%, Apple and Xiaomi are tied at 17%, and Samsung fell 20.7% to 5.8%: cheap Chinese hardware has taken the unit lead while Apple keeps the profit through attach and price. Neither line moves the group: Mac and wearables were $69.4 billion of FY2025 revenue against iPhone's $209.6 billion. [S90, S88, S5]

Services faces substitutes and rule-makers at once. Google Play substitutes on Android, Microsoft and Meta compete for advertising and subscription dollars, and Apple's disclosures are concrete: EU terms restructured in August 2026 to a 5% commission outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links from October 2026, US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02 that could bar Google from paying Apple for search distribution, and civil suits alleging monopolisation in "performance smartphones". The assistant layer was licensed rather than won: Siri was rebuilt on Google's Gemini models at WWDC in June 2026, reported at about $1 billion a year and undisclosed in either company's latest SEC filing. The 76.3%-gross-margin services stream is Apple's most valuable revenue and its most exposed. [S81, S5, S13, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 2 by Product Analyst, 8,679 characters)
Apple's strategy is a defence that is working, but it is a defence. Services at a 75.4% gross margin, a premium multi-launch product cadence and Indian assembly are turning a maturing hardware franchise into a higher-margin, less tariff-exposed annuity — while the two forces that set the ceiling, competition law in Brussels and Washington and the cost of renting intelligence from Google, are outside management's control [S115]. The plan protects cash generation; it does not restore growth.

### Services carry the margin, and the law is repricing them

Services reached $109,158m in FY2025, up 13.5% from $96,169m, at a 75.4% gross margin against 73.9% a year earlier, and grew 14% to $91,728m in the nine months to 2026-06-27 with a 75.6% margin in the June quarter. Because Apple books only its commission on third-party App Store sales, on a net basis, a dollar of services revenue carries 75 cents of gross profit against a consolidated gross margin of 46.9% in FY2025 and 50.1% in Q3 FY2026, so every point of mix shift raises group profitability without a single extra iPhone sold. That engine is now being repriced by courts and regulators rather than by competitors. On 2025-04-30 the California District Court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction and barred it from imposing any commission on purchases made outside an app, referring the matter to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt, with the Ninth Circuit hearing Apple's expedited appeal in October 2025; in Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 and its Article 6(4) investigation into Apple's contract terms remains open, carrying potential fines of up to 10% of worldwide net sales; and the Department of Justice's antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21, seeks equitable relief over the same conduct [S5]. Because Apple has already introduced alternative fee structures and external purchase links in the EU, some revenue migrates rather than vanishing, but the direction is one-way: from commission, which scales with third-party commerce and costs nothing, to advertising, subscriptions and device price, which Apple must earn back every year.

### Manufacturing diversification is real but partial

India assembled 23% of global iPhone output in 2025, up from 14% in 2024, and is projected to reach 28% in 2026, while China's share fell from 83% to 74% [S119, S6]. That is the fastest supply-chain shift in Apple's history and it is being paid for twice: duplicated tooling and lower ramp yields on one side, dependence on Chinese components on the other, since Indian final assembly still imports much of what it screws together. Scale is the offset. Apple secured components for 80 million new-model phones for the second half of 2026 and plans more than 220 million units of production in 2026, which lets it pre-buy memory while Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo cut targets below 100 million units each, and inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m in nine months. Tariff policy remains live: the U.S. Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple has applied for refunds, while Section 301 duties and the Section 232 semiconductor investigation continue.

### China: revenue up, units down, share up

Greater China revenue rose 22% to $18,816m in Q3 FY2026 and 30% to $64,839m in nine months, after falling 4% in FY2025 and 8% in FY2024. The unit picture is different: China's smartphone market fell 15.4% year on year in Q3 2026, Apple's shipments fell 4.3%, its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%, and Huawei grew 17.3% to 21.1% [S5, S122]. Apple is therefore monetising a shrinking market through mix and price rather than winning volume — defensible while the installed base upgrades to Pro and foldable models, fragile if Huawei's domestic supply chain keeps improving or price elasticity bites. The "China share loss" bear case was right about the trend through FY2025 and wrong about 2026 so far.

### Capital allocation is the strategy's quiet centre

Apple spent $6,799m on property, plant and equipment in nine months, 1.9% of revenue, while raising R&D 33% to $34,035m: the AI build is an operating cost, not a capital programme. That leaves cash for shareholders — $10.0bn of accelerated share repurchases entered in May 2026 and a $0.27 quarterly dividend — against $146.5bn of cash and marketable securities and $82.3bn of term debt at 2026-06-27. Net income rose 27% and diluted EPS 29% in the June quarter, so buybacks added 1.6 points of per-share growth [S6, S47]. The risk is not leverage but under-investment: buying capability from Google protects the margin while leaving Apple without owned compute or models, and gross intangibles rising from $24,950m to $38,220m in nine months suggests more value is being purchased than built.

### Resources fit the plan, with one exception

The organisation changed at the top on 2026-09-01, when John Ternus moved from Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering to CEO and Tim Cook became Executive Chair. A hardware engineer running a hardware-led strategy is continuity, and the first launch under him came in on schedule [S54]. The exception is political capital: the decisions that matter most over the next three years — the DMA Article 6(4) remedy, the Ninth Circuit appeal and the DOJ case — are legal negotiations in which a product engineer has less experience than the chair he replaced.

| Ninth Circuit ruling on the Epic contempt appeal | Argued October 2025 | Pending | Whether U.S. commissions can be restored | S5 |

### Partners and dependencies
