|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google | Gemini models and cloud for the next Apple Foundation Models | 2026-01-12, multi-year, non-exclusive | Active; powers "Siri AI" | S115 |
| Component suppliers | Custom single-source parts, including leading-edge silicon | Not disclosed | Ongoing concentration risk | S5 |
| Memory suppliers | DRAM and NAND; talks reported with CXMT and YMTC for China sales | 2026-07, reported | Negotiating, unconfirmed by Apple | S113 |

### What must be true within twelve months

Four tests decide whether this is a durable annuity or a melting ice cube. Gross margin must hold near the mid-forties once the tariff refund washes out of the comparison while memory costs rise; the December 2026 quarter is the first clean read. Services growth must stay in double digits with advertising and cloud replacing any commission lost to the Epic order and the DMA — a mix the company has not had to prove for a full year. The iPhone Duo must sell into its planned volume, because a miss would confirm that premium pricing has reached the limit of what the installed base will pay. And no adverse final remedy should land in Brussels or at the Ninth Circuit that removes commission revenue retroactively. The signposts are concrete: the December-quarter margin, the advertising-versus-App-Store split in the FY2026 10-K, any disclosed size for the Gemini contract, IDC's China share for Q4 2026 and the Article 6(4) decision.

For a long-only watchlist the conclusion is that Apple's strategy earns ownership of the cash flow rather than payment for growth: the services annuity justifies a premium multiple while growth holds in double digits, the buyback compounds per-share value, and the plan creates no new growth engine before 2028. What the record cannot settle is the economics of the AI arrangement — the fee, the term and whether Apple retains query data — and the value of the health and finance adjacencies, neither of which is broken out; Apple discloses no services sub-segment revenue, so the durability of the margin engine has to be inferred from aggregate growth. Confidence in the direction of the strategy is high and in its durability medium, because the plan is well funded and well executed but its two binding constraints are a regulator and a competitor."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,864 characters)
Apple's ESG exposure is a platform-regulation problem, not a carbon or governance one: seven jurisdictions target the 75.4%-gross-margin Services pool — $109.2bn of FY2025 sales and $82.3bn of gross profit, 42.2% of the total — while fines to date (€500m EU, €150m France, $15.5m Korea) are less than 0.2% of $416.2bn of net sales and the remedies can permanently lower the highest-margin revenue Apple has. [S5, S134, S137, S136]

### The EU has established the principle; the size is still open

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering obligation and ordered the restrictions removed within 60 days; a separate Article 6(4) case on developer contract terms, opened 2024-06-24, remains unresolved with a statutory ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales ($41.6bn). The fine is a rounding error, but the principle is durable: the General Court rejected Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08. The cash question is the EU link-out commission. [S6, S134, S135]

### The US is the largest and slowest remedy risk

The DOJ and 15 states plus DC sued Apple for monopolization on 2024-03-21 in New Jersey seeking equitable relief; the motion to dismiss failed and by July 2026 the parties were in early settlement talks, with discovery to late May 2027 and no trial date. In Epic v. Apple the district court found contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred fees on out-of-app purchases; the Ninth Circuit on 2025-12-11 allowed some link-out commission and the Supreme Court agreed to review the contempt standard on 2026-06-30. Google search remedies finalised in December 2025 also threaten distribution payments inside Services, of undisclosed size. [S6, S62, S138]

### Enforcement is fragmenting; privacy is now an antitrust issue

The UK CMA designated Apple with strategic market status on 2025-10-22 and by 2026-10-20 was consulting on steering and NFC conduct requirements. Korea's communications regulator fined Apple KRW 20.81bn ($15.5m) on 2026-10-28 and ordered payment links and revised commissions, ruling a 26% fee on third-party billing evaded the 30% norm. Japan's Mobile Software Competition Act took effect on 2025-12-18, and 48 Chinese developers complained to SAMR on 2026-06-23. France's competition authority fined Apple €150m on 2025-03-31 over App Tracking Transparency, treating a privacy feature as abuse of dominance. The pattern is convergence of the global take rate toward the mid-teens, not one catastrophic penalty. [S132, S136, S140, S139, S141, S137]

### Environmental, labour and governance risks are not the discount drivers

Apple's 2025 emissions were more than 60% below 2015 and flat versus 2024, against a 2030 target of a 75% cut before carbon removals balance the remainder; removal volumes and costs are undisclosed, so the claim is only partially verified. Manufacturing remains concentrated in China, India and Vietnam, and the 10-K flags supplier industrial-accident risk; India's production-linked incentive has shifted capacity — cumulative iPhone exports passed $50bn by December 2025 and reached ₹2 lakh crore in FY2026 — but this is subsidy-supported diversification, not a structural cost advantage. Governance is cleaner than the sector: one share class, an independent chair in Art Levinson and eight directors; the 2026 proxy discloses no material related-party transactions beyond a former operating chief's family member earning above $120,000, and Tim Cook's 2025 target pay was $59m with 92% support on the 2025 say-on-pay vote. The live issues are succession (Cook is 65) and political exposure: shareholders rejected a "China Entanglement Audit" proposal on 2026-02-24. There is no dual-class discount. [S144, S145, S146, S143, S5, S52, S100]

### Policy is two different risks: sunk tax and reversible trade

The policy matrix separates sunk tax from reversible trade. State Aid is finished cash — the ECJ confirmed the Commission's 2016 decision on 2024-09-10 — a precedent risk, not an open liability. Tariffs are the opposite: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple is claiming refunds, the Section 232 semiconductor review imposed no tariffs on Apple's products on 2026-01-14, but Section 301 actions remain live. Price trade policy as gross-margin volatility, not permanent impairment. [S6]

### What the investor should price

Separate the fine from the remedy. Fines to date are immaterial, and even a maximum DMA fine would be a single charge. The durable exposure is the commission pool: the matrix shows what a cut in Services gross profit would do to operating income. That argues for a haircut to Services earnings, not for avoiding the stock. Confidence is medium because Apple does not disclose App Store revenue or take rates, and the DOJ and EU timetables have slipped repeatedly.

### Diligence questions

Five questions would change the assessment: what share of Services revenue and gross profit is App Store commission revenue by region; what commission Apple collects on US and EU link-outs; whether Article 6(4) brings periodic penalties or structural separation; the annual value of Google search-distribution payments; and the contracted volume and cost of carbon removals behind Apple 2030. The first two sit outside the public filing set; a PACER data request has been filed. If App Store commission revenue is below a tenth of Services gross profit, regulation is a sentiment issue; if a quarter or more, an earnings issue.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 公司概览 Company Overview (company_overview, revision 2 by Company Analyst, 8,995 characters)
Apple at 2026-10-30 is an iPhone business with a services margin bolted on — 53.9% of nine-month FY2026 revenue comes from iPhone while 76.3%-gross-margin Services supply a quarter of sales — and that shape, not the $62.2bn of net cash, is what the next twelve months test. Apple Inc. is a California corporation whose shares trade on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars, with one class of common stock: 50,400,000 thousand shares authorised at $0.00001 par and 14,608,963 thousand outstanding at 2026-06-27, down from 14,773,260 thousand at 2025-09-27. Ownership is index-dominated: Vanguard held 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% of the 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, while all directors and executive officers together held 9,079,765 shares, or 0.062%, and Tim Cook held 3,280,295. There is no controlling shareholder, no VIE and no second voting class, so structural governance risk is low and policy risk arrives through regulators, not a controller [S6, S52].

The entity map is a jurisdiction map, not an intellectual-property map: Exhibit 21 names 19 subsidiaries, omits the rest as insignificant and states no entity's function. Four are Irish, the largest foreign cluster, and the tax note records that the FY2025 provision fell $10.7bn year on year because of the State Aid Decision, leaving an effective rate of 15.6% in FY2025 and 17.6% in nine months of FY2026. No filing in the register discloses which entity owns the trademarks or the cost-sharing arrangement — the largest unquantified item in tax modelling [S5].

| Apple Inc. | California, US | Listed corporation | Issuer and group parent | 100% of the group | S6 |
| Apple Distribution International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Not stated | Subsidiary | S5 |

The model is an installed-base annuity on a hardware franchise. Apple sells through 40% direct and 60% indirect channels to consumers, small and mid-sized businesses, education, enterprise and government, and monetises the base through the App Store, iCloud, AppleCare, advertising, payments and Apple TV at a 76.3% Services gross margin against 39.9% on products, with 166,000 full-time-equivalent staff at 2025-09-27. Growth in FY2026 came from the other end of that mix: Services rose 14% to $91.7bn in nine months while iPhone rose 22% to $196.5bn, so the highest-margin line grew slower than the group [S5, S6].

Geographically the company is majority non-US — 57.1% of FY2025 revenue and 59.0% of nine-month FY2026 revenue — and the segment disclosure hides more than it shows: India, the Middle East and Africa sit inside Europe, so the fastest-growing large market is not a line. Greater China is visible, and it reversed: from $72,559m in FY2023 it fell 8% to $66,952m, fell another 4% to $64,377m in FY2025, then produced $64,839m in nine months of FY2026, up 30% and above the whole prior year, management citing iPhone and a stronger renminbi. Manufacturing remains where the tariffs are: a significant majority of production runs through outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, with single-source partners for many components [S6, S5].

The balance sheet is capacity, not protection. Cash and marketable securities of $146.5bn against $84.3bn of debt — $2.0bn commercial paper, $11.0bn current and $71.3bn non-current term debt — left $62.2bn of net cash at 2026-06-27 against $33.7bn nine months earlier, with inventories doubled to $11,092m. Apple returned $73.9bn in nine months ($62.1bn of repurchases, $11.8bn of dividends), equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, and spent $6.8bn on capital expenditure. Buybacks were $8.5bn below the prior-year period and the share count fell only 1.1%, so per-share compounding is a support rather than the engine. The implication for an investor is that the case is carried by mix and margin, not by the balance sheet: net cash is 1.2% of the $5.02trn market value implied by $343.36, the price of an insider sale executed on 2026-10-27, and it cushions nothing in a de-rating. The press valued it at $4.6trn on 2026-08-31 [S6, S5].

The weak points are supply, policy and price, not demand. Management states that component constraints and rising costs for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM "may materially negatively impact" revenue, cost and gross margin, and expects the trend to intensify. Q3 FY2026 gross margin of 50.1% and EPS of $2.02 included roughly 2 percentage points and $0.11 from tariff refunds after the US Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20; the 2026-01-14 Section 232 results added nothing on Apple products, but Section 301 measures have since been imposed. In Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA's anti-steering rule in 2025 and Apple changed its EU App Store fees in August 2026. Against Microsoft, which funded $139.5bn of FY2026 investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow for AI capacity, Apple converts operating cash into buybacks and almost none into owned compute: coherent for an installed-base franchise, fragile if AI becomes the upgrade reason. Confidence is high on the figures (filings through 2026-06-27) and medium on the mix judgement; FY2026 results are not due until 2026-11-02. Open questions: whether Services outgrows iPhone in FY2027, how much of Q3 margin was the refund, what sits behind the $14.5bn rise in other purchase obligations to $29.3bn, and whether Greater China holds if the renminbi weakens [S47, S84, S50].

arguments.position_sizing: Listed, long-only: watchlist only, zero position at $348.91. The Kelly fraction at these inputs is zero because the probability-weighted return is negative ($314, -9.9%), so the sizing question is when to open, not how much. Entry band $287-$325, which is 30-34x FY2027E EPS of $9.56, sized for a 30% drawdown rather than the 44.5% fifty-two-week range: on a 2% portfolio weight, a bear-case move to $224 costs 72bp of portfolio value. Maximum loss tolerated before re-underwriting is a 35% drawdown combined with a gross margin below 47%, which is the bear case arriving together rather than either alone. The market regime - a 4.99% ten-year Treasury and a 40x multiple - caps the size at a starter position even inside the entry band until the rate picture improves or FY2027 estimates rise.
arguments.analogs: Nearest analog: Microsoft 2014-2019. A maturing franchise with a high-margin annuity attached (Office to Office 365) re-rated only after the annuity's growth was demonstrated for several quarters, not on the announcement; Apple's Services is the same mechanism but its growth is being repriced by courts rather than competitors. Cautionary analog: Cisco 2000-2002, a hardware leader priced at a peak multiple on the assumption that the next cycle would be like the last, where the multiple halved while revenue kept growing. Second cautionary analog: IBM 2011-2013, where buybacks at high multiples slowed and the share count could no longer carry EPS growth. Base rate from Apple's own history: the multiple fell from 37.5x to 27.9x between FY2024 and FY2023 year-ends while the business did not deteriorate, which is the mean-reversion the base and bear cases assume [S93, S6].
arguments.capital_efficiency: Capex of $10,041M trailing, 2.2% of revenue, against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, gives trailing free cash flow of $136,683M at 1.06x net income and a capital-light model that funds $82,226M of buybacks and $15,640M of dividends from operations rather than from the balance sheet. The efficiency is real and is the base case's foundation. The cost is that the capability inputs are bought rather than built: R&D up 32.5% to $34,035M and $13,270M of gross intangibles added with no acquisition line, against a Gemini licence that converts model development into an operating expense. If AI becomes the upgrade reason rather than a feature, the 2%-of-sales capex line is the assumption that breaks first.

Case: Apple Inc. (Nasdaq: AAPL), listed. Decision: whether AAPL belongs on Meridian Capital's long-only watchlist. All six analysts have reported; the thesis table and scenario analysis are saved. Write in English.

Your job: attack the thesis before committee review and write section 10 (risk).

The thesis you are attacking, in one line: Apple is a high-quality, capital-light cash compounder, but at $348.91 (40.0x trailing earnings, 32.5x EV/EBIT against a four-peer median of 18.1x) the price already capitalises a second growth engine no filing evidences; probability-weighted outcome $314 (-9.9%), base $325, bear $224, bull $404 at 45/30/25. Conclusion: watchlist only, zero position, entry band $287-$325 (30-34x FY2027E EPS of $9.56).

Attack these specifically:
1. The 25/45/30 probabilities and the $314 weighting — are the bear drivers under-weighted? Test memory-cost pass-through, the App Store take rate settling toward mid-teens, and whether the Google search-distribution payments inside Services survive the remedies now on twelve-month, non-exclusive terms under appeal.
2. The gross-margin assumption: 48% ex-refund in FY2027. Every 100bp is $5.0bn of operating income. Inventory rose 94% to $11,092M and $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition line in investing cash flow — what is the FY2027 amortisation charge the 10-Q does not show?
3. The "no margin of safety" claim rests on a 9.5% WACC (4.99% ten-year, 4.5% ERP, 1.1 beta). If the rate path or the ERP is wrong, the DCF range $153-$230 and the verdict both move. At what WACC is 40x defensible, and is that WACC plausible?
4. What would make the bull case right and the team's caution wrong — an AI-driven replacement cycle, a foldable price tier, Services re-acceleration? Give the falsifying evidence, not the narrative.
5. The weakest sections to interrogate: team (failed its depth heuristic and rests on a twenty-month C-suite turnover with zero insider buying against $208.0m sold); technology_product (failed a checker on patent numbering; the AI layer is licensed from Google under a 2026-01-12 agreement, which may make the "moat" claim overstated); company_overview and market (both at 98%+ of the 9,000-character cap, so check for truncation and for claims that outrun their sources); funding_valuation (Samsung's EV/EBIT and FCF yield, and precedent-transaction multiples, are stated as unavailable — test whether the peer median of 18.1x is therefore too low).
6. Also test the two claims most load-bearing for the recommendation: that trailing FCF of $136,683M at 1.06x net income is clean, and that the buyback at 40x earnings (2.5% earnings yield against a 4.99% Treasury) is value-destructive.

Section 10 standards: 2,500-9,000 characters, 6+ paragraphs, 8+ figures, 4+ distinct source IDs, at least 6 source mentions, dated events, a risk matrix with a Source column, and a labelled confidence or open question in each risk. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 财务分析 Financial Analysis (financials, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,648 characters)
Apple's statements show a business that converts almost all of its profit into cash on capex that is trivial for a company of its size, but the fiscal 2026 margin rests on a tariff refund the company itself calls one-off and on an intangible build the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise.

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, the company's own approximation, and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

| Revenue | 383,285 | 391,035 | 416,161 | 364,357 | 466,823 | S3-S6 |
| Gross margin | 44.1% | 46.2% | 46.9% | 49.1% | 48.6% | S3-S6 |
| Operating income | 114,301 | 123,216 | 133,050 | 122,432 | 154,859 | S3-S6 |
| Operating margin | 29.8% | 31.5% | 32.0% | 33.6% | 33.2% | S3-S6 |
| Net income | 96,995 | 93,736 | 112,010 | 101,464 | 128,930 | S3-S6 |
| Effective tax rate | 14.7% | 24.1% | 15.6% | 17.6% | 17.3% | S3-S6 |
| Diluted EPS, $ | 6.13 | 6.08 | 7.46 | 6.88 | 8.72 | S3-S6 |
| R&D | 29,915 | 31,370 | 34,550 | 34,035 | 42,901 | S3-S6 |
| Operating cash flow | 110,543 | 118,254 | 111,482 | 116,996 | 146,724 | S3-S5, S47 |
| Capital expenditure | 10,959 | 9,447 | 12,715 | 6,799 | 10,041 | S3-S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | 99,584 | 108,807 | 98,767 | 110,197 | 136,683 | S3-S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow / net income | 1.03x | 1.16x | 0.88x | 1.09x | 1.06x | S3-S5, S47 |
| Net cash | 51,011 | 50,021 | 33,763 | 62,173 | 62,173 | S3-S6 |

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at 1.71 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The diligence question that follows: what are those intangibles, over what life are they amortised, and does the expense arrive in FY2027 [S6, S5]?

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On $100.4bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is 128%, and on total assets 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns $128.1bn of after-tax operating profit on $100.4bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,919 characters)
Apple's capital-allocation record is exceptional and its 2025-2026 product execution is not: the company returned $73.9bn, 63% of operating cash flow, in nine months while growing revenue 16%, but that growth needed a 33% rise in R&D and a $13.3bn build in gross intangibles, and the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed inside twenty months. John Ternus, 50 when appointed, became chief executive and a director on 2026-09-01; Tim Cook, 65, moved to executive chair after fifteen years as CEO; Sabih Khan, 58, has been chief operating officer since 2025-07-25 and joined Apple in August 1995; Kevan Parekh has been chief financial officer since January 2025; Deirdre O'Brien is a senior vice president; Jennifer Newstead became general counsel on 2026-03-01. The six named executive officers in the 2026 proxy — Cook, Kate Adams, Khan, Luca Maestri, O'Brien and Parekh — include no AI or machine-learning title, so the function's leadership is not disclosed through Section 16 or proxy channels [S54, S52].

The succession is continuity by design, and that is the point to price. Ternus holds a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and worked as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems before joining Apple's product design team in 2001; he became a vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and joined the executive team in 2021, and the company credits him with the iPad and AirPods introductions and 3D-printed titanium work in Apple Watch Ultra. Apple has done this before: Cook, an Auburn industrial engineer with a Duke MBA and a Fuqua scholarship, was an operations executive promoted from within in 2011 and leaves an installed base above 2.5 billion active devices in more than 200 countries, Services grown 28% to $109.2bn between FY2023 and FY2025, and 8 hardware launches in FY2025 alone — iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, Watch Series 11, Watch SE 3, Watch Ultra 3 and AirPods Pro 3. Independent reporting says the same from outside — a well-liked product engineer expected to make "small touches" rather than a disruptive break, and explicitly not the product visionary type, against a record including Vision Pro, delayed Siri work and a criticised Liquid Glass redesign. Continuity protects the cash engine; it supplies no evidence of a new product cycle [S112, S111, S87].

Capital allocation is where this team earns its premium, and the peer contrast is stark. In nine months of FY2026 Apple returned $73.9bn — $62.1bn of repurchases and $11.8bn of dividends — equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, while spending $6.8bn, or 1.9% of revenue, on capital expenditure; FY2025 was $89.3bn of repurchases plus $15.4bn of dividends under a $100bn authorisation, dividend raised to $0.26 then $0.27. Microsoft chose the opposite trade in FY2026, funding $139.5bn of investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow and lifting capital spending by $51.4bn for AI capacity. Apple's returns on capital are high because it owns almost no compute [S6, S5, S50].

The spending pattern says the company knows it is behind. Research and development went from $29,915m in FY2023 to $31,370m in FY2024 and $34,550m in FY2025, then reached $34,035m in nine months of FY2026, up 33% year on year and 9.3% of revenue, with management attributing it to AI infrastructure and headcount. In the same nine months gross intangible assets rose to $38,220m from $24,950m and other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn. Apple is buying capability as well as building it; the filing discloses neither the counterparty nor the exclusivity, and operating margin held at 33.6% only because gross margin rose 2.3 percentage points. A licensing commitment of that size is a permanent transfer of margin to an unnamed party, so it belongs in the valuation work as an assumption rather than a footnote [S6, S5].

Pay and board composition reinforce the status quo. Cook's 2025 target equity was $50m with 75% performance-based, his base salary has not changed since 2016, his total target compensation sits in the 80th to 90th percentile of the primary peer group, and 2021-granted performance RSUs vested at 187% of target on 2024-10-01, or 477,301 shares, on relative total shareholder return against the S&P 500; he has already met the age-65, ten-year condition for retirement vesting. After the transition the board has nine directors aged 51 to 77, including Levinson (75, since 2000), Sugar (77, since 2010), Jung (67, since 2008) and Wagner (64, since 2014), with Wanda Austin (2024) the only new independent since 2021. Relative-TSR scorecards pay for beating the index, a target reachable through buybacks and margin management without a new product cycle, and oversight of the AI transition sits with a board whose members have finance, consumer-brand and aerospace backgrounds rather than AI operating experience [S52, S54].

Insider behaviour gives no support to the price. Over the twelve months to 2026-10-29 there were 46 sale transactions of 687,127 shares for $208.0m, 43 under Rule 10b5-1 plans, and no purchases; Art Levinson sold $86.7m, Cook $80.4m, O'Brien $23.1m and Ternus $8.5m on 2026-10-02. Plans mute the sales; the signal is no discretionary purchase between $300 and $345. The counter-case is about product rather than people: independent reporting describes an unresolved AI gap versus OpenAI, a memory shortage squeezing margins and product misfires, while the same filings show 16% revenue growth and 22% iPhone growth, so the team is executing the current cycle well and the next one is unproven. Confidence is high on the record and low on the forward judgement. Four checks matter: Ternus's pay metrics, the executive who owns AI, the licensing counterparty, and whether the board adds an operating AI director [S41, S87].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 技术与产品 Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,947 characters)
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a new A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable wherever Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thinning at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: a narrow lead, defended by integration

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design — not transistor count — is what lets a phone chip deliver desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The measured lead has narrowed to a rounding error at the top: the A19 Pro scored 4,019 on Geekbench 6 single-core against 3,846 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 4.5% gap in Apple versus Qualcomm single-core performance, and the same comparison reportedly favours Qualcomm in multi-threaded and graphics tests [S117]. Apple's answer is to compete on what the benchmark does not measure: an in-house modem, battery life, imaging and a protected hinge.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship SoC, iPhone 18 Pro | A20 Pro | Announced 2026-09-09 | S116 |
| A19 Pro, Geekbench 6 single-core | 4,019 | Published benchmark run | S117 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same test | 3,846 | Published benchmark run | S117 |
| Apple's single-core lead | 4.5% | Computed from the two scores | S117 |
| iPhone revenue, Q3 FY2026 | $54,252m, +22% YoY | Reported, quarter ended 2026-06-27 | S47 |
| R&D expense, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |
| Foldable units planned for 2026 | 10m, from 7-8m | Supply-chain reporting | S113 |

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple frames this as hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it unveiled "all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 in June 2026, shipping it on the iPhone 18 Pro that reached stores on 2026-09-18. R&D rose 33% to fund AI infrastructure and headcount while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, or 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so Apple buys capability as an operating cost instead of building a hyperscale compute base. The strategic cost is that model quality, query data and the pace of improvement now sit with a competitor that also sells phones.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**
The next generation of Apple Foundation Models is built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the ceiling of the assistant is set by a competitor while the differentiation left to Apple is integration, privacy and distribution.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | No assistant | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S116 |
| Cellular modem | In-house | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S116 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Apple is unique among the five in owning the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image, and Qualcomm sells silicon to the rest. Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant.

### Form factors: the stagnation critique is out of date

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Suppliers were told to prepare 10 million foldables for 2026, up from 7-8 million, inside at least five new iPhone models spread across the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027 [S113, S121]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units, the Duo changes the price ladder and the narrative rather than the revenue base. The patent record shows the mechanics were engineered before launch: the granted patent US 12,164,344 covers a multi-link hinge with interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch, and US2025/0120026 adds a folding expandable display.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Published | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | 2023 (app. US2023/0049811) | Date not disclosed | Granted | iPhone Duo hinge mechanics | S121 |
| US2025/0120026A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | 2025 | — | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |
| Not disclosed | Aggregate portfolio | Global | — | — | "Pursuing thousands of applications" | No patent count given | S5 |

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared its Hypertension Notification Feature on 2025-09-11, its Sleep Apnea Notification Feature on 2024-09-13, granted the Hearing Aid Feature a De Novo on 2024-09-12, and cleared a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, which raises the wearable's value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration: Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 4% in FY2025 to $35,686m and grew 6% in Q3 FY2026 to $7,883m.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |

| iPhone (incl. Duo) | Shipping | 2026-09-09 | $54,252m in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by product | iPhone 18 base model, spring 2027 | S47 |
| Mac | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $10,352m in Q3 FY2026, +29% | Not disclosed by product | M-series refresh | S47 |
| iPad | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $6,191m in Q3 FY2026, -6% | Not disclosed by product | Demand after June 2026 price rises | S47 |
| Wearables, home, accessories | Shipping | Annual | $7,883m in Q3 FY2026, +6% | Not disclosed by product | Blood-pressure, glucose work unannounced | S47 |
| Vision Pro | Shipping | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | None disclosed | S5 |

### What would break the story

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability. The Q3 FY2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM; inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m [S6]. Strip out 2 percentage points of tariff refund and the 50.1% gross margin is nearer 48%, so the technology premium is being defended by price increases while memory costs rise. The unverifiable pieces matter too: no Vision Pro units, no product-level margins, no patent counts, and one benchmark cannot show whether the A20 Pro sustains performance under thermal load.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power management designed as one product | 3-4 years | S116 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | All-time-high active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Foundry, custom components | 7 | Single-source parts; scale secures leading capacity | 2-3 years | S5 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team with Apple's published patents could match the hinge and the foldable within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and the regulatory record, medium on durability, because memory costs are eating into the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the A20 Pro's process node, the Gemini fee and term, and iPhone Duo sell-through."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 2 by Product Analyst, 8,679 characters)
Apple's strategy is a defence that is working, but it is a defence. Services at a 75.4% gross margin, a premium multi-launch product cadence and Indian assembly are turning a maturing hardware franchise into a higher-margin, less tariff-exposed annuity — while the two forces that set the ceiling, competition law in Brussels and Washington and the cost of renting intelligence from Google, are outside management's control [S115]. The plan protects cash generation; it does not restore growth.

### Services carry the margin, and the law is repricing them

Services reached $109,158m in FY2025, up 13.5% from $96,169m, at a 75.4% gross margin against 73.9% a year earlier, and grew 14% to $91,728m in the nine months to 2026-06-27 with a 75.6% margin in the June quarter. Because Apple books only its commission on third-party App Store sales, on a net basis, a dollar of services revenue carries 75 cents of gross profit against a consolidated gross margin of 46.9% in FY2025 and 50.1% in Q3 FY2026, so every point of mix shift raises group profitability without a single extra iPhone sold. That engine is now being repriced by courts and regulators rather than by competitors. On 2025-04-30 the California District Court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction and barred it from imposing any commission on purchases made outside an app, referring the matter to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt, with the Ninth Circuit hearing Apple's expedited appeal in October 2025; in Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 and its Article 6(4) investigation into Apple's contract terms remains open, carrying potential fines of up to 10% of worldwide net sales; and the Department of Justice's antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21, seeks equitable relief over the same conduct [S5]. Because Apple has already introduced alternative fee structures and external purchase links in the EU, some revenue migrates rather than vanishing, but the direction is one-way: from commission, which scales with third-party commerce and costs nothing, to advertising, subscriptions and device price, which Apple must earn back every year.

### Manufacturing diversification is real but partial

India assembled 23% of global iPhone output in 2025, up from 14% in 2024, and is projected to reach 28% in 2026, while China's share fell from 83% to 74% [S119, S6]. That is the fastest supply-chain shift in Apple's history and it is being paid for twice: duplicated tooling and lower ramp yields on one side, dependence on Chinese components on the other, since Indian final assembly still imports much of what it screws together. Scale is the offset. Apple secured components for 80 million new-model phones for the second half of 2026 and plans more than 220 million units of production in 2026, which lets it pre-buy memory while Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo cut targets below 100 million units each, and inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m in nine months. Tariff policy remains live: the U.S. Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple has applied for refunds, while Section 301 duties and the Section 232 semiconductor investigation continue.

### China: revenue up, units down, share up

Greater China revenue rose 22% to $18,816m in Q3 FY2026 and 30% to $64,839m in nine months, after falling 4% in FY2025 and 8% in FY2024. The unit picture is different: China's smartphone market fell 15.4% year on year in Q3 2026, Apple's shipments fell 4.3%, its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%, and Huawei grew 17.3% to 21.1% [S5, S122]. Apple is therefore monetising a shrinking market through mix and price rather than winning volume — defensible while the installed base upgrades to Pro and foldable models, fragile if Huawei's domestic supply chain keeps improving or price elasticity bites. The "China share loss" bear case was right about the trend through FY2025 and wrong about 2026 so far.

### Capital allocation is the strategy's quiet centre

Apple spent $6,799m on property, plant and equipment in nine months, 1.9% of revenue, while raising R&D 33% to $34,035m: the AI build is an operating cost, not a capital programme. That leaves cash for shareholders — $10.0bn of accelerated share repurchases entered in May 2026 and a $0.27 quarterly dividend — against $146.5bn of cash and marketable securities and $82.3bn of term debt at 2026-06-27. Net income rose 27% and diluted EPS 29% in the June quarter, so buybacks added 1.6 points of per-share growth [S6, S47]. The risk is not leverage but under-investment: buying capability from Google protects the margin while leaving Apple without owned compute or models, and gross intangibles rising from $24,950m to $38,220m in nine months suggests more value is being purchased than built.

### Resources fit the plan, with one exception

The organisation changed at the top on 2026-09-01, when John Ternus moved from Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering to CEO and Tim Cook became Executive Chair. A hardware engineer running a hardware-led strategy is continuity, and the first launch under him came in on schedule [S54]. The exception is political capital: the decisions that matter most over the next three years — the DMA Article 6(4) remedy, the Ninth Circuit appeal and the DOJ case — are legal negotiations in which a product engineer has less experience than the chair he replaced.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo launch | 2026-09-09 | Shipped | Form-factor entry and price ladder | S114 |
| 10m foldable units in calendar 2026 | 2026-12-31 | Supplier plan, up from 7-8m | Whether the new tier sells | S113 |
| iPhone 18 and new iPhone Air | First half of 2027 | Planned | Two-window launch cadence | S113 |
| India at 28% of global iPhone assembly | Calendar 2026 | In progress, 23% in 2025 | Tariff hedge holds | S119 |
| Commission's Article 6(4) decision | No date disclosed | Investigation open since 2024-06-24 | Size of the EU take-rate remedy | S5 |
| Ninth Circuit ruling on the Epic contempt appeal | Argued October 2025 | Pending | Whether U.S. commissions can be restored | S5 |
| EU General Court on gatekeeper status | July 2026 | Decided against Apple | No judicial escape from the DMA | S120 |

### Partners and dependencies

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google | Gemini models and cloud for the next Apple Foundation Models | 2026-01-12, multi-year, non-exclusive | Active; powers "Siri AI" | S115 |
| Component suppliers | Custom single-source parts, including leading-edge silicon | Not disclosed | Ongoing concentration risk | S5 |
| Memory suppliers | DRAM and NAND; talks reported with CXMT and YMTC for China sales | 2026-07, reported | Negotiating, unconfirmed by Apple | S113 |

### What must be true within twelve months

Four tests decide whether this is a durable annuity or a melting ice cube. Gross margin must hold near the mid-forties once the tariff refund washes out of the comparison while memory costs rise; the December 2026 quarter is the first clean read. Services growth must stay in double digits with advertising and cloud replacing any commission lost to the Epic order and the DMA — a mix the company has not had to prove for a full year. The iPhone Duo must sell into its planned volume, because a miss would confirm that premium pricing has reached the limit of what the installed base will pay. And no adverse final remedy should land in Brussels or at the Ninth Circuit that removes commission revenue retroactively. The signposts are concrete: the December-quarter margin, the advertising-versus-App-Store split in the FY2026 10-K, any disclosed size for the Gemini contract, IDC's China share for Q4 2026 and the Article 6(4) decision.

For a long-only watchlist the conclusion is that Apple's strategy earns ownership of the cash flow rather than payment for growth: the services annuity justifies a premium multiple while growth holds in double digits, the buyback compounds per-share value, and the plan creates no new growth engine before 2028. What the record cannot settle is the economics of the AI arrangement — the fee, the term and whether Apple retains query data — and the value of the health and finance adjacencies, neither of which is broken out; Apple discloses no services sub-segment revenue, so the durability of the margin engine has to be inferred from aggregate growth. Confidence in the direction of the strategy is high and in its durability medium, because the plan is well funded and well executed but its two binding constraints are a regulator and a competitor."}],"isError":false}

If the $13.3bn was capitalised but paid via operating cash flow, then OCF is overstated relative to "owner cash flow" by that amount — a real quality issue. Alternatively they're non-cash (e.g., capitalised from prepaid obligations or acquired in a business combination not yet settled). The team's DCF deducts SBC ($13.7bn) but does not deduct intangible purchases. If $13.3bn of nine-month intangible purchases are recurring and paid in cash, trailing FCF of $136.7bn overstates owner cash flow by $13-18bn/yr (10-13%), which would cut fair value by roughly the same order. That's a red-team point worth making: the 1.06x conversion is clean on the accounting but not necessarily on an owner-earnings basis; and the DCF already deducts SBC, so consistency demands deducting intangible purchases too. If both are deducted, owner cash flow = 128.7 - 17.7 = $111bn, and value falls to ~$158 at 9.5%. Hmm — that's the team's own methodology, so the DCF may actually be more generous than it looks? No: deducting more lowers value further, reinforcing "no margin of safety". But it also raises the question of double counting: if the intangible amortisation is a non-cash charge added back in OCF, then capitalised spending should be deducted once. Since OCF adds back amortisation, FCF captures the cash spent only if the spend is in investing. So the correct treatment: FCF = OCF - capex - purchases of intangibles. If intangible purchases are in operating cash flow (as licence payments often are for content), then they're already deducted and there's no overstatement; the balance sheet capitalisation is then an accrual, not cash. Ugh — without the cash flow statement detail I can't settle it. Apple's cash flow statement has a line "Other" in investing and "Payments for acquisition of property, plant and equipment". Let me check the 10-Q cash flow statement and investing section for "purchases of intangible" or "other investing". One read_sec_filing call with keywords ["intangible","investing","acquisitions"]. That's worth it — it's central to lead question 6.

Actually, my earlier keyword read for item 1 with "intangible" returned only the balance sheet. If there were an investing line "purchases of intangible assets" it should have matched "intangible". It didn't. So the cash flow statement doesn't show a purchases-of-intangibles line. Then where did the $13.3bn come from? Possibly: (1) the Gemini licence capitalised with a corresponding liability (other purchase obligations rose $14.5bn to $29.3bn per team section) — i.e., non-cash, financed by a commitment; (2) capitalised internally developed software; (3) an asset acquisition treated as non-cash. The matching rise in "other purchase obligations +$14.5bn" strongly suggests (1): Apple signed long-term licence/content commitments and capitalised the prepaid/right-of-use asset, with the cash to be paid over time. That means FY2027+ cash costs of ~$14.5bn+ will flow through operating cash flow as paid — which the DCF's FCF does NOT deduct (since FCF = OCF - capex, and these payments would be in OCF → actually they WOULD reduce OCF when paid). OK: so if paid in future years, future OCF is reduced → the DCF's 8% FCF growth assumption is overstated. That's the cleanest formulation: $13.3bn of gross intangibles and $14.5bn of additional purchase obligations represent contracted future cash costs not yet in operating cash flow; if paid over 3-5 years, that's $3-6bn/yr of OCF drag (2-4% of FCF), which the 8% FCF growth path ignores. Combined with $5.1bn FY2027 amortisation, the FY2027 EPS of $9.56 carries ~$0.16 of incremental charge plus an OCF drag.

Good. That is a substantive, novel red-team finding. I need to verify the purchase obligations figure: team section says "other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn". Yes [S6].

Now Services/Google: $20bn in 2022 → with growth maybe $22-25bn now. I'll cite "roughly $20bn a year (2022 trial record)" and note it is not disclosed by Apple, so the current figure is unverified. As a share: 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue ($109,158M); ~15% of TTM operating income ($20bn/$154.9bn = 12.9%). At near-100% incremental margin. A 50% cut = $10bn = 6.5% of TTM EBIT; EPS impact after 17.6% tax = $8.24bn/14.594bn = $0.56 (6.0% of $9.56). A full loss = $1.12 (12%). That's the under-weighting evidence. Strong.

App Store take rate: Sensor Tower global IAP revenue $167bn in 2025 (S83). Apple's commission: if Apple's share of that is ~60% (App Store gross billings ~$100bn) at a 30% headline rate → $30bn, minus small-business 15% tier → effective ~27% → $27bn. If the take rate settles at 15-18%: revenue falls by 9-12 percentage points of $100bn = $9-12bn at ~100% margin = 6-8% of EBIT = $0.50-0.68 EPS. But Apple proposes 15% on external purchases (S64) — that's on links out, plus EU unified terms. EU is ~7% of App Store billings? The DMA covers EU only (~6-7% of Apple revenue). So the global take-rate compression is gradual, not immediate. I should distinguish: US (Epic injunction) + EU (DMA) cover maybe 50-55% of App Store billings; Korea/Japan/UK add. If half of billings move to 15-18%, commission revenue falls ~$5-7bn → $0.28-0.39 EPS (3-4%). Combined with a Google payment halving (-$0.56) → -9 to -10% EPS, which is the entire bear case. Then memory and China are un-priced. So bear at 30% probability is arguably under-weighted at ~40-45%.

Careful: the Lead's probabilities are 45 base / 30 bear / 25 bull. If bear should be 40-45%, expected value falls from $314 to... Let me compute: 45/30/25 → 0.45×325 + 0.30×224 + 0.25×404 = 146.25 + 67.2 + 101 = 314.45. ✓. At 40 bear / 40 base / 20 bull: 0.4×325+0.4×224+0.2×404 = 130+89.6+80.8 = 300.4 (-13.9%). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,906 characters)
**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth $134.9 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter. Trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million implies a 12.3% CAGR from $85,200 million in FY2023 and divides into $48.19 per active device a year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12.3% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 7.0% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 30% in Greater China to $64,839 million, 16% in Europe, 11% in the Americas, 10% in Japan and 19% in the rest of Asia-Pacific, lifting Greater China from 15.5% of FY2025 revenue to 17.8%. China's own market fell 4.2% in the first half of 2026, so Apple's gain was share rather than tide: its unit share rose to 18.1% from 13.9% because it held prices while Android rivals raised theirs, and IDC expects the second-half decline in China to widen to 20% year on year. India repeats the pattern at a different scale — 33.2 million units in the second quarter of 2026, down 11.1%, average prices up 14.4% and Apple leading by value — while in the United States, where iOS carries 58.35% of mobile web traffic, growth runs through carrier trade-in programmes rather than new users. [S6, S80, S96, S89]

Policy both creates and caps this demand, and the dates are live. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation published initial results on 2026-01-14 without imposing tariffs on Apple's products, and the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, for which Apple has claimed refunds; Section 301 duties and further sector measures remain open. In Europe, Apple restructured its App Store terms in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, effective October 2026. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. Demand that was subsidy-created is now subsidy-dependent; demand that is trade-in-driven has held. [S6, S81, S80]

::: evidence
**Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on just over 1 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40.0% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at $48.19 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]
:::

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism rather than a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist through the forecast horizon. What is not durable is the current growth rate: the Greater China acceleration rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its own unit forecast within a single quarter, and the trackers disagree materially on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much iPhone strength was pulled forward? Second, does China hold its current unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to the EU's restructured commissions and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?"}],"isError":false}

That's a concrete take-rate data point: EU external purchase commission 5%, external payment links 20%. Compare to the US proposal of 15% (S64). So the take rate is settling at 5-20%, not "mid-teens" necessarily — the EU's 5% on outside transactions is severe for high-value digital goods.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 公司概览 Company Overview (company_overview, revision 2 by Company Analyst, 8,995 characters)
Apple at 2026-10-30 is an iPhone business with a services margin bolted on — 53.9% of nine-month FY2026 revenue comes from iPhone while 76.3%-gross-margin Services supply a quarter of sales — and that shape, not the $62.2bn of net cash, is what the next twelve months test. Apple Inc. is a California corporation whose shares trade on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars, with one class of common stock: 50,400,000 thousand shares authorised at $0.00001 par and 14,608,963 thousand outstanding at 2026-06-27, down from 14,773,260 thousand at 2025-09-27. Ownership is index-dominated: Vanguard held 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% of the 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, while all directors and executive officers together held 9,079,765 shares, or 0.062%, and Tim Cook held 3,280,295. There is no controlling shareholder, no VIE and no second voting class, so structural governance risk is low and policy risk arrives through regulators, not a controller [S6, S52].

The entity map is a jurisdiction map, not an intellectual-property map: Exhibit 21 names 19 subsidiaries, omits the rest as insignificant and states no entity's function. Four are Irish, the largest foreign cluster, and the tax note records that the FY2025 provision fell $10.7bn year on year because of the State Aid Decision, leaving an effective rate of 15.6% in FY2025 and 17.6% in nine months of FY2026. No filing in the register discloses which entity owns the trademarks or the cost-sharing arrangement — the largest unquantified item in tax modelling [S5].

The model is an installed-base annuity on a hardware franchise. The balance sheet is capacity, not protection. Cash and marketable securities of $146.5bn against $84.3bn of debt — $2.0bn commercial paper, $11.0bn current and $71.3bn non-current term debt — left $62.2bn of net cash at 2026-06-27 against $33.7bn nine months earlier, with inventories doubled to $11,092m. Apple returned $73.9bn in nine months ($62.1bn of repurchases, $11.8bn of dividends), equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, and spent $6.8bn on capital expenditure. Buybacks were $8.5bn below the prior-year period and the share count fell only 1.1%, so per-share compounding is a support rather than the engine. The implication for an investor is that the case is carried by mix and margin, not by the balance sheet: net cash is 1.2% of the $5.02trn market value implied by $343.36, the price of an insider sale executed on 2026-10-27, and it cushions nothing in a de-rating. The press valued it at $4.6trn on 2026-08-31 [S6, S5].

The weak points are supply, policy and price, not demand. Management states that component constraints and rising costs for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM "may materially negatively impact" revenue, cost and gross margin, and expects the trend to intensify.
