arguments.markdown:
Apple scores 5.7 out of 10, and the score is a verdict on price rather than on quality. The business earns a 9 and the ecosystem an 8, but valuation earns a 2 and regulatory exposure a 4, and those two dimensions carry 30% of the weight against a 36.5x forward multiple that the market has already paid. The composite is the weighted average of the table below; quality justifies a premium multiple, not the size of the premium the shares now carry [S93].

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Business quality and unit economics | 15% | 9 | Nine-month FY2026 revenue of $364,357M at a 49.1% gross margin, with $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income on capex of 2.2% of sales | S6, S47 |
| Competitive moat and ecosystem | 15% | 8 | More than 2.5bn active devices and 65% of the $600-plus tier; the assistant layer is licensed from Google, so the intelligence moat is rented | S6, S115 |
| Market growth | 10% | 5 | Shipments fall 16.7% while ASPs rise 27.6%, so growth is price and mix; FY2027 consensus EPS growth decelerates to 8.1% | S79, S93 |
| Margin durability and pricing power | 10% | 6 | Memory costs may materially hurt gross margin; mobile DRAM contract prices rose 78-83% quarter on quarter for LPDDR5X in Q2 2026, and 2 points of the June-quarter margin were tariff refunds | S6, S148 |
| Management and capital allocation | 10% | 6 | $82,226M of trailing buybacks at 40.0x earnings give a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.99% Treasury; the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed within twenty months | S6, S47 |
| Earnings quality and balance sheet | 5% | 8 | Free cash flow converts at 1.06x net income with net cash of $62,173M, but $13,270M of gross intangibles were added in nine months and $5,075M is already current | S6, S47 |
| Regulatory and policy risk | 10% | 4 | The Google payment is reported at $20bn a year, 12.9% of trailing operating income; the EU Article 6(4) case carries a 10%-of-sales cap with terms live since 2026-10-01 | S147, S134 |
| Valuation and margin of safety | 20% | 2 | 40.0x trailing, 32.5x EV/EBIT and 36.5x FY2027E against an 18.1x peer median and an 18.59x S&P 500 forward multiple; the DCF returns $183 | S7, S93, S153 |
| Catalysts and exit path | 5% | 5 | The 2026-11-02 print and the May 2027 buyback authorisation are dated, but the largest technology deal ever is 1.35% of enterprise value | S92, S91 |
| Composite | 100% | 5.7 | Weighted average of the nine dimensions | S6, S93 |

The quality scores are not in dispute. A franchise that converts a quarter of its revenue into gross profit and funds its buybacks from operations rather than from the balance sheet deserves a premium to the market, and the four-peer median is pulled down by a memory maker whose earnings multiple is lowest exactly when its earnings peak. But the premium now paid is at a cyclical high in gross margin and at the top of a five-year re-rating, so the table separates the franchise, which is the strongest in mega-cap technology, from the entry price, which is not.

### The recommendation and what changes it

The rating is Watchlist with a zero position, a 12-24 month horizon and medium evidence confidence. It changes in three directions. Downside: the bear case already carries a 40% weight at $224 (-35.8%); at 26x on bear EPS of $8.00 the value is $208 (-40%), and a final EU structural remedy that removes commission makes the bear the base at $270. Upside: at an 8.0% required return the same cash flows support $259-$330, so a ten-year yield below 4% would move the rating to Hold and raise the valuation score to 4. Operating: a December-2026 quarter with gross margin at 48% or better excluding refunds and Services growth in double digits would justify a starter position inside the band. None of the three is in evidence today [S7, S10].

### Position sizing and the regime

Position sizing is where the negative expected return becomes an instruction. The Kelly fraction, with its inputs in the table below, is negative because the probability-weighted outcome sits below the current price, so the optimal bet is zero. A long-only fund that wants the name would cap it at the weight in the table once the entry conditions are met, because the downside is a multiple event rather than a solvency event: net cash and the services annuity survive every stress in the risk matrix.

| Position and regime input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Bull probability and outcome | 20% and +15.8% to $404 | S93 |
| Base probability and outcome | 40% and -6.9% to $325 | S93 |
| Bear probability and outcome | 40% and -35.8% to $224 | S93 |
| Upside-to-downside ratio | 0.44 | S93 |
| Kelly fraction | -1.62, so zero position | S93 |
| Cap once entry conditions are met | 3-5% of the portfolio | S6 |
| S&P 500 | 7,720.39, +12.8% year to date, 1.6% below the high | S8 |
| VIX | 17.20, 52nd percentile of the past year | S9 |
| Ten-year Treasury and 2s10s curve | 4.99% and +37bp | S10, S37 |
| Technology ETF against the S&P 500, one month | -3.0% against +0.7% | S17, S25 |
| Credit spreads | 86bp investment grade, 314bp high yield | S39, S40 |

The regime supports patience rather than exposure. The index is near a record with volatility mid-range and credit spreads tight, yet technology is being rotated out and the ten-year yield stands near its cycle high, so a cash yield well below it has no valuation cushion. In a rotation-out regime with open EU and DOJ cases, the regime-appropriate approach is to discount the target multiple, which puts the top of the buy band below the level the scenario table implies.

| 5 | The buyback continues at 1.6% of shares a year | 1.6% | A May 2027 authorisation materially below $100bn | Halving it removes 0.8 points of annual EPS growth | low | The May 2027 authorisation | S5, S6 |

### Next diligence and the conditions to invest

Three actions come before any purchase. First, read the FY2026 10-K due with the 2026-11-02 results for the intangible note — lives, counterparty and the $5,075M current portion that implies $0.16 of FY2027 amortisation — and for the fourth-quarter buyback pace. Second, wait for the December-2026 quarter and test two numbers: gross margin at 48% or better excluding tariff refunds, and Services growth at 10% or more with the EU's post-October commission card in force. Third, ask Apple investor relations, and if necessary the court record, for the share of Services revenue from App Store commission and from the Google default payment. The conditions for a starter position are a price at or below $309, a gross margin print at or above 48% excluding refunds, and double-digit Services growth; the conditions to pass are a gross margin below 47% like-for-like or a final remedy that removes commission [S6, S147].

::: takeaways
1. Apple earns a composite of 5.7: a 9 for business quality and an 8 for its moat are outweighed by a 2 for valuation at 40.0x trailing earnings against an 18.1x peer median, so the watchlist rating is a price judgement rather than a quality one [S93].
2. The position is zero at $348.91: the Kelly fraction is -1.62 on a 20/40/40 distribution whose probability-weighted value is $300 (-14.0%), and the maximum loss to the bear case is -35.8% [S6].
3. Buy only at $273-$309 on $9.10 of risk-adjusted FY2027 EPS, and only after the December-2026 quarter shows gross margin at 48% or better excluding tariff refunds with Services growth in double digits [S7].
:::

arguments.hypothesis: Apple is a high-quality cash compounder whose installed base and services mix support durable free cash flow, but at $348.91 (40.0x trailing earnings, 32.5x EV/EBIT, 36.5x FY2027E against an 18.1x four-peer median) the price offers no margin of safety. The 2026 acceleration came from hardware mix, memory-driven competitor retreat and 2 points of one-off tariff refunds; the probability-weighted outcome is $300 (-14.0%) on a 20/40/40 distribution. View: Watchlist, zero position, conditional starter at $273-$309 on $9.10 of risk-adjusted FY2027 EPS, subject to a December-2026 quarter with gross margin at 48% or better excluding refunds and double-digit Services growth.
arguments.industry_map: Consumer electronics and platform-services value chain: upstream semiconductors and components (TSMC leading-edge SoCs; memory, displays, cameras, RF from Korea, Japan and the US) → assembly and test (Foxconn, Luxshare and Tata in India; concentrated in China with an India ramp to 28% of iPhone assembly in 2026) → distribution (carriers, retailers, direct online; 40% direct and 60% indirect) → installed base of more than 2.5bn active devices → monetization through hardware plus services (App Store, iCloud, advertising, Apple Pay, subscriptions, licensing) → replacement and upgrade cycle. Decisive bottleneck: control of the silicon/OS/developer ecosystem at the premium end, which sustains pricing and the installed-base annuity; binding constraints are advanced-node supply, memory cost, China/India manufacturing geopolitics and platform-regulation limits on services take rates. Apple's place: the integrator with pricing power at the premium end and 65% of the $600-plus handset tier, monetizing the installed base through services at a 76% gross margin.
arguments.policy_lens: Material. Jurisdictions mapped: United States (DOJ antitrust case filed 2024-03-21, App Store remedy risk, the Epic contempt finding of 2025-04-30 and Supreme Court review agreed 2026-06-30, IEEPA tariffs struck down 2026-02-20, Section 232 semiconductor review with no Apple tariffs on 2026-01-14, Section 301 measures live), European Union (DMA Article 6(4) case with a 10% of worldwide sales cap, the €500m fine of 2025-04-23, the new fee card live 2026-10-01, General Court upholding gatekeeper status 2026-07-08), China (SAMR, 48 developers' complaint of 2026-06-23, data-security rules), India (production-linked incentives; ₹2 lakh crore of iPhone exports in FY2026), plus UK CMA strategic market status of 2025-10-22, Korea's KRW 20.81bn fine of 2026-10-28 and Japan's MSCA effective 2025-12-18. Policy affects App Store take rate, services margin, supply-chain geography and China demand; the report prices a regulatory haircut to services rather than a binary outcome.

arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at a record $348.91 on 2026-10-29, a market capitalisation of $5,092.1B and an enterprise value of $5,029.9B, 5.0% above its 50-day average and 17.8% above its 200-day. The shares have returned 28.6% over twelve months against 13.2% for the S&P 500, and essentially the whole gain arrived after April 2026, so the move since the 2026-07-31 third-quarter results extends an already extended re-rating. The market backdrop is risk-on but narrow: the S&P 500 is at 7,720.39, +12.8% year to date and 1.6% below its high, the VIX is 17.20 at the 52nd percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99% with the 2s10s curve at +37bp. Technology is being rotated out even as the index sits near a record — the sector ETF is 3.0% lower over one month against the S&P 500's +0.7% — and Apple is 7.25% of SPY, so passive flows cut both ways [S7, S8, S9, S10, S17, S97].

The report's answer is Watchlist with a zero position. Apple passes the tests that describe a great business and fails the one that describes a good purchase: the need is real, the capability is defensible and the economics scale, but at $348.91 the price already capitalises a second growth engine that no filing evidences. Consensus agrees on quality — 43 analysts carry a $332.39 average target, 4.7% below the close, and Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one to six between May and October 2026 — so the difference is not about the franchise but about the multiple, and on quality the thesis is consensus. Our view is that the 2026 acceleration came from hardware mix, Android retreat under memory costs and 2 points of tariff refunds rather than from a new cycle; the probability-weighted outcome is $300, -14.0%, on a 20/40/40 distribution [S93, S6].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Watchlist | Zero position at $348.91; conditional starter at $273-$309 | 5.7 | Medium | 12-24 months | S93, S6 |
:::

The strongest positives are cash generation, the services annuity and the balance sheet: free cash flow exceeds the two largest peers' combined, net cash is intact, and Services earns the highest gross margin in the group. The most important risks are repricing events already dated: memory costs that management calls a hundred-year flood, an App Store take rate being set by courts rather than by competitors, and a Google payment on annual non-exclusive terms under appeal. The bear case is a multiple event rather than a solvency event, which is why the position is zero rather than short. Follow-up diligence is specific: the FY2026 annual report's intangible note due with the fourth-quarter results, the December-quarter gross margin excluding refunds, and Services sub-segment disclosure.

### Company claims and their status

| Claim | Status | Evidence | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| The App Store ecosystem is worth $1.4trn | Company framing | Only $149bn of it is commission-bearing digital goods | S95, S150 |
| Siri AI and the iPhone 18 Pro feature set | Company claim, not independently tested | Apple newsroom description of the 2026-09-18 launch | S116 |
| Apple Foundation Models run on Google Gemini | Partially verified | Agreement announced 2026-01-12 and corroborated by Reuters; scope, fee and term not disclosed | S115 |
| Ten million foldable units planned for 2026 | Supplier plan, not an Apple disclosure | Reported by CNBC/Nikkei | S113 |
| The Greater China rebound reflects renminbi strength and mix | Unverified management explanation | Revenue of $64,839M is filed; the cause is not disclosed | S6 |
| Memory is a hundred-year flood for hardware costs | Management statement, corroborated | Mobile DRAM contract prices rose 78-83% quarter on quarter for LPDDR5X in Q2 2026 | S97, S148 |

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Business | Nine-month FY2026 revenue of $364,357M, +16.1%; iPhone is 53.9% of it at $196,515M and Services $91,728M at a 76% gross margin | S6 |
| Price | $348.91 at the 2026-10-29 close, $5,092.1B market cap; 40.0x trailing and 36.5x FY2027E earnings against an 18.1x four-peer median | S7, S93 |
| Growth | Global shipments fall 16.7% while ASPs rise 27.6%; FY2027 consensus EPS growth decelerates to 8.1% | S79, S93 |
| Margins | 49.1% gross margin in nine months includes 2 points of tariff refunds; memory is the named cost risk | S6, S97 |
| Regulation | The Google default payment is reported at $20bn a year, 12.9% of trailing operating income; the EU Article 6(4) case carries a 10%-of-sales cap | S147, S134 |
| Balance sheet | Trailing free cash flow of $136,683M at 1.06x net income on capex of 2.2% of sales; net cash $62,173M | S47 |
| Management | John Ternus became CEO on 2026-09-01; buybacks at 40.0x give a 2.5% earnings yield; no insider bought a share in twelve months | S54, S6 |
:::

::: efficiency
| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $364,357M, +16.1% | S6 |
| Gross margin | 49.1%, including 2 points of tariff refunds | S6 |
| Operating margin | 33.6% | S6 |
| Free cash flow, trailing | $136,683M | S47 |
| Cash conversion | 1.06x net income | S47 |
| Capex | $10,041M, 2.2% of revenue | S47 |
| Net cash | $62,173M | S47 |
| Buybacks, trailing | $82,226M, 1.6% of shares | S6 |
| Dividend | $15,640M, 0.31% yield | S47 |
| Valuation | 40.0x TTM, 32.5x EV/EBIT, 36.5x FY2027E | S7, S93 |
:::

::: one-question
What share of Services revenue and gross profit comes from App Store commissions and from Google's search-distribution payments, the two cash flows the EU, US courts and the DOJ are directly repricing?

It decides whether regulation is a sentiment issue or an earnings event: Services produced $82.3bn of gross profit in FY2025 at a 75.4% margin, and a tenth of that pool is $8.2bn, 6.2% of operating income, which would turn the bear case from a multiple event into an earnings event. Apple discloses neither figure, so only the court exhibits and the Article 6(4) decision can settle it [S147, S134].
:::

::: takeaways
1. Watchlist, not buy: at $348.91 the shares cost 40.0x trailing earnings against an 18.1x peer median, and the probability-weighted value is $300, -14.0% [S93].
2. The business is not the problem: $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income and a 76% services gross margin are the strongest in mega-cap technology; the multiple is the risk [S47].
3. Buy at $273-$309 on $9.10 of risk-adjusted FY2027 EPS, only after a December-2026 quarter with gross margin at 48% or better excluding refunds and double-digit Services growth [S6].
:::

# Investor Reviewer Lens — Investment Committee Challenge

Use this lens after drafting the report and before final QA. The purpose is to simulate a skeptical investment committee partner who reads the report with fresh eyes and asks the uncomfortable questions that the analyst may have overlooked.

This is NOT the same as the red-team pass (which challenges the thesis at a strategic level). The investor reviewer focuses on **detail sharpness, completeness, and unverified claims**.

## Role

You are an experienced investment committee member with 20+ years of experience in both primary and secondary markets. You have reviewed thousands of investment memos and your specialty is finding the gaps — the competitor the analyst forgot, the founder detail that was glossed over, the market number that's cited without a source, the product comparison that's too vague to be useful.

You are skeptical but constructive. Your goal is not to kill the deal but to make the analysis bulletproof.

## Review Protocol

### Round 1: Completeness Sweep

Scan the entire report and flag anything missing or insufficient:

#### Company Overview
- [ ] Is the legal entity structure mapped with **exact ownership percentages**? If "approximately" or "estimated," flag it.
- [ ] Is the timeline specific (YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD), or does it use vague language like "recently," "soon," "currently"?
- [ ] Does the cap table distinguish between share classes (ordinary, preferred A/B/C, super-voting)?
- [ ] Are liquidation preferences, anti-dilution provisions, and board composition addressed?
- [ ] Is the VIE structure (if any) explained with the names of nominee shareholders and the specific contracts?

#### Team
- [ ] For **each** founder and C-suite executive: is education specified (institution + degree + year)?
- [ ] For each: is the career chronology specific (company + role + dates + achievements), or just "worked at Google"?
- [ ] Are prior exits, patents, publications, and industry recognition listed?
- [ ] Is the "why this team for this problem" argument explicit and evidence-backed?
- [ ] Are reference check targets identified?

#### Technology & IP
- [ ] Are patents listed with **numbers, dates, jurisdictions, and legal status**?
- [ ] Is the technology explained in accessible but precise terms (not just buzzwords)?
- [ ] Is there a technology comparison table vs. competitors?
- [ ] Are third-party dependencies (APIs, cloud, hardware, licensed IP) identified?
- [ ] Is the TRL (Technology Readiness Level) assessed with evidence?

#### Products
- [ ] For **each** product: is the competitive alternative landscape mapped?
- [ ] For medical/biotech: is the current standard of care detailed with specific drugs/procedures, efficacy data, and limitations?
- [ ] For SaaS: is the customer's current workflow ("before this product") described?
- [ ] Are unit economics broken down (price, COGS, CAC, LTV, payback)?
- [ ] Are customer concentration risks quantified?

#### Market
- [ ] Is the market **bifurcated** into domestic and international (by region)?
- [ ] For each region: market size, growth rate, regulatory barriers, competitors?
- [ ] Are TAM/SAM/SOM built from bottom-up estimates, not just citing an industry report?
- [ ] Is the "why now" argument specific to this market and time?

#### Competition
- [ ] Are **ALL** material competitors listed? Challenge: "I can think of [X] — why aren't they here?"
- [ ] For each competitor: product comparison, funding, team, market share?
- [ ] Is the company's true differentiator clearly articulated vs. each major competitor?
- [ ] Are substitutes and "do nothing" (status quo) included as competitors?

#### Financials
- [ ] Are revenue/profit figures sourced and dated? If estimated, is this clearly stated?
- [ ] Are margins broken down by product line (not just blended)?
- [ ] Is burn rate, runway, and next financing need calculated?
- [ ] For public equities: are consensus estimates, guidance, and earnings surprise history included?

#### Valuation
- [ ] Are multiple valuation methods used (not just one)?
- [ ] Are comparable companies justified (not just cherry-picked to make the target look cheap)?
- [ ] Is the margin of safety explicitly calculated?

### Round 2: Claim Verification Challenge

For each **positive claim** in the report, ask:

1. **What is the exact source of this claim?** (Company pitch deck? Media article? Regulatory filing? Analyst estimate?)
2. **Has this claim been independently verified?** If only company-provided, mark as low-confidence.
3. **Is there a specific number or is it vague?** "Market-leading" → "What is the exact market share? From what year? According to whom?"
4. **Is the comparator fair?** "Better than competitors" → "Which competitors? On what dimension? Measured how?"

### Round 3: Missing Competitor Challenge

Actively think of competitors the analyst may have missed:

- **Geographic blind spot**: "You only listed US competitors. What about the Chinese company [X] doing the same thing at half the price?"
- **Adjacent entrant**: "Has [Amazon/Google/Tencent/Alibaba] shown any interest in this space? Could they enter with their existing infrastructure?"
- **Substitute**: "What if customers just use [manual process / generic tool / internal build] instead of buying this product?"
- **Open-source**: "Is there an open-source alternative that could commoditize this?"
- **Academic/lab**: "Are there research groups or university spin-outs working on the same problem?"

### Round 4: Product/Market Fit Challenge

- "What is the single hardest thing about selling this product? (Not building it — selling it.)"
- "Who is the actual budget owner? Does the buyer have authority to spend, or do they need approval from someone else?"
- "What is the typical sales cycle? Has it been validated with real customers or is it an estimate?"
- "If the product is so good, why aren't customers adopting it faster?"
- "What do the **lost deals** tell us? Which competitor did they choose and why?"

### Round 5: Number Stress-Test

For each key number in the report:

- "Where did this number come from? Is it a company projection, an industry average, or an analyst estimate?"
- "If this number is 30% worse than stated, does the investment thesis still hold?"
- "What is the range of estimates from different sources? If only one source, why?"
- "Is this number annual, quarterly, cumulative, or 'run-rate'? These are not the same thing."

The reviewer produces a structured challenge document at `_work/investor_review.md`:

## Integration with Harness Loop

After the reviewer produces `_work/investor_review.md`:

1. The harness `gate` command checks that the review exists and that all "Critical" items are resolved
2. The analyst must address each item — either by adding the missing information, or by explicitly stating why it cannot be obtained
3. Unexplained "Critical" items block the gate
4. The loop re-runs the reviewer after each revision until no Critical items remain

### Reviewer Severity Levels

| Level | Gate Behavior |
|-------|--------------|
| **Critical** | Blocks gate. Must be resolved or explicitly acknowledged as unobtainable with confidence impact stated. |
| **Important** | Warning. Should be resolved but does not block gate. Unresolved items listed in report appendix as "areas for further diligence." |
| **Minor** | Informational. Does not block. |

## Reviewer Style Guide

The reviewer should be:

- **Specific, not generic.** "The competitor section is weak" → "You listed 3 competitors. I count at least 7 in this space: [A, B, C, D]. Also, what about the Chinese companies [E, F] that are doing this at 40% of the price point?"
- **Constructive, not destructive.** "This analysis is shallow" → "The unit economics section has the right structure, but needs: (1) actual CAC numbers broken down by channel, not a blended estimate; (2) LTV calculated from cohort data, not a top-down assumption; (3) payback period in months, not years."
- **Evidence-demanding, not evidence-replacing.** "You claim 80% market share. According to whom? What year? What geography? Consumer or enterprise? Units or revenue? If you can't source this, either find the data or downgrade the claim."
- **Investor-perspective, not academic.** "Interesting technology. But how does the company make money from it? What's the unit economics of one deployment? Who pays — the hospital, the insurer, or the patient? What's the reimbursement code?""}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 公司概览 Company Overview (company_overview, revision 2 by Company Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,995 characters)
Apple at 2026-10-30 is an iPhone business with a services margin bolted on — 53.9% of nine-month FY2026 revenue comes from iPhone while 76.3%-gross-margin Services supply a quarter of sales — and that shape, not the $62.2bn of net cash, is what the next twelve months test. Apple Inc. is a California corporation whose shares trade on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars, with one class of common stock: 50,400,000 thousand shares authorised at $0.00001 par and 14,608,963 thousand outstanding at 2026-06-27, down from 14,773,260 thousand at 2025-09-27. Ownership is index-dominated: Vanguard held 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% of the 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, while all directors and executive officers together held 9,079,765 shares, or 0.062%, and Tim Cook held 3,280,295. There is no controlling shareholder, no VIE and no second voting class, so structural governance risk is low and policy risk arrives through regulators, not a controller [S6, S52].

The entity map is a jurisdiction map, not an intellectual-property map: Exhibit 21 names 19 subsidiaries, omits the rest as insignificant and states no entity's function. Four are Irish, the largest foreign cluster, and the tax note records that the FY2025 provision fell $10.7bn year on year because of the State Aid Decision, leaving an effective rate of 15.6% in FY2025 and 17.6% in nine months of FY2026. Against Microsoft, which funded $139.5bn of FY2026 investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow for AI capacity, Apple converts operating cash into buybacks and almost none into owned compute: coherent for an installed-base franchise, fragile if AI becomes the upgrade reason. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 5 by Company Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,919 characters)
Apple's capital-allocation record is exceptional and its 2025-2026 product execution is not: the company returned $73.9bn, 63% of operating cash flow, in nine months while growing revenue 16%, but that growth needed a 33% rise in R&D and a $13.3bn build in gross intangibles, and the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed inside twenty months. John Ternus, 50 when appointed, became chief executive and a director on 2026-09-01; Tim Cook, 65, moved to executive chair after fifteen years as CEO; Sabih Khan, 58, has been chief operating officer since 2025-07-25 and joined Apple in August 1995; Kevan Parekh has been chief financial officer since January 2025; Deirdre O'Brien is a senior vice president; Jennifer Newstead became general counsel on 2026-03-01. The six named executive officers in the 2026 proxy — Cook, Kate Adams, Khan, Luca Maestri, O'Brien and Parekh — include no AI or machine-learning title, so the function's leadership is not disclosed through Section 16 or proxy channels [S54, S52].

The succession is continuity by design, and that is the point to price. Ternus holds a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and worked as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems before joining Apple's product design team in 2001; he became a vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and joined the executive team in 2021, and the company credits him with the iPad and AirPods introductions and 3D-printed titanium work in Apple Watch Ultra. Apple has done this before: Cook, an Auburn industrial engineer with a Duke MBA and a Fuqua scholarship, was an operations executive promoted from within in 2011 and leaves an installed base above 2.5 billion active devices in more than 200 countries, Services grown 28% to $109.2bn between FY2023 and FY2025, and 8 hardware launches in FY2025 alone — iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, Watch Series 11, Watch SE 3, Watch Ultra 3 and AirPods Pro 3. Independent reporting says the same from outside — a well-liked product engineer expected to make "small touches" rather than a disruptive break, and explicitly not the product visionary type, against a record including Vision Pro, delayed Siri work and a criticised Liquid Glass redesign. Continuity protects the cash engine; it supplies no evidence of a new product cycle [S112, S111, S87].

Capital allocation is where this team earns its premium, and the peer contrast is stark. In nine months of FY2026 Apple returned $73.9bn — $62.1bn of repurchases and $11.8bn of dividends — equal to 63% of $117.0bn of operating cash flow, while spending $6.8bn, or 1.9% of revenue, on capital expenditure; FY2025 was $89.3bn of repurchases plus $15.4bn of dividends under a $100bn authorisation, dividend raised to $0.26 then $0.27. Microsoft chose the opposite trade in FY2026, funding $139.5bn of investing outflows from $182.9bn of operating cash flow and lifting capital spending by $51.4bn for AI capacity. Apple's returns on capital are high because it owns almost no compute [S6, S5, S50].

The spending pattern says the company knows it is behind. Research and development went from $29,915m in FY2023 to $31,370m in FY2024 and $34,550m in FY2025, then reached $34,035m in nine months of FY2026, up 33% year on year and 9.3% of revenue, with management attributing it to AI infrastructure and headcount. In the same nine months gross intangible assets rose to $38,220m from $24,950m and other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn. Apple is buying capability as well as building it; the filing discloses neither the counterparty nor the exclusivity, and operating margin held at 33.6% only because gross margin rose 2.3 percentage points. A licensing commitment of that size is a permanent transfer of margin to an unnamed party, so it belongs in the valuation work as an assumption rather than a footnote [S6, S5].

Pay and board composition reinforce the status quo. Cook's 2025 target equity was $50m with 75% performance-based, his base salary has not changed since 2016, his total target compensation sits in the 80th to 90th percentile of the primary peer group, and 2021-granted performance RSUs vested at 187% of target on 2024-10-01, or 477,301 shares, on relative total shareholder return against the S&P 500; he has already met the age-65, ten-year condition for retirement vesting. After the transition the board has nine directors aged 51 to 77, including Levinson (75, since 2000), Sugar (77, since 2010), Jung (67, since 2008) and Wagner (64, since 2014), with Wanda Austin (2024) the only new independent since 2021. Relative-TSR scorecards pay for beating the index, a target reachable through buybacks and margin management without a new product cycle, and oversight of the AI transition sits with a board whose members have finance, consumer-brand and aerospace backgrounds rather than AI operating experience [S52, S54].

Insider behaviour gives no support to the price. Over the twelve months to 2026-10-29 there were 46 sale transactions of 687,127 shares for $208.0m, 43 under Rule 10b5-1 plans, and no purchases; Art Levinson sold $86.7m, Cook $80.4m, O'Brien $23.1m and Ternus $8.5m on 2026-10-02. Plans mute the sales; the signal is no discretionary purchase between $300 and $345. The counter-case is about product rather than people: independent reporting describes an unresolved AI gap versus OpenAI, a memory shortage squeezing margins and product misfires, while the same filings show 16% revenue growth and 22% iPhone growth, so the team is executing the current cycle well and the next one is unproven. Confidence is high on the record and low on the forward judgement. Four checks matter: Ternus's pay metrics, the executive who owns AI, the licensing counterparty, and whether the board adds an operating AI director [S41, S87].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 技术与产品 Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 4 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,947 characters)
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a new A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable wherever Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thinning at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: a narrow lead, defended by integration

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design — not transistor count — is what lets a phone chip deliver desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The measured lead has narrowed to a rounding error at the top: the A19 Pro scored 4,019 on Geekbench 6 single-core against 3,846 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 4.5% gap in Apple versus Qualcomm single-core performance, and the same comparison reportedly favours Qualcomm in multi-threaded and graphics tests [S117]. Apple's answer is to compete on what the benchmark does not measure: an in-house modem, battery life, imaging and a protected hinge.

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple frames this as hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it unveiled "all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 in June 2026, shipping it on the iPhone 18 Pro that reached stores on 2026-09-18. R&D rose 33% to fund AI infrastructure and headcount while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, or 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so Apple buys capability as an operating cost instead of building a hyperscale compute base. The strategic cost is that model quality, query data and the pace of improvement now sit with a competitor that also sells phones.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**
The next generation of Apple Foundation Models is built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the ceiling of the assistant is set by a competitor while the differentiation left to Apple is integration, privacy and distribution.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Cellular modem | In-house | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S116 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Apple is unique among the five in owning the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image, and Qualcomm sells silicon to the rest. Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant.

### Form factors: the stagnation critique is out of date

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Suppliers were told to prepare 10 million foldables for 2026, up from 7-8 million, inside at least five new iPhone models spread across the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027 [S113, S121]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units, the Duo changes the price ladder and the narrative rather than the revenue base. The patent record shows the mechanics were engineered before launch: the granted patent US 12,164,344 covers a multi-link hinge with interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch, and US2025/0120026 adds a folding expandable display.

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared its Hypertension Notification Feature on 2025-09-11, its Sleep Apnea Notification Feature on 2024-09-13, granted the Hearing Aid Feature a De Novo on 2024-09-12, and cleared a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, which raises the wearable's value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration: Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 4% in FY2025 to $35,686m and grew 6% in Q3 FY2026 to $7,883m.

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability. Strip out 2 percentage points of tariff refund and the 50.1% gross margin is nearer 48%, so the technology premium is being defended by price increases while memory costs rise. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,906 characters)
**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth $134.9 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter. Trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million implies a 12.3% CAGR from $85,200 million in FY2023 and divides into $48.19 per active device a year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12.3% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 7.0% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 30% in Greater China to $64,839 million, 16% in Europe, 11% in the Americas, 10% in Japan and 19% in the rest of Asia-Pacific, lifting Greater China from 15.5% of FY2025 revenue to 17.8%. China's own market fell 4.2% in the first half of 2026, so Apple's gain was share rather than tide: its unit share rose to 18.1% from 13.9% because it held prices while Android rivals raised theirs, and IDC expects the second-half decline in China to widen to 20% year on year. India repeats the pattern at a different scale — 33.2 million units in the second quarter of 2026, down 11.1%, average prices up 14.4% and Apple leading by value — while in the United States, where iOS carries 58.35% of mobile web traffic, growth runs through carrier trade-in programmes rather than new users. [S6, S80, S96, S89]

Policy both creates and caps this demand, and the dates are live. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation published initial results on 2026-01-14 without imposing tariffs on Apple's products, and the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, for which Apple has claimed refunds; Section 301 duties and further sector measures remain open. In Europe, Apple restructured its App Store terms in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, effective October 2026. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. Demand that was subsidy-created is now subsidy-dependent; demand that is trade-in-driven has held. [S6, S81, S80]

::: evidence
**Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on just over 1 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40.0% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at $48.19 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]
:::

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism rather than a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist through the forecast horizon. What is not durable is the current growth rate: the Greater China acceleration rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its own unit forecast within a single quarter, and the trackers disagree materially on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much iPhone strength was pulled forward? Second, does China hold its current unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? Third, how much of services revenue is exposed to the EU's restructured commissions and to the US remedies ordered against Google's search-payment arrangements, and what services margin has Apple assumed?"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 2 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,937 characters)
**Apple wins the value pool and only holds the unit pool, and the competitor that matters most is Samsung.** In Q2 2026 Apple's global smartphone market share rose 3.9 points to 20.2% and its units 14.9% in a market that fell 7.4%, while it held 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales in the first half and took 84% of that tier together with Samsung. In PCs it is fourth at 9.9% and in wrist-worn devices second at 17%; Apple's annual report concedes "a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables markets". It is not losing, but the position is concentrated in one tier whose most dangerous attacker makes the memory Apple must buy. [S79, S77, S90, S88, S5]

iPhone competition is now a contest of supply and balance sheets rather than features. Samsung grew units 8.1% and leads at 22.7%; Xiaomi fell 26.4%, OPPO 17.1% and vivo 19.6% as memory costs exceeded 65% of the bill of materials at the low end. Apple's counter is scale and early supply commitments, and IDC has it on track for a record 22% annual share in 2026. Counterpoint has Samsung at 24% and the market 11% smaller; both agree on direction. The asymmetry is that Samsung's memory division sits on the winning side of the same cost shock squeezing Xiaomi and OPPO, so Samsung can fund handset price competition longer than any Android rival — that, not product superiority, makes it the most dangerous competitor. [S79, S78]

Inside China the constraint has a name. Huawei leads with 22.6% of a market that fell 4.3% in the second quarter of 2026, growing 19.4%, while Apple rose to 18.1% from 13.9% and grew 24.4%, taking share from OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi and Honor, which fell 9.5% to 21.7%. Huawei is the only rival that has beaten Apple in a large premium market, on 2025 revenue of CNY880.9 billion, net profit of CNY68 billion and R&D of CNY192.3 billion (21.8% of revenue). Its weakness is geographic: without Google Mobile Services it cannot convert that position outside China, so the threat is a ceiling on Apple's China premium share rather than a global assault. Apple's China revenue grew 30% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 because it did not follow Android vendors into price increases; that advantage ends when they stop raising prices. [S80, S82, S6]

PCs and wearables show what happens without a premium monopoly. Mac shipments grew about 10% in a quarter when the PC market fell 4.9% to 68.2 million units, yet Apple is fourth at 9.9% behind Lenovo, HP and Dell, with Mac at 8.1% of FY2025 revenue ($33,708 million). In wrist-worn devices Huawei leads at 20.2%, Apple and Xiaomi are tied at 17%, and Samsung fell 20.7% to 5.8%: cheap Chinese hardware has taken the unit lead while Apple keeps the profit through attach and price. Neither line moves the group: Mac and wearables were $69.4 billion of FY2025 revenue against iPhone's $209.6 billion. [S90, S88, S5]

Services faces substitutes and rule-makers at once. Google Play substitutes on Android, Microsoft and Meta compete for advertising and subscription dollars, and Apple's disclosures are concrete: EU terms restructured in August 2026 to a 5% commission outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links from October 2026, US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02 that could bar Google from paying Apple for search distribution, and civil suits alleging monopolisation in "performance smartphones". The assistant layer was licensed rather than won: Siri was rebuilt on Google's Gemini models at WWDC in June 2026, reported at about $1 billion a year and undisclosed in either company's latest SEC filing. The 76.3%-gross-margin services stream is Apple's most valuable revenue and its most exposed. [S81, S5, S13, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,814 characters)
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for its life at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the growth came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth. The investor implication is that earnings durability has to be underwritten as a hardware cycle with a services annuity attached, not the other way round [S5, S6].

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Europe 16.1% and the Americas 11.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle with Pro-model mix plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, or 6.4%, against 16.1% revenue growth. iPhone concentration also rose to 53.9% of sales from 50.4%, which is the number to watch if the upgrade cycle rolls over.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is $48.9 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case from 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect lands on the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

The table below is the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow: an estimate in its construction, disclosed in its dollars.

|---|---|---|---|

| — Products / Services | $123 / $44 | $145 / $49 | S5, S6 |
| Gross profit (margin) | $78 (46.9%) | $95 (49.1%) | S5, S6 |
| R&D | $13.8 | $18.2 | S5, S6 |
| SG&A, the acquisition-cost proxy | $11.0 | $11.9 | S5, S6 |
| Operating profit (margin) | $53 (32.0%) | $65 (33.6%) | S5, S6 |
| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | $40 | $59 | S5, S47 |
| LTV at a four-year device life (assumption) | $312 | $381 | S5, S6 |
| LTV : acquisition cost | 28:1 | 32:1 | S5, S6 |

Beyond the waterfall, two numbers set the risk envelope, both computed on the disclosed 2.5-billion-device base with nine months annualised at four-thirds. The operating structure breaks even at an estimated $153bn of annual revenue, 31.5% of the current run-rate, because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6.4% a year, so a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable; and the 32:1 lifetime-to-acquisition ratio is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates more services revenue than an iPad or Mac buyer, Apple does not disclose the split, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin (Source: S6).
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA (Source: S56, S65).
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify (Source: S59).
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months (Source: S11, S13).
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow, but partly diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years — $4.4bn a year of extra expense — or over ten."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 财务分析 Financial Analysis (financials, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,648 characters)
Apple's statements show a business that converts almost all of its profit into cash on capex that is trivial for a company of its size, but the fiscal 2026 margin rests on a tariff refund the company itself calls one-off and on an intangible build the 10-Q does not explain, so the current margin is a peak to discount rather than a run-rate to capitalise.

### Growth re-accelerated, and the tax line explains two years of noise

Nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 16.1% to $364,357M and operating income 21.7% to $122,432M, lifting the operating margin to 33.6% from 32.0% in FY2025 and 29.8% in FY2023. That acceleration sits beside a FY2023-FY2025 revenue CAGR of 4.2%, so it is a cycle, not a trend. Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, the company's own approximation, and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at 1.71 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin. The diligence question that follows: what are those intangibles, over what life are they amortised, and does the expense arrive in FY2027 [S6, S5]?

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On $100.4bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is 128%, and on total assets 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns $128.1bn of after-tax operating profit on $100.4bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity. The capital-allocation version of the same point: trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow and retired 1.6% of diluted shares, lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth; but at $348.91 on 2026-10-29, or 40.0 times trailing EPS, each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%, so it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, covered 1.4 times by free cash flow and already slowing — $62,094M in nine months against $70,579M [S7, S10, S11, S13, S47].

### Base, upside and downside: gross margin is the variable that moves the outcome

On a base case of $504bn of FY2027 revenue (+6% on an estimated FY2026 of $475bn), a 48.0% gross margin and 15.6% operating expense, operating income is $163.3bn (32.4%) and EPS $9.30; an upside case of 10% revenue growth with a 49.5% margin gives $10.24, and a downside of a 2% revenue decline with a 45.0% margin gives $7.58. Every 100bp on gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, 3.1% of base-case net income; 100bp on the tax rate is $1.6bn, 1.2%. Gross margin dominates, and it is the line management has already flagged: memory and storage costs that price increases "may not" offset. That is the variable to underwrite — whether Apple can hold a 48% margin when Samsung is earning 55% on the components inside its phones [S59, S60].

::: info warning
The fiscal 2026 margin is not a clean run-rate: 2 percentage points of the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin came from tariff refunds the company calls a one-off, inventories rose 94% to $11,092M from the FY2025 year-end close, and $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition in investing cash flow and no note disaggregating them (Source: S6, S47). Amortisation of that build is the most likely source of an FY2027 operating-margin surprise that no current line item shows.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 2 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,679 characters)
Apple's strategy is a defence that is working, but it is a defence. Services at a 75.4% gross margin, a premium multi-launch product cadence and Indian assembly are turning a maturing hardware franchise into a higher-margin, less tariff-exposed annuity — while the two forces that set the ceiling, competition law in Brussels and Washington and the cost of renting intelligence from Google, are outside management's control [S115]. The plan protects cash generation; it does not restore growth.

### Services carry the margin, and the law is repricing them

Services reached $109,158m in FY2025, up 13.5% from $96,169m, at a 75.4% gross margin against 73.9% a year earlier, and grew 14% to $91,728m in the nine months to 2026-06-27 with a 75.6% margin in the June quarter. Because Apple books only its commission on third-party App Store sales, on a net basis, a dollar of services revenue carries 75 cents of gross profit against a consolidated gross margin of 46.9% in FY2025 and 50.1% in Q3 FY2026, so every point of mix shift raises group profitability without a single extra iPhone sold. That engine is now being repriced by courts and regulators rather than by competitors. On 2025-04-30 the California District Court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction and barred it from imposing any commission on purchases made outside an app, referring the matter to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt, with the Ninth Circuit hearing Apple's expedited appeal in October 2025; in Europe the Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 and its Article 6(4) investigation into Apple's contract terms remains open, carrying potential fines of up to 10% of worldwide net sales; and the Department of Justice's antitrust suit, filed on 2024-03-21, seeks equitable relief over the same conduct [S5]. Because Apple has already introduced alternative fee structures and external purchase links in the EU, some revenue migrates rather than vanishing, but the direction is one-way: from commission, which scales with third-party commerce and costs nothing, to advertising, subscriptions and device price, which Apple must earn back every year.

### Manufacturing diversification is real but partial

India assembled 23% of global iPhone output in 2025, up from 14% in 2024, and is projected to reach 28% in 2026, while China's share fell from 83% to 74% [S119, S6]. That is the fastest supply-chain shift in Apple's history and it is being paid for twice: duplicated tooling and lower ramp yields on one side, dependence on Chinese components on the other, since Indian final assembly still imports much of what it screws together. Scale is the offset. Apple secured components for 80 million new-model phones for the second half of 2026 and plans more than 220 million units of production in 2026, which lets it pre-buy memory while Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo cut targets below 100 million units each, and inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m in nine months. Tariff policy remains live: the U.S. Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20 and Apple has applied for refunds, while Section 301 duties and the Section 232 semiconductor investigation continue.

### China: revenue up, units down, share up

Greater China revenue rose 22% to $18,816m in Q3 FY2026 and 30% to $64,839m in nine months, after falling 4% in FY2025 and 8% in FY2024. The unit picture is different: China's smartphone market fell 15.4% year on year in Q3 2026, Apple's shipments fell 4.3%, its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%, and Huawei grew 17.3% to 21.1% [S5, S122]. Apple is therefore monetising a shrinking market through mix and price rather than winning volume — defensible while the installed base upgrades to Pro and foldable models, fragile if Huawei's domestic supply chain keeps improving or price elasticity bites. The "China share loss" bear case was right about the trend through FY2025 and wrong about 2026 so far.

### Capital allocation is the strategy's quiet centre

Apple spent $6,799m on property, plant and equipment in nine months, 1.9% of revenue, while raising R&D 33% to $34,035m: the AI build is an operating cost, not a capital programme. That leaves cash for shareholders — $10.0bn of accelerated share repurchases entered in May 2026 and a $0.27 quarterly dividend — against $146.5bn of cash and marketable securities and $82.3bn of term debt at 2026-06-27. Net income rose 27% and diluted EPS 29% in the June quarter, so buybacks added 1.6 points of per-share growth [S6, S47]. The risk is not leverage but under-investment: buying capability from Google protects the margin while leaving Apple without owned compute or models, and gross intangibles rising from $24,950m to $38,220m in nine months suggests more value is being purchased than built.

### Resources fit the plan, with one exception

The organisation changed at the top on 2026-09-01, when John Ternus moved from Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering to CEO and Tim Cook became Executive Chair. A hardware engineer running a hardware-led strategy is continuity, and the first launch under him came in on schedule [S54]. The exception is political capital: the decisions that matter most over the next three years — the DMA Article 6(4) remedy, the Ninth Circuit appeal and the DOJ case — are legal negotiations in which a product engineer has less experience than the chair he replaced.

### What must be true within twelve months

Four tests decide whether this is a durable annuity or a melting ice cube. Gross margin must hold near the mid-forties once the tariff refund washes out of the comparison while memory costs rise; the December 2026 quarter is the first clean read. Services growth must stay in double digits with advertising and cloud replacing any commission lost to the Epic order and the DMA — a mix the company has not had to prove for a full year. The iPhone Duo must sell into its planned volume, because a miss would confirm that premium pricing has reached the limit of what the installed base will pay. And no adverse final remedy should land in Brussels or at the Ninth Circuit that removes commission revenue retroactively. The signposts are concrete: the December-quarter margin, the advertising-versus-App-Store split in the FY2026 10-K, any disclosed size for the Gemini contract, IDC's China share for Q4 2026 and the Article 6(4) decision.

For a long-only watchlist the conclusion is that Apple's strategy earns ownership of the cash flow rather than payment for growth: the services annuity justifies a premium multiple while growth holds in double digits, the buyback compounds per-share value, and the plan creates no new growth engine before 2028. What the record cannot settle is the economics of the AI arrangement — the fee, the term and whether Apple retains query data — and the value of the health and finance adjacencies, neither of which is broken out; Apple discloses no services sub-segment revenue, so the durability of the margin engine has to be inferred from aggregate growth. Confidence in the direction of the strategy is high and in its durability medium, because the plan is well funded and well executed but its two binding constraints are a regulator and a competitor."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 风险评估 Risk Assessment (risk, revision 2 by Red Team Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,780 characters)
Apple's risk is not a broken franchise but three repricings arriving together — the memory inside its phones, the two services cash flows it does not disclose, and the discount rate — and the valuation prices only the third. Nine-month FY2026 revenue of $364,357M and a 49.1% gross margin describe a cyclical high, which is when a 40.0x trailing multiple has least room. I keep the recommendation and change the weights: bear from 30% to 40%, bull from 25% to 20%, because the bull's central assumption, an AI-driven replacement cycle, has no unit evidence while the bear's drivers are dated events already in motion. That moves the weighted outcome from $314 to $300, and to $294 if bear EPS is $8.00 rather than $8.60; the entry band should fall from $287-$325 to $273-$309 on $9.10 of risk-adjusted FY2027 EPS. Memory is the likeliest single driver at 65% probability: mobile DRAM contract prices rose 78-83% quarter on quarter for LPDDR5X and 70-75% for LPDDR4X in the second quarter of 2026, average DRAM content still rises to 8.5GB a handset in 2026, and the July 2026 10-Q says component costs may materially negatively impact gross margin and revenue. Every 100bp of gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, $0.30 of EPS and 3.1% of base-case net income, so a 300bp miss costs $0.90, or 9.4% of the $9.56 consensus. The pass-through test is already running: the iPhone 18 Pro opened at $1,199 and pre-order wait times were "lukewarm", with GF Securities' Jeff Pu cutting production estimates in the week of 2026-09-15. Price defends the margin and price suppresses the units, so the two levers cannot both work at full strength; a December-2026 quarter below 47% gross margin like-for-like settles it. [S6, S148, S151]

### Services is named but not sized

Google's payment to be Safari's default has been reported at $20bn a year since the 2022 trial record; Apple discloses neither the sum nor its margin, so the figure is unverified by the company. At $20bn it is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue of $109,158M and 12.9% of trailing operating income of $154,859M. The US remedy kept the payments lawful, banned exclusivity and moved contracts to annual renegotiation; Google filed its defence of the Safari agreement by 2026-05-22 and the remedy is under cross-appeal. Half of it is $0.56 of EPS, 5.9% of consensus. The App Store: $149bn of the $1.4trn ecosystem is commission-bearing digital goods, and Apple's EU terms from August 2026 charge 5% on transactions outside the store and 20% on external payment links from 2026-10-01, against a 15% US proposal. A 1,000bp cut on half that pool is another $0.42. Together $0.98 — 10.3% of $9.56, the whole of the bear case's EPS haircut before memory, China or the renminbi. [S147, S150, S81]

### The bear case is too narrow, not too harsh

It applies a defensible multiple to a haircut two services items exhaust and leaves nothing for the cost shock already contracted. Refinancing is the stress that does not bind on $62,173M of net cash. A 30% free-cash-flow cut takes the discounted value to $128, which no committee should believe for a franchise earning 76% margins on a quarter of revenue, so the honest form of that stress is EPS minus 17% at 26x, or $206. Policy is priced the same way rather than listed: the €500m fine of 2025-04-23 showed the Commission will fine, the Article 6(4) case carries a statutory cap near $41.6bn of FY2025 revenue, the General Court upheld gatekeeper status on 2026-07-08, and Korea fined Apple and Google a combined $47.6m on 2026-10-28 — cash small beside the precedent that the commission is contestable. [S93, S47, S134, S136]

### The FY2027 charge the 10-Q hides in the current portion

Earnings are clean in the narrow sense and the margin is not. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, but the amortisation that never appears as a line item is visible on the balance sheet: the current portion of intangible assets, net rose to $5,075M from $2,208M, putting $2.9bn more amortisation into the next twelve months — 55bp of FY2027 revenue, $0.16 of EPS, 1.7% of consensus. Gross intangibles of $38,220M grew $13,270M in nine months while other purchase obligations rose $14.5bn to $29.3bn, so the item is a contracted cash cost as well as an accrual; paid over three years it is $4.8bn a year, 3.5% of trailing free cash flow. That is why 1.06x conversion is arithmetically sound and economically incomplete: had the $13,270M been cash, conversion was 0.96x. Inventories rose 94% to $11,092M, and the discount model deducts $13.7bn of stock compensation but not the $17.7bn annualised intangible purchases — which flatters value. [S6, S47]

### 40x needs a discount rate no long-only fund can underwrite

On the valuation's cash flows and 3.5% terminal growth, $348.91 is fair at a WACC near 6.8% — an equity risk premium of 1.6% over a 4.99% Treasury at a 1.1 beta. At 8.0% the value is $259, at 8.5% $233, at 9.5% $183; a 150bp fall in the ten-year to 3.5% still leaves $233, so 40x needs a required return below 7%. Two supports are weaker than the conclusion: the 18.1x peer median includes Samsung at 12.9x, a memory maker whose P/E is lowest exactly when its earnings peak, and the three US peers alone give 21.3x, so the premium is 88% rather than 122%. The $158 peer value and $183 DCF are below any multiple a premium franchise trades at, leaving the reverse DCF — 6.8% perpetual growth at 9.5% — as the argument to carry into committee. The buyback is not value-destructive because 2.5% compares badly with a 4.99% coupon; it is value-destructive because the price exceeds the valuation's own intrinsic value, and management agrees: repurchases fell 12.0% to $62,094M in nine months and no insider bought a share in the twelve months to 2026-10-29 while $208.0m was sold. [S93, S10, S41]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,919 characters)
Apple passes the first three tests of the thesis and fails the fourth, which is the only one that decides a purchase at today's price. The need is real and measured: more than 2.5 billion active devices generated $364,357M of revenue in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone at $196,515M and Services at $91,728M, and the group turned 49.1% of that revenue into gross profit and $136,683M of trailing revenue into free cash flow at 1.06 times net income on capex of 2.2% of sales. The capability is defensible: silicon-OS co-design, an in-house modem, four FDA clearances and 65% of the $600-plus handset tier are not replicable within a product cycle. The economics scale: Services earns a 76% gross margin on a quarter of revenue and needs no new distribution. What fails is the price. At $348.91 the buyer pays 40.0x trailing earnings, 32.5x EV/EBIT and 36.5x FY2027E EPS against a four-peer median of 18.1x and an S&P 500 forward multiple of 18.59x, for a company whose consensus EPS growth decelerates to 8.1% in FY2027 [S6].

### The disagreement is about what produced 2026

Our difference with consensus is about the durability of the current growth rate, not about quality. The 43-analyst consensus target of $332.39 sits 4.7% below the close, and Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one to six between May and October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6%, so the sell side is behind the price rather than bearish on the franchise. We agree with the quality call and disagree that 2026 revealed a second growth engine: global shipments fall 16.7% while ASPs rise 27.6%, so growth is price and mix; Apple's share gain came partly from Android vendors retreating under memory costs; and 2 points of the June-quarter 50.1% gross margin were one-off tariff refunds. The edge is narrow and it is about price rather than insight — if the ten-year yield falls below 4%, the same cash flows support a materially higher value and the caution weakens [S93].

The bear's three drivers are dated events already in motion — memory contracts repricing handsets, EU commission terms live since 2026-10-01, and a Google default payment on annual, non-exclusive terms under cross-appeal — while the bull's driver, an AI replacement cycle, has no unit evidence. That moves the weighted outcome from $314 to $300. At $348.91 the arithmetic gives an 8.4% annual return only if the multiple holds at 40x, below the 9.5% required return, so the buyer is paying for the bull case and receiving the base case [S6, S93].
