arguments.markdown:
Apple passes the first three tests of the thesis and fails the fourth, which is the only one that decides a purchase at today's price. The need is real: more than 2.5 billion active devices generated $364,357M of revenue in nine months of FY2026, with a 49.1% gross margin and $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income on capex of 2.2% of sales. The capability is defensible: silicon-OS co-design, an in-house modem, four FDA clearances and 65% of the $600-plus handset tier are not replicable within a product cycle. The economics scale: Services earns a 76% gross margin on a quarter of revenue. What fails is the price. At $348.91 the buyer pays 40.0x trailing earnings, 32.5x EV/EBIT and 36.5x FY2027E EPS against a four-peer median of 18.1x and an S&P 500 forward multiple of 18.59x on 2026-10-29, for a company whose consensus EPS growth decelerates to 8.1% in FY2027 [S6].

### The disagreement is about what produced 2026

Our difference with consensus is about the durability of the current growth rate, not about quality. The 43-analyst consensus target of $332.39 sits 4.7% below the close, and Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one to six between May and October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6%: the sell side is behind the price, not bearish on the franchise. We agree with the quality call and disagree that 2026 revealed a second growth engine: global shipments fall 16.7% while ASPs rise 27.6%, so growth is price and mix; Apple's share gain came partly from Android vendors retreating under memory costs; and 2 points of the June-quarter 50.1% gross margin were one-off tariff refunds. The edge is about price more than insight: below a 4% ten-year yield, the same cash flows support a higher value [S93].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 20% | AI replacement cycle extends; the foldable iPhone Duo opens a new price tier; Services holds double-digit growth with advertising and cloud replacing lost commission; gross margin near 49%; multiple stays at 40x | $404, +15.8% before the 0.31% dividend; 40x FY2027E EPS of $10.10 | December-quarter unit growth above 5%; Duo pre-orders; Services above 13% | S6, S93 |
| Base | 40% | Revenue growth decelerates to 10.3% and EPS to 8.1%; gross margin normalises to 48% as refunds wash out; regulation trims rather than removes commission; multiple drifts to the FY2025 year-end 34x | $325, -6.9%; 34x FY2027E EPS of $9.56 | FY2026 results on 2026-11-02; December-quarter margin near 48% excluding refunds | S93, S6 |
| Bear | 40% | Memory costs compress hardware margin; the App Store take rate settles toward the mid-teens and the Google payments are curtailed; FY2027 EPS $8.60; multiple mean-reverts to the FY2023 26x | $224, -35.8%; 26x FY2027E EPS of $8.60 | Gross margin below 47% like-for-like; a final EU remedy; a 2027 renewal below $20bn | S134, S147, S93 |
| Probability-weighted | 100% | 20% bull, 40% base, 40% bear | $300, -14.0% | — | S6, S93 |
:::

The 20/40/40 weighting rests on three dated drivers rather than on a narrative. Memory contracts are repricing handsets now: mobile DRAM contract prices rose 78-83% quarter on quarter for LPDDR5X in Q2 2026, and inventory is up 94% to $11,092M. The EU's new commission card has been live since 2026-10-01, with the Article 6(4) case still open. And the Google default payment, reported at $20bn a year and 12.9% of trailing operating income, now runs on annual, non-exclusive terms under cross-appeal. Against that, the bull case needs an AI replacement cycle in units, and the December-2026 quarter is the first place it could show; the filings carry features, not volume. Three dated downside mechanisms against one undated upside is why base and bear carry 40% each and the bull 20%, and why the weighted outcome is $300, 14.0% below the price [S148, S134, S147, S6].

### What has to be true

| Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gross margin holds at or above 48% excluding tariff refunds through FY2027 | medium-low | A December-2026 quarter below 47% like-for-like, or iPhone 18 price increases that do not stick | Each 100bp is $5.0bn of operating income, $0.30 of EPS and 3.1% of base-case net income | Mobile DRAM and NAND contract prices; Samsung's memory-division margin | S6, S148 |
| The App Store take rate settles at 15-26% and the Google payments survive in some form | medium | A final EU Article 6(4) structural remedy, or a US order terminating the search payments | A 10% cut in Services gross profit is $8.2bn, 6.2% of operating income | Article 6(4) decision; the Supreme Court's Epic ruling; DOJ settlement terms | S134, S147 |
| Services grows at double digits and Greater China share holds near 18% | medium | Services growth below 8% for two quarters, or China unit share below 15% | A 300bp Services shortfall is 2.2% of operating income; China is 17.8% of nine-month revenue | Quarterly Services growth; IDC China share for Q4 2026 | S6, S80 |
| The exit multiple is 34x FY2027E EPS rather than 40x | medium | A ten-year Treasury materially below 4%, or FY2028 consensus EPS above $11 | Ten points of multiple move the two-year total return by 30 percentage points | Ten-year yield; sell-side target dispersion | S93, S10 |
| The buyback continues at 1.6% of shares a year and Q4 lands near $113.3bn of revenue and $1.96 of EPS | medium-high | A May 2027 authorisation materially below $100bn, or a September-quarter miss | Halving the buyback removes 0.8 points of annual EPS growth | The 2026-11-02 print; the May 2027 authorisation | S93, S5 |

### The analogs say the multiple, not the business, decides

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | cautionary | 1999-2012 | Free cash flow per share tripled from $1.15 to $3.45 while the share price fell 54% from $58.38 to $26.71 and $100 became $51 with dividends reinvested; the P/FCF multiple went from 51x to 8x | S154 |
| Cisco | cautionary | 2000-2025 | The split-adjusted record of $80.06 set on 2000-03-27 was not exceeded until 2025-12-10, a 25-year round trip, while revenue kept growing | S155 |
| Apple | cautionary | 2005-2014 | Apple's own P/E fell from 45.25x to 12.46x while earnings grew, so a low-teens multiple is in this company's history | S156 |
:::

No best-case analog is close enough to carry the bull case, and that absence is a finding: no mega-cap franchise in the register has re-rated upward from 40x without an acceleration in reported growth. The three cautionary cases teach a decision rule rather than a forecast: when the entry multiple is the main contributor to expected return, growth has to be demonstrated before the multiple is paid. Apple at 40.0x on 8.1% consensus EPS growth is a milder version of the same configuration — 37.3x price-to-free-cash-flow against Microsoft's 51x — but the mechanism is identical, and half of Apple's last five years of return came from the multiple rather than from earnings [S154, S155].

The strongest counter-case is that the quality deserves the multiple. Apple's trailing free cash flow of $136,683M is 1.71 times Microsoft and Alphabet combined, its 2.68% cash yield grows at 8% a year, and at an 8.0% required return the reverse DCF needs only 5.3% perpetual growth, which the 8.9% five-year free-cash-flow compound has already cleared. A long-only fund that owns the S&P 500 already holds 7.25% Apple through the index, so the active decision is whether to hold more than the benchmark; at 36.5x forward earnings the answer is no until the price or the growth changes [S97, S93].

### The price at which the case turns

The case turns at a price. Risk-adjusted FY2027 EPS of $9.10 is the base and bear cases weighted 60/40 — 0.60 × $9.56 + 0.40 × $8.42, where $8.42 is the bear's $8.60 less the $0.18 of FY2027 amortisation on the FY2026 intangible additions; the bull is excluded because it needs unit evidence the filings do not yet show. At 30-33x that gives an entry band of $273-$300, and the top is the probability-weighted value itself, so nothing above $300 should be bought. The decision tree: watch at zero position until the FY2026 fourth-quarter print on 2026-11-02 and the December quarter; buy a starter at or below $300 if gross margin holds at 48% or better excluding refunds with double-digit Services growth; pass if memory takes gross margin below 47% or a final remedy removes commission. Confidence is high that the current price has no margin of safety and medium on the level of fair value, because the WACC moves the discounted value from $153 to $230. Open diligence: does the FY2026 10-K disclose intangible lives and the licensing counterparty, and does the December quarter hold 48% gross margin ex-refund? The fastest falsifier is evidence that the AI cycle is producing units rather than features [S7].

The same partner asks why the base case exits at 34x when it simultaneously assumes EPS growth decelerating to 8.1%, and why 40.0x is treated as a peak when the FY2024 and FY2025 year-ends were 37.5x and 34.2x (S7, S93). The answer has to be the reverse DCF — 6.8% perpetual growth at a 9.5% required return — not the $183 point estimate, and the section should say so before it is asked.
answers.most_damaging_fact: The size and durability of Google's search-distribution payment. It is reported at $20bn a year (S147), equivalent to 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and 12.9% of trailing operating income (S6), it is not disclosed by Apple, and the remedy that preserved it put the contract on annual, non-exclusive terms that both parties are appealing (S149). If the true figure is $12-14bn and the 2027 renewal clears lower, the base case's 48% gross margin and $9.56 EPS are overstated by 4-6%, the bear becomes the base, and the entry band falls below $273 — the lower bound the recommendation names. If instead the payment is intact and rising, the bear's principal earnings driver disappears and the 40% bear weight is too high. The second most damaging fact is the 4.99% ten-year yield (S10): at a 7.0% required return the same cash flows give roughly $330 and the verdict softens to fairly valued.
answers.company_only_claims: Four positive claims rest on company material. The AI capability narrative — "all-new Siri AI" and the iPhone 18 Pro feature set — comes from Apple's newsroom (S116) and is not independently tested; the Gemini arrangement is corroborated by Reuters (S115) but its scope, fee and term are Apple's description. The $1.4trn App Store ecosystem is Apple's own framing (S95), and only $149bn of it is commission-bearing digital goods (S150). The 10 million foldable units planned for 2026 is a supplier plan reported by CNBC/Nikkei (S113), not an Apple disclosure, and the technology section presents it as the form-factor test. The attribution of the 30% Greater China rebound to renminbi strength and mix is management's explanation; the revenue is filed (S6) but the cause is unverified. By contrast, revenue, margins, buybacks, cash and the Microsoft and Alphabet capex comparisons are filing-verified (S5, S6, S47, S11, S13).
answers.generic_section: technology_product is the most generic. Its barrier table assigns difficulty scores of 8, 9, 7, 7 and 3, a composite of 7 and "3-4 years to replicate" with no method and no source, which is exactly the kind of unsourced scoring the rest of the report avoids. The silicon moat rests on one Geekbench 6 single-core run from a low-confidence blog (S117) showing a 4.5% lead, a gap inside normal run-to-run variance, and the section itself concedes that the benchmark cannot show sustained thermal performance. Its central judgement — that the moat is hardware and regulatory rather than intelligence — is probably right but needs a second independent benchmark, the Gemini fee and term, and the A20 Pro process node before a committee can lean on it. The exit section is second weakest: it is market data plus arithmetic, with no judgement about the buyer base.
answers.unpriced_risk: The services repricing is named in the thesis table but not carried into the recommendation's price. The bear case's 10% EPS haircut ($9.56 to $8.60) is fully consumed by the two services items — $0.56 from halving the Google payment and $0.42 from a 1,000bp cut on half the $149bn App Store pool — leaving nothing for a 300bp gross-margin miss worth $0.90, a 30% China decline worth $0.45, or the $0.16 FY2027 amortisation charge (S147, S150, S6). The second unpriced item is the $14.5bn rise in other purchase obligations to $29.3bn, a contracted cash cost that the 8% free-cash-flow growth path ignores.

Free cash flow 30% lower takes the DCF to $128, which no committee should accept for a 76%-margin franchise, so the honest statement of that stress is EPS minus 17% at 26x, or $206. Refinancing does not bind: $62,173M of net cash, $12,393M of 2026 term maturities covered by maturing securities and positive net interest income (S6, S47). An inventory write-down of 20% on $11,092M costs $2.2bn pre-tax, $0.12 of EPS. Even a 50%-smaller premium tier, which would halve iPhone revenue, leaves Apple with net cash and a services annuity, so the bear case is a multiple event rather than a solvency event — which is why zero position at $348.91 is defensible and a short is not.

arguments.markdown:
Apple scores 5.7 out of 10, and the score is a verdict on price rather than on quality. The business earns a 9 and the ecosystem an 8, but valuation earns a 2 and regulatory exposure a 4, and those two dimensions carry 30% of the weight against a 36.5x forward multiple that the market has already paid. The composite is the weighted average of the table below; quality justifies a premium multiple, not the size of the premium the shares now carry [S93].

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Business quality and unit economics | 15% | 9 | Nine-month FY2026 revenue of $364,357M at a 49.1% gross margin, with $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income on capex of 2.2% of sales | S6, S47 |
| Competitive moat and ecosystem | 15% | 8 | More than 2.5bn active devices and 65% of the $600-plus tier; the assistant layer is licensed from Google, so the intelligence moat is rented | S6, S115 |
| Market growth | 10% | 5 | Shipments fall 16.7% while ASPs rise 27.6%, so growth is price and mix; FY2027 consensus EPS growth decelerates to 8.1% | S79, S93 |
| Margin durability and pricing power | 10% | 6 | Memory costs may materially hurt gross margin; mobile DRAM contract prices rose 78-83% quarter on quarter for LPDDR5X in Q2 2026, and 2 points of the June-quarter margin were tariff refunds | S6, S148 |
| Management and capital allocation | 10% | 6 | $82,226M of trailing buybacks at 40.0x earnings give a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.99% Treasury; the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed within twenty months | S6, S47 |
| Earnings quality and balance sheet | 5% | 8 | Free cash flow converts at 1.06x net income with net cash of $62,173M, but $13,270M of gross intangibles were added in nine months and $5,075M is already current | S6, S47 |
| Regulatory and policy risk | 10% | 4 | The Google payment is reported at $20bn a year, 12.9% of trailing operating income; the EU Article 6(4) case carries a 10%-of-sales cap with terms live since 2026-10-01 | S147, S134 |
| Valuation and margin of safety | 20% | 2 | 40.0x trailing, 32.5x EV/EBIT and 36.5x FY2027E against an 18.1x peer median and an 18.59x S&P 500 forward multiple on 2026-10-29; the DCF returns $183 | S7, S93, S153 |
| Catalysts and exit path | 5% | 5 | The 2026-11-02 print and the May 2027 buyback authorisation are dated, but the largest technology deal ever is 1.35% of enterprise value | S92, S91 |
| Composite | 100% | 5.7 | Weighted average of the nine dimensions | S6, S93 |

The quality scores are not in dispute. A franchise that converts a quarter of its revenue into gross profit and funds its buybacks from operations rather than from the balance sheet deserves a premium to the market, and the four-peer median is pulled down by a memory maker whose earnings multiple is lowest exactly when its earnings peak. But the premium now paid is at a cyclical high in gross margin and at the top of a five-year re-rating, so the table separates the franchise, which is the strongest in mega-cap technology, from the entry price, which is not.

### The recommendation and what changes it

The rating is Watchlist with a zero position, a 12-24 month horizon and medium evidence confidence. It changes in three directions. Downside: the bear case already carries a 40% weight at $224 (-35.8%); at 26x on bear EPS of $8.00 the value is $208 (-40%), and a final EU structural remedy that removes commission makes the bear the base at $270. Upside: at an 8.0% required return the same cash flows support $259-$330, so a ten-year yield below 4% would move the rating to Hold and raise the valuation score to 4. Operating: a December-2026 quarter with gross margin at 48% or better excluding refunds and Services growth in double digits would justify a starter position inside the band. The band is $273-$300: $9.10 of risk-adjusted FY2027 EPS — the base and bear cases weighted 60/40, with the bull excluded until units appear — at 30-33x, capped at the $300 probability-weighted value so that no purchase inside it is negative-expectation [S7, S10].

### Position sizing and the regime

Position sizing is where the negative expected return becomes an instruction. The Kelly fraction, with its inputs in the table below, is negative because the probability-weighted outcome sits below the current price, so the optimal bet is zero. A long-only fund that wants the name would cap it at the weight in the table once the entry conditions are met, because the downside is a multiple event rather than a solvency event: net cash and the services annuity survive every stress in the risk matrix.

| Position and regime input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Bull probability and outcome | 20% and +15.8% to $404 | S93 |
| Base probability and outcome | 40% and -6.9% to $325 | S93 |
| Bear probability and outcome | 40% and -35.8% to $224 | S93 |
| Upside-to-downside ratio | 0.44 | S93 |
| Kelly fraction | -1.62, so zero position | S93 |
| Cap once entry conditions are met | 3-5% of the portfolio | S6 |
| S&P 500 | 7,720.39, +12.8% year to date, 1.6% below the high | S8 |
| VIX | 17.20, 52nd percentile of the past year | S9 |
| Ten-year Treasury and 2s10s curve | 4.99% and +37bp | S10, S37 |
| Technology ETF against the S&P 500, one month | -3.0% against +0.7% | S17, S25 |
| Credit spreads | 86bp investment grade, 314bp high yield | S39, S40 |

The regime supports patience rather than exposure. The index is near a record with volatility mid-range and credit spreads tight, yet technology is being rotated out and the ten-year yield stands near its cycle high, so a cash yield well below it has no valuation cushion. In a rotation-out regime with open EU and DOJ cases, the appropriate approach is to discount the target multiple rather than to pay it.

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Exit multiple 34x FY2027E rather than 40x | 34x | A ten-year Treasury materially below 4%, or FY2028 consensus EPS above $11 | Ten points of multiple move the two-year return by 30 points; 26x gives -28.7% | high | Ten-year yield; sell-side target dispersion | S93, S10 |
| 2 | Gross margin holds at 48% excluding tariff refunds | 48% | A December-2026 quarter below 47% like-for-like | 100bp is $5.0bn of operating income and $0.30 of EPS; a 300bp miss removes 9.4% of consensus EPS | high | Mobile DRAM and NAND contract prices | S6, S148 |
| 3 | The Google payments survive and the take rate settles at 15-26% | $20bn payment intact | A final EU Article 6(4) remedy or a 2027 renewal below current terms | Halving the payment is $0.56 of EPS, 5.9% of consensus; losing it entirely is $1.13 | high | Article 6(4) decision; renewal terms | S147, S134 |
| 4 | FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.56 is delivered | $9.56 | A September-quarter miss or a weak December guide | A 5% revenue miss is $2.30 of EPS at a 48% gross margin | medium | The 2026-11-02 print | S93, S6 |
| 5 | The buyback continues at 1.6% of shares a year | 1.6% | A May 2027 authorisation materially below $100bn | Halving it removes 0.8 points of annual EPS growth | low | The May 2027 authorisation | S5, S6 |
:::

### Next diligence and the conditions to invest

Three actions come before any purchase. First, read the FY2026 10-K due with the 2026-11-02 results for the intangible note — lives, counterparty and the $5,075M current portion that implies $0.16 of FY2027 amortisation — and for the fourth-quarter buyback pace. Second, wait for the December-2026 quarter and test two numbers: gross margin at 48% or better excluding tariff refunds, and Services growth at 10% or more with the EU's post-October commission card in force. Third, ask Apple investor relations, and if necessary the court record, for the share of Services revenue from App Store commission and from the Google default payment. The conditions for a starter position are a price at or below $300, a gross margin print at or above 48% excluding refunds, and double-digit Services growth; the conditions to pass are a gross margin below 47% like-for-like or a final remedy that removes commission [S6, S147].

::: takeaways
1. Apple earns a composite of 5.7: a 9 for business quality and an 8 for its moat are outweighed by a 2 for valuation at 40.0x trailing earnings against an 18.1x peer median, so the watchlist rating is a price judgement rather than a quality one [S93].
2. The position is zero at $348.91: the Kelly fraction is -1.62 on a 20/40/40 distribution whose probability-weighted value is $300 (-14.0%), and the maximum loss to the bear case is -35.8% [S6].
3. Buy only inside $273-$300 — 30-33x $9.10, the 60/40 base-bear EPS — and only after the December-2026 quarter shows gross margin at 48% or better excluding tariff refunds with Services growth in double digits [S7].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 3 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,814 characters)
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for its life at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the growth came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth. The investor implication is that earnings durability has to be underwritten as a hardware cycle with a services annuity attached, not the other way round [S5, S6].

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Europe 16.1% and the Americas 11.4%. Apple reports segments geographically and discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists in the filings; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle with Pro-model mix plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, or 6.4%, against 16.1% revenue growth. iPhone concentration also rose to 53.9% of sales from 50.4%, which is the number to watch if the upgrade cycle rolls over.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is $48.9 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case from 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect lands on the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| Offer | Pricing metric | Rate | Effective | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| App Store In-App Purchase, EU | % of developer transaction | 26% (15% for small-business, mini-app and video programmes and auto-renewing subscriptions after year one) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, alternative in-app payment | % of developer transaction | 20% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| Alternative marketplaces and web distribution, EU | % of digital transactions | 5% Core Technology Commission; per-install Core Technology Fee removed | 2026-10-01 | S56, S57 |
| App Store, US, In-App Purchase | % of developer transaction | 15-30% by developer size and category | current | S65 |
| App Store, US, external-link purchases | % (proposed, needs court approval) | 5-15% tiers; 0% was ordered in April 2025 | 2026-08-14 | S64 |
| iPhone | $ of revenue per unit | not disclosed; the 10-K reports iPhone net sales with no unit count | n/a | S5 |

### Unit economics: $194 of revenue and $65 of operating profit per device

The table below is the closest thing to a unit P&L that Apple's disclosures allow: an estimate in its construction, disclosed in its dollars.

| Line, per active device per year | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 (estimate) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $166 | $194 | S5, S6, S58 |
| — Products / Services | $123 / $44 | $145 / $49 | S5, S6 |
| Gross profit (margin) | $78 (46.9%) | $95 (49.1%) | S5, S6 |
| R&D | $13.8 | $18.2 | S5, S6 |
| SG&A, the acquisition-cost proxy | $11.0 | $11.9 | S5, S6 |
| Operating profit (margin) | $53 (32.0%) | $65 (33.6%) | S5, S6 |
| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | $40 | $59 | S5, S47 |
| LTV at a four-year device life (assumption) | $312 | $381 | S5, S6 |
| LTV : acquisition cost | 28:1 | 32:1 | S5, S6 |

Beyond the waterfall, two numbers set the risk envelope, both computed on the disclosed 2.5-billion-device base with nine months annualised at four-thirds. The operating structure breaks even at an estimated $153bn of annual revenue, 31.5% of the current run-rate, because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6.4% a year, so a 10% revenue decline would still leave the company solidly profitable; and the 32:1 lifetime-to-acquisition ratio is closer to a subscription business than to a hardware assembler [S6, S47, S58]. The caveat is that these are averages: an iPhone buyer generates more services revenue than an iPad or Mac buyer, Apple does not disclose the split, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin (Source: S6).
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA (Source: S56, S65).
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify (Source: S59).
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months (Source: S11, S13).
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow, but partly diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation of those intangibles will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years — $4.4bn a year of extra expense — or over ten."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at a record $348.91 on 2026-10-29, a market capitalisation of $5,092.1B and an enterprise value of $5,029.9B, 5.0% above its 50-day average and 17.8% above its 200-day. The shares have returned 28.6% over twelve months against 13.2% for the S&P 500, and essentially the whole gain arrived after April 2026, so the move since the 2026-07-31 third-quarter results extends an already extended re-rating. The market backdrop is risk-on but narrow: the S&P 500 is at 7,720.39, +12.8% year to date and 1.6% below its high, the VIX is 17.20 at the 52nd percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99% with the 2s10s curve at +37bp. Technology is being rotated out even as the index sits near a record — the sector ETF is 3.0% lower over one month against the S&P 500's +0.7% — and Apple is 7.25% of SPY, so passive flows cut both ways [S7, S8, S9, S10, S17, S97].

The report's answer is Watchlist with a zero position. Apple passes the tests that describe a great business and fails the one that describes a good purchase: the need is real, the capability is defensible and the economics scale, but at $348.91 the price already capitalises a second growth engine that no filing evidences. Consensus agrees on quality — 43 analysts carry a $332.39 average target, 4.7% below the close, and Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one to six between May and October 2026 — so the difference is not about the franchise but about the multiple, and on quality the thesis is consensus. Our view is that the 2026 acceleration came from hardware mix, Android retreat under memory costs and 2 points of tariff refunds rather than from a new cycle; the probability-weighted outcome is $300, -14.0%, on a 20/40/40 distribution [S93, S6].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Watchlist | Zero position at $348.91; conditional starter at $273-$300 | 5.7 | Medium | 12-24 months | S93, S6 |
:::

The strongest positives are cash generation, the services annuity and the balance sheet: free cash flow exceeds the two largest peers' combined, net cash is intact, and Services earns the highest gross margin in the group. The most important risks are repricing events already dated: memory costs that management calls a hundred-year flood, an App Store take rate being set by courts rather than by competitors, and a Google payment on annual non-exclusive terms under appeal. The bear case is a multiple event rather than a solvency event, which is why the position is zero rather than short. Follow-up diligence is specific: the FY2026 annual report's intangible note due with the fourth-quarter results, the December-quarter gross margin excluding refunds, and Services sub-segment disclosure.

### Company claims and their status

:::

::: one-question
What share of Services revenue and gross profit comes from App Store commissions and from Google's search-distribution payments, the two cash flows the EU, US courts and the DOJ are directly repricing?

It decides whether regulation is a sentiment issue or an earnings event: Services produced $82.3bn of gross profit in FY2025 at a 75.4% margin, and a tenth of that pool is $8.2bn, 6.2% of operating income, which would turn the bear case from a multiple event into an earnings event. Apple discloses neither figure, so only the court exhibits and the Article 6(4) decision can settle it [S147, S134].
:::

::: takeaways
1. Watchlist, not buy: at $348.91 the shares cost 40.0x trailing earnings against an 18.1x peer median, and the probability-weighted value is $300, -14.0% [S93].
2. The business is not the problem: $136,683M of trailing free cash flow at 1.06x net income and a 76% services gross margin are the strongest in mega-cap technology; the multiple is the risk [S47].
3. Buy only inside $273-$300 — 30-33x $9.10, the 60/40 base-bear EPS — and only after a December-2026 quarter with gross margin at 48% or better excluding refunds and double-digit Services growth [S6].
:::

Two accounting items explain most of the reported profit volatility either side of it: the $10.2bn one-time State Aid charge in FY2024 pushed the effective tax rate to 24.1% and cut net income to $93,736M, while the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, the company's own approximation, and $0.11 of the $2.02 diluted EPS. Apple publishes no adjusted EPS, so there is no non-GAAP reconciliation to police; the reported line is the only line, and the normalisation is the reader's job. What is not accounting is the cost trend: R&D rose 32.5% to $34,035M in nine months and stock-based compensation was 2.9% of revenue, so the operating margin is being defended with pricing and mix rather than operating leverage [S5, S6, S47].

### Cash conversion is better than the FY2025 ratio suggests

FY2025's 0.88x free-cash-flow conversion is the one ratio a screen will flag, and it is an artefact. The $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement was still in escrow at 2024-09-28 and was paid during FY2025, so cash taxes for the nine months to 2025-06-28 were $37,332M against $26,555M a year later; adjust for it and FY2025 conversion is 1.0x. In nine months to 2026-06-27, operating cash flow of $116,996M exceeded net income by $15,532M and working capital was a net $2.9bn drag rather than a source of cash, with an $8,316M receivables release and $5,671M of vendor receivables offset by a $16,266M build in other assets and a $5,461M inventory build. The structural reason conversion is high is the negative cash cycle — receivables 24.5 days, payables 98.3 days — and the structural reason it beats peers is capex: $10,041M trailing against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, which leaves Apple's free cash flow at 1.71 times the two combined [S47, S5, S11, S13].

### The balance sheet is a net-cash position with one unexplained line

At 2026-06-27 Apple held $146,517M of cash and marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M at the FY2025 year-end. Term-debt maturities are $12,393M in 2026, $10,078M in 2027 and $9,300M in 2028, covered by maturities in the securities portfolio, and the company earns net interest income (+$670M in nine months), so coverage does not bind. Commitments are modest: $4,752M of unconditional purchase obligations due in 2026, lease liabilities of $13.7bn, deferred revenue of $14.9bn (64% current) and $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits, of which $10.6bn would hit the tax rate if recognised. The line that needs explaining is intangibles: gross intangibles rose $13,270M to $38,220M in nine months with $5,075M already current, and there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow, so this is licensed or purchased capability rather than a bought business, and its amortisation is not yet in the margin. The diligence question that follows: what are those intangibles, over what life are they amortised, and does the expense arrive in FY2027 [S6, S5]?

### Returns are extraordinary, but the reported ROIC is arithmetic, not economics

Return on assets is 36.1% on the trailing twelve months and return on equity 148.8%, both far above Microsoft's 20.1% and 30.6% and lifted by a shrinking equity base. The computed ROIC of 320.6% is meaningless: buybacks of $263,210M in FY2023-FY2025 shrank invested capital to near zero, so the denominator, not the numerator, produces the number. On $100.4bn of net operating assets the after-tax return is 128%, and on total assets 33% — a wide premium to an estimated 9-10% cost of capital built on a 4.99% ten-year Treasury yield, and the honest statement is that Apple earns $128.1bn of after-tax operating profit on $100.4bn of operating capital. Against Microsoft's 35.2% and Alphabet's 30.1% TTM ROIC the comparison is not like-for-like, because those two now carry the data-centre capital Apple does not; that is the trade an investor is making — higher returns on lighter capital, in exchange for depending on partners for AI capacity. The capital-allocation version of the same point: trailing buybacks of $82,226M plus $15,640M of dividends absorbed 72% of free cash flow and retired 1.6% of diluted shares, lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth; but at $348.91 on 2026-10-29, or 40.0 times trailing EPS, each buyback dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield while the ten-year Treasury yields 4.99%, so it is per-share engineering with a below-risk-free return, covered 1.4 times by free cash flow and already slowing — $62,094M in nine months against $70,579M [S7, S10, S11, S13, S47].

### Base, upside and downside: gross margin is the variable that moves the outcome

On a base case of $504bn of FY2027 revenue (+6% on an estimated FY2026 of $475bn), a 48.0% gross margin and 15.6% operating expense, operating income is $163.3bn (32.4%) and EPS $9.30; an upside case of 10% revenue growth with a 49.5% margin gives $10.24, and a downside of a 2% revenue decline with a 45.0% margin gives $7.58. Every 100bp on gross margin is $5.0bn of operating income, 3.1% of base-case net income; 100bp on the tax rate is $1.6bn, 1.2%. Gross margin dominates, and it is the line management has already flagged: memory and storage costs that price increases "may not" offset. That is the variable to underwrite — whether Apple can hold a 48% margin when Samsung is earning 55% on the components inside its phones [S59, S60].

DSO = receivables / revenue x 365; DIO = inventory / cost of revenue x 365; DPO = accounts payable / cost of revenue x 365, all from closing balances; cash conversion cycle = DSO + DIO - DPO. Interest coverage = operating income / interest expense; goodwill and intangibles count what is tagged; capex / D&A = capital expenditure / depreciation and amortization. n/m = not meaningful (a base that is not positive). Interest expense = InterestExpense as tagged. Debt = LongTermDebtNoncurrent + LongTermDebtCurrent + CommercialPaper as tagged; finance leases are not included.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,906 characters)
**Apple's markets are shrinking in units and growing in value, and Apple already owns the value.** Global smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units, the steepest annual contraction IDC has recorded, while the average selling price rises 27.6% to $581 and total market value grows 6.3% to a record $613 billion. That inverts the usual market question. Sold at the market's average price, Apple's record 22% unit share would be worth $134.9 billion of that pool; its actual iPhone revenue of $245,540 million in the twelve months to 2026-06-27 is 1.8 times that. Sized in value, Apple is a 40-share business; sized in units, it is a fifth of a contracting market. [S79, S6]

The bottom-up method reaches the same place from the installed base. Apple reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter. Trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478 million implies a 12.3% CAGR from $85,200 million in FY2023 and divides into $48.19 per active device a year, earned at a 76.3% gross margin in the nine months to 2026-06-27 against 36.8% for products in FY2025. The consumer app market that feeds it spent $167 billion on in-app purchases in 2025, up 10.6%, with non-gaming outspending games for the first time. The unit of growth is no longer the handset sold but the revenue extracted per device already in a pocket, which is why a 12.3% services growth rate adds more gross profit than a 7.0% iPhone growth rate. [S58, S6, S83, S5]

Why now is a cost event, not a demand event. Memory prices are up nearly 300% year on year and exceed 65% of the bill of materials at the low end, which has erased the sub-$100 tier that absorbed 173 million units in 2025. Vendors with secured supply and premium mix gained — Apple by 14.9% and Samsung by 8.1% in units in a quarter when the market fell 7.4% — while Xiaomi fell 26.4%. Counterpoint's independent series puts the same quarter at -11%, a 3.6-point disagreement on magnitude that makes any single quarter's rate indicative only. The premium tier absorbed the shock: devices above $600 rose to a record 29% of unit sales in the first half of 2026 from 25% a year earlier, and Apple took 65% of them, with Apple and Samsung combined at 84%. [S79, S78, S77]

Geography moves the number more than product mix does. Nine-month FY2026 revenue grew 30% in Greater China to $64,839 million, 16% in Europe, 11% in the Americas, 10% in Japan and 19% in the rest of Asia-Pacific, lifting Greater China from 15.5% of FY2025 revenue to 17.8%. China's own market fell 4.2% in the first half of 2026, so Apple's gain was share rather than tide: its unit share rose to 18.1% from 13.9% because it held prices while Android rivals raised theirs, and IDC expects the second-half decline in China to widen to 20% year on year. India repeats the pattern at a different scale — 33.2 million units in the second quarter of 2026, down 11.1%, average prices up 14.4% and Apple leading by value — while in the United States, where iOS carries 58.35% of mobile web traffic, growth runs through carrier trade-in programmes rather than new users. [S6, S80, S96, S89]

Policy both creates and caps this demand, and the dates are live. The Section 232 semiconductor investigation published initial results on 2026-01-14 without imposing tariffs on Apple's products, and the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, for which Apple has claimed refunds; Section 301 duties and further sector measures remain open. In Europe, Apple restructured its App Store terms in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, effective October 2026. In China, the government subsidies that supported 2025 demand faded in the second quarter of 2026 and "618" smartphone sales fell close to 15%. Demand that was subsidy-created is now subsidy-dependent; demand that is trade-in-driven has held. [S6, S81, S80]

**Two sizing methods converge: Apple competes in a value pool it already dominates, not a volume pool it can outgrow.**

Top-down, the handset pool is worth $613 billion in 2026 on just over 1 billion units, and Apple's $245.5 billion of iPhone revenue equals 40.0% of it on a 22% unit share. Bottom-up, more than 2.5 billion active devices at $48.19 of services each produce the $120.5 billion services base, and the app-store spend feeding it grew 10.6% in 2025. [S79, S77, S58, S6, S83]
:::

The judgement this supports is narrower than a growth story. Apple's revenue can compound while its unit market shrinks, because price, premium mix and services attach do the work; that is a durable mechanism rather than a cyclical accident, since the cost structure squeezing low-end Android vendors is expected to persist through the forecast horizon. What is not durable is the current growth rate: the Greater China acceleration rests on price discipline that works only while rivals raise prices, on renminbi strength and on demand pulled forward ahead of Apple's own price increases.

Confidence in direction is high: the value pool and Apple's share of it are documented in filed revenue and two independent trackers. Confidence in magnitude is lower: IDC cut its own unit forecast within a single quarter, and the trackers disagree materially on the most recent quarter. Three gaps would change the picture and none is publicly disclosed — the commission-bearing slice of the App Store ecosystem, services revenue by category (to separate the Google-licensing and EU-exposed portions), and Apple's India revenue.

Three diligence questions follow. First, what share of growth in the next four quarters is price rather than units, and how much iPhone strength was pulled forward? Second, does China hold its current unit share once Android vendors stop raising prices, or was that a one-quarter window? {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 2 by Market Analyst, 8,937 characters)
**Apple wins the value pool and only holds the unit pool, and the competitor that matters most is Samsung.** In Q2 2026 Apple's global smartphone market share rose 3.9 points to 20.2% and its units 14.9% in a market that fell 7.4%, while it held 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales in the first half and took 84% of that tier together with Samsung. In PCs it is fourth at 9.9% and in wrist-worn devices second at 17%; Apple's annual report concedes "a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables markets". It is not losing, but the position is concentrated in one tier whose most dangerous attacker makes the memory Apple must buy. [S79, S77, S90, S88, S5]

iPhone competition is now a contest of supply and balance sheets rather than features. Samsung grew units 8.1% and leads at 22.7%; Xiaomi fell 26.4%, OPPO 17.1% and vivo 19.6% as memory costs exceeded 65% of the bill of materials at the low end. Apple's counter is scale and early supply commitments, and IDC has it on track for a record 22% annual share in 2026. Counterpoint has Samsung at 24% and the market 11% smaller; both agree on direction. The asymmetry is that Samsung's memory division sits on the winning side of the same cost shock squeezing Xiaomi and OPPO, so Samsung can fund handset price competition longer than any Android rival — that, not product superiority, makes it the most dangerous competitor. [S79, S78]

Inside China the constraint has a name. Huawei leads with 22.6% of a market that fell 4.3% in the second quarter of 2026, growing 19.4%, while Apple rose to 18.1% from 13.9% and grew 24.4%, taking share from OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi and Honor, which fell 9.5% to 21.7%. Huawei is the only rival that has beaten Apple in a large premium market, on 2025 revenue of CNY880.9 billion, net profit of CNY68 billion and R&D of CNY192.3 billion (21.8% of revenue). Its weakness is geographic: without Google Mobile Services it cannot convert that position outside China, so the threat is a ceiling on Apple's China premium share rather than a global assault. Apple's China revenue grew 30% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 because it did not follow Android vendors into price increases; that advantage ends when they stop raising prices. [S80, S82, S6]

PCs and wearables show what happens without a premium monopoly. Mac shipments grew about 10% in a quarter when the PC market fell 4.9% to 68.2 million units, yet Apple is fourth at 9.9% behind Lenovo, HP and Dell, with Mac at 8.1% of FY2025 revenue ($33,708 million). In wrist-worn devices Huawei leads at 20.2%, Apple and Xiaomi are tied at 17%, and Samsung fell 20.7% to 5.8%: cheap Chinese hardware has taken the unit lead while Apple keeps the profit through attach and price. Neither line moves the group: Mac and wearables were $69.4 billion of FY2025 revenue against iPhone's $209.6 billion. [S90, S88, S5]

Services faces substitutes and rule-makers at once. Google Play substitutes on Android, Microsoft and Meta compete for advertising and subscription dollars, and Apple's disclosures are concrete: EU terms restructured in August 2026 to a 5% commission outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links from October 2026, US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02 that could bar Google from paying Apple for search distribution, and civil suits alleging monopolisation in "performance smartphones". Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a new 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. ### Silicon: the lead widened, then narrowed again

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design — not transistor count — is what lets a phone chip deliver desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16, and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, run by one outlet on its own handsets, it scored 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. A second outlet's independent units scored 4,735 and 12,800 for the iPhone 18 Pro, and 4,741 and 12,789 for the Pro Max [S158]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the CPU difference is large enough to measure, and it rests on a process-node lead as much as on design.

rows.benchmark: Prior owner-cash build of $128.7B; reported FCF conversion of 1.06x net income; risk section's finding that $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition in investing cash flow.

rows.mechanism: With 85% of the price in the terminal value, the multiple and the discount rate, not the near-term cash flow, set the value.
rows.benchmark: Peer-median P/E method at $158 (18.1x x $8.72) and own four-year average year-end P/E at $271 (31.1x x $8.72).

rows.follow_up: What beta and equity-risk premium does the committee underwrite for a 40x mega-cap?
rows.confidence: medium — sensitive to WACC

rows.finding: At a 9.5% required return the $5,029.9B enterprise value needs free cash flow to compound at about 17% a year for ten years — 3.1x the 5.5% revenue CAGR from FY2021 to FY2026E and 1.9x Apple's 8.9% five-year FCF compound; at an 8.0% required return the bar falls to 5.7% in perpetuity.
rows.mechanism: The price is a call option on a second growth engine: only an acceleration far above the company's own history justifies it at a 9.5% discount rate.
rows.benchmark: 5.5% revenue CAGR FY2021-FY2026E; 8.9% five-year FCF CAGR; 17% is 3.1x and 1.9x those rates respectively.
rows.weakens: At an 8.0% required return the requirement is already met by history, so the bear case rests on the discount rate rather than on the cash flows.
rows.implication: The buyer is underwriting AI devices, Services or a new category that no filing yet evidences; wait for evidence or a lower price.
rows.follow_up: Which reported line would first show a second growth engine — Services sub-segments, wearables, or units?

rows.mechanism: A premium multiple on decelerating growth compresses when the growth evidence fails or the discount rate rises; the sell side lags the price rather than leading it.
rows.benchmark: Four-peer median 18.1x; three US peers 21.3x; Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 range 24.6-37.5x.

rows.mechanism: When the cash yield is below the risk-free rate, the buyer's return depends on growth and multiple, not on cash return.

plan.comparison_set: The report's own 20/40/40 distribution in sections 10, 11 and 14; Apple's 2021-2026 return decomposition; the largest technology transactions against Apple's enterprise value; the 30-34x entry band on blended FY2027 EPS.
plan.counter_evidence: Re-rating has punished patience — a holder who trimmed at 37.5x in fiscal 2024 missed the following 50% — and 1.6% share shrinkage plus 8.1% EPS growth plus the dividend is an 8-10% annual return with no re-rating, an acceptable long-only outcome.
plan.decision_question: For a long-only holder, what drives total return from here and what is the exit or trim discipline?
plan.mechanism: With the multiple at a five-year high, expected return is the weighted multiple change plus EPS change plus the dividend; no takeover premium exists at $5T, so the secondary market is the only exit and the entry price sets the return.
plan.prohibited: No 'well positioned', 'strong team', 'attractive entry', 'manageable risk'; no vague timing; no sentence about report construction; no rating language.
plan.thesis_sentence: Half of Apple's 134% five-year price gain came from its multiple rising from 26.6x to 40.0x, and with the probability-weighted outcome at $300 — 14.0% below the $348.91 close — the discipline for a long-only holder is a trim rule tied to the multiple and an entry band of $273-$300, not an exit on news.
plan.visual: Scenario table (Exit multiple x FY2027E EPS | Price | Return | Weight | Source) and the return decomposition table.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that prices the way out: the return decomposition, the named exit routes, precedent transactions and the entry/trim discipline, where the valuation section prices the business.

rows.benchmark: The previous 25/45/30 split gave $314 and -9.9%; sections 10, 11 and 14 run 20/40/40.
rows.confidence: medium — the weights are judgement, the arithmetic is exact
rows.finding: On the report's unified 20/40/40 distribution the outcomes are bull $404 (+15.8%, 40x x $10.10) at 20%, base $325 (-6.9%, 34x x $9.56) at 40% and bear $224 (-35.8%, 26x x $8.60) at 40%, giving a probability-weighted $300 and -14.0% from $348.91 (0.2 x 404 + 0.4 x 325 + 0.4 x 224 = $300.4).
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026-11-02 print move the bear weight above 40%?
rows.implication: No position at $348.91; the expected return is negative before the 0.31% dividend and the entry band sits at $273-$300.
rows.mechanism: The weighted exit multiple (32.0x) is 12.3 points below the 36.5x paid on FY2027E EPS, and the weighted EPS is 2.9% below consensus because the bear carries 40% weight; the two effects plus their interaction produce the -14.0%.
rows.weakens: The bull's driver, an AI replacement cycle, has no unit evidence, so the 20% weight could be too high; a ten-year yield below 4% would justify a higher multiple and a positive expected return.

rows.benchmark: S&P 500 at $217 and Dow Jones U.S. Technology at $287 per $100 over the five years to September 2025; Apple 18.5% a year against 16.8% and 23.5%.
rows.confidence: high — computed from dated closes and reported EPS
rows.finding: From the $148.96 close on 2021-11-01 to $348.91 on 2026-10-29 the shares returned 134.2%: diluted EPS $5.61 to $8.72 (+55.4%, 9.2% a year), the P/E 26.6x to 40.0x (+50.7%) and dividends 3.3% cumulative; multiple expansion is 48% of the log return.
rows.follow_up: What multiple is paid at the next entry, and does it leave any re-rating?
rows.implication: The historical return cannot repeat from a 40x starting multiple; the forward case must be earned from EPS and dividends.
rows.mechanism: Decomposition of total return into earnings growth, the price paid for earnings and cash returned identifies how much of the past is repeatable.
rows.weakens: The starting multiple was depressed by the 2022 compression, and a 12.8% share-count reduction flatters EPS growth versus net income.

rows.benchmark: Largest technology deal ever, Microsoft/Activision at $68.7B; $250M position is 1.9% of one day's $13.22B traded value.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: The only exit is the secondary market: no strategic buyer exists (the largest technology transaction ever is 1.35% of Apple's $5,029.9B enterprise value), the buyback retires 1.6% of shares a year on $82.2B, the dividend yields 0.31% and 38.67M shares trade daily.
rows.follow_up: Does the May 2027 authorisation match the $100B of 2025, and at what average price?
rows.implication: Size for a 30% drawdown and exit in the market; there is no premium to negotiate and no lock-up.
rows.mechanism: At $5T of equity the bid side is index and active flows, so the price realized is whatever multiple prevails at sale.
rows.weakens: Index weight of 7.25% means passive flows support the price on the way up and amplify the way down; a $100B buyback at a lower price would retire more stock.

rows.benchmark: Current 36.5x forward P/E on FY2027E EPS of $9.56; 34x on $9.10 is $309, above the $300 expected value.
rows.confidence: medium-high
rows.finding: The entry band is $273-$300: 30-34x the $9.10 blended FY2027 EPS (60% x $9.56 + 40% x $8.42), capped at the $300 probability-weighted value.
rows.follow_up: Is $8.42 the right bear EPS once the FY2027 amortisation is known?
rows.implication: Add only below $300; $287 is no longer the entry point and $309 must not be paid.
rows.mechanism: The cap binds because paying above expected value for a 40%-weighted downside is a negative-expectation trade even at a lower multiple.
rows.weakens: If FY2027 EPS lands at consensus $9.56 and the multiple holds 34x, the base case value of $325 exceeds the $300 cap.

rows.benchmark: Fourteen points of exit multiple produce the whole spread; two-year dividends add about 0.6%.
rows.confidence: medium — the exit multiple and horizon dominate
rows.finding: Holding two years to FY2028 EPS of $10.32, an exit at 40x returns +18.9% including dividends, at 34x +1.2% and at 26x -22.5% — a 41.4-point spread from the same three multiples as the distribution.
rows.follow_up: What would make 26x the wrong exit multiple — a lower ten-year yield or faster EPS?
rows.implication: The trim rule is a multiple rule, not a news rule.
rows.mechanism: Total return equals EPS growth times the change in the multiple plus dividends; the multiple term dominates when it moves fourteen points.
rows.weakens: A two-year horizon is arbitrary and a 40x exit requires the AI cycle to arrive after all.

rows.benchmark: The stock's 44.5% fifty-two-week range ($243.42-$351.73) and its five-year closing low of $125.02.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: The shares traded at $243.42 within the past year, 30.2% below the $348.91 close, and the five-year closing low of $125.02 is 64.2% below it.
rows.follow_up: What drawdown does the position sizing assume if the multiple reverts to 26x?
rows.implication: Size the position for a 30% drawdown as the ordinary case, not the tail.
rows.mechanism: At a 40x entry the same 26-40x multiple range that produced the last five years' gains produces the next five years' drawdowns.
rows.weakens: Both lows occurred at far lower multiples, so they understate the compression risk rather than overstate it.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a new 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable wherever Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thinning at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: the lead is measurable again, and narrower than it looks

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design — not transistor count — is what lets a phone chip deliver desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16, and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, run by one outlet on its own handsets, it scored 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the CPU difference is large enough to measure, and it rests as much on the process node as on design.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship SoC, iPhone 18 Pro | A20 Pro, TSMC N2 (2nm), 6-core CPU to 4.93GHz, 7-core GPU | Announced 2026-09-09 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, Geekbench 6 | 4,707 single-core / 12,598 multi-core | Outlet's own iPhone 18 Pro Max | S157 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same build | 3,588 / 10,207 | Outlet's own iQOO 15 | S157 |
| Apple's lead on that run | +31% single-core, +23% multi-core | Computed from the two runs | S157 |
| A20 Pro, second outlet | 4,735 / 12,800 | Independent iPhone 18 Pro unit | S158 |
| Sustained graphics, 20 loops | 80% stability vs 25% | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme, best to lowest loop | S157 |
| Geekbench AI 1.7 | 69,245 vs 83,047 | iPhone 18 Pro vs Galaxy S26 Ultra | S158 |
| iPhone revenue, Q3 FY2026 | $54,252m, +22% YoY | Reported, quarter ended 2026-06-27 | S47 |
| R&D expense, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |
| Wearables, Home and Accessories, FY2025 | $35,686m, -4% | Reported | S47 |
| Foldable units planned for 2026 | 10m, up from 7-8m | Supply-chain reporting | S113 |

### Sustained performance is the stronger claim, and it is not pure silicon

Peak scores flatter a chip; the 20-loop 3DMark stress test shows what a buyer actually gets after ten minutes. The A20 Pro held 80% of its best score, falling from 8,793 to 7,032, while the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 fell from 6,867 to 1,715, or 25% stability; a second outlet measured graphics stability rising to 79.4% from 65.2% a year earlier [S157, S158]. Apple's vapour chamber is three times larger and the memory no longer sits on the die, so part of the end-of-test gap is chassis rather than chip, and pairing Apple's largest phone with a thinner Android device overstates the silicon margin. Two counters keep this honest. Qualcomm's next part, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, is vendor-quoted at 4,257 single-core and 12,710 multi-core — about 11% behind on single-core and level on multi-core — before retail devices are tested. And on Geekbench AI 1.7 a Qualcomm-powered Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 83,047 against 69,245 for the iPhone 18 Pro, so the second neural engine did not buy AI throughput leadership [S158]. Benchmarks also move with the test build: the same iPhone 18 Pro scores 4,022 single-core on Geekbench 7 against 4,735 on Geekbench 6, so no single headline number settles durability.

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple frames this as hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it unveiled "all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 in June 2026, shipping it on the iPhone 18 Pro that reached stores on 2026-09-18. R&D rose 33% to fund AI infrastructure and headcount while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, or 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so Apple buys capability as an operating cost instead of building a hyperscale compute base. The Geekbench AI result above is the mechanism in miniature: Apple's own silicon is optimised for efficient on-device inference, and everything heavier is routed to a competitor's data centre at a price Apple has not disclosed. Model quality, query data and the pace of improvement sit with a company that also sells phones.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**

The next generation of Apple Foundation Models is built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the ceiling of the assistant is set by a competitor while the differentiation left to Apple is integration, privacy and distribution.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | No assistant | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro on TSMC N2 | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S157 |
| Cellular modem | In-house C2 5G | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S157 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Apple is unique among the five in owning the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image, and Qualcomm sells silicon to the rest. Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant.

### Form factors: the stagnation critique is out of date on hardware, not on cadence

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Apple has announced the Duo; supply-chain reporting places it in the September 2026 shipping window, and neither Apple's filings nor a document verified here give unit volumes or price, so the plan below is a target rather than a result [S113, S114]. Suppliers were told to prepare 10 million foldables for 2026, up from 7-8 million, inside at least five new iPhone models spread across the second half of 2026 and the first half of 2027. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units, the Duo changes the price ladder and the narrative more than the revenue base. The mechanics were engineered long before launch: the granted patent US 12,164,344 B2 covers a hinge of interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch, and the record shows a 2021 priority date, a 2024 grant and a 2042 expiry rather than a 2025 invention.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed / published | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 B2 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Filed 2022-07-07; priority 2021-08-11 | 2024-12-10 | Active to 2042-07-07; assignee Apple Inc. | iPhone Duo hinge: interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch | S159, S121 |
| US 2023/0049811 A1 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Published 2023-02-16 | — | Application publication, later granted as US 12,164,344 B2 | Pre-grant publication of the same family | S121 |
| US 2025/0120026 A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | Published 2025-04-17 | — | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |
| EP4134784A1, KR20230024218A, CN115904004A | Hinge family outside the US | EP, KR, CN | 2022-2023 | — | Family members of US 12,164,344 B2 | Freedom-to-operate cover in Europe, Korea and China | S159 |

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared its Hypertension Notification Feature on 2025-09-11, its Sleep Apnea Notification Feature on 2024-09-13, granted the Hearing Aid Feature a De Novo on 2024-09-12, and cleared a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, which raises the wearable's value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration, and the revenue line remains volatile quarter to quarter.

### What would break the story

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability. The Q3 FY2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM; inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m, and strip out two percentage points of tariff refund and the 50.1% gross margin is nearer 48%, so the technology premium is being defended by price increases while memory costs rise. The unverifiable pieces matter too: no Vision Pro units, no product-level margins, no patent counts, and the AI throughput gap above shows the neural engine is not where the assistant's capability comes from.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power management designed as one product, on a leading node | 3-4 years | S157 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | All-time-high active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Foundry, custom components | 7 | Single-source parts; scale secures leading capacity | 2-3 years | S5 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team of fifty with Apple's published patents could match the hinge and the foldable within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts, the benchmarks and the regulatory record, medium on durability, because Qualcomm's next generation closes most of the CPU gap and memory costs are eating into the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the Gemini fee and term, the share of queries processed on-device, and iPhone Duo sell-through.

| P/E multiple | 26.6x → 40.0x, +50.7% | +8.5% | 48% | S6, S7 |
| Dividends per share | $0.90 → $1.07, 3.3% cumulative | 0.65% | 2% | S6, S93 |

That history is the base rate a buyer is fighting. Apple's own filing puts $100 invested in September 2020 at $234 five years later, against $217 for the S&P 500 and $287 for the Dow Jones U.S. Technology index — 18.5% a year against 16.8% and 23.5%, so the quality compounder beat the index by 8% cumulatively and lagged its own sector by 24%. The bull case's 8.4% annual return at a held 40x — 8.1% EPS growth, of which 1.6 points is buyback, plus a 0.31% dividend — is a 20% branch, not the base case [S5, S93].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
