{"url":"https://www.idc.com/resource-center/blog/smart-glasses-growth-cools-to-35-as-meta-doubles-down-on-distribution/","title":"Smart Glasses Growth Cools to 35% as Meta Doubles Down on Distribution","text":"Global shipments of XR headsets and glasses rose 35.3% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, strong growth but a significant moderation from the 130.2% increase IDC tracked in the prior quarter. Much of that slowdown reflects tougher comparisons and a pause between major product cycles rather than any softening in consumer interest. Growth should pick back up as the next wave of product launches arrives later this year.

Audio glasses, the display-less category that includes devices like Ray-Ban Meta, represented the largest portion of shipments, capturing 70.3% share during the quarter, up from 61.9% a year ago. Display glasses represented 14.3% share, up from 11% a year ago, while headsets held the remaining 15.4%. Glasses overall have turned a corner and are quickly being recognized by a mainstream audience. Recent privacy backlash over always-on recording shows not all of that attention is flattering.

Meta continued to dominate the market with 68.7% share. Its growth this quarter came from pushing into two additional segments: prescription eyewear, with the launch of its Blayzer and Scriber Optics lines, and lower-cost options that skip the fashion branding EssilorLuxottica normally provides. That expansion is only part of the story. Meta’s lead also rests on distribution scale, brand recognition, and AI features built across its product line, advantages that are harder for challengers to replicate than any single hardware launch.

CompanyQ2 2026 Market ShareMeta68.7%RayNeo3.6%Alibaba Group2.6%XREAL2.5%Xiaomi2.3%Others20.4%

RayNeo ranked second with 3.6% share, up 83.3% year over year, on the strength of its low-cost, personal-theater-style devices. Alibaba, a relative newcomer to the category, ranked third at 2.6% share thanks to the popularity of Qwen and the company’s already-established presence in China. XREAL and Xiaomi rounded out the top five, though Xiaomi’s share nearly halved from a year ago as competition in its home market intensified.

What’s coming next: The launches that could reshuffle the board

A lot is going to change in the remaining months of 2026 as next-gen products arrive from multiple vendors, each chasing a similar set of goals: more capable AI experiences, lighter hardware, and use cases that go beyond entertainment into everyday productivity. Those shared priorities, more than any single launch, will shape competition through the rest of the year.

Snap is launching its Specs, which bring genuine AR capabilities packaged into the most consumer-friendly design the category has seen yet, backed by a marketing campaign built around fashion icons.

Samsung and XREAL are both readying Android XR products. XREAL’s Aura pairs the company’s personal-theater-style hardware, already strong for content consumption, with Google’s Android XR platform, putting productivity use cases on equal footing with entertainment. Samsung’s audio glasses, meanwhile, bring Google’s Gemini assistant together with the distribution and design sensibility of Gentle Monster and Warby Parker.

Meta’s upcoming Connect event is widely expected to launch a more premium mixed reality headset with better visuals and a slimmer, lighter form factor that should appeal to enthusiasts. IDC also anticipates new display and audio glasses at the show, with the display glasses aimed at broader availability and a more accessible price point.

Beyond these headline launches, products from Pico, RayNeo, Viture, and a growing list of other brands will help drive further growth in 2026 and into the years ahead.

The road ahead: Forecast 2026–2028

IDC forecasts total unit shipments will grow 26.3% in 2026, then accelerate to 40.5% growth in 2027 and another 26.4% in 2028. Audio glasses will keep leading the category, though display glasses and headsets will continue to ramp alongside them.

For consumers, that growth will be driven by a wider range of products, price points, and channels, plus the spread of AI and friction-reducing use cases like easy photo and video capture. Among businesses, training and design use cases will keep driving adoption, since IDC has tracked ROI gains in early enterprise pilots, and more businesses continue to start them.

Growing pains: Privacy and business-model tension

There are also growing concerns behind the scenes that need to be addressed, as they stand to reshape the adoption curve going forward.

Privacy and shifting consumer attitudes. Many products and services surrounding XR glasses have clear, tangible benefits, though IDC has tracked growing concern over the need for privacy controls. IDC has also observed a shift from early jokes about social acceptance to more serious concerns about the lack of meaningful notice and consent mechanisms while recording, along with AI-enabled data collection, raising the stakes for how vendors respond. Meta, the current leader, has taken action to reduce misuse of its products, but those steps came only after public backlash forced its hand. That leaves room for a competitor willing to build privacy safeguards in before launch, not after a headline forces the issue.

Competing business models. XR glasses are a relatively new category, and tech companies are quickly partnering with fashion companies to leverage their expertise in design, manufacturing, and distribution. There’s tension between these camps, though, as fashion companies often operate on higher margins while tech companies are willing to sacrifice margin in favor of ongoing subscription or advertising-based models, where the hardware can be offered at a lower upfront cost to keep the consumer inside the ecosystem. This is likely one reason Meta launched glasses without EssilorLuxottica’s branding. It also puts smaller players at a disadvantage, since they face pricing pressure on hardware from incumbents like Meta and potentially Google and Samsung, and will likely have to adjust their own business models to offer subscription services alongside their XR products going forward.

What this means for the industry

Smart glasses are genuinely being worn now, not just tested, and that changes the competitive picture. Meta still holds the lead, but the next round of launches from Snap, Samsung, XREAL, and Meta’s own Connect event will show whether that lead holds up. The rest of 2026 will be shaped as much by these launches as by the numbers themselves. Even with this quarter’s slower growth, consumer awareness keeps building and AI is unlocking new use cases — the vendors that move first on privacy may be the ones who convert that awareness into share.

{"url":"https://www.idc.com/resource-center/blog/smartphone-shipments-set-for-record-16-7-drop-in-2026-as-the-memory-crisis-hits-full-force/","title":"Smartphone Shipments Set for Record 16.7% Drop in 2026, as the Memory Crisis Hits Full Force","text":"The smartphone market has changed character this year. Units are dropping while prices are climbing sharply, with consumers expected to absorb the cost.

According to IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker, worldwide smartphone shipments will fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1 billion units.

That is a sharp downgrade from the 13.9% decline we forecast only one quarter ago, and it is the steepest annual contraction the industry has ever recorded. What makes this moment unusual is that the market is shrinking and getting more valuable at the same time. Total market value will still grow 6.3% to $613 billion, because higher prices are now doing the heavy lifting that volume once did.

Why did the outlook get worse?

The memory shortage, which started in late 2025, is striking hard in the second half of 2026, with shipments forecast to drop by 27.2% YoY. NAND and DRAM costs continue to rise, up over 300% YoY, and vendors are running out of options to absorb the increased costs. As memory prices are expected to continue increasing until at least 2028, vendors are adapting their portfolios to a permanently higher cost structure. The 173 million smartphones below $100, which shipped last year, are facing an existential crisis. Android players focused on low-end devices, which were already operating on razor-thin margins, are cutting low-end models and pushing a higher-end product mix. In Q2 2026, this segment saw an almost 60% YoY drop and is expected to fall faster in the second half.

How much are smartphone prices expected to increase?

This is where the forecast has moved most. The average selling price of a smartphone will reach $581 in 2026, up 27.6% in a single year and revised upward from the $550 projected last quarter. More brands are passing the increased cost to the end consumer, with prices rising faster than expected. The premium end will remain more resilient to the price hikes as long-term interest-free financing options are more prevalent in developed markets like the US and UK. The mass market does not hold up, especially in emerging markets, which are expected to drop over 20% this year. This is why the unit decline continues to deepen while the value line keeps rising.

“
The memory tsunami that we warned about is now hitting the market in full, and consumers are starting to pay the AI bill. The components that make AI possible are the same ones in short supply, and their cost is being passed straight through to the shelf. Average selling prices are up 27.6% this year and will keep rising well into 2027. The era of the cheap smartphone has ended. From here, the winners will be the vendors with the scale and supply leverage to hold demand at prices consumers have never had to pay before.

Who is winning the crisis, iOS or Android?

The crisis is not hitting everyone equally. Android bears almost the entire decline, falling 24.3% in 2026 as its most exposed vendors retreat from the entry tiers they can no longer serve profitably. Android share drops seven percentage points in a single year. iOS share moves in the opposite direction, increasing almost four percentage points from last year to a record-high 23.6% share, as shipments remain relatively resilient, down just 1.3% YoY in 2026. HarmonyOS sees strong growth off a small base, nearly tripling to 51 million units in 2026 as Huawei maintains a disciplined pricing strategy, taking full advantage of the crisis to gain share in China as the rest of the Android market contracts.

Is there any segment that is still growing?

Almost nothing in this forecast grows, except foldables. The category will grow 12.6% in 2026 to 22.9 million units, then accelerate to 18% growth in 2027, reaching roughly 27 million units. The rapid growth is thanks to Apple’s entry into the category in the second half of this year. Apple is not only adding a new model or increasing competition in the foldables category; it is converting a segment that was about to decline into the fastest-growing part of the industry.

“
Apple’s entry into the foldable market has done more than reignite growth in a category that was losing momentum. It has fundamentally altered the market’s trajectory. Without Apple, foldable shipments would have declined at a double-digit rate year over year. We forecast Apple will ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027, capturing roughly 40% of the global foldables market. With an average selling price exceeding $2,550, Apple is expected to generate more than $45.7 billion in value and account for over half of the category’s total value. Perhaps most notably, Apple is positioned to challenge Huawei and Samsung for leadership in markets where they have long dominated, an extraordinary outcome for a product expected to be less than two years into its lifecycle.

What does this mean for consumers?

The days of the cheap smartphone are ending. The average handset now costs roughly $147 more than it did a couple of years ago, and the cheapest models are the ones leaving the shelves fastest. Buyers in price-sensitive markets will feel this loss the most, as the sub-$100 phones many of them relied on are being cut from vendor line-ups. For everyone else it means holding a device for longer and paying more at the point of upgrade. On-device AI is arriving, but the memory it runs on is scarce and expensive, and consumers are covering that cost directly.

What does this mean for vendors?

The next 18 months will separate the vendors who can operate in a structurally more expensive market from those who cannot. Apple, Samsung, and Huawei have the scale and pricing power to turn this challenge to their advantage. Smaller Android brands anchored in the entry tiers face the hardest stretch in the industry’s history, and some will not clear it. The market that emerges on the other side of the crisis, when the memory supply finally stabilizes in 2028, will be smaller in units, larger in value, and far more concentrated at the top. The cheap smartphone era is not pausing. It is over.

Apple at $348.91 is priced at 40.0x trailing earnings — an 88% premium to its three US peers' median and above every fiscal year-end multiple since FY2022 — so the share price, not the business, is the risk: it requires free cash flow to compound at about 17% a year for a decade at a 9.5% discount rate, or 5.7% perpetual growth accepted at an 8.0% required return, and leaves a long-only buyer no margin of safety. The quote is unambiguous: $348.91 at the NasdaqGS close on 2026-10-29 20:00 UTC, market capitalisation $5,092.1B, enterprise value $5,029.9B, trailing diluted EPS $8.72, free cash flow $136.7B. The shares made a record close, sit at 97% of the $243.42-$351.73 fifty-two-week range and 5.0% above the 50-day average of $332.37; the twelve-month return of +28.6% against +13.2% for the S&P 500 and +25.7% for the technology sector ETF means essentially the whole gain arrived after April 2026 [S6, S7, S17].

A record price is where valuation discipline matters most, and the peer table explains why. On trailing figures Apple trades at 40.0x earnings and 32.5x EV/EBIT against 23.9x and 21.5x for Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta; adding Samsung at 12.9x pulls the four-peer median P/E to 18.1x and widens Apple's premium to 122%. Only the cash-flow multiples look less extreme — Apple's 2.7% free-cash-flow yield and 37.3x price-to-FCF beat all three peers — but that is capital intensity, not cheapness: Alphabet's 177.8x price-to-FCF and 0.6% yield reflect an AI capital-expenditure cycle Apple has so far avoided by spending $10.0B on capex against $146.7B of operating cash flow [S6, S93].

Against its own history the message is sharper. At the last four fiscal year ends Apple traded at 24.6x (2022), 27.9x (2023), 37.5x (2024) and 34.2x (2025) earnings, with EV/Sales of 6.1x, 6.9x, 8.8x and 9.1x; today's 40.0x and 10.8x sit above all four years on both measures. The re-rating is not random: revenue growth accelerated to 14.8% in FY2026 from 6.4% in FY2025 on consensus, gross margin rose to 48.6% from 46.9%, and Services reached $91.7B of the $364.4B nine-month revenue. A faster-growing, self-funding stream deserves more than the 24.6x of fiscal 2022; whether it deserves 40.0x is a question only a discount-rate-and-growth model can answer [S5, S6, S7].

The DCF's inputs are worth stating plainly, because its precision is false comfort. Consensus FY2026 free cash flow of $142.36B less $13.7B of stock-based compensation and $17.7B of contracted intangible purchases — licensed intellectual property, content and distribution rights that the 10-Q lists among unconditional purchase obligations — gives $111.0B of owner cash flow [S6, S47]. Terminal value is 56% of the $2,246B enterprise value, so the grid matters more than the point estimate: $132 a share at a 10.5% WACC and 2.5% terminal growth, $198 at 8.5% and 3.5%. The reverse calculation is the cleanest statement of what the price assumes: at a 9.5% required return, today's $5,029.9B enterprise value needs free cash flow to compound at about 17% a year for ten years — 3.1 times the 5.5% revenue compound from FY2021 ($365.8B) to FY2026E ($477.6B) and 1.9 times Apple's own 8.9% five-year free-cash-flow compound; at an 8.0% required return the bar falls to 5.7% in perpetuity, which that 8.9% compound has already cleared. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16 and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. ### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. The consensus of 43 analysts polled by S&P Global carries an average 12-month target of $332.39 and a median of $337.50, 3.3-4.7% below the $348.91 close, with a high of $405 and a low of $245. Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one in May 2026 to six in October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6%. Forward numbers are respectable — consensus FY2026 revenue $477.64B (+14.8%) and EPS $8.84 (+18.5%), FY2027 $526.79B (+10.3%) and $9.56 (+8.1%) — but they already imply a sharp deceleration: subtracting nine-month actuals from the full-year estimate gives a September quarter of $113.3B and $1.96 of EPS, or +10.6% and +6.5%, against +16.4% and +29% in the June quarter. Apple publishes no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance — the July 2026 results release contains none — so consensus is the only forward anchor [S93].

The strongest case against my conclusion is that the acceleration is real and broad. June-quarter revenue rose 16.4% with double-digit growth in iPhone, Mac and Services and in every geographic segment, Greater China rebounded 22.4% to $18.8B, and R&D rose 32.2% to $11.7B. Against that, the 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds, so underlying margin was 48.1%, and a 50% margin carried into FY2027 overstates gross profit by $10.5B on consensus revenue; peak margin plus peak multiple plus a 4.99% ten-year yield is the combination that hurt Apple in 2022, when the multiple fell from 37.5x to 27.9x in a year while the business did not deteriorate. For a long-only watchlist the implication is a price, not a story: at $348.91 there is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return, the probability-weighted value of $300 is 14.0% below the price, and the buyback does not defend a 40x multiple at a 2.18% owner cash yield. The conditions that would justify adding are concrete — revenue growth of 10% or more in FY2027 with gross margin of 48% or higher excluding tariff refunds, and an entry multiple of 30-34x the $9.10 blended FY2027 EPS, or $273-$300. Two open questions move the value more than 5% of price: how much of Services gross profit is the Google default payment, and what buyback authorisation replaced the May 2025 programme [S47, S5, S93].

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable where Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thin at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: the lead is measurable again, and narrower than it looks

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design, not transistor count, is what puts desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip, on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16 and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, one outlet measured 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core on its iPhone 18 Pro Max against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the difference is large enough to measure, and it rests as much on the node as on design.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flagship SoC, iPhone 18 Pro | A20 Pro, TSMC N2, 6-core CPU to 4.93GHz | Announced 2026-09-09 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, Geekbench 6 | 4,707 single / 12,598 multi | Outlet's iPhone 18 Pro Max | S157 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same build | 3,588 / 10,207 | Outlet's iQOO 15 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, second outlet | 4,735 / 12,800 | Independent iPhone 18 Pro | S158 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 4,257 / 12,710 | Qualcomm reference-device claim | S157 |
| Sustained graphics, 20 loops | 80% stability vs 25% | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme | S157 |
| R&D, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |
| Capital expenditure, nine months FY2026 | $6,799m, 1.9% of revenue | Reported | S6 |

### Sustained performance is the stronger claim, and it is not pure silicon

Peak scores flatter a chip; the 20-loop stress test in the table shows what a buyer gets after ten minutes. The A20 Pro held 80% of its best score, 8,793 falling to 7,032, while the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 fell to 25%, 6,867 to 1,715; a second outlet measured graphics stability of 79.4% against 65.2% a year earlier [S158]. Apple's vapour chamber is three times larger and memory no longer sits on the die, so part of that gap is chassis, and pairing Apple's largest phone with a thinner Android device overstates the silicon margin. Two counters keep this honest. Qualcomm's next part is vendor-quoted at 4,257 single-core and 12,710 multi-core, about 11% behind on single-core and level on multi-core before retail testing. And on Geekbench AI 1.7 a Qualcomm-powered Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 83,047 against 69,245 for the iPhone 18 Pro, so the second neural engine did not buy AI throughput leadership [S158].

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple calls this hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it shipped "all-new Siri AI" in September 2026 on the iPhone 18 Pro. R&D rose 33% while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so capability is bought as an operating cost rather than built on owned compute. Model quality, query data and the pace of improvement sit with a competitor that also sells phones; the Geekbench AI gap is that dependency in miniature.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**

The next Apple Foundation Models are built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the assistant's ceiling is set by a competitor while integration, privacy and distribution are what Apple keeps.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | None | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro, TSMC N2 | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S157 |
| Cellular modem | In-house C2 5G | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S157 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant. Apple is unique among the five in owning the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image.

### Form factors: late, not rushed

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Apple has announced the Duo; supply-chain reporting places it in the September 2026 shipping window, and no document verified here gives its unit volumes or price, so the 10 million foldables planned for 2026 are a target, not a result [S113]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units the Duo changes the price ladder more than the revenue base, and the hinge patent shows why the hardware is late rather than rushed: a 2021 priority date, a 2024 grant, an expiry in 2042.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Dates | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 B2 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Filed 2022-07-07; priority 2021-08-11; granted 2024-12-10 | Active to 2042-07-07; assignee Apple Inc. | iPhone Duo hinge: interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch | S159, S121 |
| EP4134784A1, KR20230024218A, CN115904004A | Hinge family outside the US | EP, KR, CN | 2022-2023 | Family of US 12,164,344 B2 | Freedom to operate in Europe, Korea, China | S159 |
| US 2025/0120026 A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | Published 2025-04-17 | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared Hypertension Notification on 2025-09-11, Sleep Apnea Notification on 2024-09-13, granted Hearing Aid a De Novo on 2024-09-12 and cleared Medical Imaging Calibration on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, raising value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration, though the segment grew again in the June 2026 quarter.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (incl. Duo) | Shipping; Duo announced, shipment per supply-chain reporting | 2026-09-09 | $54,252m in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by product | iPhone 18, spring 2027 | S47, S113 |
| Mac | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $10,352m in Q3 FY2026, +29% | Not disclosed by product | M-series refresh | S47 |
| iPad | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $6,191m in Q3 FY2026, -6% | Not disclosed by product | Demand after June 2026 price rises | S47 |
| Wearables, home, accessories | Shipping | Annual | $35,686m FY2025, -4%; $7,883m Q3 FY2026, +6% | Not disclosed by product | Blood-pressure and glucose work unannounced | S47 |
| Vision Pro | Shipping | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | None disclosed | S5 |

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability: the June 2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM, and inventories nearly doubled in nine months, so the technology premium is being defended by price while memory costs rise. No Vision Pro units, no product-level margins and no patent counts are disclosed.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power management designed as one product on a leading node | 3-4 years | S157 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | All-time-high active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Foundry, custom components | 7 | Single-source parts; scale secures leading capacity | 2-3 years | S5 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team of fifty with Apple's published patents could match the hinge within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and benchmarks, medium on durability, because Qualcomm's next generation closes most of the CPU gap and memory costs are eating the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the Gemini fee and term, the share of queries processed on-device, and iPhone Duo sell-through.

arguments.markdown:
Apple taxes a 2.5-billion-device installed base twice — once at a 39.9% product gross margin when a device is sold, then for its life at a 76.3% services margin — but in fiscal 2026 the growth came from the hardware leg that memory suppliers are now repricing, not the software leg that regulators are repricing, so the durable half of the model is the smaller half of the growth. The investor implication is that earnings durability has to be underwritten as a hardware cycle with a services annuity attached, not the other way round [S5, S6].

### The mix rotated back to hardware, and that is where the profit came from

In the nine months to 2026-06-27 Apple booked $364,357M of net sales, up 16.1% year on year: iPhone $196,515M (+22.4%), Services $91,728M (+14.1%), Mac $27,137M (+8.6%), iPad $21,700M (+3.0%) and Wearables, Home and Accessories $27,277M (+2.3%). Full-year FY2025 was $416,161M (+6.4%), with iPhone at 50.4% of sales and Services at 26.2%, against a FY2023 mix of 52.3% and 22.2%. Greater China grew 30.0% to $64,839M, Europe 16.1% and the Americas 11.4%. Apple discloses gross margin only for Products and Services, so no iPhone-level margin exists; but of the $31,922M increase in nine-month gross profit, $22,629M — 71% — came from Products, a reversal of FY2025, when Services supplied 77.6% of the $14,518M gross-profit increase [S5, S6, S47]. The driver is a device upgrade cycle with Pro-model mix plus a favourable euro and renminbi swing, not a step-change in the base: the company reported more than 2.5 billion active devices in the December 2025 quarter, up 150 million year on year, or 6.4%, against 16.1% revenue growth. iPhone concentration rose to 53.9% of sales from 50.4%, the number to watch if the upgrade cycle rolls over.

### Services is a toll on the base, and the toll rate is now set outside the company

Services is the structurally superior asset: a 76.3% gross margin in 9M FY2026, up from 75.4% in FY2025 and 70.8% in FY2023, on revenue recognised net of the developers' share. On the disclosed base it is $48.9 of services revenue per active device per year, against $43.7 in FY2025, while device count grew 6.4%, so most of services growth is monetisation per device — advertising, cloud, App Store — rather than more devices. The margin is not a free parameter. Apple's EU rate card from 2026-10-01 cuts the base App Store commission to 26% from the 30% standard, adds a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed outside the App Store, and sets 20% for in-app alternative payments and 15% for link-outs; in the US Apple has proposed 5-15% on purchases through external links after a 2025 contempt finding, and the Department of Justice's Section 2 case from 2024-03-21 is unresolved while the two sides reportedly discuss settlement [S56, S62]. Each point off the commission moves third-party developer revenue out of a 76%-margin line, so the effect lands on the highest-margin slice of Services rather than spread across it.

### Pricing: what Apple charges, and who now sets it

| App Store, EU, link-out to web purchase | % of developer transaction | 15% (10% for reduced-rate programmes) | 2026-10-01 | S56 |
| Alternative marketplaces and web distribution, EU | % of digital transactions | 5% Core Technology Commission; per-install Core Technology Fee removed | 2026-10-01 | S56, S57 |
| App Store, US, In-App Purchase | % of developer transaction | 15-30% by developer size and category | current | S65 |
| App Store, US, external-link purchases | % (proposed, needs court approval) | 5-15% tiers; 0% was ordered in April 2025 | 2026-08-14 | S64 |
| iPhone | $ of revenue per unit | not disclosed; the 10-K reports iPhone net sales with no unit count | n/a | S5 |

| Capex | $5.1 | $3.6 | S5, S47 |
| Free cash flow | $40 | $59 | S5, S47 |
| LTV : CAC, four years matched ($312 vs $44) | 7.1:1 | 8.0:1 | S5, S6 |
| CAC payback, months (CAC ÷ gross profit per year) | 6.8 | 6.0 | S5, S6 |

Beyond the waterfall, two numbers set the risk envelope on the 2.5-billion-device base, with nine months annualised at four-thirds. The operating structure breaks even at an estimated $153bn of annual revenue, 31.5% of the current run-rate, because R&D and SG&A are largely fixed against a base growing 6.4% a year, so a 10% revenue decline leaves it solidly profitable. The acquisition multiple only survives a period match: four years of gross profit per device ($78.1 × 4 = $312) against four years of SG&A per device ($11.0 × 4 = $44) is 7.1:1, repaid in 6.8 months, where one year of SG&A would overstate it four-fold [S5, S6]. Since the CAC input is all of SG&A, not a marketing line Apple discloses, 7.1:1 is the floor. These are averages: an iPhone buyer generates more services revenue than an iPad buyer, and the average hides the concentration that matters.

::: evidence
**Claim: the hardware leg is doing the growth and the services leg is doing the margin, and both are being repriced at the same time.**

- Products produced 71% of the $31,922M nine-month gross-profit increase ($22,629M) even though Services carries the 76.3% margin (Source: S6).
- The EU rate card effective 2026-10-01 sets a 26% base App Store commission and 5% for distribution outside the App Store, against the 30% standard Apple charged before the DMA (Source: S56, S65).
- Samsung Electronics earned a 55.0% operating margin in Q3 2026 on record memory earnings, the mirror image of the component-cost pressure Apple says will intensify (Source: S59).
- Apple's capital-light model keeps cash intact: $10,041M of trailing capex against $135,921M at Microsoft and $159,804M at Alphabet, while R&D rose 32.5% in nine months (Source: S11, S13).
:::

### Capital allocation is part of the model, not an afterthought

The model funds itself from a negative cash cycle: payables of 98 days against receivables of 24 days and inventory of 17 days give a cash conversion cycle of -56.8 days, and that is what pays for the buyback. Over the trailing twelve months Apple repurchased $82,226M of stock and paid $15,640M of dividends, retiring 1.6% of diluted shares a year and lifting nine-month EPS growth to 22.4% against 20.0% net income growth. The direction of travel in FY2026 is the signal: buybacks fell from $70,579M to $62,094M year on year while R&D rose 32.5% and gross intangible assets rose $13,270M, which the 10-Q does not disaggregate and for which there is no acquisition line in investing cash flow [S47, S11, S13]. Apple is redirecting cash from share retirement into capability it buys or licenses rather than builds — which protects free cash flow but diverts the per-share compounding engine, and the amortisation will land in future operating expense.

### What breaks the economics

The strongest counter-evidence is not that services is legally exposed; it is that both legs are exposed at once. IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 while the industry ASP rises 27.6% to $581, and Counterpoint measured Apple's Q2 2026 shipments up 13% on an ASP up 17%: Apple is winning share in a market shrinking in units and inflating in price, which works only while demand is inelastic [S59, S60]. Apple's own 10-Q says memory and storage costs will intensify and that price increases may not offset them. If hardware gross margin gives back the 300bp it gained in nine months, and the App Store commission settles at 15-26% rather than 30%, the model still earns a 30%-plus operating margin on a fixed cost base — the economics do not break, they normalise. The open questions that would move confidence are iPhone unit volume, which Apple no longer discloses; the EU share of Services revenue, which Apple does not break out; and whether the $13.3bn intangible addition is amortised over three years — $4.4bn a year of extra expense — or over ten.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable where Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thin at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: the lead is measurable again, and narrower than it looks

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design, not transistor count, is what puts desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip, on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16 and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, one outlet measured 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core on its iPhone 18 Pro Max against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the difference is large enough to measure, and it rests as much on the node as on design.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro, Geekbench 6 | 4,707 single / 12,598 multi | Outlet's iPhone 18 Pro Max | S157 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same build | 3,588 / 10,207 | Outlet's iQOO 15 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, second outlet | 4,735 / 12,800 | Independent iPhone 18 Pro | S158 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 4,257 / 12,710 | Qualcomm reference-device claim | S157 |
| Sustained graphics, 20 loops | 80% stability vs 25% | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme | S157 |
| R&D, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |

### Sustained performance is the stronger claim, and it is not pure silicon

Peak scores flatter a chip; the 20-loop stress test in the table shows what a buyer gets after ten minutes. The A20 Pro held 80% of its best score, 8,793 falling to 7,032, while the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 fell to 25%, 6,867 to 1,715; a second outlet measured graphics stability of 79.4% against 65.2% a year earlier [S158]. Apple's vapour chamber is three times larger and memory no longer sits on the die, so part of that gap is chassis and pairing Apple's largest phone with a thinner Android device overstates the silicon margin. Two counters keep this honest. Qualcomm's next part is vendor-quoted at 4,257 single-core and 12,710 multi-core, about 11% behind on single-core and level on multi-core before retail testing. And on Geekbench AI 1.7 a Qualcomm-powered Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 83,047 against 69,245 for the iPhone 18 Pro, so the second neural engine did not buy AI throughput leadership [S158].

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple calls this hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it shipped "all-new Siri AI" in September 2026 on the iPhone 18 Pro. R&D rose 33% while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so capability is bought as an operating cost rather than built on owned compute. Model quality, query data and the pace of improvement sit with a competitor that also sells phones; the Geekbench AI gap is that dependency in miniature.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**

The next Apple Foundation Models are built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the assistant's ceiling is set by a competitor while integration, privacy and distribution are what Apple keeps.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | None | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro, TSMC N2 | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S157 |
| Cellular modem | In-house C2 5G | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S157 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant. Apple alone owns the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image.

### Form factors: late, not rushed

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Apple has announced the Duo; supply-chain reporting places it in the September 2026 shipping window, and no document verified here gives its unit volumes or price, so the 10 million foldables planned for 2026 are a target, not a result [S113]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units the Duo changes the price ladder more than the revenue base, and the hinge patent shows why the hardware is late rather than rushed: a 2021 priority date, a 2024 grant, an expiry in 2042.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Dates | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 B2 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Filed 2022-07-07; priority 2021-08-11; granted 2024-12-10 | Active to 2042-07-07; assignee Apple Inc. | iPhone Duo hinge: interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch | S159, S121 |
| EP4134784A1, KR20230024218A, CN115904004A | Hinge family outside the US | EP, KR, CN | 2022-2023 | Family of US 12,164,344 B2 | Freedom to operate in Europe, Korea, China | S159 |
| US 2025/0120026 A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | Published 2025-04-17 | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |

No assistant or foundation-model patent with an Apple assignee surfaced in the public record, which is consistent with a licensed-model strategy and caps how much of the AI stack Apple can protect.

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared Hypertension Notification on 2025-09-11, Sleep Apnea Notification on 2024-09-13, granted Hearing Aid a De Novo on 2024-09-12 and cleared Medical Imaging Calibration on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, raising value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration, though the segment grew again in the June 2026 quarter.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (incl. Duo) | Shipping; Duo announced, shipment per supply-chain reporting | 2026-09-09 | $54,252m in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by product | iPhone 18, spring 2027 | S47, S113 |
| Mac and iPad | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $10,352m (+29%) and $6,191m (-6%) in Q3 FY2026 | Not disclosed by product | M-series and iPad refresh | S47 |
| Wearables, home, accessories | Shipping | Annual | $35,686m FY2025, -4%; $7,883m Q3 FY2026, +6% | Not disclosed by product | Blood-pressure and glucose work unannounced | S47 |
| Vision Pro | Shipping | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | None disclosed | S5 |

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability: the June 2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM, and inventories nearly doubled in nine months, so the technology premium is being defended by price while memory costs rise. No Vision Pro units, no product-level margins and no patent counts are disclosed.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power design on a leading node | 3-4 years | S157 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | Record active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Foundry, custom components | 7 | Single-source parts; scale secures capacity | 2-3 years | S5 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team of fifty with Apple's published patents could match the hinge within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and benchmarks, medium on durability, because Qualcomm's next generation closes most of the CPU gap and memory costs are eating the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the Gemini fee and term, the share of queries processed on-device, and iPhone Duo sell-through.

That history is the base rate a buyer is fighting. Run forward, the same decomposition produces the expected return: on the 20/40/40 split the weighted exit multiple is 32.0x FY2027E earnings against the 36.5x paid today (−12.3 points) and the weighted EPS is 2.9% below consensus because the bear's $8.60 carries 40% weight (−2.9 points), with the interaction taking the total to −14.0%. The bull case's 8.4% annual return at a held 40x — 8.1% EPS growth, of which 1.6 points is buyback, plus a 0.31% dividend — is a 20% branch, not the base case [S5, S93].

Every incremental dollar of return has to come from the market, and the market will pay whatever multiple prevails when the holder sells; there is no bid to negotiate, no premium to extract and no lock-up to wait out. arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable where Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thin at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: the lead is measurable again, and narrower than it looks

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design, not transistor count, is what puts desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip, on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16 and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, one outlet measured 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core on its iPhone 18 Pro Max against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the difference is large enough to measure, and it rests as much on the node as on design.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro, Geekbench 6 | 4,707 single / 12,598 multi | Outlet's iPhone 18 Pro Max | S157 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same build | 3,588 / 10,207 | Outlet's iQOO 15 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, second outlet | 4,735 / 12,800 | Independent iPhone 18 Pro | S158 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 4,257 / 12,710 | Qualcomm reference-device claim | S157 |
| Sustained graphics, 20 loops | 80% stability vs 25% | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme | S157 |
| R&D, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |

### Sustained performance is the stronger claim, and it is not pure silicon

Peak scores flatter a chip; the 20-loop stress test in the table shows what a buyer gets after ten minutes. The A20 Pro held 80% of its best score, 8,793 falling to 7,032, while the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 fell to 25%, 6,867 to 1,715; a second outlet measured graphics stability of 79.4% against 65.2% a year earlier [S158]. Apple's vapour chamber is three times larger and memory no longer sits on the die, so part of that gap is chassis and pairing Apple's largest phone with a thinner Android device overstates the silicon margin. Two counters keep this honest. Qualcomm's next part is vendor-quoted within 11% on single-core and level on multi-core before retail testing, and on Geekbench AI 1.7 a Qualcomm-powered Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 83,047 against 69,245 for the iPhone 18 Pro, so the second neural engine did not buy AI throughput leadership [S158].

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple calls this hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it shipped "all-new Siri AI" in September 2026 on the iPhone 18 Pro. R&D rose 33% while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so capability is bought as an operating cost rather than built on owned compute. Model quality, query data and the pace of improvement sit with a competitor that also sells phones; the Geekbench AI gap is that dependency in miniature.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**

The next Apple Foundation Models are built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the assistant's ceiling is set by a competitor while integration, privacy and distribution are what Apple keeps.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | None | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro, TSMC N2 | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S157 |
| Cellular modem | In-house C2 5G | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S157 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant, and the buyer in 2026 is being sold the assistant. Apple alone owns the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image.

### Form factors: late, not rushed

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Apple has announced the Duo; supply-chain reporting places it in the September 2026 shipping window, and no document verified here gives its unit volumes or price, so the 10 million foldables planned for 2026 are a target, not a result [S113]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units the Duo changes the price ladder more than the revenue base, and the hinge patent shows why the hardware is late rather than rushed: a 2021 priority date, a 2024 grant, an expiry in 2042.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Dates | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 B2 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Filed 2022-07-07; priority 2021-08-11; granted 2024-12-10 | Active to 2042-07-07; assignee Apple Inc. | iPhone Duo hinge: interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch | S159, S121 |
| EP4134784A1, KR20230024218A, CN115904004A | Hinge family outside the US | EP, KR, CN | 2022-2023 | Family of US 12,164,344 B2 | Freedom to operate in Europe, Korea, China | S159 |
| US 2025/0120026 A1 | Electronic Devices Having Folding Expandable Displays | US | Published 2025-04-17 | Application, Apple Inc. | Second foldable form factor | S131 |

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared Hypertension Notification on 2025-09-11, Sleep Apnea Notification on 2024-09-13, granted Hearing Aid a De Novo on 2024-09-12 and cleared Medical Imaging Calibration on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, raising value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration, though the segment grew again in the June 2026 quarter.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (incl. Duo) | Shipping; Duo announced, shipment per supply-chain reporting | 2026-09-09 | $54,252m in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by product | iPhone 18, spring 2027 | S47, S113 |
| Mac and iPad | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $10,352m (+29%) and $6,191m (-6%) in Q3 FY2026 | Not disclosed by product | M-series and iPad refresh | S47 |
| Wearables, home, accessories | Shipping | Annual | $35,686m FY2025, -4%; $7,883m Q3 FY2026, +6% | Not disclosed by product | Blood-pressure and glucose work unannounced | S47 |
| Vision Pro | Shipping | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | None disclosed | S5 |

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability: the June 2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM, and inventories nearly doubled in nine months, so the technology premium is being defended by price while memory costs rise. No Vision Pro units, no product-level margins and no patent counts are disclosed.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power design on a leading node | 3-4 years | S157 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | Record active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team of fifty with Apple's published patents could match the hinge within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and benchmarks, medium on durability, because Qualcomm's next generation closes most of the CPU gap and memory costs are eating the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the Gemini fee and term, the share of queries processed on-device, and iPhone Duo sell-through.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable where Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thin at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: the lead is measurable again, and narrower than it looks

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design, not transistor count, is what puts desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip, on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16 and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, one outlet measured 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core on its iPhone 18 Pro Max against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the difference is large enough to measure, and it rests as much on the node as on design.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro, Geekbench 6 | 4,707 single / 12,598 multi | Outlet's iPhone 18 Pro Max | S157 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same build | 3,588 / 10,207 | Outlet's iQOO 15 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, second outlet | 4,735 / 12,800 | Independent iPhone 18 Pro | S158 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 4,257 / 12,710 | Qualcomm reference-device claim | S157 |
| Sustained graphics, 20 loops | 80% stability vs 25% | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme | S157 |
| R&D, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |

### Sustained performance is the stronger claim, and it is not pure silicon

Peak scores flatter a chip; the 20-loop stress test in the table shows what a buyer gets after ten minutes. The A20 Pro held 80% of its best score, 8,793 falling to 7,032, while the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 fell to 25%, 6,867 to 1,715; a second outlet measured graphics stability of 79.4% against 65.2% a year earlier [S158]. Apple's vapour chamber is three times larger and memory no longer sits on the die, so part of that gap is chassis and pairing Apple's largest phone with a thinner Android device overstates the silicon margin. Two counters keep this honest. Qualcomm's next part is vendor-quoted within 11% on single-core and level on multi-core before retail testing, and on Geekbench AI 1.7 a Qualcomm-powered Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 83,047 against 69,245 for the iPhone 18 Pro, so the second neural engine did not buy AI throughput leadership [S158].

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple calls this hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it shipped "all-new Siri AI" in September 2026 on the iPhone 18 Pro. R&D rose 33% while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m, 1.9% of nine-month revenue [S6], so capability is bought as an operating cost rather than built on owned compute. Model quality, query data and the pace of improvement sit with a competitor that also sells phones; the Geekbench AI gap is that dependency in miniature.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**

The next Apple Foundation Models are built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the assistant's ceiling is set by a competitor while integration, privacy and distribution are what Apple keeps.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | None | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro, TSMC N2 | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S157 |
| Cellular modem | In-house C2 5G | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S157 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant. Apple alone owns the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image.

### Form factors: late, not rushed

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Apple has announced the Duo; supply-chain reporting places it in the September 2026 shipping window, and no document verified here gives its unit volumes or price, so the 10 million foldables planned for 2026 are a target, not a result [S113]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units the Duo changes the price ladder more than the revenue base; the patent's 2021 priority date shows why the hardware is late rather than rushed.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Dates | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 B2 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Filed 2022-07-07; priority 2021-08-11; granted 2024-12-10 | Active to 2042-07-07; assignee Apple Inc. | iPhone Duo hinge: interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch | S159, S121 |
| EP4134784A1, KR20230024218A, CN115904004A | Hinge family outside the US | EP, KR, CN | 2022-2023 | Family of US 12,164,344 B2 | Freedom to operate in Europe, Korea, China | S159 |

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared Hypertension Notification on 2025-09-11, Sleep Apnea Notification on 2024-09-13, granted Hearing Aid a De Novo on 2024-09-12 and cleared Medical Imaging Calibration on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, raising value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (incl. Duo) | Shipping; Duo announced, shipment per supply-chain reporting | 2026-09-09 | $54,252m in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by product | iPhone 18, spring 2027 | S47, S113 |
| Mac and iPad | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $10,352m (+29%) and $6,191m (-6%) in Q3 FY2026 | Not disclosed by product | M-series and iPad refresh | S47 |
| Wearables, home, accessories | Shipping | Annual | $35,686m FY2025, -4%; $7,883m Q3 FY2026, +6% | Not disclosed by product | Blood-pressure and glucose work unannounced | S47 |

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability: the June 2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM, and inventories nearly doubled in nine months, so the technology premium is being defended by price while memory costs rise. No Vision Pro units, no product-level margins and no patent counts are disclosed.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power design on a leading node | 3-4 years | S157 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | Record active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team of fifty could match the hinge within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and benchmarks, medium on durability, because Qualcomm's next generation closes most of the CPU gap and memory costs are eating the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the Gemini fee and term, and iPhone Duo sell-through.

arguments.claims_weakened: No European revenue or ASP is given in the extract; the 34% Apple share is not cross-checked against a second tracker and sits well above Apple's global unit share, so it may reflect a value or premium-weighted cut.

arguments.claims: Japan's smartphone market declined 1% YoY in Q2 2026 after two years of growth; the Middle East and Africa market fell 10% YoY (paywalled regional report page, retrieved as a search extract, HTTP 403).

arguments.title: CIRP: How is the Android to iOS Pipeline?
arguments.claims: 12% of new US iPhone buyers in the March 2026 quarter reported moving from an Android smartphone; the switching rate has held at 11-15% of new iPhone buyers in recent years (Consumer Intelligence Research Partners quarterly survey).
arguments.claims_weakened: US-only survey of buyers, not the installed base; the rate is inside its historical range, so it shows no acceleration in conversion from Android.

arguments.title: MacRumors: iPhone Loyalty Rate Climbs to 87% as Switching to Android Slows
arguments.claims: CIRP puts iPhone loyalty at 87% in Q1 2026, up from 84% a year earlier, with Android switchers at 12% of new US iPhone buyers versus 14% a year earlier.
arguments.claims_weakened: Survey-based and US-only; loyalty measures repeat purchase among buyers, not retention across the whole installed base.

arguments.title: IDC: Smart Glasses Growth Cools to 35% as Meta Doubles Down on Distribution
arguments.claims: Global XR headset and glasses shipments rose 35.3% YoY in Q2 2026 after 130.2% in Q1; audio glasses were 70.3% of units and display glasses 14.3%; Meta held 68.7% share; IDC forecasts unit growth of 26.3% in 2026, 40.5% in 2027 and 26.4% in 2028, with Samsung and XREAL Android XR products due later in 2026.
arguments.claims_weakened: The article gives no absolute units or revenue; the category is small against smartphone volumes, and today's glasses pair with a phone rather than replace one, so near-term substitution is an attach risk, not a handset-loss risk.

arguments.title: TechCrunch: OpenAI's first hardware device is reportedly a screenless speaker that can move
arguments.claims: On 2026-07-14 Bloomberg-sourced reporting described OpenAI's first hardware product as a screen-free, movable AI companion speaker built with former Apple engineers and still in development; Apple sued OpenAI over trade secrets in July 2026.
arguments.claims_weakened: No confirmed launch date, price or specification; nothing has shipped, so it takes no measurable revenue from Apple's pool yet, and the report rests on unnamed sources.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's silicon and operating-system advantage is still real, but it is no longer self-sufficient. In the September 2026 cycle Apple shipped a 2nm A20 Pro processor, its first foldable iPhone and a rebuilt "Siri AI", and the assistant at the centre of the launch runs on Google's Gemini models under a multi-year agreement announced 2026-01-12 [S115]. The moat is durable where Apple controls the whole stack — processor, OS, power management, hinge, sensors, factory loading — and thin at the intelligence layer, where the next premium is being priced.

### Silicon: the lead is measurable again, and narrower than it looks

Apple designs the processor, the operating system and the power-management logic together, and that co-design, not transistor count, is what puts desktop-class single-thread performance inside a phone power envelope. The A20 Pro, announced 2026-09-09, is Apple's first 2nm phone chip, on TSMC's N2 node: a 6-core CPU with two performance cores at up to 4.93GHz, a 7-core GPU, a dual 16-core Neural Engine rated at 44 TOPS FP16 and Apple's own C2 5G modem [S157]. On Geekbench 6, one outlet measured 4,707 single-core and 12,598 multi-core on its iPhone 18 Pro Max against 3,588 and 10,207 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in an iQOO 15 — a 31% single-core and 23% multi-core lead [S157]. The 4.5% gap quoted in earlier coverage was an A19 Pro comparison inside run-to-run variance; on the shipping generation the difference is large enough to measure, and it rests as much on the node as on design.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro, Geekbench 6 | 4,707 single / 12,598 multi | Outlet's iPhone 18 Pro Max | S157 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, same build | 3,588 / 10,207 | Outlet's iQOO 15 | S157 |
| A20 Pro, second outlet | 4,735 / 12,800 | Independent iPhone 18 Pro | S158 |
| Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 | 4,257 / 12,710 | Qualcomm reference-device claim | S157 |
| Sustained graphics, 20 loops | 80% stability vs 25% | 3DMark Wild Life Extreme | S157 |
| R&D, nine months FY2026 | $34,035m, +33% YoY | Reported | S6 |
| Capital expenditure, nine months FY2026 | $6,799m, 1.9% of revenue | Reported | S6 |
| Foldable units planned, 2026 | 10m, up from 7-8m | Supply-chain reporting | S113 |

### Sustained performance is the stronger claim, and it is not pure silicon

Peak scores flatter a chip; the 20-loop stress test in the table shows what a buyer gets after ten minutes. The A20 Pro held 80% of its best score, 8,793 falling to 7,032, while the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 fell to 25%, 6,867 to 1,715; a second outlet measured graphics stability of 79.4% against 65.2% a year earlier [S158]. Apple's vapour chamber is three times larger and memory no longer sits on the die, so part of that gap is chassis and pairing Apple's largest phone with a thinner Android device overstates the silicon margin. Two counters keep this honest. Qualcomm's next part, in the table, closes the single-core gap to about 11% before retail testing, and on Geekbench AI 1.7 a Qualcomm-powered Galaxy S26 Ultra scored 83,047 against 69,245 for the iPhone 18 Pro, so the second neural engine did not buy AI throughput leadership [S158].

### The intelligence layer is rented, not owned

The most consequential technical fact about Apple in 2026 is a contract: the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology. Apple calls this hybrid — on-device processing for privacy, licensed models for capability — and it shipped "all-new Siri AI" in September 2026 on the iPhone 18 Pro. R&D rose 33% while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to 1.9% of nine-month revenue, so capability is bought as an operating cost rather than built on owned compute. Model quality, query data and the pace of improvement sit with a competitor that also sells phones; the Geekbench AI gap is that dependency in miniature.

::: evidence
**Apple converted its largest technology gap into a recurring cost rather than closing it.**

The next Apple Foundation Models are built on Google's Gemini under a non-exclusive multi-year licence, so the assistant's ceiling is set by a competitor while integration, privacy and distribution are what Apple keeps.
:::

### Who owns which layer

| Dimension | Apple | Qualcomm | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant model | Licensed Gemini | None | Owns Gemini | No public figure | No public figure | S115 |
| SoC design | In-house A20 Pro, TSMC N2 | Merchant Snapdragon | In-house Tensor | Partly in-house | In-house | S157 |
| Cellular modem | In-house C2 5G | Merchant 5G | Merchant | Merchant | In-house | S157 |
| Foldable phone | Launched 2026 | No device | None identified | Shipping since 2019 | Shipping | S114 |

Owning the stack guarantees a good phone and a high price; it no longer guarantees the best assistant. Apple alone owns the processor, the OS and the modem but not the assistant; Google is the mirror image.

### Form factors: late, not rushed

The 2026-09-09 event introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the foldable iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Apple has announced the Duo; supply-chain reporting places it in the September 2026 shipping window, and no document verified here gives its unit volumes or price, so the foldable volume in the table is a target, not a result [S113]. At 4.5% of more than 220 million units the Duo changes the price ladder more than the revenue base; the patent's 2021 priority date shows why the hardware is late rather than rushed.

| Patent or application number | Title | Jurisdiction | Dates | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 12,164,344 B2 | Hinges for folding display devices | US | Filed 2022-07-07; priority 2021-08-11; granted 2024-12-10 | Active to 2042-07-07; assignee Apple Inc. | iPhone Duo hinge: interdigitated fingers in a friction clutch | S159, S121 |
| EP4134784A1, KR20230024218A, CN115904004A | Hinge family outside the US | EP, KR, CN | 2022-2023 | Family of US 12,164,344 B2 | Freedom to operate in Europe, Korea, China | S159 |

### Health is the most defensible new technology

Apple's health claims are regulator-verified rather than marketing: the FDA cleared Hypertension Notification on 2025-09-11, Sleep Apnea Notification on 2024-09-13, granted Hearing Aid a De Novo on 2024-09-12 and cleared Medical Imaging Calibration on 2026-04-01 [S68]. Each clearance turns sensor data into a claim a rival cannot copy by shipping the same sensor, raising value per unit. It has not yet reversed category deceleration.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (incl. Duo) | Shipping; Duo announced, shipment per supply-chain reporting | 2026-09-09 | $54,252m in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by product | iPhone 18, spring 2027 | S47, S113 |
| Mac and iPad | Shipping | 2025-2026 | $10,352m (+29%) and $6,191m (-6%) in Q3 FY2026 | Not disclosed by product | M-series and iPad refresh | S47 |
| Wearables, home, accessories | Shipping | Annual | $35,686m FY2025, -4%; $7,883m Q3 FY2026, +6% | Not disclosed by product | Blood-pressure and glucose work unannounced | S47 |

The counter-case is cost and dependency, not capability: the June 2026 filing warns of shortages and rising prices for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM, and inventories nearly doubled in nine months, so the technology premium is being defended by price while memory costs rise. No Vision Pro units, no product-level margins and no patent counts are disclosed.

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon-OS co-design | 8 | Chip, OS and power design on a leading node | 3-4 years | S157 |
| Installed base, switching costs | 9 | Record active base in every category | 5+ years | S47 |
| Regulated health claims | 7 | Four FDA clearances since 2024 | 3-5 years | S68 |
| Foundation models, assistant | 3 | Licensed from Google | Already conceded | S115 |
| **Composite** | **7** | **Durable hardware moat, thin AI layer** | **Minimum 3 years** | — |

A funded team of fifty could match the hinge within a couple of product cycles; matching the silicon, the health clearances and the installed base would take a decade. The moat is a hardware and regulatory moat, not an AI one.

The investment implication is to value Apple as a premium hardware franchise with a services annuity at three quarters gross margin rather than as an AI option, and not to pay for proprietary intelligence the company has chosen to rent. Confidence is high on the dated facts and benchmarks, medium on durability, because Qualcomm's next generation closes most of the CPU gap and memory costs are eating the margin that funds the model. Open questions: the Gemini fee and term, and iPhone Duo sell-through.
