rows.finding: iPhone supplied $196,515m of the $364,357m revenue in the nine months to 2026-06-27, 53.9% of the total, up from 50.4% in FY2025 ($209,586m of $416,161m); iPhone grew 22% against 16% for the group.
rows.mechanism: Growth re-concentrated in the shortest-cycle, most tariff- and component-exposed product while Services, the 76.3%-gross-margin annuity, grew 14% and fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2%.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 iPhone 52.3% and Services 22.2% of $383,285m; FY2025 Services 26.2%.
rows.weakens: Group gross margin still rose to 49.1% from 46.8% and operating margin to 33.6% from 32.1%, so hardware mix did not damage profitability.
rows.implication: Underwrite the services-annuity story at a lower weight than 2025 results implied; revenue quality fell in FY2026 even as growth doubled.
rows.confidence: high on figures (audited comparatives and 10-Q tables); medium on the mix judgement
rows.follow_up: Does Services outgrow iPhone in FY2027, and at what App Store take rate after the EU changes?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue was $64,839m in nine months of FY2026, up 30% from $49,884m, already above the whole of FY2025 ($64,377m) after declines of 8% in FY2024 and 4% in FY2025; it is 17.8% of group revenue.
rows.mechanism: iPhone-led rebound amplified by renminbi strength, in the one geography where iPhone is a higher proportion of segment sales (management's own disclosure).
rows.benchmark: FY2023 peak of $72,559m, then $66,952m in FY2024 and $64,377m in FY2025.
rows.weakens: Part of the increase is currency (renminbi strength noted by management), so local-demand growth is below the reported 30%.
rows.implication: China exposure is rising again into a year of US-China tariff and export-control risk; the rebound is a large part of the 16% group growth.
rows.confidence: high on figures; medium on durability
rows.follow_up: What is Greater China growth in constant currency, and how concentrated is it in Pro models?

rows.finding: Cash and marketable securities of $146,517m against debt of $84,344m ($1,997m commercial paper, $11,007m current and $71,340m non-current term debt) gave net cash of $62,173m at 2026-06-27, versus about $33,700m at 2025-09-27 ($132.4bn cash versus $91.3bn notes plus $8.0bn commercial paper).
rows.mechanism: Operating cash flow of $116,996m outran capital returned of $73,872m and capex of $6,799m, and inventories doubled to $11,092m from $5,718m ahead of component shortages.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 net cash of roughly $33.7bn; net cash equals about 1.2% of a ~$5.0trn market value.
rows.weakens: The cash build partly reflects buybacks running $8.5bn below the prior-year period ($62.1bn versus $70.6bn), not only stronger operations.
rows.implication: Balance-sheet capacity is not the constraint on the investment case and cannot support the valuation; the constraint is revenue durability.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Will the cash build be deployed into AI infrastructure, licensing or faster buybacks in FY2027?

rows.finding: Apple returned $73.9bn in nine months of FY2026 ($62.1bn of repurchases and $11.8bn of dividends), 63% of operating cash flow, and retired 164m shares (-1.1%) to 14,608,963 thousand; FY2025 was $89.3bn of repurchases plus $15.4bn of dividends under a $100bn May 2025 authorisation with the dividend at $0.26 rising to $0.27 in FY2026.
rows.mechanism: Per-share compounding is partly financial: diluted EPS rose 22% ($6.88 versus $5.62) faster than net income, but a 1.1% annual shrink adds only about 1pp.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft used FY2026 to fund $139.5bn of investing outflows with $182.9bn of operating cash flow, retaining capital for AI capacity rather than returning it.
rows.weakens: Apple has no debt constraint on returning more: net cash still rose $28.5bn in nine months.
rows.implication: The buyback is a support to EPS, not the engine; if the pace stays below FY2025, EPS growth decelerates toward net income growth.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the board raise the authorisation again in 2027, and does capex step up under the new CEO?

rows.finding: Ownership is index-dominated and single-class: Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% of 14,697,926,000 shares at 2026-01-02, all directors and executive officers 0.062%, 50.4bn shares authorised at $0.00001 par and no second voting class.
rows.mechanism: No controlling holder and no dual-class veto means structural governance risk is low, while policy risk arrives through regulators rather than controllers.
rows.benchmark: Alphabet and Meta carry multi-class voting; Apple does not.
rows.weakens: A board aged 51-77 with only one new independent since 2021 and a chair of 26 years' tenure (Levinson, director since 2000) is a soft governance negative.
rows.implication: Governance discounts are not warranted on structure, but there is no strategic anchor shareholder either; the register will follow index flows.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Will Ternus's arrival trigger board refresh, including an AI-operator director?

rows.finding: Tariffs and component costs are now a margin variable: Q3 FY2026 gross margin of 50.1% and EPS of $2.02 included about 2 percentage points and $0.11 from tariff refunds after the US Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, while management expects semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints to intensify.
rows.mechanism: One-off refunds flattered the quarter while a genuine input-cost squeeze is building, so the margin base is overstated and the forward cost line is understated.
rows.benchmark: Nine-month products gross margin of 39.9% versus 36.9% a year earlier, partly refund-driven.
rows.weakens: The 2026-01-14 Section 232 semiconductor initial results imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products.
rows.implication: Normalise Q3 margins before extrapolating; the FY2027 gross-margin assumption is the single most sensitive input, and this is a regulatory item to hand to the policy workstream.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How much of the tariff refund is non-recurring, and what Section 301 exposure applies to Apple's China-built products?

plan.decision_question: What exactly is Apple today - legal entity, listing, capital structure, business mix and geographic exposure - and does that structure support a long-only case at a market value near $5.0trn?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple at 2026-10-30 is an iPhone business with a services margin bolted on - 53.9% of nine-month FY2026 revenue comes from iPhone while 76.3%-gross-margin Services supply a quarter of sales - and that shape, not the $62.2bn net cash, is what the next twelve months test.
plan.why_different: It fixes the entity, ownership, revenue-mix and balance-sheet facts every other section assumes; it does not judge the market, the competition, the technology or the price.
plan.mechanism: Revenue quality: FY2026 growth came from iPhone and Greater China rather than from Services, lifting revenue and gross margin while concentrating the case in the product and geography most exposed to tariffs, memory pricing and US-China policy; the $62.2bn net cash position funds a 63%-of-cash-flow return rather than new capacity.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 trajectory; peer filings (Microsoft FY2026 operating cash flow $182.9bn against $139.5bn investing outflows; Alphabet Q3 2026 10-Q for a multi-class contrast); base rate: hardware companies rarely repeat mid-teens growth on a >50% single-product concentration without a new category.
plan.counter_evidence: Memory/NAND/DRAM shortage management expects to intensify; one-off tariff refunds inside Q3 FY2026 margins; iPhone at 53.9% of revenue; a China rebound partly driven by renminbi strength; a EUR 500m DMA fine and an EU fee overhaul; four top-team changes in twenty months; a ~$5.0trn market value on 16% growth.
plan.visual: A 12-row dated timeline of 2025-2026 events plus product-mix and geography tables covering FY2023 to nine months of FY2026.
plan.prohibited: well positioned, strong ecosystem, huge market, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, about/many/several, recently

rows.finding: Q2 2026 global smartphone units: Samsung 22.7% (+8.1% YoY), Apple 20.2% (+14.9% YoY, +3.9pp share), Xiaomi 11.3% (-26.4%), OPPO 10.5% (-17.1%), vivo 7.7% (-19.6%) in a market down 7.4% to 276.3M units.
rows.mechanism: Vendors that secured memory supply early and sell where memory is a smaller share of bill of materials gain; vendors whose volume sits below $200 absorb the cost shock and lose both volume and pricing room.
rows.benchmark: Q2 2025: Apple 16.3%, Samsung 19.4%, Xiaomi 14.2%; Apple is on track for a record 22% full-year share in 2026 against about 20% in 2025.
rows.weakens: Some of Apple's unit growth is demand pulled forward by fear of its own second-half price increases, so the share gain may not repeat; Xiaomi's decline is partly deliberate low-end pruning to protect margin.
rows.implication: Apple is taking share in a contracting market, which is the opposite of commoditisation — the competitive risk is at the margin (price-led Android flagships, Huawei in China), not in the core.
rows.confidence: High — final IDC historical data; the share direction is confirmed by Counterpoint's independent Q2 2026 series, though Counterpoint puts Samsung at 24%.
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's FY2027 share hold once the pull-forward from expected price rises fades and Android vendors reprice?

rows.finding: Premium handsets ($600+ wholesale) reached a record 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026; Apple held 65% of premium units with sales up 9% YoY, and Apple plus Samsung held 84%, up from 82% a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: Trade-in, financing and buyback programmes let consumers absorb higher prices, and the premium tier is where the memory cost increase is a smaller share of the price, so it grows as a share of a shrinking market.
rows.benchmark: H1 2025: Apple 62% of premium units; premium was 25% of the market. Apple's premium volumes grew 9% YoY.
rows.weakens: Unit share is not profit share; Huawei is the third-largest premium brand globally and the leader in China, where Apple's premium position is contested.
rows.implication: The profit pool is concentrating in two vendors; Apple's pricing power is intact, but at 65% share the incremental gain has to come from price and mix rather than from taking more of the segment.
rows.confidence: Medium — one research house, and the release was available only as a search extract rather than a full page.
rows.follow_up: What is Huawei's share of China's $600+ segment specifically, and how much premium profit does Apple earn per unit outside the US?

rows.finding: China Q2 2026: Huawei 22.6% (+19.4% YoY), Apple 18.1% (+24.4%), OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% (-21.7%), Honor 11.3%; the top six hold about 96% of the market.
rows.mechanism: Huawei's domestic brand loyalty, policy-backed prestige and widening price ladder let it hold price while Android rivals raised theirs; Apple matched with price holds and trade-in, so both took share from the price-raising middle.
rows.benchmark: Q2 2025 China: Huawei 18.1%, Apple 13.9%, Xiaomi 15.1%. China's total market fell 4.2% in H1 2026 to 134M units, and IDC expects the decline to widen to about 20% YoY in H2 2026.
rows.weakens: Apple grew faster than Huawei in Q2 2026, so Huawei is not gaining on Apple right now; and Huawei's reach outside China is limited by the absence of Google Mobile Services.
rows.implication: Huawei caps Apple's China premium ceiling at a level Apple has not exceeded since 2023; plan on 18% share, not on a return to former highs.
rows.confidence: High on the shares (IDC table); low on the durability of the relative position, since both leaders gained by holding prices rather than by winning on product.
rows.follow_up: What happens to Huawei's and Apple's China shares when Android vendors stop raising prices, and how much of Apple's China revenue is services and accessories rather than iPhone?

rows.finding: Mac shipments grew about 10% in Q2 2026 while the PC market fell 4.9%, leaving Apple at 9.9% unit share against Lenovo's 24.4%, HP's 19.1% and Dell's 13.6%.
rows.mechanism: Memory shortages hit low-priced consumer PCs hardest while Apple's M-series pricing and vertical integration protect gross margin; AI-PC replacement demand favours premium configurations.
rows.benchmark: Global PC market Q2 2026 fell 4.9% to 68.2M units after nine quarters of growth; Lenovo 24.4%, HP 19.1%, Dell 13.6%, Apple 9.9%.
rows.weakens: Apple reports Mac revenue of $33.7bn in FY2025, only 8% of total revenue, so even strong Mac growth moves the group by less than a point.
rows.implication: Mac is a share-taker at the margin, not a growth engine: a 10% unit share cannot move group revenue the way iPhone or services can.
rows.confidence: Medium — IDC figures via trade press rather than IDC's release; unit share understates Apple's revenue share.
rows.follow_up: What is Mac revenue share of the PC market, and how much of the Q2 2026 growth is AI-PC refresh versus education and enterprise wins?

rows.finding: Q1 2026 wrist-worn shipments of 47.05M units: Huawei 20.2%, Apple 17%, Xiaomi 17%, Samsung 5.8% (-20.7%), Garmin 5.1%.
rows.mechanism: Huawei and Xiaomi win on price and breadth in China and emerging markets; Apple competes on health sensing and iPhone attach, which supports ASP rather than unit share.
rows.benchmark: Wrist-worn category grew 2.2% in Q1 2026; Counterpoint's smartwatch-only series put Apple at 23% share with 21% growth, so category definition changes the ranking.
rows.weakens: The category bundles smartwatches with basic bands, and Apple does not sell a band, so the headline share understates its position in the profitable segment.
rows.implication: Apple has lost the unit lead in wrist-worn devices to cheaper Chinese hardware but likely retains profit leadership; the wearables line fell 4% in FY2025 to $35.7bn, so this is a shrinking contributor.
rows.confidence: Low — trade-press summary of IDC, category mix distorts the comparison.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's share of smartwatch revenue and of attach rates to iPhone, and is Huawei's lead inside China only?

rows.finding: Apple's App Store terms face three simultaneous pressures: EU terms restructured in August 2026 to a 5% commission on transactions outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links from October 2026; US remedies ordered on 2025-09-02 in the Google search case could bar Google from paying Apple for distribution; and US civil antitrust suits allege monopolisation in smartphones.
rows.mechanism: Regulation compresses the take rate on the only part of the ecosystem where Apple charges a commission, while the assistant layer commoditises: Siri was rebuilt on Google's Gemini models at WWDC in June 2026, reported at about $1bn a year and not disclosed in either company's latest SEC filing.
rows.benchmark: App Store ecosystem billings of over $1.4tn in 2025 (company-commissioned study), more than 90% commission-free; services gross margin 76.3% in the nine months to 2026-06-27.
rows.weakens: Most of the $1.4tn ecosystem was already commission-free, the EU is a minority of services profit (not disclosed), and Apple still charges on external distribution, so the revenue loss may be smaller than the headlines imply.
rows.implication: Price a haircut to the highest-multiple revenue stream rather than a binary break-up: each point of services gross margin is worth more than a point of hardware share.
rows.confidence: High on the policy facts and the remedies timeline; medium on the revenue at risk, which Apple does not disclose.
rows.follow_up: How much services revenue comes from App Store commission, Google licensing and EU-exposed commerce, and what has Apple guided for services margin in FY2027?

gate: 1+ primary or near-primary source checked where available
2+ numeric facts/proxies or explicit missing-data note
source IDs mapped to source register

plan.decision_question: In each market Apple sells into, is it gaining or losing share and share of the profit pool?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is winning the value pool and merely holding the unit pool: it holds 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales and 20.2% of global smartphone units in Q2 2026, about 10% of PCs and second place in wrist-worn devices, and the most dangerous competitor is Samsung — the only rival gaining share at scale in a shrinking market while its memory division profits from the shortage that is squeezing everyone else — with Huawei the binding constraint on Apple inside China's premium tier.
plan.why_different: This section maps rivals product by product and measures share and profit-pool movement; the market section sizes the pool and its growth; the strategy section asks what Apple should do about it; the risk section prices the failure modes. Competition answers 'who is taking the pool and how'.
plan.mechanism: Three different competitive mechanisms operate at once: vertical integration in memory (Samsung) converts an input-cost shock into share and profit; domestic brand plus policy protection (Huawei) caps Apple inside China's premium tier; and platform regulation plus AI commoditisation erode the services take rate and the assistant layer where Apple's differentiation was software.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own premium share of 62% in H1 2025 rising to 65% in H1 2026; Q2 2025 unit shares (Apple 16.3%, Samsung 19.4%) against Q2 2026 (20.2% and 22.7%); Huawei's 18.1% China share a year ago against 22.6% now; PC unit share of about 10% against a 25% revenue-share proxy implied by Mac ASPs.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple gained 3.9pp of global unit share and 3pp of premium share in the same periods, so the 'Android is closing the gap' case is contradicted at the high end; Huawei cannot compete outside China without Google Mobile Services, which caps its threat; and the EU's new 5% fee still leaves Apple a take on external distribution.
plan.visual: A per-product competitor table (iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, services) with share, price position and source, a positioning table by product, and a SWOT component carrying the share-gain counter-evidence.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; well positioned; strong moat; best-in-class; dominant ecosystem; robust pipeline

competition.author: Market Analyst
queries: IDC global smartphone vendor share Q2 2026 Apple Samsung Xiaomi OPPO vivo
IDC China smartphone market Q2 2026 Huawei Apple share
IDC PC shipments Q2 2026 Lenovo HP Dell Apple
IDC wrist-worn devices Q1 2026 Huawei Apple Xiaomi Samsung Garmin
EU DMA alternative app marketplaces Apple commission 2026
Apple v Epic Games Supreme Court 2026 external purchase links
Meta smart glasses market share Q2 2026 IDC
OpenAI first hardware device 2026 screenless speaker Apple lawsuit

rows.finding: In Q2 2026 Apple's global smartphone unit share rose 3.9 points to 20.2% and units 14.9% while the market fell 7.4%; Samsung led at 22.7% with units +8.1%, Xiaomi fell 26.4% to 11.3%, OPPO 17.1% and vivo 19.6%. IDC has Apple at a record 22% annual share in 2026.
rows.mechanism: The memory shock rewards vendors with supply commitments and premium mix; Samsung's memory division profits from the same cost increase that squeezes Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo, so Samsung can fund handset competition longest.
rows.benchmark: Market -7.4% (IDC) or -11% (Counterpoint); Apple 20.2% versus Samsung 22.7%
rows.weakens: The two trackers disagree on the size of the decline and Counterpoint puts Samsung at 24%, so the gap between Samsung and Apple may be wider than IDC shows.
rows.implication: Apple is gaining share in a shrinking market and Samsung is the most dangerous competitor because it is the only rival with a profit pool on the other side of the cost shock.
rows.confidence: high on direction, medium on the point estimates
rows.follow_up: Does Samsung's memory profit translate into sustained handset price competition through 2027?

rows.finding: Apple held 65% of $600-plus premium unit sales in H1 2026, with Apple and Samsung together at 84%; the premium tier was a record 29% of all units, up from 25% a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: The premium tier is where the profit pool sits, and Apple's share there is three times its share of the total unit market.
rows.benchmark: Premium share of 25% in H1 2025; Apple's total unit share of 20.2%
rows.weakens: Measured in units, not revenue or profit; Counterpoint does not disclose the tier's value in the material opened.
rows.implication: Competition for the profit pool is a two-vendor contest; Xiaomi and OPPO compete for units that carry little profit.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of premium revenue and gross profit does Apple hold, and is it rising?

rows.finding: In China, Huawei led Q2 2026 at 22.6% (+19.4%) while Apple rose to 18.1% from 13.9% (+24.4%) and OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi and Honor fell 9.5% to 21.7%; Huawei's 2025 revenue was CNY880.9bn with net profit of CNY68bn and R&D of CNY192.3bn (21.8% of revenue); IDC expects HarmonyOS to nearly triple to 51m units in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Huawei's domestic brand and policy standing plus HarmonyOS give it a premium position Apple cannot contest on software ecosystem; outside China, the absence of Google services caps Huawei.
rows.benchmark: Apple's China unit share of 13.9% a year earlier; Huawei at 22.6%
rows.weakens: Huawei's revenue is group-wide, not smartphone-specific, and its unit share is in a market that fell 4.3% in Q2 2026 and 15.4% in Q3 2026.
rows.implication: Huawei is a ceiling on Apple's China premium share, not a global competitor; the China recovery depends on Huawei's supply and pricing as much as on Apple.
rows.confidence: high on shares, medium on Huawei's smartphone economics
rows.follow_up: What is Huawei's premium share within China's $600-plus tier, and how much of its volume is subsidised or government-directed?

rows.finding: In PCs Apple is fourth at 9.9% while the market fell 4.9% to 68.2m units, behind Lenovo at 24.4%, HP at 19.1% and Dell at 13.6%; in wrist-worn devices Huawei leads at 20.2%, Apple and Xiaomi are tied at 17% and Samsung fell 20.7% to 5.8%.
rows.mechanism: Outside the phone, Apple competes on differentiation rather than ecosystem lock-in, and cheap Chinese hardware takes the unit lead while Apple keeps the profit through attach and price.
rows.benchmark: Mac revenue of $33,708m (8.1% of FY2025 revenue); Mac plus wearables $69.4bn against iPhone's $209.6bn
rows.weakens: The wrist-worn source is a secondary report of IDC data with low confidence, and PC share varies by quarter.
rows.implication: PCs and wearables do not move the group; they are optionality, not the thesis.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's wearable attach hold as Huawei and Xiaomi push cheaper watches into the same premium buyers?

rows.finding: Services competition is regulatory as much as commercial: Apple's EU terms from 2026-10-01 charge 5% outside the App Store and 20% on external payment links, the US remedies of 2025-09-02 left Google's search payments intact on appeal, Korea fined Apple and Google a combined $47.6m on 2026-10-28, and Siri was rebuilt on Google's Gemini models in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Regulators lower the commission Apple can charge and open distribution to rival stores and payment links, while the assistant layer is licensed from a competitor, so services margin depends on rules Apple does not set.
rows.benchmark: App Store commission of up to 30%; services gross margin of 76.3%
rows.weakens: The US search payments survived the 2025 remedies and are under appeal; the EU changes may preserve most revenue through the 5% and 20% fees.
rows.implication: The most valuable revenue stream is the most exposed; a lower take rate or a lost search payment hits gross profit directly.
rows.confidence: high on the terms, medium on the revenue effect
rows.follow_up: What share of App Store transactions now run outside Apple's payment system in the EU and US, and at what effective take rate?

rows.finding: Substitutes: Meta holds 68.7% of XR glasses, a category up 35.3% in Q2 2026 and forecast +26.3% in 2026; EU alternative app marketplaces and external links are permitted under the DMA and the US Epic injunction, with Apple proposing a 15% cut of external purchases on 2026-08-14 and the case at the Supreme Court (No. 25-1311); OpenAI's screenless AI companion was reported on 2026-07-14 and remains unshipped.
rows.mechanism: Glasses attack the next device purchase, alternative marketplaces attack the 15-30% commission, and an AI companion attacks the assistant layer Apple licenses from Google.
rows.benchmark: 2.5bn active Apple devices; App Store commission of up to 30%; Siri's Gemini licence reported at about $1bn a year
rows.weakens: Glasses pair with a phone, alternative stores remain small, and OpenAI has no ship date, so near-term revenue at risk is limited.
rows.implication: These are the three ways Apple's pool can shrink without an Android vendor winning a handset sale; none is material in 2026, and all three compound by 2028.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How fast are EU alternative marketplaces taking volume, and does Apple's 5% external fee survive the Supreme Court?

rows.finding: Counter-evidence: iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders were reported muted in September 2026, the EU General Court rejected Apple's DMA designation challenge on 2026-07-08, and the UK CMA's mobile platform case remains open.
rows.mechanism: Regulatory losses accumulate across jurisdictions and reduce Apple's ability to bundle services with hardware; weak pre-orders would expose the premium franchise to a demand shock.
rows.benchmark: Apple's 9M FY2026 revenue growth and record projected 22% unit share in 2026
rows.weakens: The pre-order note is a single analyst report, and the DMA ruling affects designation, not directly the commission rates.
rows.implication: The premium franchise is strong but not immune; the watchlist case should require evidence that the iPhone 18 cycle holds before adding on strength.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What did the iPhone 18 cycle do to Apple's premium share in Q4 2026, and does the CMA case force further App Store changes in the UK?

plan.decision_question: In each market, is Apple gaining or losing share and profit pool?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple wins the value pool and only holds the unit pool, the competitor that matters most is Samsung, and Huawei, regulators and substitute devices each cap a different part of the franchise.
plan.why_different: The market section sizes the pool and its regional split; this section names who captures it product by product and what Apple's wedge is against each rival.
plan.mechanism: Memory-cost inflation rewards vertical supply and premium mix, Samsung's memory profits fund handset price competition, Huawei's domestic brand and HarmonyOS cap Apple in China, and regulation plus substitute devices erode the services and next-device layers.
plan.comparison_set: Samsung 22.7%, Xiaomi 11.3%, Huawei 22.6% in China against Apple's 20.2% globally and 18.1% in China; Lenovo 24.4% in PCs; Huawei 20.2% in wrist-worn devices; 2025 and 2026 share points.
plan.counter_evidence: Huawei's China premium strength, Android flagships closing the performance gap, the EU and US opening of the App Store, and muted iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders.
plan.visual: The per-product competitor table and the product positioning table (leader, challenger, niche, emerging threat).
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; strong team; well positioned; high barriers to entry; risks are manageable; vague counts; any note on how the section is written

team.author: Company Analyst
queries: AAPL Form 4 activity last 12 months: purchases, sales, 10b5-1 flags, largest sellers
AAPL 8-K Item 5.02 filed 2025-07-25, 2025-12-05 and 2026-04-20: COO, general counsel and CEO transitions
AAPL 2026 DEF 14A: director biographies, tenure and ages, CEO pay structure, named executive officers, ownership
AAPL 10-Q 2026-06-27: R&D expense trend and drivers, repurchases, dividends, share count, intangible build and purchase obligations
AAPL FY2025 10-K Item 7: R&D by year, buyback authorisation, dividend increase
MSFT FY2026 10-K Item 7: operating cash flow and investing outflows (peer capital deployment)
Fortune profile of John Ternus, 2026-08-31 (independent evidence on the AI gap and succession expectations)

rows.finding: John Ternus, 50 at appointment, became CEO and a director on 2026-09-01; he joined Apple in 2001, was vice president of hardware engineering from 2013 and a member of the senior executive team from 2021; Tim Cook moved to executive chair and Art Levinson from chair to lead independent director.
rows.mechanism: A planned insider succession preserves operational continuity and product cadence but leaves the AI strategy owned by the same executive team that produced the 2024-2026 Siri delays.
rows.benchmark: Cook himself was an operations executive promoted internally in 2011, a base rate of Apple preferring continuity; Fortune reports Gassée and Munster expect continuity rather than a reset.
rows.weakens: Ternus has run hardware engineering since 2021 and is credited with the Mac silicon transition, so continuity may be an asset rather than a weakness.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a strategy reset: the premium should rest on the installed base and margin, not on a new-category bet from the new CEO.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does Ternus change capital allocation (capex, M&A, licensing) or only product cadence in FY2027?

rows.finding: Four of the top jobs turned over in twenty months: CFO (Kevan Parekh, January 2025), COO (Sabih Khan, 2025-07-25, aged 58, at Apple since August 1995), general counsel (Jennifer Newstead from 2026-03-01, with Kate Adams, GC since 2017, retiring late 2026) and CEO (2026-09-01).
rows.mechanism: A retirement wave in a long-tenured leadership cohort replaced operating experience with operating experience, not with new capability.
rows.benchmark: Apple's tenured cohort: Khan joined in 1995 (31 years), Ternus in 2001 (25 years), Cook in 1998 (28 years); the GC replacement is the only external senior hire in the group.
rows.weakens: Three of the four moves were planned retirements with internal successors, so the turnover may signal a managed bench rather than instability.
rows.implication: Institutional knowledge is intact but external refresh is thin; key-person dependency concentrates in Ternus and Khan at the moment of an AI transition.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Who is the designated AI/product leader below the CEO, and is that role on the executive team?

rows.finding: Capital allocation is disciplined and shareholder-first: $73.9bn returned in nine months of FY2026 ($62.1bn repurchases, $11.8bn dividends) equal to 63% of $117.0bn operating cash flow while capex was only $6.8bn; FY2025 returned $104.7bn ($89.3bn plus $15.4bn) and the share count fell 1.1% in nine months.
rows.mechanism: Returning most operating cash flow and holding capex near 2% of revenue maximises per-share metrics and ROIC while leaving AI compute to partners and licensing.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft in FY2026 retained capital: $182.9bn operating cash flow against $139.5bn investing outflows with capex up $51.4bn.
rows.weakens: Apple's asset-light model is why it earns a 49% gross margin and a high return on capital; heavy capex is not automatically better capital allocation.
rows.implication: The record justifies a premium for capital discipline but not for reinvestment; a buyer paying ~$5trn is paying for returns of capital, not for a new growth engine.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Is Apple buying capability it used to build - and at what price and exclusivity?

rows.finding: R&D rose from $29,915m (FY2023) to $31,370m (FY2024) to $34,550m (FY2025) and reached $34,035m in nine months of FY2026, up 33% year on year, or 9.3% of revenue, with the quarter at 10.7%; at the same time gross intangible assets rose to $38,220m from $24,950m and other purchase obligations to $29.3bn from $14.8bn.
rows.mechanism: AI catch-up is being funded through the P&L (infrastructure and headcount) and through licensed IP on the balance sheet, which is why operating margin (33.6%) held only because gross margin rose 2.3pp.
rows.benchmark: R&D was 8% of revenue in FY2023-FY2025, so 9.3% is a step change, not a drift.
rows.weakens: The intangible increase could be routine content and distribution rights rather than AI licensing; the filing does not attribute it.
rows.implication: Apple is buying capability as well as building it; that is a rational catch-up route but it transfers margin to a licensor whose identity is not disclosed.
rows.confidence: high on figures; medium on what the spend buys
rows.follow_up: What is the counterparty, term and exclusivity of the licensing commitments behind the intangible build?

rows.finding: Pay is tied to relative total shareholder return, not to AI or product milestones: Cook's 2025 target equity was $50m, 75% performance-based, his base salary is unchanged since 2016, and 2021-granted performance RSUs vested at 187% of target on 2024-10-01 (477,301 shares); he has already met the age-65, ten-year retirement-vesting condition.
rows.mechanism: Relative-TSR scorecards pay for outperforming the S&P 500, a target reachable through buybacks and margin management without a new product cycle.
rows.benchmark: Apple positions Cook's total target pay at the 80th-90th percentile of its peer group by its own statement.
rows.weakens: The 2022-granted PSUs paid out at 187% of target only because Apple beat the S&P 500 on TSR, which is a demanding hurdle rather than a soft one.
rows.implication: Alignment with shareholder returns is strong and alignment with strategic transformation is weak - the incentive structure rewards the status quo the market is worried about.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is Ternus's pay package and does it include AI or product-cycle metrics?

rows.finding: Insiders sold and did not buy: 46 sale transactions of 687,127 shares for $208.0m in the twelve months to 2026-10-29, 43 of them under Rule 10b5-1 plans, with zero purchases; the largest were director Art Levinson at $86.7m, executive chair Tim Cook at $80.4m and Deirdre O'Brien at $23.1m, and new CEO John Ternus sold $8.5m on 2026-10-02.
rows.mechanism: Scheduled plans mute the information content of sales, so the informative signal is the absence of any discretionary purchase at a ~$5trn valuation.
rows.benchmark: A 14,608,963-thousand-share company where no officer or director bought a share at $300-345.
rows.weakens: Senior executives at a company this size rarely buy on the open market because most of their wealth is already in Apple stock and equity grants dominate.
rows.implication: Treat as neutral-to-negative corroboration, not a thesis driver: scheduled diversification explains the sales, but no informed buyer is signalling that the shares are cheap.
rows.confidence: high on the facts; low as a standalone signal
rows.follow_up: Does any officer buy after the 2026-11-02 results, and does Ternus keep selling on the same schedule?

rows.finding: The board is experienced but stale: after the transition it has nine directors aged 51-77, including Levinson (75, a director since 2000), Sugar (77, since 2010), Jung (67, since 2008) and Wagner (64, since 2014), with Wanda Austin (2024) the only new independent since 2021.
rows.mechanism: Low refresh and long tenure preserve institutional memory but reduce the external challenge a first-time CEO needs during a technology discontinuity.
rows.benchmark: Committee chairs are substantive: Ron Sugar (77, since 2010) chairs audit after serving as Northrop Grumman's CFO; Sue Wagner (64, since 2014) co-founded BlackRock.
rows.weakens: The same board oversaw the services transition and the silicon transition, and no director election has drawn majority opposition in the disclosed record.
rows.implication: Oversight of the AI transition rests with a board that has deep finance and consumer-brand experience and little current AI-operator experience.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Will the board add an operating AI or developer-platform director within twelve months?

rows.finding: Independent reporting on the handover describes an unresolved AI gap versus OpenAI, a memory-chip shortage squeezing margins, slowing revenue growth and product misfires (Vision Pro, Siri updates, the Liquid Glass redesign), while describing Ternus as a well-liked hardware engineer expected to make only 'small touches' at first.
rows.mechanism: A continuity CEO inherits both the operating discipline and the innovation gap, so the valuation premium cannot be justified by succession alone.
rows.benchmark: Fortune quotes an investor that Ternus is not 'an iconic product visionary' and reports Vision Pro as a misfire, Siri updates as a miss, the Liquid Glass redesign as criticised and the foldable phone as years behind Samsung.
rows.weakens: Apple's reported 16% revenue growth and 22% iPhone growth in nine months of FY2026 contradict the 'slowing growth' framing in the same article.
rows.implication: The counter-case is about product, not people: the team is competent and the pipeline is the open question, which is what the FY2027 cycle will settle.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Which AI features ship in the FY2027 cycle and are they Apple-built or licensed?

plan.decision_question: Does management's execution and capital-allocation record justify a premium valuation at a market value near $5.0trn, or is the premium a balance-sheet and buyback artefact?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's capital-allocation record is exceptional and its 2025-2026 product execution is not: the company returned $73.9bn, 63% of operating cash flow, in nine months while growing revenue 16%, but that growth needed a 33% rise in R&D and a $13.3bn build in gross intangibles, and the CEO, COO, CFO and general counsel all changed inside twenty months.
plan.why_different: It judges the people and their decisions - pay, succession, insider behaviour, where the cash goes - rather than the products, the market or the price.
plan.mechanism: Capital allocation substitutes for growth: the buyback adds roughly 1pp to EPS a year, so the premium depends on gross margin holding above 49% while R&D intensity rises from 8.3% to above 9% and while a first-time CEO with a hardware-engineering background runs the AI transition.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own 2011 handover from Cook's operations background; Microsoft FY2026 ($182.9bn operating cash flow against $139.5bn investing outflows, capex up $51.4bn); Apple's own stated benchmark of the 80th-90th percentile of peer CEO pay; base rate: internally promoted operations CEOs at hardware incumbents rarely deliver a new product category in their first two years.
plan.counter_evidence: Independent reporting of an unresolved AI gap, Siri misses and product misfires; zero insider purchases in twelve months against $208m of sales; a board with only one new independent since 2021; CEO, COO, CFO and GC all changed between January 2025 and March 2026; R&D intensity rising partly because of catch-up spending.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix across Ternus, Cook, Khan and Parekh, with an evidence component on the succession and the capital-allocation record.
plan.prohibited: well positioned, strong team, experienced management, clear strategy, risks are manageable, about/many/several, recently

rows.finding: AAPL trades at 40.0x TTM P/E, 32.5x EV/EBIT and 10.8x EV/Sales on a $5,092.1B market cap and $5,029.9B EV, against a three-peer median of 21.3x P/E and 21.5x EV/EBIT — an 88% P/E premium and 51% EV/EBIT premium; adding Samsung at 12.9x lowers the four-peer median to 18.1x. Apple's own fiscal-year-end P/E rose 24.6x (FY2022) to 27.9x (FY2023), 37.5x (FY2024) and 34.2x (FY2025), so 40.0x is above every year-end multiple since 2021.
rows.mechanism: The premium is the price of mix (Services $91.7B of the $364.4B nine-month revenue) and of a revenue acceleration to 14.8% in FY2026 from 6.4% in FY2025; the market is capitalising a higher-quality, faster-growing stream at a lower discount rate than the peer set receives.
rows.benchmark: Peer median 21.3x P/E and 21.5x EV/EBIT (MSFT, GOOGL, META); Samsung 12.9x; Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 year-end P/E range 24.6x-37.5x and EV/Sales range 6.1x-9.1x.
rows.weakens: Apple's FY2026 revenue growth of 14.8% is far above the peer set, and its EV/Sales premium is only 51% against a 88% P/E premium, so part of the gap is earned by mix rather than pure re-rating; Alphabet's 14.8x trailing P/E appears depressed by a trailing item and drags the median down.
rows.implication: An entry at 40x means the multiple, not the business, determines the return: hold the multiple and the buyer earns EPS growth of about 8%; lose a third of the multiple and two years of compounding is erased. Price lower or wait.
rows.confidence: high — multiples computed from SEC XBRL filings and 2026-10-29 closing prices, with two independent consensus reads agreeing.
rows.follow_up: What Services growth and gross margin does a 40x multiple capitalise, and does the FY2027 consensus of +10.3% revenue support it?

rows.finding: A two-stage DCF on $128.7B of owner free cash flow (consensus FY2026 FCF $142.36B less $13.7B stock-based compensation) at a 9.5% WACC, 8% growth for five years, 4% for five more and 3% terminal, values the equity at $2,667B or $183 a share — 48% below the $348.91 close. Across an 8.5%-10.5% WACC and 2.5%-3.5% terminal grid the range is $153-$230; each 100bp on the discount rate moves the value 15-18%.
rows.mechanism: Duration: at 40x earnings the cash flows that matter sit a decade out, so the discount rate and terminal growth set the price. Terminal value is 56% of the $2,605B enterprise value, which is why the grid, not the point estimate, is the honest output.
rows.benchmark: Revenue CAGR of 5.5% from FY2021 ($365.8B) to FY2026E ($477.6B); consensus FY2027 revenue growth of 10.3%; 10-year Treasury at 4.99%.
rows.weakens: The terminal assumption dominates: a single-stage perpetual-growth reverse DCF needs only 5.3% perpetual FCF growth at an 8.0% WACC (6.9% at 9.5%) to justify $5,030B, and Apple has compounded FCF at about 9% a year for five years — so the DCF is not proof of overvaluation, it is proof that the price depends on assumptions I cannot verify.
rows.implication: There is no margin of safety against a 9.5% required return; a buyer is underwriting a second growth engine (AI devices, Services) that is not in the model. Position size for a 15-25% drawdown if the required return rises.
rows.confidence: medium — the arithmetic is exact and reproducible, but the growth path is judgement, and the peer-consistent discount rate is an assumption (beta 1.1 is mine, not sourced).
rows.follow_up: Which disclosed cash flows would have to arrive by FY2031 for the 15%-growth case to be visible in filings rather than in narrative?

rows.finding: Consensus already sits below the market: average 12-month target $332.39 across 43 analysts (median $337.50, low $245, high $405) is 4.7% below the $348.91 close, corroborated by a 44-analyst median of $338; Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from 1 in May 2026 to 6 in October 2026 while the shares gained 28.6% in twelve months.
rows.mechanism: The sell side's own discounted values do not support the price, so the marginal buyer is not rating-driven; when targets lag the price, upgrades cannot supply the next leg and downgrades become the asymmetric risk.
rows.benchmark: 43 analysts polled by S&P Global; the high target of $405 implies +16.1% and the low of $245 implies -29.8%.
rows.weakens: Targets lag prices mechanically in a momentum run, and five named houses (Evercore ISI $380, HSBC $366, JPMorgan $360, BofA $370, Monness $355) sit above the average; the average is dragged by a long tail of low targets.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a re-rating to consensus — there is none. The watchlist case must rest on earnings beats, not on multiple expansion.
rows.confidence: medium-high — two independent consensus aggregators agree within 1.6% on the median.
rows.follow_up: How much of the FY2027 EPS estimate depends on the Google default payment and on tariff-refund gross margin?

rows.finding: At a $5,092.1B market cap Apple's trailing earnings yield is 2.50% against a 4.99% 10-year Treasury yield — a negative spread of 249bp — with the 10-year up 93bp year on year, the 2-year at 4.67%, fed funds at 4.00%, VIX at 17.20 (52nd percentile) and investment-grade spreads at 86bp.
rows.mechanism: A negative earnings-yield spread means the buyer is paid less for owning the equity than for owning the bond and must recover the difference through growth; it also makes the multiple mechanically sensitive to any further rise in the discount rate, which is the exact channel through which 2022 compressed Apple's P/E from 37.5x to 24.6x.
rows.benchmark: 10-year Treasury 4.99%, 2-year 4.67%, fed funds upper limit 4.00%, IG OAS 86bp versus 76bp a year earlier, VIX 17.20 versus a 13.47-31.05 one-year range.
rows.weakens: Credit spreads at 86bp and a VIX in the middle of its range describe a calm market, not a stressed one; a fall in the 10-year yield would re-expand the multiple and my scenario weights would be wrong.
rows.implication: Size the position for rate duration, not just for earnings risk: a 100bp rise in the required return removes 15-18% of my DCF value without any change in Apple's business.
rows.confidence: high on the data, medium on the causal link between yields and this multiple.
rows.follow_up: What is the historical beta of Apple's P/E to the 10-year yield in 2022-2026, and has it fallen as Services grew?

rows.finding: FQ3 FY2026 (quarter ended 2026-06-27) revenue rose 16.4% to $109.4B with gross margin of 50.1% that included about 2 percentage points of tariff refunds, iPhone +21.7%, Greater China +22.4%, Services +12.1% and R&D +32.2%; the release contains no quantitative revenue or EPS guidance.
rows.mechanism: The margin peak is partly a refund, and R&D growing twice as fast as revenue is the cost of the AI build; extrapolating a 50.1% gross margin into FY2027 overstates earnings power by roughly two points, which on $527B of consensus FY2027 revenue is about $10B of gross profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 gross margin 46.9% and revenue growth 6.4%; FQ3 FY2025 gross margin 46.5% ($43.7B on $94.0B).
rows.weakens: The growth is broad-based — every geographic segment and iPhone, Mac and Services all grew double digits — and Greater China's 22.4% rebound contradicts the share-loss narrative, so the acceleration is not a one-product or one-refund artefact.
rows.implication: Underwrite FY2027 margins at 48-49%, not 50%, and discount the first clean quarter from the new CEO on 2026-11-02 rather than extrapolating the refund-flattered one.
rows.confidence: high — read from the 8-K exhibit filed with the SEC.
rows.follow_up: What is the gross margin excluding tariff refunds, and how much of the refund is recurring?

rows.finding: Trailing free cash flow of $136.7B is flattered by a working-capital release: days sales outstanding fell to 24.5 from 34.9 a year earlier with receivables $8.4B lower, so FCF/net income is 1.06x against 0.88x in FY2025 and a 0.98-1.16x five-year range; normalised FCF is about $129B, a 2.5% yield rather than 2.7%.
rows.mechanism: Cash conversion mean-reverts: a one-off collection of receivables raises reported FCF without changing earnings power, so anyone valuing Apple on trailing FCF yield overstates the cash return by roughly 20bp.
rows.benchmark: FY2021-FY2025 FCF/net income 0.98x, 1.12x, 1.03x, 1.16x, 0.88x; consensus FY2026 FCF $142.36B.
rows.weakens: Apple's conversion has averaged about 1.03x over five years, so 1.06x is not an outlier and the adjustment is small relative to the multiple question.
rows.implication: Use $129-142B of FCF as the base and resist the 2.7% yield headline; on either figure the cash yield is below the 4.99% Treasury, which is the whole valuation argument in one line.
rows.confidence: medium-high — the working-capital swing is in the filed balance sheet; the normalisation is my judgement.
rows.follow_up: Is the receivables decline a vendor-non-trade-receivable reclassification or genuine collection, and does it reverse in FQ4?

plan.decision_question: What is Apple worth, and what does the $348.91 share price imply about future cash flow and risk?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple at $348.91 is priced at 40.0x trailing earnings — an 88% premium to its peer median and above every fiscal-year-end multiple since 2021 — so the share price rather than the business is the risk: it requires roughly 15% annual free-cash-flow growth for a decade at a 9.5% discount rate, or a 5-7% perpetual growth rate accepted at a sub-9% required return, and leaves a long-only buyer no margin of safety at today's quote.
plan.why_different: The other sections judge the business, its products, its market and its risks; this one prices them, converting the filed numbers into per-share value and stating which growth the market has already paid for so the Lead can size a position rather than describe a company.
plan.mechanism: Multiple duration: a 40x P/E is a claim on cash flows a decade out, so the discount rate (10-year Treasury 4.99%) and the terminal growth rate set the value more than the next quarter does; with a 2.50% earnings yield sitting 249bp under the risk-free rate, each 100bp of required return removes 15-18% of my DCF value.
plan.comparison_set: Four named peers (MSFT 27.7x, GOOGL 14.8x, META 21.3x, Samsung 12.9x; median 18.1x), Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 fiscal-year-end P/E of 24.6x/27.9x/37.5x/34.2x and EV/Sales of 6.1x-9.1x, consensus FY2027 EPS of $9.56, and a 5.5% revenue CAGR from FY2021 to FY2026E.
plan.counter_evidence: Revenue grew 16.4% in FQ3 FY2026 with Greater China up 22.4% and gross margin at 50.1%, consensus FY2026 EPS was revised up 18.5%, the shares made a new high on 2026-10-29 and VIX sits at its 52nd percentile — a genuine AI-driven acceleration could hold a 40x multiple, and with terminal value at 56% of my DCF the $183 figure is an assumption rather than an observation.
plan.visual: Trading snapshot table, then the peer multiples table with Samsung added to the four-peer median, then the valuation methods table carrying peer P/E, own-history P/E, the two-stage DCF range and the reverse DCF.
plan.prohibited: 'expensive', 'overvalued' or 'bubble' as standalone labels without the arithmetic; 'huge market', 'strong team', 'high barriers to entry', 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned'; vague counts ('about 5', 'many'); any sentence about how the section or report is written.

rows.finding: Consensus FY2026 free cash flow of $142.36B less $13.7B of stock-based compensation and $17.7B of contracted intangible purchases (licensed intellectual property, content and distribution rights, listed in the 10-Q's unconditional purchase obligations note) gives $111.0B of owner cash flow, not the $128.7B used before this revision.
rows.mechanism: Reported free cash flow overstates distributable cash when capability is bought through contracted licences rather than built through capex; the cash leaves through investing and operating commitments that capex does not capture.
rows.benchmark: Prior owner-cash build of $128.7B; reported FCF conversion of 1.06x net income; risk section's finding that $13,270M of gross intangibles were added with no acquisition in investing cash flow.
rows.weakens: The $17.7B is an annualisation of a nine-month build, and the 10-Q does not disaggregate the commitment table by year or counterparty, so the deduction could be too high or too low by several billion.
rows.implication: Cut the DCF base from $183 to $158 a share and raise the reverse-DCF growth requirement from 15% to about 17%; the conclusion (no margin of safety at $348.91) survives and strengthens.
rows.confidence: medium — the direction is certain from the filing, the size is an estimate
rows.follow_up: Does the FY2026 10-K disclose the intangible lives and the licensing counterparty, and does the amortisation arrive in FY2027?

rows.finding: Two-stage DCF at a 9.5% WACC gives $158 a share (range $132-$198 at 8.5-10.5% WACC and 2.5-3.5% terminal growth), against the $348.91 close; terminal value is 56% of the $2,246B enterprise value.
rows.mechanism: With 85% of the price in the terminal value, the multiple and the discount rate, not the near-term cash flow, set the value.
rows.benchmark: Peer-median P/E method at $158 (18.1x x $8.72) and own four-year average year-end P/E at $271 (31.1x x $8.72).
rows.weakens: The 1.1 beta and 4.5% equity-risk premium are my assumptions, not sourced figures; a WACC near 6.8% would make $348.91 fair.
rows.implication: No margin of safety at the current price; the two independent methods now agree at $158.
rows.confidence: medium — sensitive to WACC
rows.follow_up: What beta and equity-risk premium does the committee underwrite for a 40x mega-cap?

rows.finding: At a 9.5% required return the $5,029.9B enterprise value needs free cash flow to compound at about 17% a year for ten years — 3.1x the 5.5% revenue CAGR from FY2021 to FY2026E and 1.9x Apple's 8.9% five-year FCF compound; at an 8.0% required return the bar falls to 5.7% in perpetuity.
rows.mechanism: The price is a call option on a second growth engine: only an acceleration far above the company's own history justifies it at a 9.5% discount rate.
rows.benchmark: 5.5% revenue CAGR FY2021-FY2026E; 8.9% five-year FCF CAGR; 17% is 3.1x and 1.9x those rates respectively.
rows.weakens: At an 8.0% required return the requirement is already met by history, so the bear case rests on the discount rate rather than on the cash flows.
rows.implication: The buyer is underwriting AI devices, Services or a new category that no filing yet evidences; wait for evidence or a lower price.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the growth comparison
rows.follow_up: Which reported line would first show a second growth engine — Services sub-segments, wearables, or units?

rows.finding: Apple trades at 40.0x trailing earnings, 32.5x EV/EBIT and 10.8x EV/Sales with a 2.7% FCF yield, against a four-peer median of 18.1x and above every fiscal year-end multiple since FY2022 (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x); the 43-analyst consensus target is $332.39, 4.7% below the close, and Sell plus Strong Sell ratings rose from one to six between May and October 2026.
rows.mechanism: A premium multiple on decelerating growth compresses when the growth evidence fails or the discount rate rises; the sell side lags the price rather than leading it.
rows.benchmark: Four-peer median 18.1x; three US peers 21.3x; Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 range 24.6-37.5x.
rows.weakens: Samsung at 12.9x is a memory maker whose multiple is lowest at peak earnings, so the US-peer premium is 88%, not 122%.
rows.implication: There is no re-rating left to buy; the entry case requires 30-34x forward earnings.
rows.confidence: high — market data and consensus are dated
rows.follow_up: Do target cuts follow the 2026-11-02 print, and does the multiple hold above 36x forward?

rows.finding: The valuation methods table now spans $158 (peer median and DCF), $271 (own-history P/E) and a $132-$198 DCF sensitivity band; the owner cash yield at the price is 2.18% against a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a -281bp spread.
rows.mechanism: When the cash yield is below the risk-free rate, the buyer's return depends on growth and multiple, not on cash return.
rows.benchmark: Reported FCF yield of 2.68% (S6, S10); ten-year Treasury 4.99%.
rows.weakens: Apple's cash yield grows with the business and the Treasury's does not, so a static spread understates the equity case.
rows.implication: The buyback retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield funded by 4.99% risk-free alternatives; it does not defend a 40x price.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: At what price does the owner cash yield exceed the ten-year Treasury?

rows.finding: Over the five years to 2026-10-29 Apple's price rose 134.2% (18.5% a year) on diluted EPS growth of 55.4% ($5.61 in FY2021 to $8.72 trailing) and a P/E re-rating from 26.6x to 40.0x (+50.7%), with dividends adding about 2.3% cumulatively; multiple expansion accounts for roughly 48% of the logarithmic return.
rows.mechanism: Re-rating, not earnings, supplied half the return: with the multiple now at a five-year high the same mechanism cannot repeat from a higher base, so the return distribution is asymmetric — earnings still compound, the multiple can only give back.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 10-K total-return graph to September 2025: Apple $234, S&P 500 $217, Dow Jones U.S. Technology $287 on a $100 base — 18.5% a year against 16.8% for the S&P and 23.5% for the technology index.
rows.weakens: EPS still compounded at 9.2% a year through a pandemic, a China slowdown and a tariff cycle, so the underlying engine did two-thirds of the work even though the multiple did half of the return.
rows.implication: A repeat of the last five years requires the multiple to reach 60x on 8% EPS growth; without that, the holding-period return is the EPS growth rate plus the dividend, about 8.4% a year, which is below the 9.5% required return used in the valuation.
rows.confidence: high — every component is from a filing or a dated price series and the three components multiply back to the actual price change.
rows.follow_up: What multiple would a holding-period return of 8% a year require at exit, and what would force it down?

rows.finding: Apple has $99.779B of buyback authorisation left at 2025-09-27 under the May 2025 $100B programme, of which $62.1B was used in the nine months to 2026-06-27, leaving roughly $37.7B absent a new programme; trailing repurchases of $82.2B equal 1.6% of market cap, and in FQ4 FY2025 Apple bought 89.5M shares for about $20.0B at roughly $223.5 each, 36% below today's close.
rows.mechanism: A buyback adds value only when the price is below intrinsic value; above it, each repurchased share is a transfer from continuing holders to selling ones, so the 1.6% buyback yield is a share-count effect rather than a return source at a 40x multiple.
rows.benchmark: Buyback yield 1.6% against a 2.5% normalised FCF yield; $82.2B trailing repurchases against $90.7B in FY2025 and $94.9B in FY2024.
rows.weakens: The programme is large, recurring and renewed annually, and 1.6% of annual share shrinkage is a real contributor to EPS growth that my 8% EPS estimate already embeds.
rows.implication: Do not treat the buyback as a bid under the stock: at 40x it shrinks the share count 1.6% a year while transferring value to sellers, and its capacity is about 2% of market cap a year, far too small to absorb index selling.
rows.confidence: high — authorisation, spend and prices are filed figures; only the residual balance is my arithmetic.
rows.follow_up: What did Apple authorise in May 2026, and is the buyback being slowed as the multiple rises?

rows.finding: No strategic exit exists: the largest technology acquisition ever, Microsoft's $68.7B purchase of Activision Blizzard, equals 1.35% of Apple's $5,029.9B enterprise value, every comparable deal since 2016 was struck for a company one to two orders of magnitude smaller, and a leveraged buyout would need more than $5T of equity that no sponsor or consortium can raise.
rows.mechanism: Deal size is bounded by the acquirer's balance sheet and by antitrust review; at $5.03T Apple is roughly 73 times the largest technology deal ever, so the distribution of exit outcomes has no takeover premium in it at all.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft/Activision Blizzard $68.7B (2023), Dell/EMC $67B (2016), Broadcom/VMware $61B (2023) — the three largest technology transactions ever.
rows.weakens: A stock-for-stock merger with another mega-cap, an activist-driven break-up, or a sovereign-backed consortium are theoretical routes my arithmetic rules out by assumption rather than by evidence.
rows.implication: The exit is the secondary market, full stop; a holder should not pay anything for takeover optionality, and the trim decision must be made on valuation and catalyst dates rather than on a bid.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the deal values, which come from one near-primary release and one ranking.
rows.follow_up: Is there any regulatory or political path to a foreign or domestic acquisition of a US$5T company, and would antitrust review not end it first?

rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: 38.67M shares a day worth $13.22B trade in Apple, so a $250M position is 1.9% of one day's volume and can be exited in under a day at a fifth of normal participation; the shares sit 0.8% below their 52-week high of $351.73 and above the 50-day ($332.37) and 200-day ($296.13) averages.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity cuts both ways: it lets a holder leave without a discount, and it lets index-driven selling arrive without a discount too, so concentration in the index amplifies drawdowns rather than protecting the price.
rows.benchmark: Average daily value traded $13.22B (20 days) and $13.55B (3 months); Apple is one of three stocks that together make up 21% of the S&P 500.
rows.weakens: An all-time-high price with a 44.5% fifty-two-week range ($243.42 to $351.73) shows the stock can lose 30% in a year even with this liquidity, so liquidity protects the exit, not the return.
rows.implication: Exit cost is not the risk and does not argue for a smaller position; the risk is the price at which the exit happens, which is set by the multiple rather than by the order book.
rows.confidence: high on liquidity; medium on the index concentration, which comes from a single media report without Apple's individual weight.
rows.follow_up: What share of Apple's float is held by index and passive vehicles, and how does that change the drawdown behaviour versus 2022?

rows.finding: A twelve-to-eighteen-month scenario set on FY2027 EPS of $9.56 gives $404 in the bull case (40x, +16%), $325 in the base case (34x, -7%) and $224 in the bear case (26x on a margin reversal, -36%); at 25/45/30 weights the probability-weighted outcome is $314, or -10% plus the 0.3% dividend.
rows.mechanism: With EPS growth fixed at 8% by consensus, the exit multiple does most of the work: each 6x of P/E is about 15% of terminal value, so a return to the FY2025 year-end multiple alone erases two years of compounding.
rows.benchmark: Consensus average target $332.39 and median $337.50 (43 analysts); 40.0x current P/E against 34.2x at FY2025 year end and 30-34x across FY2022-FY2025.
rows.weakens: If revenue growth holds at 14-16% and the AI device cycle extends, 40x is defensible and the bull case is the base case; my 30% bear weight is the single most consequential judgement in the table.
rows.implication: The expected return at today's price is negative, so a long-only holder's discipline is to wait for 30-34x (about $287-$325 on FY2027 EPS) or to trim into strength above 40x, rather than to add at an all-time high.
rows.confidence: medium — the multiples and EPS are sourced; the probabilities and the exit multiples are my judgement.
rows.follow_up: Which single disclosure on 2026-11-02 would move the base case to the bull case, and how much would the multiple have to expand for the position to earn its cost of capital?

rows.finding: The catalyst calendar is dated and near: FQ4 and full-year FY2026 results on 2026-11-02, the first call chaired by CEO John Ternus, who replaced Tim Cook on 2026-09-01; the December-quarter print in late January 2027 (FQ1 FY2026 was released 2026-01-29); the annual buyback authorisation with FQ2 results in May 2027; and an unresolved D.C. plan.decision_question: For a long-only holder, what drives total return from here and what is the exit or trim discipline?
plan.thesis_sentence: Half of Apple's 134% five-year price gain came from its multiple rising from 26.6x to 40.0x, and with the consensus target already 4.7% below the $348.91 close, the next five years can be earned only from earnings and dividends — about 8-9% a year if the multiple holds and a negative return if it reverts to 34x — so the right discipline for a long-only holder is a trim rule tied to the multiple, not an exit on news.
plan.why_different: It starts where the valuation section stops: that section asks what Apple is worth, this one asks how a holder gets paid and how the position gets out, so it works on return decomposition, catalyst dates, scenario prices and realisation mechanics rather than on intrinsic value.
plan.mechanism: The return comes from three sources only: EPS growth, the multiple paid at exit, and the 1.9% total shareholder yield; because a buyback at 40x transfers value to selling holders rather than compounding value for staying ones, the programme cannot put a floor under the price, so the multiple at entry sets the exit outcome and a re-rating above 40x is the only upside the fundamentals do not already pay for.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own five-year total shareholder return certified in the 10-K (Apple $234 versus S&P 500 $217 versus Dow Jones U.S. Technology $287 on a $100 base to September 2025); a 5.3-6.9% perpetual growth rate implied by today's price; 40.0x today against 34.2x at FY2025 year end and a 30-34x FY2022-FY2025 average; and the largest technology acquisitions ever at $61-69B.
plan.counter_evidence: A 1.6% buyback yield plus 8% EPS growth and a 0.3% dividend is an 8-10% annual return with no re-rating at all, which is an acceptable long-only outcome, and mean reversion has not paid in this cycle: the stock's 52-week low of $243.42 is 30% below today's close and a holder who trimmed at 37.5x in FY2024 would have missed the next 50% of the move.
plan.visual: Exit routes table naming the venue and the buyer for each route, then the return decomposition table, then the bull/base/bear price-target table with its probability-weighted outcome.
plan.prohibited: 'expensive', 'overvalued', 'bubble' as labels without arithmetic; 'huge market', 'strong team', 'high barriers to entry', 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned'; vague counts; any sentence about how the report is written; 'IPO or M&A' as a generic exit route.

rows.mechanism: The weighted exit multiple (32.0x) is 12.3 points below the 36.5x paid on FY2027E EPS, and the weighted EPS is 2.9% below consensus because the bear carries 40% weight; the two effects plus their interaction produce the -14.0%.
rows.benchmark: The previous 25/45/30 split gave $314 and -9.9%; sections 10, 11 and 14 run 20/40/40.
rows.weakens: The bull's driver, an AI replacement cycle, has no unit evidence, so the 20% weight could be too high; a ten-year yield below 4% would justify a higher multiple and a positive expected return.

rows.finding: From the $148.96 close on 2021-11-01 to $348.91 on 2026-10-29 the shares returned 134.2%: diluted EPS $5.61 to $8.72 (+55.4%, 9.2% a year), the P/E 26.6x to 40.0x (+50.7%) and dividends 3.3% cumulative; multiple expansion is 48% of the log return.
rows.mechanism: Decomposition of total return into earnings growth, the price paid for earnings and cash returned identifies how much of the past is repeatable.
rows.benchmark: S&P 500 at $217 and Dow Jones U.S. Technology at $287 per $100 over the five years to September 2025; Apple 18.5% a year against 16.8% and 23.5%.
rows.weakens: The starting multiple was depressed by the 2022 compression, and a 12.8% share-count reduction flatters EPS growth versus net income.
rows.implication: The historical return cannot repeat from a 40x starting multiple; the forward case must be earned from EPS and dividends.
rows.confidence: high — computed from dated closes and reported EPS
rows.follow_up: What multiple is paid at the next entry, and does it leave any re-rating?

rows.finding: The only exit is the secondary market: no strategic buyer exists (the largest technology transaction ever is 1.35% of Apple's $5,029.9B enterprise value), the buyback retires 1.6% of shares a year on $82.2B, the dividend yields 0.31% and 38.67M shares trade daily.
rows.mechanism: At $5T of equity the bid side is index and active flows, so the price realized is whatever multiple prevails at sale.
rows.benchmark: Largest technology deal ever, Microsoft/Activision at $68.7B; $250M position is 1.9% of one day's $13.22B traded value.
rows.weakens: Index weight of 7.25% means passive flows support the price on the way up and amplify the way down; a $100B buyback at a lower price would retire more stock.
rows.implication: Size for a 30% drawdown and exit in the market; there is no premium to negotiate and no lock-up.

rows.follow_up: Does the May 2027 authorisation match the $100B of 2025, and at what average price?

rows.finding: The entry band is $273-$300: 30-34x the $9.10 blended FY2027 EPS (60% x $9.56 + 40% x $8.42), capped at the $300 probability-weighted value.

rows.benchmark: Current 36.5x forward P/E on FY2027E EPS of $9.56; 34x on $9.10 is $309, above the $300 expected value.
rows.weakens: If FY2027 EPS lands at consensus $9.56 and the multiple holds 34x, the base case value of $325 exceeds the $300 cap.

rows.confidence: medium-high
rows.follow_up: Is $8.42 the right bear EPS once the FY2027 amortisation is known?

rows.finding: Holding two years to FY2028 EPS of $10.32, an exit at 40x returns +18.9% including dividends, at 34x +1.2% and at 26x -22.5% — a 41.4-point spread from the same three multiples as the distribution.

rows.benchmark: Fourteen points of exit multiple produce the whole spread; two-year dividends add about 0.6%.
rows.weakens: A two-year horizon is arbitrary and a 40x exit requires the AI cycle to arrive after all.

rows.confidence: medium — the exit multiple and horizon dominate
rows.follow_up: What would make 26x the wrong exit multiple — a lower ten-year yield or faster EPS?

rows.finding: The shares traded at $243.42 within the past year, 30.2% below the $348.91 close, and the five-year closing low of $125.02 is 64.2% below it.
rows.mechanism: At a 40x entry the same 26-40x multiple range that produced the last five years' gains produces the next five years' drawdowns.
rows.benchmark: The stock's 44.5% fifty-two-week range ($243.42-$351.73) and its five-year closing low of $125.02.

rows.finding: Apple's new A20 Pro shipped in iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max on 2026-09-09 (in stores 2026-09-18) alongside "Siri AI"; the prior A19 Pro scored 4,019 on Geekbench 6 single-core versus 3,846 for Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a 4.5% lead.

rows.benchmark: Qualcomm flagship of the 2025-2026 generation; Apple's own prior generations led by double digits in single-core in previous cycles (not retrieved for 2022-2024).
rows.weakens: Benchmark is from a low-confidence aggregator; thermals, multi-core and graphics results reportedly favour Qualcomm; A20 Pro's process node and transistor count were not in any retrieved source.

rows.follow_up: TechInsights teardown of A20 Pro for node, die area and cost, and multi-core/GPU bench results.

rows.finding: On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multi-year, non-exclusive deal under which the next generation of Apple Foundation Models is based on Gemini models and Google cloud technology; the rebuilt Siri was still "coming later this year" in January 2026 and Apple showed "all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 in June 2026.
rows.mechanism: Apple converts an open-ended model-development race into a variable licensing cost while keeping the user interface and on-device processing; it protects gross margin and avoids hyperscale capex but cedes the intelligence layer, the query data and the ability to differentiate on model quality.
rows.benchmark: Google (in-house Gemini), Microsoft (in-house plus OpenAI), Samsung (licenses Google models) - Apple now sits closer to Samsung's model than to Google's.
rows.weakens: Apple's own 8-K quotes the CEO describing the Siri AI launch as a source of pride, and the deal is non-exclusive, so Apple retains optionality; the reported ~$1bn annual fee is not confirmed in any retrieved source.
rows.implication: Treat AI as a licensed input with a recurring cost and strategic dependency; the moat narrows at exactly the layer investors pay the highest multiple for.
rows.confidence: high on the deal and dates; low on the fee and on model performance.
rows.follow_up: Do Google's or Apple's filings disclose the contract value or minimum commitments? What share of Siri queries still run on-device after the rebuild?

rows.finding: R&D expense reached $34,035m in the nine months to 2026-06-27 (+33% year on year) with Q3 FY2026 at $11,729m (+32%), driven by AI infrastructure and headcount, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6,799m from $9,473m (1.9% of nine-month revenue).
rows.mechanism: Apple funds AI as operating expense rather than capital investment, so the AI build does not create a depreciation drag or a capex race with hyperscalers, but it also does not create owned compute capacity that could be rented out or that compounds as a fixed-cost advantage.
rows.benchmark: Capital intensity of 1.9% of revenue is far below cloud hyperscalers that capitalise AI infrastructure (their ratios were not retrieved in this run).
rows.weakens: R&D growth of one third in a single year is a large step-up for Apple and may signal catch-up rather than leadership; the split between AI and other programmes is not disclosed.
rows.implication: Margin protection is credible; the missing asset is proprietary compute and model capability, which is what would justify an AI premium in the multiple.
rows.confidence: high: primary filing figures.
rows.follow_up: How much of the R&D step-up is recurring (model licensing, cloud compute) versus one-off?

rows.finding: Apple's health claims are regulator-verified: FDA 510(k) K250507 Hypertension Notification Feature cleared 2025-09-11, K240929 Sleep Apnea Notification Feature cleared 2024-09-13, De Novo DEN230081 Hearing Aid Feature granted 2024-09-12, and K253582 Medical Imaging Calibration Feature cleared 2026-04-01.
rows.mechanism: Clearances turn sensor data into regulated claims that competitors cannot copy by shipping the same sensor; they raise the wearable's value per unit and lengthen the replacement cycle, but do not by themselves create a subscription.
rows.benchmark: Wearables, Home and Accessories revenue fell 4% in FY2025 to $35,686m and grew 6% in Q3 FY2026 to $7,883m - clearances have not yet reversed category deceleration.
rows.weakens: Each clearance is a feature notification, not a diagnostic; sensitivity and specificity data behind K250507 were not in the retrieved record, and no peer clearance comparison was retrieved.
rows.implication: Health is a defensible but slow monetisation: value accrues through device ASP and retention, so it supports the installed base rather than services growth.
rows.confidence: high on the regulatory facts; low on clinical performance.
rows.follow_up: What are the published sensitivity/specificity of the hypertension notification, and which jurisdictions outside the US have approved it?

rows.finding: Apple launched its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, at the 2026-09-09 event and told suppliers to prepare about 10 million foldable units in 2026 (up from 7-8 million), within at least five new iPhone models across H2 2026-H1 2027 and 2026 production above 220 million units; Apple-assigned patent US2023/0049811 claims the multi-link hinge.
rows.mechanism: Apple enters a category years after Samsung but with component pre-purchase scale: 10 million units is about 4.5% of 2026 production, enough to set a premium price and absorb panel supply, not enough to change the revenue base; the hinge patent shows the mechanics were engineered well before launch.
rows.benchmark: Samsung has shipped foldables since 2019; Apple's planned 10m units is a niche share of its own 220m output.
rows.weakens: Nikkei's earlier reporting pointed to a possible slip to early 2027, and some sources reported yield failures at engineering validation; the 10m figure is a supplier plan, not a shipped number.
rows.implication: The foldable answers the innovation-stagnation critique qualitatively but is immaterial to earnings; do not underwrite revenue growth on it.
rows.confidence: medium-high: multiple independent reports plus Apple newsroom; unit plans are third-party estimates.
rows.follow_up: Did Apple disclose iPhone Duo pricing and first-weekend demand, and what is the panel yield?

rows.finding: The counter-case is supply and cost, not capability: the Q3 FY2026 10-Q warns of component shortages and rising costs for advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM, inventories rose to $11,092m from $5,718m, and Apple raised MacBook and iPad prices in late June 2026; total gross margin of 50.1% in Q3 FY2026 included about 2 percentage points from tariff refunds.
rows.mechanism: Memory inflation converts unit growth into margin risk; Apple's scale lets it pre-buy and pass costs through, which protects share at the expense of price leadership and gives low-cost Chinese rivals a relative opening.
rows.benchmark: Underlying gross margin excluding the tariff refund is about 48%; iPhone revenue grew 22% in Q3 FY2026 and nine months, so volume and mix are currently outrunning cost inflation.
rows.weakens: The refund is non-recurring, so the headline margin overstates run-rate profitability; a memory-cost shock could compress margins faster than services mix can offset.
rows.implication: Model gross margin at roughly 48% and treat the 50.1% print as flattered; supply cost is the main near-term risk to the technology premium.
rows.confidence: high: filing language and figures.
rows.follow_up: What share of FY2027 memory needs is contracted at fixed prices, and how much of the tariff refund is still to be received?
